title: ThreatLocker IT Infrastructure Assessment Prep
tagline: Zero-to-hero hands-on prep for a 3-hour terminal assessment: Windows Server, AD, networking, VPNs, Hyper-V, SQL Server, storage, PowerShell, and hardening.
disclaimer: Independent interview-prep material by Interstitium Labs. Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by ThreatLocker or Crawford Thomas. Confers no certificate. All scenarios are original practice content; no exam or vendor-training content is reproduced.

scenarios.title: What Is a Server, Really?
scenarios.situation: You just started at a small company with 15 employees. The owner points at a humming rack in the closet and says "that's our server," then points at the laptops on desks and says "those are desktops." Tomorrow you'll be asked to keep that rack machine running. Before you touch it, you need to understand what makes a server different from a desktop — and why it matters.
objectives: Define what a server is in one sentence
Name two ways server hardware differs from desktop hardware
Explain why a desktop OS is a poor choice for server work
evidence: Can state: a server is a computer that provides services to other computers (clients) over a network
scenarios.prompt: Which statement best describes a server?
choices: A server is a computer whose main job is providing services — files, logins, websites, email — to other computers (clients) over a network.
A server is the monitor and keyboard connected to the network closet.
A server is any expensive computer with lots of blinking lights in a rack.
A server is just a desktop computer running Windows 11 with the screen turned off.
scenarios.hint: Forget what it looks like. Ask instead: what is its JOB?
scenarios.why:
The correct answer is B. A server is defined by its ROLE, not its shape: it provides services to clients. This is the client-server model — clients ask, servers answer. A laptop sharing files for the office IS acting as a server; a rack of blinking lights with nothing installed is furniture.

Why the others are wrong:
- A ("blinking lights"): looks don't matter. Some of the most important servers in a company are virtual machines (VMs) with no physical presence at all.
- C ("Windows 11 with the screen off"): a desktop OS is a bad server for three concrete reasons. (1) Windows 11 forces update reboots — your file share dies at 3 AM during patching. (2) Desktop Windows caps inbound network connections at 20; a server OS (operating system) like Windows Server is licensed for many simultaneous connections. (3) Desktop Windows cannot host server roles — installable jobs like AD (Active Directory), DNS (Domain Name System), or DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) — that Windows Server provides.
- D ("monitor and keyboard"): those are peripherals. Unplug them and the server keeps serving — in fact most servers run "headless" (no monitor at all) and are managed remotely.

The hardware differences that matter: ECC (Error-Correcting Code) RAM fixes single-bit memory errors instead of crashing; redundant power supplies let one PSU die without downtime; hot-swap drive bays let you pull a failed disk while running. Desktops skip all of this to stay cheap — which is exactly why a desktop "server" fails at the worst moment.

Logic Check — here's the reasoning: if you forget every fact above, keep the single constraint — NO HUMAN PRESENT. Ask of any server feature 'what happens at 3 AM when this fails and nobody's here?' ECC: the hardware fixes the flipped bit itself. Redundant PSUs: the dead one is bypassed automatically. No forced reboots: the machine never takes itself offline. Server OS roles: the jobs (AD, DNS, DHCP) must run whether or not anyone logs in. Every correct answer on server questions can be derived from that constraint; every wrong answer violates it.

scenarios.title: What Is an IP Address?
scenarios.situation: Every device on the office network has a sticker on it: 192.168.1.42, 192.168.1.43, 192.168.1.44... Your trainer says "memorize nothing yet — first understand what those numbers ARE." You're going to learn what an IP (Internet Protocol) address identifies, how to read one, and why some addresses never appear on the public internet.
objectives: Read an IPv4 address as four octets
State what an IP address identifies (a network interface, not a device)
Name the three private address ranges and explain why they can be reused
evidence: Can explain: an IP address is a 32-bit number written as four decimals 0-255, identifying a device's network connection; 192.168.x.x is private
scenarios.prompt: Your laptop shows 192.168.1.42 and the office printer shows 192.168.1.60. What does this tell you?
choices: Both devices are on the same local network, because their addresses share the same first three numbers (the network portion) — and these are private addresses, meaning they work inside the office but are not directly reachable from the internet.
Those addresses are public, so anyone on the internet can reach the laptop directly.
The laptop is on the internet but the printer is not, because printers can't have IP addresses.
192.168.1.42 is the laptop's serial number burned in at the factory, and it never changes.
scenarios.hint: Look at what the two addresses have in common — and notice both start with 192.168.
scenarios.why:
The correct answer is A. An IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) address is a 32-bit number written as four decimal numbers separated by dots. Each of the four numbers is an octet (8 bits) ranging 0–255. With a typical 255.255.255.0 mask, the first three octets are the network ("the street") and the last is the device ("the house number") — so 192.168.1.42 and 192.168.1.60 are neighbors on the same street and can talk directly.

Private vs public: three ranges are reserved by RFC 1918 (the standards document that set them aside) for internal use and are NEVER routed on the public internet: 10.0.0.0/8 (10.anything), 172.16.0.0/12 (172.16–172.31.anything), 192.168.0.0/16 (192.168.anything). Every home and office reuses them — your 192.168.1.5 and your neighbor's 192.168.1.5 coexist because NAT (Network Address Translation) on each router translates them to one public address at the internet boundary. A public address is globally unique, assigned by your ISP (Internet Service Provider).

Why the others are wrong:
- B: printers absolutely have IP addresses — that's how your laptop finds them. "Being on the internet" isn't a property of the device; anything behind the office NAT router reaches the internet through it.
- C: confuses IP with MAC. The MAC (Media Access Control) address is the factory-burned hardware address on the network card and never changes; the IP address is logical, assigned by DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol), and WILL change (that's why you never hard-code one into documentation).
- D: backwards. 192.168.x.x is the textbook private range — it is specifically NOT reachable from the internet, which is why the whole world reuses it safely.

Logic Check — here's the reasoning: ask 'what breaks if private ranges didn't exist?' Every home router, every office printer, every lab VM would need a globally unique address — and IPv4 only has 4.3 billion total. The internet would have run out of addresses in the 1990s instead of the 2010s. NAT plus the three RFC 1918 ranges bought the world 20 extra years by exploiting one insight: an address only needs to be unique where it's routed. That's also why your home 192.168.1.1 and your office 192.168.1.1 never collide — they're in different routing universes, joined only at the NAT boundary.

scenarios.title: Binary and Decimal: Your First Conversion
scenarios.situation: IP addresses and subnet masks are really 32 ones and zeros underneath. To work with them, you must convert between binary (base 2) and decimal (base 10) without fear. There is exactly one trick: the place values 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. This drill teaches it — the same method you'll use for every subnetting question on Tuesday.
objectives: List the eight bit place values from memory
Convert binary 10101000 to decimal using place values
Convert decimal 168 to binary using repeated subtraction
evidence: Correctly converts 10101000 → 168 and 168 → 10101000, showing the place-value work
scenarios.prompt: Using the place values 128-64-32-16-8-4-2-1, what is binary 10101000 in decimal?
scenarios.hint: Add up the place values sitting under each 1: 128 + 32 + 8.
scenarios.why:
The correct answer is 168. A bit is one binary digit (0 or 1); eight bits make a byte = one octet of an IP address. The eight place values are powers of two: 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 (that's 2⁷ down to 2⁰).

Line up 10101000 under the place values:
  128(1) 64(0) 32(1) 16(0) 8(1) 4(0) 2(0) 1(0)
Add the values under each 1: 128 + 32 + 8 = 168.

The reverse direction (decimal → binary) is repeated subtraction: take the largest place value that fits, mark it 1, subtract, repeat. 168: 168−128=40 → 1; 64 doesn't fit in 40 → 0; 40−32=8 → 1; 16 doesn't fit → 0; 8−8=0 → 1; rest are 0. Result: 10101000. Verify by adding back: 128+32+8=168.

Why this matters: a subnet mask like 255.255.255.0 is 24 ones followed by 8 zeros in binary. The "/24" in CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) notation literally counts those ones. And 255 — the biggest octet — is all eight bits on: 128+64+32+16+8+4+2+1 = 255. Any octet over 255 is impossible; that's your built-in error check.

Why the wrong answers are wrong:
- 160 = 10100000 (the 8 got dropped — the most common slip: skipping a middle place value).
- 192 = 11000000 (that's the famous first octet of 192.168.x.x — your brain pattern-matched instead of adding).
- 176 = 10110000 (added the 16 instead of the 8).

Logic Check — here's the reasoning: the place values HAVE to double because each new bit doubles the combinations — that's not a convention, it's combinatorics. And 255 HAS to be the max because 8 wires × 2 states = 256 patterns (0–255). Once you see that the numbers are forced by the physics (two voltage states) and the math (doubling combinations), there's nothing to memorize — the table derives itself. Subnetting is just this table applied to the question 'where does the street end and the house number begin?'

scenarios.title: One Machine Pretending to Be Many
scenarios.situation: The office server closet has ONE physical server, but the admin says it "runs" six servers: a file server, a domain controller, a backup server, and three more. How? You're about to meet virtualization — the single idea that makes modern IT infrastructure possible, and the reason you'll be tested on Hyper-V on Tuesday.
objectives: Define virtualization and hypervisor in plain language
Give two business reasons companies virtualize
evidence: Can state: a hypervisor lets one physical computer run multiple isolated virtual machines, each with its own OS
scenarios.prompt: The company needs a new file server but has no budget for hardware. The admin creates one on the existing Hyper-V host instead. What just happened?
choices: The admin renamed a folder 'File Server' — folders aren't servers.
Virtualization means the server is now in the cloud, so the physical box can be thrown away.
A new virtual machine (VM) was created: a software-emulated computer with its own virtual CPU, RAM, disk, and OS, running isolated on the existing physical hardware under the hypervisor's control.
The admin split the physical server's motherboard in half so each half runs independently.
scenarios.hint: The physical computer didn't multiply. Something ON it is pretending to be a separate computer.
scenarios.why:
The correct answer is A. The hypervisor — the software layer between the hardware and the VMs — carved slices of physical CPU, RAM, and disk into a new virtual machine. Each VM has its own virtual hardware and its own operating system, believes it is a real standalone machine, and is isolated: one guest crashing cannot crash the others. The physical machine is the host; the VMs are guests. Hyper-V is Microsoft's hypervisor (a Type 1 / "bare-metal" hypervisor: it installs directly on hardware, no desktop OS underneath — that's why nearly all the machine's power goes to guests).

Why companies do it — the three business reasons: (1) Consolidation: one physical server does the work of ten — less hardware to buy, power, cool, and rack. (2) Isolation: the file server and the domain controller are separate VMs, so patching one can't break the other. (3) Agility: a new "server" is a file copy that boots in minutes, not a purchase order that ships in weeks; broken VM? Roll back to yesterday's checkpoint.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: hardware isn't split. Virtualization is software pretending to be hardware — the motherboard is untouched; the hypervisor just schedules slices of it.
- C: a folder is not a server (though a folder CAN be a file share served by a server — don't confuse the share with the machine serving it).
- D: virtualization ≠ cloud. The cloud is just someone else's virtualized datacenter that you rent by the hour — the physical hosts still exist, in their building. Here, the physical box stays; it's doing all the work.

Logic Check — here's the reasoning: the pre-virtualization world forced a bad choice — isolation (one app per physical box, so crashes don't spread; expensive, 90% idle) versus efficiency (many apps per box; one crash takes down everything). The hypervisor dissolves the trade-off by moving isolation into software: the guest's 'hardware' is a fiction the hypervisor maintains, so crashes stay inside the fiction. That's why a VM can be copied, snapshotted, and live-migrated — you can't live-migrate a physical motherboard, but you CAN copy the files that fully describe a virtual one.

scenarios.title: On-Call at 2 AM: Write the SOP as You Go
scenarios.situation: You are the junior on call. 2:07 AM: the site-to-site VPN tunnel to the Miami branch drops and the warehouse scanners go offline — they cannot reach the file server. There is no SOP for a VPN outage. The senior admin who 'just knows how to fix it' is on a plane. The SLA promises 4-hour recovery, and the clock is running.
objectives: Documenting during an incident instead of after it
What to capture: timestamps, exact commands, outputs, dead ends
Turning raw notes into a real SOP the same morning
evidence: ALERT: Tunnel VPN-MIA-01 down 12m. Packet loss 100%. Warehouse scanners offline. No recent config change logged.
A sticky note on the monitor reads: 'VPN dies sometimes - restart the tunnel - Dave'. Dave left the company in March.
scenarios.prompt: It is 2:15 AM, the tunnel is down, and there is no SOP. What do you do in the first 30 minutes?
choices: Touch nothing until the senior admin lands at 6 AM. Making it worse is worse than being slow, and undocumented changes are a firing offense.
Open a timestamped notes file and log every step as you take it: time, exact command, output, result. Fix the tunnel, then turn those notes into a proper SOP the same morning.
Fix it first, write it up later from memory. Speed matters most — you will remember the important parts, and the post-mortem can be filled in tomorrow morning.
Write the complete SOP first — purpose, prerequisites, rollback plan — then start troubleshooting. Documentation discipline means the document comes before the fix.
scenarios.hint: At 9 AM tomorrow, what will you actually remember about the exact command that brought the tunnel back at 2:40 AM?
scenarios.why: Under stress, memory keeps the story and drops the details — the exact command, the output line that told you it worked, the dead end you must not repeat. A timestamped log written AS you work captures all three for free, and it converts directly into an SOP: your notes are the first draft, already in the right order with real commands and real outputs. Fix-first-remember-later produces confident fiction (studies of incident recall show techs misremember commands within hours). Doc-first delays the fix past the 4-hour SLA — you cannot write accurate steps for a failure you have not diagnosed yet. Waiting burns the SLA and teaches nothing. The professional habit is: narrate into the log while you work, publish the SOP before you sleep.

scenarios.title: The Diagram Nobody Can Read
scenarios.situation: You inherit the network diagram for a 40-person office one week before a firewall migration. It is a single page: 23 unlabeled rectangles, arrows pointing both ways with no labels, no legend, no IP addresses, no VLAN IDs, no hostnames. The one person who understood it left last month. The new firewall's rules must replicate the old ones, and those rules reference source IPs, destination IPs, and zones (LAN, WAN, DMZ). This diagram is the only documentation that exists.
objectives: Reading a diagram critically: what questions must it answer?
Physical vs logical views — why one page cannot do both
evidence: Rectangles labeled 'box1' through 'box7', 'router?', and 'switch (old)'. One cloud shape labeled 'internet??'. Double-headed arrows between most boxes. A red X drawn on one box with no note. Zero IP addresses, zero VLAN IDs, zero hostnames, zero interface names, no legend.
Migration requirement from the firewall engineer

Every existing rule must be recreated on the new firewall. Rules are defined by source IP, destination IP, port, and zone. Quote: 'If I can't tell which box is the DMZ web server and what its IP is, I can't migrate a single rule.'
scenarios.prompt: The firewall migration is Friday and this diagram is all you have. What is the right move?
choices: Skip the diagram and interview the helpdesk tech instead — he has rebooted things here for two years and knows the network. Verbal knowledge is faster than redrawing.

Trace every cable and rebuild the diagram from reality: standard symbols, a legend on the page, every hostname, IP, and VLAN labeled, and two separate views — one physical (what plugs into what) and one logical (subnets, zones, traffic flows with protocol and port on each arrow).
Clean up the existing diagram: straighten the boxes, add colors (red = important, green = fine), keep it on one page. The information is all there — it just needs to look professional.
Add all the missing detail onto the same single page — cable runs, VLAN assignments, firewall rules, application flows. One page that contains everything is the most useful reference.
scenarios.hint: Which choice gives the firewall engineer the source IPs, destination IPs, and zones the rules require?
scenarios.why: A diagram is a tool, not art: its job is answering questions under pressure in under 30 seconds. Unlabeled boxes cannot answer 'what is the DMZ web server's IP?' Color without a legend means nothing to the next reader — and means nothing printed in black-and-white or to a colorblind engineer. Cramming physical cabling, VLANs, firewall rules, and app flows onto one page makes all four unreadable; that is exactly why the industry splits physical views (cables, ports — for the hands-on tech) from logical views (subnets, zones, flows — for design and troubleshooting), linked by hostname. Rebuilding from reality with standard symbols, an on-page legend, full labels, and protocol plus port on every flow arrow produces the only artifact the firewall migration can actually be built from. Verbal knowledge walks out the door with the tech.

scenarios.title: Function vs One-Liner vs Script
scenarios.situation: Three tasks land on your desk at once. (a) The auditor needs a one-time list of disabled AD accounts — needed in 10 minutes, never again. (b) The helpdesk keeps asking you to check locked-out accounts: the same query with different usernames, every week, run by four different techs. (c) Every night at 2 AM, someone must export the disabled-account list to CSV, email it to the security lead, and log any failures. Last month a 40-line one-liner pasted into the team chat broke silently for three weeks — nobody could tell what it was supposed to do, and there was no logging to notice.
objectives: Code granularity: one-liner vs function vs script
Matching the packaging to the task's lifecycle
When reuse justifies structure — and when it does not
evidence: (a) Once, needed in 10 minutes, run by you. (b) Weekly, run by 4 different techs with different usernames each time. (c) Nightly, unattended, must log and alert on failure.
A 40-line one-liner pasted into chat silently stopped returning correct results for 3 weeks. No parameters, no help text, no logging, no owner. The auditor's report went out wrong.
scenarios.prompt: How do you implement each of the three tasks?
choices: (a) A one-liner typed at the prompt. (b) A saved function with parameters, pipeline support, and comment-based help. (c) A scheduled script with logging, error handling, and failure alerting.
One-liners for everything, saved in a shared chat channel. Fastest to write, everyone can see them, and there is only one place to look.
(a) and (b) as scripts on a file share, (c) as a one-liner you run manually each morning before the auditor arrives.
Write a full advanced function for all three. Consistency beats convenience, one-liners are not professional, and everything should be reusable.
scenarios.hint: Match the packaging to three things: how often it runs, who runs it, and what happens when it fails silently.
scenarios.why: Granularity is a lifecycle decision, not a style preference. A one-liner is correct when the task is once, now, by you — packaging it further costs more time than it saves, and the auditor is waiting. A function is correct when humans repeat a task with variations: parameters replace editing the code each time, help text replaces asking you, pipeline support lets it compose with other commands — that is what makes four techs self-sufficient. A script is correct when a machine runs it unattended: it needs logging (so silent failures become visible), error handling (so one bad record does not kill the run), and scheduling (because nobody reliably runs anything at 2 AM). The decision rule to memorize: runs once -> one-liner; repeated by people -> function; repeated by machines -> script.

scenarios.title: Design Review: Small Business Infrastructure
scenarios.situation: A 20-person company asks you to review a contractor's infrastructure proposal before they sign. Their stated requirements: everyone must be able to log in and reach file shares even if one server dies; backups must allow recovery within 4 hours and lose no more than one day of work; 5 remote workers need secure access; year-1 budget ceiling is $25,000.
objectives: Reading a design against requirements, line by line
Single points of failure: naming them explicitly
RPO/RTO reasoning: what the numbers demand in practice
evidence: One physical server running AD, file shares, and print services. A $89 consumer router as firewall and VPN endpoint. Backups to a USB external drive, 'taken home on Fridays'. No UPS. No second domain controller. No monitoring. Quote: $11,000 — described as 'well under budget'.
Survive any single server failure. RPO 24 hours (lose at most one day of work). RTO 4 hours (fully recovered within 4 hours). Secure remote access for 5 workers. Budget is a ceiling, not a target.
scenarios.prompt: Do you approve the proposal?
choices: Reject as drawn. One server is a single point of failure — when it dies, nobody authenticates and no shares exist. A USB drive taken home weekly cannot meet RPO 24h or RTO 4h, and a consumer router gives no VPN audit trail or support. Send it back: second domain controller, tested 3-2-1 backups, a business firewall with VPN, and a UPS — priced against the $25k ceiling.
Reject and demand enterprise gear — clustered hosts, a SAN, dual ISPs. If the budget allows $25k, spend it on real redundancy.
Approve. It comes in well under budget, and a single well-built server with a USB backup is standard for a 20-person shop. Requirements are aspirational anyway.
Approve the server but require the contractor to add a second domain controller. That fixes the single point of failure, which is the only hard requirement.
scenarios.hint: Walk each requirement against the proposal: which requirement survives the death of that single server?
scenarios.why: A design review is requirements-versus-proposal, line by line — the budget is a ceiling, not a score. Kill the single server and every requirement dies with it: nobody authenticates (one domain controller is a single point of failure for all logins), file shares are gone until a bare-metal restore from a USB drive that leaves the building on Fridays (RPO and RTO both blown — a Friday-to-Friday drive loses up to 7 days, and nobody has timed a restore), and the consumer 'firewall' cannot prove who connected over VPN. The fix list is ordered by requirement-impact per dollar: tested 3-2-1 backups first (cheapest, covers RPO/RTO — and 'tested' is doing the heavy lifting, because an untested backup is a hope, not a plan), then a second domain controller (kills the authentication SPOF), then a business firewall with VPN plus a UPS. Choice 2 fixes one of three fatal gaps. Choice 3 gold-plates past the stated requirements for a 20-person shop.

choices: Keep Desktop Experience on all three for consistency. Roles and features are the same thing, both installed with Add-WindowsFeature, so the distinction does not matter in practice.
Use Desktop Experience on the file server and Core elsewhere. Roles can only be installed during the initial OS setup, so the file server needs the GUI installer.

Deploy Server Core on all three and manage them remotely via RSAT, PowerShell remoting, and SConfig. A role is the server's primary workload (AD DS, File Services, DNS); a feature is a supporting component (.NET Framework, RSAT tools, Failover Clustering).
Use Server Core only on the domain controller. Roles require the full GUI to configure, while features can be managed from the command line, so the file and utility servers need Desktop Experience.
evidence: Get-WindowsFeature excerpt from the pilot build

PS C:\> Get-WindowsFeature | Where-Object {$_.Installed} | Select-Object Name, FeatureType

Name                      FeatureType
----                      -----------
File-Services             Role
FS-FileServer             Role Service
NET-Framework-45-Core     Feature
RSAT-AD-PowerShell        Feature

Desktop Experience pilot: ~6 GB larger disk footprint, ~40% more patches per cycle.
All three servers will be managed from the admin jump box over WinRM.
scenarios.hint: Which install option gives attackers — and Windows Update — the smallest possible target?
scenarios.prompt: Which installation option should the three servers get, and how do you explain the roles-vs-features distinction to the junior admin?
scenarios.situation:
Windows Server comes in two flavors: Desktop Experience (the familiar GUI — graphical user interface) and Server Core (no desktop at all — just a terminal, with a smaller attack surface and fewer reboots). The reasoning: every GUI component is code that needs patching and can be exploited, so stripping it removes whole categories of vulnerabilities — the trade-off is you must do everything from the command line. This scenario tests whether you know what you gain and lose when the desktop disappears...

A mid-size regional distributor is deploying three new Windows Server 2025 machines: a file server, an additional domain controller, and a utility server for scheduled tasks. The junior admin chose the Desktop Experience install for all three, saying it is easier to manage. The security lead pushes back and asks you to justify a different approach before the builds proceed.
scenarios.title: Picking the Right Server Install
scenarios.why: Server Core strips the GUI shell, which shrinks the attack surface, the disk footprint, and the monthly patch burden — and every one of these workloads (file serving, AD DS, scheduled tasks) is fully manageable remotely via RSAT, PowerShell remoting, and SConfig. A role is the server's primary job; a feature supports it. There is no technical reason any of these three boxes needs a desktop.

choices: Sales-Green, from the OU-linked GPO. Group Policy applies in LSDOU order — Local, Site, Domain, OU — and the last one applied wins the conflict. Confirm the winning set with gpresult /r /scope:user.
Red, from Local Group Policy. Local policy applies first, so its settings stick and cannot be overridden by domain-based GPOs.
Corporate-Gray, from the domain-linked GPO. Domain-level policy always outranks OU-level policy because the domain is higher in the hierarchy.
Blue, from the site-linked GPO. Site policy is evaluated after both domain and OU policy, so it takes precedence over both.
evidence:
C:\> gpresult /r /scope:user

USER SETTINGS
--------------
    Last time Group Policy was applied: 10/10/2026 at 9:41:03 AM
    Applied Group Policy Objects
    -----------------------------
        Corporate-Wallpaper
        Site-Branding
        Sales-Team-Wallpaper
GPMC link report (enforced: none, block inheritance: none)

Local Group Policy       sets Wallpaper = Red
Site: HQ-Site            sets Wallpaper = Blue
Domain: corp.local       sets Wallpaper = Corporate-Gray
OU: Sales                sets Wallpaper = Sales-Green
scenarios.hint: Policies apply in LSDOU order — when two settings collide, which letter is last?
scenarios.prompt: The user sits in OU=Sales,DC=corp,DC=local. No GPO is Enforced and no OU blocks inheritance. Which wallpaper does the user actually get, and what is the first command you run to confirm it?
scenarios.situation:
Group Policy is how Windows administrators push settings (wallpaper, password rules, security lockdowns) to hundreds of computers automatically instead of touching each one. When several policies overlap, they apply in LSDOU order — Local, Site, Domain, Organizational Unit — each layer overwriting the last, so the OU (closest to the user) wins unless a higher layer is Enforced. The logic: the most specific scope knows the most about the user, so it gets the final word...

Help desk ticket: a sales rep's desktop wallpaper policy is not applying. The corporate wallpaper GPO is linked at the domain level, a branding GPO is linked at the site level, and the Sales OU has its own wallpaper GPO — all three configure the exact same policy setting. The tech already ran gpupdate /force and rebooted twice, but the wrong wallpaper persists.
scenarios.title: Whose Wallpaper Wins?
scenarios.why: LSDOU is the processing order: Local, then Site, then Domain, then OU — each layer overwrites conflicting settings from the earlier ones, so the OU-linked Sales-Team-Wallpaper wins here. (Enforced on a parent GPO or Block Inheritance on the OU would change this, but neither is set.) gpresult /r with /scope:user shows exactly which user GPOs applied and is always the first confirmation step before guessing.

choices: Run ipconfig /flushdns on every workstation and wait for AD replication to fix the records on its own.
Convert the zone from AD-integrated to a standard primary zone and rebuild every record from scratch.
Add a forwarder to 8.8.8.8 on dc01 so external DNS resolution repairs mail.corp.local.

Correct the stale A record for mail.corp.local to 10.1.0.50 and recreate the missing MX record on the authoritative server, then audit the Sunday cleanup script and the zone's scavenging/aging settings.
evidence:
C:\> nslookup mail.corp.local
Server:  dc01.corp.local
Address:  10.1.0.11

Name:    mail.corp.local
Address:  10.1.0.99

C:\> nslookup -q=mx corp.local
Server:  dc01.corp.local
Address:  10.1.0.11

*** No mail exchanger (MX) records available for corp.local

10.1.0.99 was the decommissioned Exchange 2016 server, retired 3 weeks ago.
Current mail server: 10.1.0.50. Sunday cleanup script deleted 'unused' records.
scenarios.hint: nslookup is quoting the authoritative server's answer — does the lie live in a cache, or in the zone itself?
scenarios.prompt: nslookup shows mail.corp.local resolving to a stale IP and the zone has no MX record at all. What do you fix first, and what do you investigate so it does not recur?
scenarios.situation:
Email delivery depends on a special DNS (Domain Name System) record called the MX (Mail Exchanger) record — the entry that says 'mail for this domain goes to THAT server.' When mail stops flowing but the mail server itself is healthy, the MX record (or the DNS server answering for it) is suspect number one. The reasoning: sending servers don't know your mail server's address — they ASK DNS, so a missing or wrong MX record means mail has literally nowhere to go...

Monday 8:12 AM: nobody can reach the mail server by name and Outlook clients are failing to connect, though the server itself is up and reachable by IP. The DNS admin insists nothing changed, but an automated cleanup script ran against the DNS zones on Sunday night. The zone is AD-integrated.
scenarios.title: Mail Is Down, DNS Is Suspect
scenarios.why: The authoritative zone itself is wrong: the A record points at a decommissioned IP and the MX record that tells SMTP where to deliver mail is gone — no amount of client cache-flushing or forwarding fixes bad authoritative data, and forwarders only help with names this server is not authoritative for. Fix the A and MX records directly, then find out whether the cleanup script or overly aggressive DNS scavenging deleted them so Monday does not repeat.

choices: Convert every reservation into an exclusion so the printers keep their current IPs permanently.
Enable DHCP failover in Hot Standby mode. The partner server will serve the extra clients the primary cannot handle.

Shorten the lease duration for transient devices, reconcile and reclaim stale leases, then add capacity by expanding the scope or building a superscope. Keep exclusions for statically-addressed devices and reservations for MAC-pinned devices — they solve different problems.
Delete all exclusions to free up addresses immediately. Exclusions waste address space that clients could be using.
evidence:
PS C:\> Get-DhcpServerv4ScopeStatistics -ScopeId 10.4.0.0

ScopeId   Free  InUse PercentageInUse
-------   ----  ----- ---------------
10.4.0.0    12    500  98%

Lease duration: 8 days (default). Client mix: handheld scanners (transient, many per day),
printers (fixed, need stable IPs). Failover: not configured.
scenarios.hint: Failover gives you a spare tire, not a bigger gas tank — where does extra capacity actually come from?
scenarios.prompt: Get-DhcpServerv4ScopeStatistics shows 98% of the scope in use. What is the correct fix sequence?
scenarios.situation:
A DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) scope is the pool of IP addresses a server is allowed to hand out — say, 192.168.1.50 through 192.168.1.200. When the pool runs dry, new devices get no address and, to the user, 'the network is down.' The reasoning: without an address a device can't even start talking, so an empty pool looks exactly like a dead network — this scenario teaches you to tell the two apart...

A new warehouse wing just opened with 60 new scanners, printers, and handhelds. Now random devices across the site intermittently fail to get DHCP addresses. The scope is 10.4.0.0/23. The previous admin mixed exclusions and reservations for the printers and nobody documented which is which.
scenarios.title: No IP for You
scenarios.why: Exclusions are ranges the server never leases (for devices with static IPs); reservations are leases pinned to a MAC address — deleting or converting them breaks the printers. The real problem is capacity: an 8-day lease on transient scanners hoards addresses, so shorten leases, reclaim stale ones, and grow the address space with a larger scope or a superscope. DHCP failover is about availability, not capacity — a standby partner does not create new addresses.

choices: Seize only the Schema Master role. The other four roles are optional and the forest functions without them.
Transfer the roles with ntdsutil. A transfer works fine even when the current role holder is offline.
Wait for a replacement DC01. FSMO roles are not required for logons or password changes, so nothing urgent is broken.

Seize the four roles to DC02 with Move-ADDirectoryServerOperationMasterRole -Identity DC02 -OperationMasterRole SchemaMaster,DomainNamingMaster,PDCEmulator,RIDMaster -Force. Seizure is the tool for a permanently offline holder; the -Force flag performs the seize.
evidence:
C:\> netdom query fsmo
Schema master               dc01.corp.local
Domain naming master        dc01.corp.local
PDC                         dc01.corp.local
RID pool manager            dc01.corp.local
Infrastructure master       dc02.corp.local

DC01: powered off, hardware unrecoverable, removed from the rack.
DC02: healthy, Global Catalog, DNS, all services running.
scenarios.hint: A transfer is a handshake — can you shake hands with a powered-off server?
scenarios.prompt: DC01 is never coming back. Do you seize or transfer its FSMO roles to DC02, and which PowerShell cmdlet performs the move?
scenarios.situation:
Active Directory (AD) — the database of users and computers — keeps five special jobs, the FSMO (Flexible Single Master Operations) roles, on exactly one domain controller (DC) at a time. When that DC dies you must move its roles: transfer if it's alive and cooperative, seize if it's dead and never coming back. The reasoning behind the caution: seizing tells the network 'the old holder is gone forever,' so if it ever comes back online holding the same role, you get two masters and a corrupted database — which is why a seized DC must never be allowed back...

Friday night: DC01 suffered a fatal motherboard failure and the board is end-of-life with no replacement available — the server is gone for good. DC01 held four of the five FSMO roles. Monday morning is coming, password changes are already failing for some users, and new account creation will stall once DC02 exhausts its RID pool.
scenarios.title: The PDC Emulator Just Died
scenarios.why: A transfer is a graceful handshake that requires the current holder to be online — impossible here. Seizure forcibly takes the roles for a dead holder, which is exactly this situation: the PDC Emulator is the authority for password changes and lockouts, and the RID Master feeds DC02 the RID pools it needs to create new accounts. After a seizure, the old DC must never be brought back online — it would believe it still owns the roles — so DC01 gets wiped or stays decommissioned.

choices: Demote and re-promote HQ-DC01. An RPC error means the AD database is corrupt and a rebuild is the only fix.

RPC connectivity to HQ-DC01 is broken — verify DNS name resolution, confirm TCP 135 plus the RPC dynamic port range are open through the new firewall rules, then run dcdiag /test:replications to validate the fix.
Force replication with repadmin /syncall and move on. Error 1722 is cosmetic and clears itself once the schedule catches up.
Seize the FSMO roles from HQ-DC01. Replication failures mean the FSMO role holders are broken and must be moved.
evidence:
C:\> repadmin /replsummary
Replication Summary Start Time: 2026-10-10 12:00:00

Source DSA     largest delta   fails/total    error
HQ-DC01        06h:12m         5 / 5  100%    (1722) The RPC server is unavailable.
BR-DC02        12m             0 / 5    0%

Firewall rule change between HQ and branch: 2026-10-03.
Password replication from HQ to branch last succeeded: 2026-10-10 05:48.
scenarios.hint: 1722 is the network telling you 'I cannot reach it' — and something in the path changed last week. What was it?
scenarios.prompt: repadmin /replsummary shows 100% failures from HQ-DC01 with error 1722 and a 6-hour largest delta. What is your diagnosis path?
scenarios.situation:
Every domain controller (DC) holds a copy of the Active Directory (AD) database, and replication is the background sync keeping all copies identical — a password changed in Orlando must reach the Miami DC. When replication breaks, the copies drift apart: users can log in at one site but not the other. The reasoning for the fix order: DCs locate each other through DNS (Domain Name System) records, so you check DNS first, then the network path, then the AD service itself — each layer assumes the one below it works...

A user changed her password at headquarters, but the branch-office domain controller keeps rejecting the new password hours later. The firewall team tightened rules between sites last week. You suspect replication is broken rather than the password change itself.
scenarios.title: Password Changed Here, Not There
scenarios.why: Error 1722, 'The RPC server is unavailable,' is a connectivity error, not database corruption — AD replication rides on RPC, so a firewall change blocking TCP 135 or the ephemeral port range breaks it exactly this way. Check name resolution first (replication failures are DNS problems more often than not), then the firewall rules, then prove health with dcdiag. Demoting a DC over a firewall issue would be destroying a healthy server.

choices: Create OUs by object type (All-Users, All-Computers) and make the help desk technicians Domain Admins, with a written policy telling them to be careful outside their office.
Keep the flat default containers and do everything with security groups. OUs are a legacy concept and containers work fine for delegation.
Create one OU per user so that Group Policy and delegation are maximally granular for every individual.

Create OUs by office (HQ, Orlando, Tampa, Remote) with child OUs for Users and Workstations, then use the Delegation of Control Wizard to grant a per-office Help Desk security group the 'Reset user passwords and force password change at next logon' task scoped to that office's Users OU.
evidence:
DC=corp,DC=local
  CN=Users        <- 800 user objects (default container: cannot link GPOs)
  CN=Computers    <- 650 computer objects (default container: cannot link GPOs)
  (no organizational units exist)

Each office's help desk: reset passwords + unlock accounts for their office only.
GPO needs: per-office WSUS targeting and drive mappings.
scenarios.hint: OUs exist for two things: aiming Group Policy and aiming permissions — which boundary needs both aimed at once?
scenarios.prompt: Which OU design do you propose, and how do you grant the help desk password-reset rights without making anyone a Domain Admin?
scenarios.situation:
An OU (Organizational Unit) is a folder inside Active Directory used to organize users and computers — and, crucially, to attach Group Policies and delegate control ('the helpdesk can reset passwords, but ONLY for the Sales OU'). The reasoning: OUs exist so authority can be sliced to match the real organization — good design mirrors who actually administers whom, while flat or random OUs mean policies spray everywhere and nobody can tell who controls what...

The company has four offices and a completely flat Active Directory: all 800 users sit in the default Users container and all 650 computers in the default Computers container — there are no OUs at all. The help desk needs to reset passwords and unlock accounts for their own office only. A consultant proposes OUs organized by object type; you think that misses the point.
scenarios.title: Help Desk Needs Keys, Not the Kingdom
scenarios.why: OUs exist for two purposes: aiming Group Policy and aiming delegated permissions — so design them around administrative boundaries (offices, departments), not object types, and keep the hierarchy shallow. Default containers cannot have GPOs linked to them, which is why the per-office GPO needs are unmet today. The Delegation of Control Wizard grants granular rights like password reset scoped to a single OU, giving each help desk exactly their office and nothing more — no Domain Admins required.

scenarios.title: Think Aloud: 'The Trust Relationship Failed' on 20 Workstations
scenarios.situation: Monday 8:05 AM: twenty workstations — all deployed from the same golden image last month — greet users with 'The trust relationship between this workstation and the primary domain failed.' The other 600 machines are fine. The junior tech's plan is to rejoin all twenty to the domain before lunch.
scenarios.prompt: Narrate your thinking aloud as you work: what do you check first and why? Then: what is the least-disruptive fix for the twenty machines, and what do you investigate so this does not repeat next month?
evidence:
PS C:\> Test-ComputerSecureChannel
False

PS C:\> nltest /sc_query:corp.local
Trusted DC Connection Status Status = 1787 0x6fb ERROR_NO_TRUST_SAM_ACCOUNT
AD check on one machine account

PS C:\> Get-ADComputer WS-114 | Select-Object Enabled, PasswordLastSet
Enabled        PasswordLastSet
-------        ---------------
True           2026-09-02  (38 days ago — normal rotation)
All 20 imaged from GOLD-2026-09 without sysprep — 'it was faster'. No two machines were ever on the network at the same time during staging.
choices: Rejoin all twenty to the domain immediately — disjoin, reboot, rejoin, reboot. It is the standard fix and the junior tech is right to move fast.
Reset all twenty user passwords. Trust relationship errors are authentication errors, so the user accounts are the problem.

Repair the secure channel in place with Test-ComputerSecureChannel -Repair (or Reset-ComputerMachinePassword against a DC), then investigate the imaging process — 20 identical machines failing together points at cloning without sysprep, which duplicated the machine identity.
Restore the domain controllers from Friday's backup. Twenty simultaneous trust failures means the DCs' computer-account database is corrupt.
scenarios.why: The trust relationship is between the COMPUTER account and the domain, not the user — resetting user passwords fixes nothing. Cloning without sysprep duplicated the machine SID and the machine-account password state; when two clones with the same identity talk to the DC, each password rotation invalidates the other, and the secure channel breaks fleet-wide. Test-ComputerSecureChannel -Repair (or Reset-ComputerMachinePassword -Server <DC>) re-establishes the channel in place — no disjoin, no reboot circus, no new SIDs. Then fix the process: sysprep every image, because the next golden image will do this again. Logic Check: when twenty identical machines fail identically on the same morning, the cause is in what makes them identical — always interrogate the image before touching the machines.
scenarios.hint: User passwords have nothing to do with the machine's trust — and what is identical about all twenty machines that is different from the 600 healthy ones?

scenarios.title: Four-Minute Logons Across the Floor
scenarios.situation: Help desk tickets all morning: logons take 3–4 minutes on the 3rd floor, started Monday after the weekend firewall change. Machines are healthy, the DCs are healthy, and nobody changed Group Policy — or so everyone claims.
scenarios.prompt: Logons are slow but eventually succeed. What two faults do you hunt, in what order, and which commands prove each one?
evidence: Applied GPOs include 'Drive-Maps-2024' mapping S: to \\OLDFS\shared — OLDFS was decommissioned in August.
Stuck 2m40s on 'Applying Group Policy Drive Maps policy...' then 40s on 'Waiting for network...'
choices: Add RAM to the 3rd-floor workstations and enable Folder Redirection — slow logons are a client performance problem.
Rebuild every affected user profile. Corrupt profiles are the most common cause of slow logons and a rebuild always helps.

Fix DNS first (DHCP scope option 006 must hand out the DCs, not 8.8.8.8 — external DNS cannot resolve AD SRV records, so DC location times out), then remove the dead \\OLDFS drive mapping GPO. Prove with nslookup -q=srv _ldap._tcp.corp.local and a timed logon.
Disable the Windows Firewall on the workstations — the weekend firewall change is obviously blocking Group Policy traffic.
scenarios.why: Slow-but-successful logons are timeouts, not failures — something the client waits for is not answering. DNS pointing at 8.8.8.8 means every AD SRV lookup (_ldap._tcp.corp.local) goes to a server that knows nothing about the domain; the client waits, fails over, waits again. Fix DHCP option 006 to hand out the DCs and the 40-second 'waiting for network' evaporates. The dead \\OLDFS mapping is the second timeout: the client retries an unreachable server for the full SMB timeout per mapped drive. Two timeouts, two fixes, in that order — DNS first because it affects everything. Logic Check: 'slow but eventually works' always means a timeout — find what is being waited on (DNS, unreachable server) instead of upgrading hardware that was fast on Friday.
scenarios.hint: The logon eventually SUCCEEDS — so nothing is broken, something is being waited on. What does 8.8.8.8 not know about your domain?

scenarios.title: Six Minutes of Skew Killed Kerberos
scenarios.situation: Users report 'The clocks on the client and server differ' and SSO to the file shares fails, though old NTLM logons still work. The new branch office router went in last week with a 'deny all outbound except web' rule that nobody reviewed.
scenarios.prompt: Authentication fails only for Kerberos. What is the time situation, what broke it, and what is the exact repair sequence?
evidence:
Source: Local CMOS Clock
Last Successful Sync Time: unspecified
Stratum: 0 (unspecified)
Branch edge ACL: permit TCP 80/443 out; deny UDP 123 out ('NTP is not a business requirement').
choices: Run w32tm /resync on every server — that forces an immediate sync and Kerberos will recover on its own.
Rebuild the Kerberos keytab on the file server. Clock errors are a red herring; the real fault is ticket encryption.

Repoint time to a real source and resync: w32tm /config /manualpeerlist:pool.ntp.org /syncfromflags:manual /reliable:yes /update, restart the w32time service, w32tm /resync /rediscover — then get UDP 123 reopened outbound so it stays fixed. Kerberos allows ~5 minutes of skew; +361s exceeds it.
Disable Kerberos and force NTLM everywhere via GPO — NTLM still works, so standardize on what works.
scenarios.why: Kerberos authenticates partly by timestamp — tickets carry a 5-minute validity window, so a 361-second skew means every ticket looks forged or replayed and the KDC rejects them. The server fell back to 'Local CMOS Clock' because the firewall blocks UDP 123 outbound — NTP never had a chance, and CMOS drift did the rest. /resync alone cannot fix this: there is no source to sync FROM until /config sets one, and the firewall hole must be reopened or the drift returns within weeks. NTLM 'working' is not a solution — it is the absence of mutual authentication, and downgrading the whole domain to it is a security incident wearing a workaround costume. Logic Check: when Kerberos fails and NTLM works, the cryptography is fine and the ENVIRONMENT is wrong — check the clock before you touch a single keytab.
scenarios.hint: Kerberos tickets are timestamped — how much skew does the protocol tolerate, and what does +361 seconds do to that budget?

choices: /27 (255.255.255.224): eight /27 blocks, 30 usable hosts each
/28 (255.255.255.240): sixteen /28 blocks, 14 usable hosts each
/26 (255.255.255.192): four /26 blocks, 62 usable hosts each
/25 (255.255.255.128): two /25 blocks, 126 usable hosts each
evidence:
192.168.10.0/24 -> 4 subnets
min 50 usable hosts per subnet
fewest subnets that satisfy the requirement
scenarios.hint: How many host bits do you need for 50 usable addresses? Remember the -2 for network and broadcast.
scenarios.prompt: Which subnet mask and subnet layout meets the requirement?
scenarios.situation:
Subnetting is slicing one IP network into smaller sub-networks, and a VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) is the switch's way of enforcing those slices — invisible walls so departments can't see each other's traffic. The reasoning: without carving, every broadcast packet hits every device (noise and eavesdropping scale with size), so you fence traffic into neighborhoods. This scenario makes you carve address space for real departments — each needs its own subnet with room to grow, and the math must close exactly...

You inherit a flat 192.168.10.0/24 network and must split it into 4 VLANs (servers, workstations, VoIP, guest). Each VLAN needs at least 50 usable host addresses, and you want the fewest subnets that satisfy the requirement so the address plan stays simple.
scenarios.title: Carving a /24 into VLAN subnets
scenarios.why: 50 usable hosts needs 2^6 = 64 addresses (62 usable), so the smallest workable mask is /26. A /24 splits into exactly four /26 subnets: .0/26, .64/26, .128/26, .192/26. /27 only gives 30 usable hosts each (too small), and /25 only yields 2 subnets (too few).

scenarios.hint: AND the last octet of the IP with the mask, or use the block-size method: 256 minus the mask octet.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct network ID, broadcast address, and usable host range?
scenarios.situation:
Before you design subnets, you must do the raw conversion: dotted-decimal to binary and back, using the place values 128-64-32-16-8-4-2-1. The reasoning: a subnet mask is really a string of ones and zeros, and every 'how many hosts' question is answered by counting in binary — there is no formula to memorize, only the conversion. This is the arithmetic drill: a workstation's address and mask, decoded by hand, until the bigger problems become mechanical...

A workstation reports IP 192.168.20.130 with mask 255.255.255.192 (/26). The helpdesk argues the PC is on the 192.168.20.128/26 network, but the server team insists it should be on 192.168.20.64/26. You need to settle it with binary math, then state the network, broadcast, and usable range.
scenarios.title: Which network is this workstation on?
scenarios.why: Block size for /26 is 64 (256-192). Network boundaries fall on multiples of 64: .0, .64, .128, .192 — so .130 sits in the .128 network. Broadcast is one before the next boundary: .191. Usable range is .129 through .190. ANDing 130 (10000010) with 192 (11000000) also gives 128, confirming it.

choices: Native VLAN mismatch (1 vs 99): untagged frames leak between VLANs and CDP flags the mismatch, breaking inter-VLAN paths
Port speed/duplex mismatch: Gi0/1 autonegotiated to half-duplex and drops tagged frames
Allowed VLAN list mismatch: VLAN 10 is missing from one side so its frames are dropped
Trunk encapsulation mismatch: one side uses ISL and the other 802.1Q, so tags are unreadable
evidence:
interface Gi0/1
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk native vlan 1
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20

interface Gi0/1
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk native vlan 99
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20
scenarios.hint: 802.1Q inserts a 4-byte tag into frames — except for traffic on one special VLAN. Which one differs between the two configs?
scenarios.prompt: What is misconfigured, and why does it break connectivity?
scenarios.situation:
On a trunk — the link between switches carrying multiple VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks) — untagged traffic rides the native VLAN (VLAN 1 by default). If the two ends disagree on which VLAN is native, traffic leaks into the wrong neighborhood and loops can form. The reasoning: untagged frames have no label saying which VLAN they belong to, so each switch guesses by its own native setting — two different guesses means traffic crosses invisible walls it should never cross...

After a core switch replacement, servers on VLAN 20 can ping each other but lose connectivity to VLAN 10. The new trunk port was configured quickly from memory. You pull the trunk config from both ends of the link and spot the problem.
scenarios.title: Native VLAN mismatch drops trunk traffic
scenarios.why: The 802.1Q native VLAN carries untagged traffic, and both ends of a trunk must agree on it. A mismatch means untagged frames (control traffic, plus any device sending untagged) cross into the wrong VLAN, and CDP/LLDP raise native-VLAN-mismatch errors. Both sides list VLANs 10 and 20 as allowed, encapsulation is 802.1Q on both, and speed/duplex would show errors, not selective VLAN loss.

choices: Move the router-on-a-stick subinterfaces from the firewall to the WAN router
Collapse all 6 VLANs into one flat /22 to eliminate inter-VLAN routing entirely
Add a second firewall in active/active HA to share the inter-VLAN forwarding load
Create SVIs on the L3 switch and enable IP routing, so inter-VLAN traffic is switched in hardware at the core
evidence:
inside->inside inter-VLAN: 780 Mbps
inside->internet: 95 Mbps
CPU: 95% (packet forwarding, not inspection)

Cisco L3 switch, IP routing capable
6 VLANs, SVIs currently unconfigured
scenarios.hint: Where does the 780 Mbps of traffic actually need to go — and which device forwards it fastest?
scenarios.prompt: What is the best fix, and why does it outperform router-on-a-stick here?
scenarios.situation:
VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks) can't talk to each other without a router in the middle — that's inter-VLAN routing, and there are two classic designs. Router-on-a-stick uses one physical router interface split into sub-interfaces (one per VLAN); an SVI (Switched Virtual Interface) puts the routing inside a Layer-3 switch itself — faster, no extra box. The reasoning for the trade-off: a stick is cheap but every cross-VLAN packet squeezes through one cable (a bottleneck and a single point of failure), while an SVI routes at switch speed but costs more up front...

A branch office has 6 VLANs on a Layer 3 switch, with a single firewall uplink. The current router-on-a-stick setup funnels all inter-VLAN traffic up to the firewall and back down, and the firewall's CPU is pegged at 95% during business hours. The firewall team refuses to route internal traffic.
scenarios.title: Inter-VLAN routing design choice
scenarios.why: A Layer 3 switch routes between VLANs via SVIs in hardware (ASICs) at line rate, while router-on-a-stick hairpins every inter-VLAN packet through one physical link and a software-based router/firewall. Offloading internal routing to the L3 switch keeps the firewall CPU for what it is for: stateful inspection of internet-bound traffic.

choices: The directly connected 10.20.5.0/24: longest prefix match wins, and connected beats all AD values at equal length
The OSPF 10.20.0.0/16 via 192.168.1.2: the lower OSPF cost path is preferred
The static 10.0.0.0/8 via 192.168.1.1: static routes (AD 1) beat OSPF (AD 110)
The OSPF 10.20.5.0/24 via 192.168.1.3: OSPF routes are preferred over connected interfaces
scenarios.hint: Two different rules are in play: one picks among different prefix lengths, the other among same-length routes. Apply them in order.
scenarios.prompt: Which route forwards the packet, and what rule decides it?
scenarios.situation:
When a router knows several routes to the same destination, it picks the LONGEST prefix match — the most specific route wins (/26 beats /24, like a street address beats a zip code). OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) is the protocol routers use to learn those routes from each other inside a company network. The reasoning: the most specific route is the most informed guess about where the packet actually goes — generality is for when nothing better is known...

A packet destined for 10.20.5.44 arrives at the core router. The routing table has overlapping entries learned from OSPF and one static route. The junior admin assumes the static route wins because 'static beats OSPF' — but that is not how forwarding works.
scenarios.title: Routing table: which route wins?
scenarios.why: Forwarding uses longest-prefix-match FIRST: the router picks the most specific matching route, and both /24 entries beat the /16 and /8. Between the two /24s, administrative distance breaks the tie — connected (AD 0) beats OSPF (AD 110) and static (AD 1). AD only matters among routes of equal prefix length.

choices: TCP port 80 is blocked by the stateful inspection engine before ACL evaluation
Rule 30 is a duplicate of rule 20 and the firewall rejects duplicate entries, ignoring it
The implicit deny at rule 40 overrides all permit rules regardless of position
Rule 20 matches the workstation traffic first and denies it; ACLs stop at the first match, so rule 30 is never evaluated
evidence:
10 permit tcp 10.10.5.0 0.0.0.255 any
20 deny tcp 10.10.40.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.10.5.20 eq 80
30 permit tcp 10.10.40.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.10.5.20 eq 80   <- added fix
40 deny ip any any   (implicit)
scenarios.hint: The firewall does not read the whole list and pick the best rule. What does it do when a packet matches rule 20?
scenarios.prompt: Why does the new permit rule have no effect?
scenarios.situation:
A firewall ACL (Access Control List) is an ordered list of allow/deny rules checked top-to-bottom — the FIRST match wins and the rest are ignored, like a bouncer reading a guest list from the top. The reasoning: the firewall must decide fast on every packet, so it stops at the first rule that applies — which means a broad 'deny' sitting above a specific 'allow' silently kills legitimate traffic. This scenario hands you a misordered list and asks what's actually getting through...

A new internal web app on 10.10.5.20:80 works for the server team but times out for workstation VLAN 10.10.40.0/24. The firewall admin 'fixed' it by adding a permit at the bottom of the inbound ACL. You read the ACL top-down like the firewall does.
scenarios.title: ACL rule order silently blocks the app
scenarios.why: ACLs are evaluated top-down and the FIRST match wins — processing stops there. Traffic from 10.10.40.0/24 to 10.10.5.20:80 matches rule 20 (deny) before ever reaching rule 30, so the fix never fires. The correct repair is to place the permit ABOVE the deny (or remove the overly broad deny), then re-test. The implicit deny only catches traffic no explicit rule matched.

choices: Replace the scanners immediately; any WPA2 fallback voids the WPA3 audit requirement
Enable WPA3 transition mode (WPA3-SAE + WPA2-PSK) on CORP so SAE-capable clients use WPA3 while legacy scanners fall back to WPA2
Downgrade CORP back to WPA2-PSK and document a risk acceptance for the audit
Dedicate a separate WPA2-PSK SSID on the warehouse VLAN for the scanners and keep CORP on pure WPA3-SAE
evidence:
SSID CORP: WPA3-SAE only (transition mode disabled)
SSID GUEST: WPA2-PSK (VLAN 90)
Scanners: 802.11n, WPA2-PSK only, no SAE support
scenarios.hint: Transition mode keeps the old handshake alive on the same SSID. Is there a way to quarantine the legacy risk instead of mixing it in?
scenarios.prompt: What is the best resolution that satisfies both the audit and the scanners?
scenarios.situation:
WPA2 and WPA3 are the security standards that encrypt Wi-Fi traffic — WPA3 (using SAE, Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) fixes WPA2's weaknesses: offline password-guessing attacks and unencrypted open networks. The reasoning for the painful upgrade: you can't just flip a switch because old devices don't speak WPA3, so networks run a transition mode — and every transition mode is a compromise between security and compatibility. This scenario weighs what breaks and what's still exposed...

After enabling WPA3-SAE on the corporate SSID for a security audit, three warehouse barcode scanners drop off Wi-Fi permanently while all laptops reconnect fine. The scanners are 2019-era devices with no firmware updates available. The audit still requires stronger wireless security.
scenarios.title: WPA3 upgrade breaks legacy scanners
scenarios.why: Transition mode would technically reconnect the scanners, but it re-exposes the WPA2 4-way handshake (downgrade/dictionary-attack surface) on the corporate SSID and weakens the audit posture. A dedicated WPA2 SSID mapped to an isolated warehouse VLAN segments the legacy risk, keeps CORP on pure WPA3-SAE (Dragonfly handshake, forward secrecy, no offline dictionary attacks on the PSK), and lets firewall policy restrict what scanners can reach.

scenarios.title: Think Aloud: The Gigabit Link Negotiating 100 Mbps
scenarios.situation: The backup server's nightly copy to the NAS takes 6 hours instead of 40 minutes. The NIC is a 1 Gbps card, the switch port is a 1 Gbps port, the cable 'has always worked'. Both ends are set to Auto.
scenarios.prompt: Narrate your thinking aloud as you work: what do you check first and why? Then: what is the most likely physical cause, and what is the rule about hard-setting speed/duplex?
evidence: Jacket reads 'CAT5' (not 5e). Run is 68 meters, zip-tied tight around a fluorescent ballast housing.
choices: Hard-set the SERVER to 1000/full and leave the switch on auto — the server is the side you control, so forcing it fixes the negotiation.

Replace the cable with certified Cat5e or Cat6, re-run away from the ballast, and confirm both ends negotiate 1000/full on auto. Hard-set speed/duplex only as a last resort — and always on BOTH ends together, never one side fixed and the other auto.
Enable jumbo frames on the server and the NAS — bigger frames mean fewer interrupts and the throughput will recover.
Reboot the switch. Port negotiation state machines get stuck, and a reboot clears them.
scenarios.why: 1000BASE-T needs all four cable pairs; Cat5 (not 5e) with a long run past an EMI source loses a pair to noise, and autonegotiation gracefully falls back to 100BASE-TX which needs only two pairs — the 100 Mbps reading is the cable confessing. Hard-setting one side to 1000/full while the other stays auto is the classic way to CREATE a duplex mismatch: the auto side cannot see the fixed side's duplex intent and guesses half, giving you collisions and late collisions on top of the slow link. Auto/auto with a good cable is the correct end state; fixed/fixed is the acceptable workaround only when negotiation hardware is genuinely broken. Logic Check: autonegotiation falling back is a symptom with a physical cause — fix the wire before you override the protocol that was correctly reporting the wire is bad.
scenarios.hint: Gigabit needs all four pairs, 100-meg needs two — what does a fallback to 100 tell you about the cable, and what happens when only ONE side is hard-set?

scenarios.title: The Gateway's MAC Keeps Changing
scenarios.situation: Intermittent drops all afternoon on VLAN 20 — sessions freeze for 30–60 seconds, then recover. Nothing in the switch logs, the gateway is up, and the firewall team swears they changed nothing.
scenarios.prompt: Two arp -a snapshots, five minutes apart, show the gateway IP mapped to two different MAC addresses. What does that prove, and what is your next three commands?
evidence:
Interface: 10.2.20.44
  Internet Address      Physical Address      Type
  10.2.20.1             aa-bb-cc-dd-ee-01     dynamic

Interface: 10.2.20.44
  Internet Address      Physical Address      Type
  10.2.20.1             aa-bb-cc-dd-ee-99     dynamic
Gateway's real MAC (from the firewall console)
aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:01 — so the 14:05 entry is an impostor.
choices: Run arp -d * on every workstation to clear the bad entries, then monitor — stale ARP happens and clearing fixes it.
Reboot the core switch. Flapping ARP entries mean the CAM table is corrupt and a reboot rebuilds it.

A second device is claiming the gateway's IP — find the rogue MAC's switch port (show mac address-table | include ee-99), shut the port, and investigate the device. Clearing ARP only treats the symptom; the impostor will re-announce within seconds.
Change the gateway's IP address to 10.2.20.254 so the conflict disappears.
scenarios.why: An IP address mapping to two different MACs minutes apart is not flapping — it is two devices answering for one identity. The impostor (ee-99) is sending gratuitous ARPs claiming 10.2.20.1, so half the VLAN sends its gateway traffic to the wrong MAC and sessions black-hole until the real gateway's next ARP refresh. This is either a duplicate-IP misconfiguration (someone statically set the gateway IP on a laptop) or active ARP spoofing — either way, the fix is physical: trace the MAC to its switch port and remove the device, then find out which. arp -d buys you seconds; the liar re-announces immediately. Logic Check: an ARP table that cannot make up its mind is two devices claiming one identity — stop clearing the table and go find the second claimant.
scenarios.hint: One IP, two MACs, five minutes apart — is that a 'stale entry', or is something actively announcing?

scenarios.title: Port Forward Works Inside, Fails From the Internet
scenarios.situation: The new customer portal is published via DNAT: public 203.0.113.10:8443 → 10.1.5.20:443. From the LAN, https://10.1.5.20 works perfectly. From the internet, the connection times out. The firewall admin insists both the NAT rule and the WAN allow rule are correct.
scenarios.prompt: The server is proven healthy by the LAN test. Where is the packet dying, and what single observation proves it?
evidence:
WAN IP: 192.168.0.2/24 (DHCP from ISP CPE)
DNAT rule: 203.0.113.10:8443 -> 10.1.5.20:443  [active]
WAN allow: TCP 8443 from any -> 10.1.5.20  [active]
Internet IP: 203.0.113.10 | LAN: 192.168.0.1/24 | Mode: Router (NAT enabled)
Inbound SYN to 192.168.0.2:8443 from the ISP modem's LAN — never from a real internet source.
choices: The application is down — restart the portal services on 10.1.5.20 and retest from outside.
DNS is wrong — create a public A record for portal.example.com pointing at 203.0.113.10.

Double NAT: the ISP modem is also routing/NATing, so the firewall's 'WAN' is really a private LAN (192.168.0.2). Inbound internet traffic hits the ISP modem first, which has no forward — put the modem in bridge/IP-passthrough mode, or add the matching forward on the modem too.
The firewall is underpowered — replace it with a bigger model; the SYN packets are being dropped under load.
scenarios.why: The LAN test exonerates the server completely — the fault is strictly in the inbound translation path. The giveaway is the firewall's WAN address: 192.168.0.2 is RFC 1918, meaning there is another NAT device upstream. The ISP modem holds the real public IP (203.0.113.10) and is NATing, so internet SYNs arrive at the MODEM, which has no port-forward rule and drops them — the firewall's perfect DNAT config never sees a packet. The capture proves it: SYNs only ever arrive sourced from the modem's LAN side (its own health checks), never from the internet. Bridge the CPE (or forward 8443 on both devices), and the path completes. Logic Check: when inside works and outside fails, the server is innocent — walk the inbound path hop by hop and find the first device that does not know the packet is coming.
scenarios.hint: What kind of address is 192.168.0.2, and what does a 'WAN' interface holding one tell you about the path?

choices: NAT-T disabled: UDP 4500 is blocked and ESP cannot traverse the vendor's NAT
Phase 2 transform-set mismatch: the ESP encryption proposal differs between peers
Interesting-traffic ACL mismatch: the crypto map is not encrypting the right subnets
Pre-shared key mismatch: proposals match on paper, so the remaining Phase 1 variable is the PSK itself
evidence:
Encryption: AES-256 | Hash: SHA256 | DH group: 14 | Lifetime: 86400s
Auth: pre-shared key

IKEv1 Phase 1: no matching proposal found from peer 203.0.113.7
IKE SA negotiation FAILED
AES-256 / SHA256 / DH group 14, PSK 'correct-horse-...'(they claim)
scenarios.hint: Phase 1 must fully succeed before Phase 2 is even attempted. Which listed options belong to Phase 2 or later?
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause of the Phase 1 failure?
scenarios.situation:
IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) builds encrypted tunnels between sites in two handshakes: IKE (Internet Key Exchange) Phase 1 establishes a secure channel between the two gateways — authenticating each other and agreeing on encryption — and Phase 2 negotiates protection for the actual data. When Phase 1 fails, NO tunnel exists at all. The reasoning: the phases are sequential by design — you can't negotiate WHAT to protect until you've agreed HOW to talk — so a Phase 1 failure means the peers never even authenticated...

A new IPsec site-to-site tunnel to a vendor never comes up. The firewall log shows repeated IKE failures and the tunnel status stays at 'IKE SA negotiation'. The vendor swears their side is configured correctly. You compare the Phase 1 proposals.
scenarios.title: Site-to-site tunnel stuck at Phase 1
scenarios.why: Phase 1 (IKE SA / ISAKMP SA) requires identical proposals on both peers: encryption, hash, DH group, lifetime, AND authentication material. 'No matching proposal found' with matching cipher suites points at the one element not visible in the proposal — the pre-shared key. Phase 2, interesting traffic, and NAT-T only matter after Phase 1 completes, so they cannot cause an IKE SA negotiation failure.

choices: Interesting-traffic mirror mismatch: local encrypts 10.1<->10.2 but branch expects 10.2<->10.9, so Phase 2 proxy IDs never agree
IKE version mismatch: one side runs IKEv1 and the other IKEv2 for Phase 2 quick mode
DH group mismatch in the Phase 2 proposal: PFS group differs between peers
ESP vs AH mismatch: one side proposes ESP and the other AH in the transform set
scenarios.hint: Phase 2 negotiates which subnets get encrypted. Write each side's pair as source->destination and compare.
scenarios.prompt: What should you check first for this Phase 2 failure?
scenarios.situation:
Phase 2 of IKE (Internet Key Exchange) negotiates WHICH traffic gets encrypted — the 'interesting traffic,' defined by matching subnet pairs on both ends. If Site A says 'encrypt 10.1.0.0/24 to 10.2.0.0/24' and Site B's mirror entry is misconfigured, Phase 1 succeeds but Phase 2 dies. The reasoning: each side independently decides what deserves the tunnel, and the tunnel only forms where both sides' definitions overlap — a mismatch means zero overlap, so the tunnel blinks up, then drops...

The IKE Phase 1 SA is established to the branch office, but the IPsec SA never forms and no traffic crosses the tunnel. Phase 1 completing proves proposals and PSK are fine, so the fault is in Phase 2 negotiation.
scenarios.title: Phase 1 up, Phase 2 down: no traffic flows
scenarios.why: Phase 2 (IPsec SA via quick mode) negotiates proxy IDs — the local and remote subnet pairs — which must mirror each other exactly. Local says 'encrypt 10.1.0.0/16 to 10.2.0.0/16' while the branch expects '10.2.0.0/16 to 10.9.0.0/16'; the proxy IDs do not mirror, so quick mode fails. IKE version, ESP/AH, and PFS mismatches are possible but the ACL evidence directly shows the proxy-ID disagreement.

choices: ESP (IP protocol 50) cannot survive NAT, and NAT-T never engaged; allow UDP 4500 so ESP gets encapsulated in UDP
AH (IP protocol 51) is being used instead of ESP; change the transform set to ESP
The private address 192.168.0.2 invalidates the PSK; switch Phase 1 to certificate auth
IKE UDP 500 is blocked by the ISP router; open UDP 500 inbound on the ISP router
evidence:
UDP 500  <-> peer: IKE negotiation OK
IP proto 50 -> peer: ESP packets sent, none returned
No UDP 4500 traffic observed
NAT enabled; firewall behind it on 192.168.0.2 (private)
scenarios.hint: NAT rewrites ports. Which of the tunnel's protocols has no ports to rewrite?
scenarios.prompt: What is happening, and what must be allowed through for the fix?
scenarios.situation:
IPsec's ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) protocol doesn't survive NAT (Network Address Translation) — NAT rewrites packet headers and ESP's integrity check then fails, killing the tunnel. NAT-T (NAT Traversal) fixes this by wrapping ESP inside UDP port 4500, which NAT handles fine. The reasoning: ESP was designed before NAT existed and assumes headers arrive untouched; UDP encapsulation gives NAT a header it's allowed to rewrite while the ESP payload inside stays pristine. This scenario puts a VPN gateway behind a NAT router — the most common branch-office setup — and asks what must be enabled...

A working site-to-site tunnel broke the day the branch's ISP installed a new router that NATs the branch firewall. Phase 1 completes but the tunnel flaps and passes no traffic. You capture the ports in use during negotiation.
scenarios.title: Tunnel dies behind the new ISP router
scenarios.why: ESP is IP protocol 50 — it has no ports, so NAT devices cannot translate it and typically drop it. NAT-Traversal detects NAT in the path and wraps ESP inside UDP port 4500, which NAT handles normally. IKE on UDP 500 clearly works (Phase 1 completes), and the missing UDP 4500 traffic shows NAT-T never engaged — usually because the peer is not offering it or the port is filtered.

choices: PPTP: only needs TCP 1723 and GRE, simple for captive portals
IKEv2: faster reconnection via MOBIKE, but still needs UDP 500/4500 and ESP
SSTP: tunnels PPP over TLS on TCP 443, which hostile networks almost always allow outbound
OpenVPN in TAP mode: flexible, but requires installing the OpenVPN client
evidence:
L2TP/IPsec: needs UDP 500, UDP 4500, UDP 1701, ESP proto 50
Failure rate on hotel Wi-Fi: ~60%

Windows 10/11 native client only; no third-party installs
Must traverse captive portals and port-restricted egress
scenarios.hint: What is the one port that virtually every public network leaves open outbound?
scenarios.prompt: Which protocol best fits, and why?
scenarios.situation:
A client VPN connects one remote laptop to the office — but WHICH protocol builds the tunnel matters: IKEv2/IPsec (fast, auto-reconnects when phones switch networks), SSTP (rides HTTPS port 443, slips through strict firewalls), SSL-style VPNs (browser-friendly), and WireGuard (modern, minimal code) — versus legacy PPTP/L2TP, whose encryption is broken and which you must recognize to refuse. The reasoning: each protocol trades security, firewall-friendliness, and reconnect behavior differently, so 'best' depends on the user's network — this scenario picks the right one for the constraints...

Remote users on hotel and airport Wi-Fi report the company L2TP/IPsec VPN often fails to connect — captive portals and strict egress firewalls seem to block it. You need a client VPN protocol most likely to work from hostile networks, native to Windows, without extra client installs.
scenarios.title: Picking a client VPN for locked-down networks
scenarios.why: SSTP encapsulates VPN traffic in HTTPS (TCP 443), so it looks like ordinary web traffic and passes through captive portals and restrictive egress firewalls that block UDP 500/4500/1701 and ESP. It is built into Windows (no extra client). IKEv2 still needs UDP/ESP, PPTP is cryptographically broken (MS-CHAPv2), and OpenVPN violates the no-install constraint.

choices: Split tunneling requires a second VPN tunnel per user, doubling gateway load
Split tunneling prevents the corporate firewall from logging any user activity at all
Split tunneling breaks IPsec encryption for internet traffic, exposing credentials in cleartext
Split tunneling turns the endpoint into a dual-homed bridge: malware from the direct internet path can pivot into the corporate LAN over the VPN
evidence:
All traffic -> VPN -> corp firewall -> internet
Zoom via VPN: 180ms latency, frequent drops

10.0.0.0/8 + corp DNS -> VPN; internet direct
Risk note: endpoint becomes a bridge between internet and LAN
scenarios.hint: Draw the laptop with two active network paths. What can travel between them?
scenarios.prompt: What is the core security trade-off of split tunneling?
scenarios.situation:
Tunnel policy decides what goes through the VPN: split tunnel sends ONLY office-bound traffic through the encrypted tunnel while YouTube goes direct (faster, less office bandwidth — but the company can't inspect that traffic); full tunnel forces EVERYTHING through the office (inspectable and consistent, but slower and heavier).
