The reasoning: it's a control-versus-performance trade — full tunnel lets security see everything at the cost of hauling Netflix through the corporate firewall, split tunnel trusts the endpoint more. This scenario weighs the trade for a real workforce...

Security wants all remote-user traffic forced through the corporate firewall (full tunnel), but users complain that video calls and cloud apps crawl when tunneled from home. A split-tunnel proposal would send only 10.0.0.0/8 and internal DNS through the VPN. You must weigh the trade-off for the policy decision.
scenarios.title: Split tunneling vs full tunnel policy
scenarios.why: With split tunneling the laptop simultaneously touches the untrusted internet and the corporate LAN, so a compromise via the direct path can pivot through the VPN into the internal network — the classic dual-homed risk. Mitigations: always-on VPN with enforced EDR/firewall posture on the endpoint. Full tunnel avoids this but backhauls everything, hurting performance and gateway scale.

choices: AH (IP proto 51) encrypts the payload; tunnel mode adds a new IP header for routing across the internet
Transport mode is required gateway-to-gateway; tunnel mode only works host-to-host
ESP (IP proto 50) encrypts and authenticates the payload; tunnel mode encrypts the entire original IP packet including its header, hiding internal addressing
ESP authenticates only; encryption is provided by tunnel mode wrapping the packet in a new IP header
evidence:
Confidentiality required for all tunneled traffic
Gateway-to-gateway (not host-to-host)
scenarios.hint: Which protocol encrypts, and which mode hides the original IP header?
scenarios.prompt: Which statement correctly describes ESP in tunnel mode for this use case?
scenarios.situation:
IPsec has two protocols — ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload: encrypts AND authenticates) and AH (Authentication Header: authenticates ONLY, no encryption) — and two modes — transport (protects just the payload, host-to-host) and tunnel (wraps the ENTIRE original packet, gateway-to-gateway). The reasoning for the real-world default: site-to-site VPNs need the whole packet hidden (tunnel mode) AND the contents secret (ESP), so ESP-in-tunnel-mode dominates; AH survives only in niches where you must prove integrity without hiding anything. This scenario tests why, and when the other combinations appear...

A vendor's security questionnaire asks you to confirm the site-to-site tunnel uses ESP in tunnel mode, not AH. The junior engineer asks what the difference actually is and why the distinction matters for a gateway-to-gateway VPN carrying mixed internal traffic.
scenarios.title: ESP vs AH, tunnel vs transport
scenarios.why: ESP provides both encryption and authentication (AH authenticates but does NOT encrypt — that is why the questionnaire demands ESP for confidentiality). Tunnel mode encapsulates the whole original packet, so internal source/destination IPs are hidden from anyone watching the internet path; transport mode only protects the payload and leaves original headers visible, and is meant for host-to-host, not gateway VPNs.

scenarios.title: Think Aloud: The Tunnel That Dies Every 8 Hours
scenarios.situation: The site-to-site IPsec tunnel to the branch drops like clockwork every 8 hours, stays down 2–3 minutes, then comes back on its own. Phase 1 and Phase 2 both establish cleanly every morning. The ISP swears the circuit is clean, and it is — the drops do not correlate with any outage.
scenarios.prompt: Narrate your thinking aloud as you work: what do you check first and why? Then: what timer is killing the tunnel, and what is the permanent fix?
evidence:
09:00:00 IPsec SA established (Phase 2)
17:00:02 deleting IPsec SA after 28800 seconds   <-- exactly 8h
17:02:41 IPsec SA established (Phase 2)

Side A: Phase1 lifetime 86400, Phase2 lifetime 28800
Side B: Phase1 lifetime 86400, Phase2 lifetime 3600
Dead Peer Detection: enabled both sides, 30s interval — peer is alive at every drop.
choices: Schedule a script to clear and rebuild the tunnel every 7 hours — if it dies on a timer, beat the timer.
Increase the DPD interval to 300 seconds. Aggressive dead-peer detection is clearly tearing the tunnel down early.

Match the Phase 2 (and Phase 1) lifetimes identically on both sides — e.g., 86400/28800 on both — then clear the SAs and let them renegotiate. Mismatched lifetimes mean one side deletes the SA while the other still trusts it, and rekey negotiation fails across the disagreement.
Replace the branch firewall — hardware that drops tunnels on a timer has a failing clock or memory.
scenarios.why: Clockwork failures are configuration, not hardware — hardware fails randomly, timers fail on schedule. 28,800 seconds is exactly 8 hours: side A's Phase 2 SA lifetime. Side B believes the SA should live 3,600 seconds. When B's timer expires it tries to rekey on terms A does not expect (or A deletes the SA out from under B's rekey), the negotiation fails, traffic black-holes until the next full establishment cycle. DPD is a red herring — the peer is alive, which is exactly what the log shows. A cron job bouncing the tunnel treats the symptom and guarantees a 2-minute outage on YOUR schedule instead of the timer's. The fix is boring and permanent: identical lifetimes on both ends, the single most common IPsec interoperability setting. Logic Check: failures on a precise timer are never the ISP and never hardware — read the log's timestamps as a configuration confession.
scenarios.hint: 28,800 seconds is a very round number of hours — whose configured lifetime is it, and what does the OTHER side believe?

scenarios.title: Remote users locked out after the ZTNA rollout
scenarios.situation: Your company replaced the legacy SSL VPN with brokered ZTNA last night. This morning one remote accountant reports: 'I can sign in fine, but the file server app just spins and never connects.' Three other remote users are working normally on the same app. The accountant mentions she received a replacement laptop yesterday and set it up herself. No firewall changes were made — ZTNA uses outbound connectors only.
evidence: User: sign-in succeeds, MFA passes. App 'FileServer': connection spins, never loads. 3 other remote users on same app: OK.
DENY user=accountant app=FileServer reason=device posture check failed: unknown device certificate
User's laptop replaced under warranty. New device shipped directly to user; IT enrollment step scheduled for 'later this week.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the root cause, and what is the correct fix?
choices: The broker service is down for remote users — roll everyone back to the legacy VPN concentrator until it stabilizes

The replacement laptop was never enrolled/approved, so the broker denies the connection: ZTNA requires BOTH an authorized user AND an approved device — enroll the device (or issue a managed one) and the app connects
Split tunneling is misconfigured on her client — push the full-tunnel profile to her machine
The site-to-site IPsec tunnel to her branch office dropped — restart the tunnel on the edge firewall
scenarios.hint: Her credentials work. Read the broker log's deny reason word by word — what is ZTNA checking besides the user?
scenarios.why: This is the signature ZTNA rollout ticket. Sign-in and MFA pass because the USER is authorized; the broker still denies because the DEVICE is unknown — access in a brokered ZTNA model requires user identity AND device identity together, which is precisely what makes stolen credentials useless. The fix is enrollment/approval of the replacement device, not a rollback: the three working users prove the broker and app path are healthy, there are no tunnels to restart (connectors dial outbound), and tunnel mode is irrelevant to a per-app brokered session.

scenarios.title: Picking the right virtual switch
scenarios.situation:
Hyper-V (Microsoft's hypervisor) gives VMs virtual switches instead of physical cables: External (bridged to a real NIC — Network Interface Card — so VMs join the physical network), Internal (VMs talk to each other and the host only), Private (VMs talk only to each other — a sealed box). The reasoning: the switch type IS the VM's network boundary decision — it answers 'who is this VM allowed to reach?' before any firewall rule is even considered. This scenario diagnoses the classic 'my new VM has no network' by checking which switch it was plugged into...

You built a new Hyper-V host with one physical NIC. The host itself must stay reachable for management, the production VMs need LAN and internet access, and a malware-analysis VM must be completely isolated — no host access, no internet, no VM-to-host traffic.
scenarios.prompt: Which virtual switch layout meets all three requirements?
evidence:
Ethernet adapter Ethernet:
   IPv4 Address. . . : 10.0.5.20
   Default Gateway . : 10.0.5.1
choices: One External switch with management OS sharing disabled; every VM shares it
Private switch for production VMs, Internal switch for the malware VM
Internal switch for the production VMs and an External switch with management OS sharing disabled for the malware VM
External switch bound to the physical NIC with management OS sharing enabled, plus a separate Private switch for the malware VM
scenarios.why: An External switch binds to the physical NIC, giving VMs real LAN and internet access; AllowManagementOS keeps the host reachable through the same NIC. A Private switch allows VM-to-VM traffic only — the host cannot reach those VMs at all — which is true isolation. An Internal switch would still let the malware VM talk to the host, which breaks the isolation requirement.
scenarios.hint: Which switch type lets the malware VM 'see' the host? Eliminate any layout where that is possible.

scenarios.title: Generation 1 vs Generation 2 VMs
scenarios.situation:
Hyper-V VMs come in two generations: Gen 1 emulates legacy hardware (IDE disks, BIOS boot — needed for old operating systems), Gen 2 is modern virtual hardware (SCSI boot, UEFI, Secure Boot — faster, but requires a 64-bit modern OS). You choose at creation and can't change later. The reasoning: Gen 1 exists purely for backward compatibility (ancient OS installers that only understand BIOS/IDE), while Gen 2 drops the emulation overhead — pick wrong and the OS won't install, and there's no convert button...

You must build two VMs on the same host: a new Windows Server 2025 web server that requires UEFI boot with Secure Boot, and a legacy vendor appliance that only boots from an emulated IDE controller under a legacy BIOS. Both must PXE-boot for imaging.
scenarios.prompt: Which generation do you pick for each VM, and what constraint applies?
evidence: Creates a Gen 2 VM: UEFI firmware, Secure Boot on by default, SCSI boot only
Requires: legacy BIOS, IDE boot disk, legacy network adapter for PXE
choices: Gen 2 for the web server (UEFI + Secure Boot, PXE via synthetic NIC), Gen 1 for the legacy appliance (IDE + legacy BIOS, PXE via legacy NIC) — generation is fixed at creation and cannot be changed later
Gen 1 for both; Generation 2 was deprecated and no longer supported
Gen 2 for both; any legacy OS adapts to UEFI automatically
Gen 1 for the web server and Gen 2 for the appliance, then convert later with Set-VM
scenarios.why: Generation 2 requires a 64-bit UEFI-capable guest and brings Secure Boot, SCSI boot, and faster boot times, with PXE through the synthetic network adapter. Generation 1 keeps the emulated IDE controller, legacy BIOS, and the legacy network adapter for PXE — the only option for old appliances. The generation is chosen at creation time and is permanent, so the decision must be right up front.
scenarios.hint: Match each guest to the boot hardware it actually supports: SCSI/UEFI or IDE/legacy BIOS?

scenarios.title: Growing a data disk past the old limits
scenarios.situation:
A VM's disk is a VHDX file on the host, in one of three types: Fixed (all space allocated up front — fastest, hungriest), Dynamically expanding (grows as data is written — space-efficient, slight performance cost, dangerous if the host disk fills), Differencing (tracks only CHANGES from a parent disk — the basis of checkpoints). The reasoning: it's the classic space-versus-speed-versus-safety triangle — fixed buys deterministic performance, dynamic buys capacity efficiency, differencing buys cheap branching at the cost of chain complexity. This scenario matches disk type to workload...

A file-server VM's data disk is a 150 GB dynamically expanding VHDX and is now 95% full. The VM's old C: drive is a 127 GB fixed VHD in the legacy format. You need the data disk at 300 GB with minimal downtime, and the disk is attached to the SCSI controller with no checkpoints.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct operation to grow the data disk?
evidence:
VhdFormat : VHDX
VhdType   : Dynamic
FileSize  : 142GB
Size      : 150GB
Attached  : True
choices: Convert the disk back to VHD first, because VHDX cannot be resized
Run Resize-VHD to 300 GB (VHDX supports online resize when attached via SCSI), then extend the volume inside the guest OS
Shrink the disk; a VHDX can never grow beyond the size it was created with
Delete the VHDX and restore the VM from a checkpoint to get more space
scenarios.why: VHDX supports up to 64 TB (VHD caps at about 2 TB) and Resize-VHD grows it. On Windows Server 2012 R2 and later, a VHDX on the SCSI controller can be resized while the VM is running; then you extend the partition inside the guest. Resizing is blocked when checkpoints exist, so the clean chain here matters. As a bonus, the old fixed VHD could be modernized with Convert-VHD to a dynamic VHDX.
scenarios.hint: What is the size ceiling of VHD vs VHDX — and what must be true about checkpoints before a resize?

scenarios.title: Checkpoints are not backups
scenarios.situation:
A Hyper-V checkpoint is a save point — a differencing disk frozen at a moment in time for quick rollback — and it is NOT a backup: it lives on the same storage as the VM, so a dead disk kills both. The reasoning: a checkpoint protects against LOGICAL mistakes (bad patch, bad config — rewind the state), while a backup protects against PHYSICAL loss (dead disk, dead building — separate media, separate location). This scenario draws the hard line: when a checkpoint is the right tool, and when only a real tested backup counts...

A junior admin took nightly production checkpoints of the finance VM for a month and calls it the backup strategy. The VM folder now holds one 80 GB VHDX plus twelve 15–40 GB AVHDX files, disk space is critical, and the app team wants to roll back to last Tuesday's checkpoint.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct handling of this situation?
evidence: Get-VMCheckpoint -VMName FIN01 | Select Name, CheckpointType, CreationTime

PreMonthEnd   Standard    2026-09-08
PrePatch      Production  2026-09-15
... 12 checkpoints total ...

FIN01.vhdx  80 GB
FIN01_AutoRecovery.avhdx, ... 12 AVHDX files 15-40 GB each
choices: Apply last Tuesday's checkpoint to roll back, then delete the stale checkpoints so their AVHDX files merge back into the parent — and implement a real backup solution, because checkpoints are not backups
Delete all checkpoints with the VM running and consider the job done
Keep stacking checkpoints indefinitely; the chain itself is the backup
Copy the AVHDX files to a USB drive; that is a complete backup
scenarios.why: A checkpoint is a point-in-time differencing state (an AVHDX chain) stored alongside the VM — if the host or its storage dies, every checkpoint dies with it, so it is never a backup. Deleting a checkpoint merges its differencing data back into the parent disk, which takes time and needs free space. Production checkpoints (2016+) use VSS inside the guest for application-consistent captures, while standard checkpoints just save the VM's memory state.
scenarios.hint: If the host's RAID died tonight, which of those files would survive? That answers the backup question.

scenarios.title: Planning a Hyper-V Replica failover
scenarios.situation:
Hyper-V Replica keeps a scheduled copy of a VM on a second host — asynchronous, typically every 30 seconds to 15 minutes — as disaster insurance. Failover is MANUAL: you decide disaster struck, then boot the replica (planned, test, or unplanned failover). The reasoning for manual: only a human can declare 'the primary site is truly dead' — automatic failover risks split-brain (both copies running, diverging). And the replica is minutes behind by design, so some data loss is inherent — this scenario walks the failover decision with eyes open...

A critical VM replicates from the Orlando host to the DR host every 5 minutes. Get-VMReplication shows State=Replicating and Health=Normal. The primary site loses power during business hours and the primary host is unreachable.
scenarios.prompt: What is the expected data loss, and what is the correct recovery action?
evidence:
State         : Replicating
Health        : Normal
FrequencySec  : 300
PrimaryServer : HV-ORL-01
ReplicaServer : HV-DR-01
choices: Expect zero data loss; just power on the replica copy
Restore the primary from one of its checkpoints
Expect up to about 5 minutes of data loss (the replication interval is the RPO); run Start-VMFailover on the DR replica, then Start-VM
Run a planned failover from the (dead) primary host
scenarios.why: Hyper-V Replica sends changes on a fixed interval — 30 seconds, 5 minutes, or 15 minutes — and that interval is your recovery point objective: an unplanned failover loses everything changed since the last replication. Start-VMFailover brings the replica online at the DR site (a planned failover with -Prepare is only possible when the primary is alive). After the primary recovers, Reverse-VMReplication flips the direction for failback.
scenarios.hint: The 300-second interval is your worst-case data loss. What PowerShell verb starts a failover on the replica side?

scenarios.title: Moving running VMs between hosts
scenarios.situation:
A failover cluster groups Hyper-V hosts so VMs automatically restart on a surviving node when a host dies — high availability without human intervention. Moving VMs has flavors: live migration (a RUNNING VM moves with zero downtime), quick migration (brief pause), storage migration (move the VHDX while running). The reasoning: live migration works by copying memory pages while the VM keeps running, then freezing for milliseconds to transfer the last dirty pages — which is why it needs fast interconnects and shared (or shared-nothing with SMB) storage. This scenario picks the right move for the maintenance window...

A 4-node Hyper-V failover cluster on Cluster Shared Volumes hosts 30 VMs. You must evacuate HOST02 for firmware updates with zero VM downtime. Separately, one VM's storage must move from an old SAN LUN to a new one without stopping the VM.
scenarios.prompt: Which migration type fits each task?
evidence:
Name   State
----   -----
HOST01 Up
HOST02 Up
HOST03 Up
HOST04 Up
All CSVs in Direct I/O, healthy
choices: Live Migration to evacuate HOST02 (no downtime on shared storage), Storage Migration for the LUN move (relocates VHDX files while the VM keeps running)
Live Migration moves the storage, Storage Migration moves the running VM
Quick Migration for both tasks — it is the fastest option
Shut down all VMs and copy the VHDX files manually
scenarios.why: Live Migration moves a running VM's memory and state between hosts with no perceived downtime — it needs a failover cluster with Cluster Shared Volumes (or SMB 3 shared-nothing live migration). Quick Migration instead saves/pauses the VM, causing a brief outage. Storage Migration moves only the VM's virtual disks and configuration between storage locations while the VM keeps running — exactly the LUN move.
scenarios.hint: Which operation keeps the VM's memory running uninterrupted, and which one only touches the disks?
objectives: Live vs Quick vs Storage Migration

scenarios.title: VM fails to start after a BIOS update
scenarios.situation:
A VM that won't start is a host-side problem until proven otherwise: the usual suspects are the Hyper-V Virtual Machine Management service not running, insufficient host RAM, a locked or missing VHDX, or a virtual switch deleted out from under it. The reasoning for the triage order: the VM is a guest of the host's resources — if the host can't provide RAM, disk access, or networking, no guest setting will fix it — so you verify host health first, then the VM's configuration, instead of randomly clicking...

After a host BIOS update, the DB01 VM fails to start and sits in the Off state. Hyper-V Manager reports: 'Virtual machine DB01 could not be started because the hypervisor is not running.' No VM on the host will start, but other Windows services look fine.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause, and what do you check first?
evidence: 'Hypervisor launch failed; Either VMX not present or not enabled in BIOS.'

Hyper-V Requirements:      VM Monitor Mode Extensions: Yes
                           Virtualization Enabled In Firmware: No
choices: The VM's integration services are outdated and must be upgraded
The virtual switch binding broke during the update
The Hyper-V role must be reinstalled
The BIOS update disabled hardware virtualization (Intel VT-x / AMD-V) — re-enable it in firmware and confirm with systeminfo
scenarios.why: The hypervisor requires CPU virtualization extensions (VT-x/AMD-V) plus DEP, and BIOS updates commonly reset firmware settings to defaults — disabling them. When the hypervisor cannot launch, no VM on the host can start, which matches every VM being affected. systeminfo's 'Virtualization Enabled In Firmware' line is the definitive check. Integration services affect guest performance and time sync, not whether the hypervisor itself launches.
scenarios.hint: The error names the hypervisor itself, and ALL VMs are affected. What hardware feature does the hypervisor need from the BIOS?

scenarios.title: Import-VM Fails on the New Host
scenarios.situation: WEB01 was exported from the old Hyper-V host and copied to the new one. Import-VM fails immediately. The .vhdx files are intact, the export folder structure looks right, and the junior admin is already talking about rebuilding the VM from scratch.
scenarios.prompt: The import error names a virtual switch. What must exist on the target host BEFORE the import, and what two flags make the import safe when the source VM still exists?
evidence: Import-VM : The virtual switch 'vSwitch-Production' could not be found.

PS C:\> Get-VMSwitch | Select-Object Name, SwitchType
Name             SwitchType
----             ----------
vSwitch-Lab       External

PS C:\> Get-VMHostSupportedVersion | Select-Object Version
Version
-------
11.0   (VM config version is 9.0 — supported)
choices: Hand-edit the .vmcx file to replace 'vSwitch-Production' with 'vSwitch-Lab' — the config is just XML-ish data and a quick edit is faster than rebuilding.

Create a vSwitch named 'vSwitch-Production' (same type: External, bound to the right NIC) on the target host first, then run Import-VM -Path <vmcx> -Copy -GenerateNewId. The -Copy keeps the export pristine and -GenerateNewId prevents VM-ID/AD collisions while the original still exists.
Import with -Force to skip the switch check, then fix networking after the VM boots.
Rebuild the VM from scratch on the new host and attach the exported .vhdx files — imports across hosts are unreliable.
scenarios.why: The .vmcx references the virtual switch BY NAME — 'vSwitch-Production' does not exist on the target, so the import fails before it starts. Hand-editing the .vmcx is surgery on a binary config format: it voids supportability and usually corrupts the file. The correct sequence is environment-first: create the identically-named switch (bound to the correct physical NIC), then import. -Copy leaves the export folder untouched as your rollback, and -GenerateNewId is mandatory while the source VM still exists — without it you get duplicate VM IDs and the cloned computer account fights the original in AD. Version 9.0 on an 11.0 host is fine (downgrade direction works); it would only fail going the other way. Logic Check: a VM is files plus the environment those files expect — make the target host look like the source host (switch names, paths) BEFORE the import, not after.
scenarios.hint: The error names exactly what is missing — and the source VM still exists, so what must the import NOT duplicate?

scenarios.title: Point-in-time restore after a bad delete
scenarios.situation:
SQL Server restores work as a CHAIN applied in strict order: full backup first, then the latest differential (all changes since that full), then every transaction log backup in sequence — like stacking transparencies to rebuild the picture. Break the chain (a missing log file) and you can only restore up to the gap. The reasoning: each backup only records what changed SINCE the last one, so the full history must be replayed in order — skip a link and the later links reference changes that were never applied. This scenario rebuilds a database from a chain with a twist...

The Orders database runs in the FULL recovery model: full backup Sunday 02:00, differential backups nightly at 02:00, transaction log backups every 15 minutes. Wednesday at 10:17 someone runs DELETE FROM Orders with no WHERE clause. The last log backup covers up to 10:15.
scenarios.prompt: What restore sequence recovers Orders to 10:16, just before the delete?
evidence: SELECT name, recovery_model_desc FROM sys.databases WHERE name='Orders'
choices: RESTORE the full backup WITH NORECOVERY, then the Wednesday differential WITH NORECOVERY, then the log backups in LSN order WITH NORECOVERY — the final one with STOPAT = '2026-10-07 10:16' WITH RECOVERY
Switch the database to SIMPLE recovery and restore the full backup
RESTORE only the Wednesday differential WITH RECOVERY
RESTORE the full backup WITH RECOVERY; the log backups replay automatically
scenarios.why: A restore chain is full, then the most recent differential, then every log backup in LSN order. WITH NORECOVERY leaves the database in the restoring state so the next backup in the chain can be applied; the final step uses WITH RECOVERY (plus STOPAT for point-in-time) to bring it online. SIMPLE recovery cannot take log backups at all, so point-in-time recovery is impossible there.
scenarios.hint: Each step must leave the database ready for the NEXT backup in the chain. Which option keeps that door open until the end?

scenarios.title: Login failed for user — error 18456
scenarios.situation:
Error 18456 is SQL Server's 'login failed' — and the STATE code inside it names the real cause (wrong password, disabled login, nonexistent user), though the client only sees the generic message. The reasoning for the vagueness is deliberate security: telling the client 'password wrong' vs 'user doesn't exist' hands attackers a username oracle, so SQL Server lies to the client and tells the truth only in the server-side error log. This scenario teaches you to read that log, map the state code to the fix...

Right after a password rotation, the reporting app's service account fails with: Login failed for user 'svc_reports'. (Error 18456, Severity 14, State 8). The SQL Server error log records the same state code, and nothing else changed.
scenarios.prompt: What does State 8 mean, and what is the fix?
evidence:
2026-10-09 03:12:04.11 Logon       Error: 18456, Severity: 14, State: 8.
2026-10-09 03:12:04.11 Logon       Login failed for user 'svc_reports'.
choices: State 8 means the account is locked out — wait 30 minutes and retry
State 8 means the database is offline — bring it online first
State 8 means Windows authentication is required — switch the app off SQL auth
State 8 means password mismatch — update the password in the app's connection string (or reset the login's password) to the new value
scenarios.why: The common 18456 state codes are diagnostic: state 5 is an invalid user ID, state 8 is a bad password, and states like 38/40/46 point at database access problems. A failure immediately after a rotation with an unchanged connection string is the classic password mismatch — sync the credential on both sides. Also verify the login is enabled and not tripping a password policy.
scenarios.hint: The error started exactly when the password changed, and the app's config still holds the old value. What does the state code confirm?

scenarios.title: Can't reach the named instance remotely
scenarios.situation:
SQL Server listens on TCP port 1433 by default — if the app can't reach the database, the checklist is mechanical, in order: the SQL Server service running, TCP/IP enabled in SQL Configuration Manager, port 1433 open on the Windows Firewall, and basic network reachability to the host. The reasoning for the order: each step assumes the previous one works — a stopped service makes firewall tests meaningless, and a blocked port makes credential errors impossible to even reach — so you work service → protocol → firewall → network instead of guessing...

SSMS from a workstation cannot connect to SQL01\APPS. The SQL Server service is running. On the server itself, SSMS connects fine over shared memory. A port test from the workstation fails.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely connectivity cause?
evidence:
Server is listening on [ 'any' <ipv4> 49812 ]
SQL Server Browser service: stopped
choices: The database is in single-user mode
The named instance listens on a dynamic port and SQL Server Browser (UDP 1434) is stopped — start the Browser service or connect with the explicit port, and check the Windows Firewall
The sa password has expired
TCP/IP is disabled on the server
scenarios.why: Named instances listen on dynamic ports by default, and clients discover the current port through the SQL Server Browser service on UDP 1434. With Browser stopped and the port unknown, remote clients cannot resolve SQL01\APPS — while local shared-memory connections bypass the network entirely, which is why local SSMS works. Fix it by starting Browser, pinning a static port and connecting as SQL01,port, and allowing the port plus UDP 1434 through the firewall.
scenarios.hint: Local works but remote fails, and it is a NAMED instance. How is a client supposed to learn which port the instance is on?

scenarios.title: Least-privilege access for a developer
scenarios.situation:
SQL Server has two doors: a login grants entry to the SERVER (authenticated at the instance level), a user grants entry to a specific DATABASE (mapped from a login) — and an 'orphaned user' is a database user whose login was deleted, stranded with no way in. The reasoning for the split: one login can map to different users in different databases with different permissions — identity (who are you) is separated from authorization (what can you touch here). This scenario untangles the login → user → role chain and fixes the orphan...

A developer (DOMAIN\ana) needs to read and write data and manage objects in the Reporting database only. She must have no server-level admin rights and no access to any other database. Her login currently has only the public server role — a good starting point.
scenarios.prompt: How do you grant exactly what she needs?
evidence: SELECT r.name FROM sys.server_principals p JOIN sys.server_role_members m ON p.principal_id=m.member_principal_id JOIN sys.server_principals r ON r.principal_id=m.role_principal_id WHERE p.name='DOMAIN\ana'
Reporting database: read + write + DDL. All other databases: no access. Server roles: none beyond public.
choices: Add DOMAIN\ana to the sysadmin fixed server role
Grant her db_owner in the master database
Enable the sa account and share its password with her
CREATE LOGIN for DOMAIN\ana, then in Reporting run CREATE USER mapped to that login and ALTER ROLE db_datareader / db_datawriter ADD MEMBER — never grant sysadmin
scenarios.why: A login is a server-level principal (who can connect); a user is a database-level principal (what they can touch inside one database). Database roles like db_datareader and db_datawriter scope permissions to that single database, while the sysadmin server role would hand her the keys to the entire instance. Least privilege means granting the smallest role that covers the job — here, reader plus writer in Reporting only.
scenarios.hint: Server-level roles open the whole instance; database-level roles open one database. Which level matches the requirement?

scenarios.title: Fragmented indexes slowing reports
scenarios.situation:
Indexes are SQL Server's book index — they make reads fast but slow down writes and bloat over time through fragmentation (data pages scattered, like a shuffled card catalog). Maintenance means rebuilding or reorganizing fragmented indexes and updating statistics (the optimizer's map of the data) on a schedule. The reasoning: the query optimizer chooses execution plans based on statistics — stale statistics mean it picks terrible plans, so 'the database was fast last month' is usually a maintenance gap, not a hardware problem. This scenario diagnoses the slowdown...

Reporting queries have degraded over the quarter. sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats shows the Orders primary key at 42% average fragmentation and a smaller customer lookup index at 12%. Statistics have not been updated in weeks.
scenarios.prompt: What maintenance action does each index need?
evidence: SELECT i.name, s.avg_fragmentation_in_percent FROM sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats(DB_ID('Orders'),NULL,NULL,NULL,'LIMITED') s JOIN sys.indexes i ON s.object_id=i.object_id AND s.index_id=i.index_id
choices: Rebuild both indexes with every transaction log backup
REBUILD the 42% index (ALTER INDEX ... REBUILD), REORGANIZE the 12% index, then UPDATE STATISTICS — and keep DBCC CHECKDB on a regular schedule
Drop and recreate both indexes every week
REORGANIZE both indexes; rebuilds are never needed
scenarios.why: The standard fragmentation rule of thumb: above ~30% rebuild, between ~5% and 30% reorganize, below ~5% leave alone. A rebuild recreates the index and refreshes its statistics with a full scan; a reorganize defragments leaf pages online but does not update statistics, so UPDATE STATISTICS follows. DBCC CHECKDB belongs in the maintenance plan too, checking the database for corruption rather than performance.
scenarios.hint: One index is heavily fragmented and one is lightly fragmented — do they need the same medicine?

scenarios.title: SQL Server service won't start
scenarios.situation:
When the SQL Server service itself won't start, the database engine never loads — and the reason is in the ERRORLOG, not in random clicking. The greatest hits: the service account's password changed, the data files were moved, or TempDB's drive is full. The reasoning: the service fails at the FIRST thing it can't do during startup (its account login, finding its data files, writing to TempDB), and it writes exactly which step failed — so you read the log first, fix the actual cause, and get the engine up...

After a GPO-driven password change, the SQL Server (MSSQLSERVER) service fails to start. The System event log reports the service was unable to log on as DOMAIN\svc_sql with the currently configured password. No databases were touched.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct first fix?
evidence: Log On As: DOMAIN\svc_sql   Status: (blank — not running)
The SQL Server (MSSQLSERVER) service was unable to log on as DOMAIN\svc_sql with the currently configured password due to the following error: Logon failure: unknown user name or bad password.
choices: Disable the Windows Firewall
Update the service account password via SQL Server Configuration Manager, then start the service and check the SQL Server error log
Detach and reattach all user databases
Reinstall SQL Server
scenarios.why: The service stores its own copy of the account password, so changing the password in Active Directory breaks the logon until the service's stored credential is updated. SQL Server Configuration Manager is the right tool — it updates the password and keeps the required file and registry permissions intact. The error log then confirms a clean startup, and a managed service account (gMSA) would prevent this class of failure entirely.
scenarios.hint: What changed right before it broke — the password. Where does the Windows service keep its own copy of it?

scenarios.title: Think Aloud: SQL Server Service Will Not Start — Read the Error Log
scenarios.situation: Monday 6:40 AM: the SQL Server service (MSSQLSERVER) will not start after the weekend SAN maintenance. The application team is escalating, the junior DBA wants to reinstall SQL Server, and the SAN team says 'all our volumes are healthy'.
scenarios.prompt: Narrate your thinking aloud as you work: what do you check first and why? Then: what does the error log actually say, and who owns the real problem?
evidence: Event ID 7000: The SQL Server (MSSQLSERVER) service failed to start due to the following error: The service did not respond to the start or control request in a timely fashion.

2026-10-10 06:31:12.44 spid5s      Starting up database 'master'.
2026-10-10 06:31:12.47 spid5s      FCB::Open failed: Could not open file E:\Data\MSSQL\master.mdf for file number 1. OS error: 3 (The system cannot find the path specified.).

PS C:\> Get-Volume -DriveLetter E
Get-Volume : No MSFT_Volume objects found with property 'DriveLetter' equal to 'E'.
Disk Management: Disk 4 (SAN LUN) shows OFFLINE.
choices: Reinstall SQL Server — a service that cannot open master is corrupted and a fresh install is the clean fix.
Restore the master database from Friday's backup — master.mdf cannot be opened, so master must be restored.

Bring Disk 4 online and remount E: (SAN path recovered after maintenance — the LUN needs rescanning/reconnecting), then start the service. SQL Server is healthy; the storage path it depends on is missing. OS error 3 = path not found = storage problem wearing a SQL costume.
Start SQL with trace flag 3608 to skip master recovery, then detach and reattach the user databases.
scenarios.why: Read the evidence chain in order: Event 7000 says the SERVICE failed (not the database engine logic), the ERRORLOG names the exact file and the exact OS error — 'FCB::Open failed... OS error 3: path not found' — and Get-Volume proves E: does not exist at all. SQL cannot open a file on a volume that is not there; the SAN maintenance left Disk 4 offline. Reinstalling SQL or restoring master both fail identically, because neither creates the missing E: path — you would spend hours proving the storage was the problem all along. The fix belongs to the storage layer: rescan, bring Disk 4 online, verify E:\Data\MSSQL\master.mdf exists, then start the service. The SAN team's 'all volumes healthy' meant THEIR array, not your host's disk state. Logic Check: the error log names the file and the OS names the reason — 'path not found' is never a database problem; always verify the path exists before touching the database.
scenarios.hint: OS error 3 has a very literal meaning — and Get-Volume just told you whether E: exists at all. Who owns THAT layer?

choices: 8 TB usable, survives 1 disk failure
4 TB usable, survives 2 disk failures
6 TB usable, survives 2 disk failures
6 TB usable, survives 1 disk failure (correct: (4-1) x 2 TB = 6 TB)
evidence:
RAID 5 requires minimum 3 disks
Usable capacity = (n - 1) x smallest disk
n = 4 disks of 2 TB each
(4 - 1) x 2 TB = 6 TB usable
Survives failure of any 1 disk
scenarios.hint: Parity in RAID 5 consumes the equivalent of one whole disk. Subtract that from your total raw space.
scenarios.prompt: With four 2 TB drives in RAID 5, what is the usable capacity and fault tolerance?
scenarios.situation:
RAID 5 stripes data across disks plus parity (recovery math) so ANY one disk can die without data loss — you sacrifice one disk's worth of capacity for the privilege. The formula: usable = (n − 1) × smallest disk. The reasoning for 'smallest disk': stripes are uniform, so every disk contributes only as much as the runt — a 4TB disk in an array of 1TB disks wastes 3TB. This scenario does the capacity math with real disk sizes, including the trap of the odd-sized disk...

The Orlando office needs a new file server. You have four 2 TB drives and a hardware RAID controller. The business requirement: survive the loss of any single drive with zero data loss. Your manager asks how much usable storage you'll get from a RAID 5 configuration before you order the server.
scenarios.title: How Much Usable Space in a RAID 5 Array?
scenarios.why: RAID 5 stripes data with distributed parity. The parity overhead costs exactly one disk's worth of capacity: (n-1) x smallest disk = 3 x 2 TB = 6 TB. It survives the failure of any ONE disk; a second failure during the rebuild destroys the array, which is why large disks (multi-TB) make RAID 5 risky for long rebuild windows.

choices: RAID 10 (1+0) — 4 TB usable, best write performance, rebuild is a fast mirror copy
RAID 5 — 7 TB usable, parity write penalty acceptable for databases
RAID 0 — 8 TB usable, fastest writes, redundancy not needed for SSDs
RAID 6 — 6 TB usable, double parity is safest for SSDs
evidence:
8 x 1 TB SSDs
RAID 5: 7 TB usable, write penalty (read-modify-write per stripe)
RAID 6: 6 TB usable, double write penalty
RAID 10: 4 TB usable, no parity penalty, rebuilds are simple copies
RAID 0: 8 TB, zero redundancy
scenarios.hint: Ask what a write has to do on each level: with mirrors it's one write to two disks; with parity it's read-old-data, read-old-parity, write-new-data, write-new-parity.
scenarios.prompt: Which RAID level is the best fit for this write-heavy, redundancy-required workload, and why?
scenarios.situation:
Different RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks) levels buy different things: RAID 10 (mirrored stripes) buys speed AND survival at half capacity — the database favorite; RAID 5 buys capacity-efficient single-disk survival — the file-server favorite; RAID 6 buys two-disk survival for big slow archives. The reasoning: databases do random small I/O where RAID 5's parity calculations become a write penalty, while sequential file serving barely notices — so the workload's I/O pattern picks the level, not the marketing sheet. This scenario matches the level to a database server's actual needs...

ThreatLocker's lab runs a SQL-heavy log-ingestion VM on a box with eight 1 TB SSDs. The DBA wants maximum write throughput AND redundancy, and rebuild times matter. The junior admin proposes RAID 5 because it gives 7 TB. You need to pick the right level and explain the trade-off.
scenarios.title: Choosing RAID for a Database Volume
scenarios.why: RAID 10 (stripe of mirrors) has no parity calculation penalty on writes, so it delivers the best write throughput of any redundant level, and a rebuild is just copying a surviving mirror — fast and low-risk. Cost: 50% capacity overhead (n/2 x smallest = 4 TB here). RAID 5/6 suffer parity write penalties (worse for 6) that hurt database workloads; RAID 0 offers zero redundancy and is never acceptable for production data.

choices: A: 1, B: 1, C: 3, D: 2 — with usable capacities 2, 16, 6, 9 TB
A: 2, B: 2, C: 2 per mirror pair, D: 1 — with usable capacities 2, 12, 12, 6 TB
A: 1, B: 2, C: 1 total, D: 1 — with usable capacities 4, 12, 6, 12 TB
A: 1, B: 2, C: 1 per mirror pair (up to 3 if lucky), D: 1 — with usable capacities 2, 12, 6, 9 TB
evidence:
A: RAID 1, 2 x 2 TB -> usable 2 TB
B: RAID 6, 5 x 4 TB -> usable (5-2) x 4 = 12 TB
C: RAID 10, 6 x 2 TB -> usable 3 x 2 = 6 TB
D: RAID 5, 4 x 3 TB -> usable 3 x 3 = 9 TB
scenarios.hint: For each level, count how many disks must still hold your data: parity RAID needs all-but-n-parity-disks alive; mirrors need one per pair.
scenarios.prompt: Which statement about failure survival across these four servers is CORRECT?
scenarios.situation:
RAID is not backup — it survives DISK failure, not deletion, corruption, or fire. The reasoning: RAID protects against exactly one failure mode (a disk stops responding) by keeping redundant data live; it can't help when the data itself is wrong (deleted rows are faithfully mirrored to all disks) or when the whole box is gone. This scenario tests the survival math: which levels live through one dead disk, which through two, what happens during the vulnerable rebuild window (a second failure kills RAID 5), and why the hot spare (a standby disk that auto-rebuilds) matters...

During a disaster-recovery tabletop exercise, the team lead walks through a rack diagram: Server A has 2x2TB in RAID 1, Server B has 5x4TB in RAID 6, Server C has 6x2TB in RAID 10, Server D has 4x3TB in RAID 5. She asks the room to call out, for each server, how many simultaneous drive failures are survivable.
scenarios.title: How Many Disks Can Each Array Lose?
scenarios.why: RAID 1 survives 1 (its mirror half). RAID 6's double parity survives any 2. RAID 10 survives any 1 failure per mirror pair — worst case 1 total, best case 3 if failures land on different pairs. RAID 5 survives any 1. Capacities: RAID 1 = smallest disk (2 TB); RAID 6 = (5-2)x4 = 12 TB; RAID 10 = 3 pairs x 2 = 6 TB; RAID 5 = (4-1)x3 = 9 TB.

choices: RPO = 1 hour (needs hourly full backups); RTO = 4 hours (no change needed)
RPO = 1 hour (needs hourly transaction-log or incremental backups); RTO = 4 hours (restore runbook must complete within 4 hours)
Both are the same concept — 5 hours total downtime budget; keep nightly full backups
RTO = 1 hour (restore within 1 hour); RPO = 4 hours (backup every 4 hours)
evidence:
Max data loss: 1 hour
Max restore time: 4 hours
Current: nightly full backup at 2 AM
Ticketing DB changes constantly during business hours
scenarios.hint: One is about how far back in time your data can roll (point), the other is about how long the clock runs before users are back (time).
scenarios.prompt: How do these two requirements map to RTO/RPO, and what backup strategy meets them?
scenarios.situation:
RTO (Recovery Time Objective) = how long you may be down; RPO (Recovery Point Objective) = how much data you may lose — two numbers the BUSINESS sets, and every backup design serves them. The reasoning: these numbers convert business pain into engineering math — a 15-minute RPO demands transaction log backups every 15 minutes (you can only lose what happened since the last backup), and a 4-hour RTO demands restores you've actually timed (hope is not a recovery plan). This scenario turns business requirements into a backup schedule...

The business continuity plan for the Orlando helpdesk ticketing system states: 'The ticketing database may lose at most 1 hour of data, and service must be restored within 4 hours of a total loss.' Full backups run nightly at 2 AM. The IT director asks what these requirements are called and what backup changes they demand.
scenarios.title: RTO and RPO Drive the Backup Design
scenarios.why: RPO (Recovery Point Objective) = how much data loss is tolerable: 1 hour means you need backups (or log shipping) at least hourly — nightly fulls allow up to 24 hours of loss and fail this requirement. RTO (Recovery Time Objective) = how fast service must return: 4 hours means your restore procedure must be tested to complete in 4 hours. RPO drives backup FREQUENCY; RTO drives restore SPEED and hardware readiness.

scenarios.situation:
The 3-2-1 rule — 3 copies, 2 different media, 1 offsite — exists because disks, buildings, and regions fail independently: one disaster should never take all copies. Backup chains (full + differential + incremental) trade backup speed for restore complexity. The reasoning: incrementals are fast to take (only today's changes) but restore slowest (every link must apply in order — one corrupt link breaks everything after it), while differentials cost more backup time but restore in two steps. This scenario designs the chain and the offsite copy for a real workload...

A workstation department backup policy says: weekly full backups on Sunday, differential backups Monday–Saturday. After a cryptolocker hits on Friday afternoon, the restore team argues about which media is needed. Separately, the auditor asks whether the offsite tape copy satisfies the 3-2-1 rule.
scenarios.title: Full, Incremental, Differential — and the 3-2-1 Rule
scenarios.why: Differential backups capture ALL changes since the last full, so Friday's differential plus Sunday's full is a complete two-media restore (this is the differential advantage over incremental, which would need Sun + Mon + Tue + Wed + Thu + Fri chained). The 3-2-1 rule demands 3 total copies, on 2 different media types, with 1 offsite. Here there are only 2 copies (NAS + tape), so a third copy — e.g., immutable cloud storage — is required for full compliance.

scenarios.situation:
An untested backup is a rumor, not a recovery plan — restores fail for boring reasons: corrupt media, missing encryption keys, a chain with a gap nobody noticed, a backup job that's been 'succeeding' while writing empty files. The reasoning: a backup is a CLAIM about the future ('we can recover'), and untested claims in engineering are called hope — the test restore is the experiment that converts hope into evidence. This scenario makes the case for scheduled test restores (to an isolated environment, never overwriting production) and shows what a restore test actually verifies...

The new hire proudly reports: 'Backups have been green for 18 months — Windows Server Backup runs every night and completes with status Success.' The senior admin asks three follow-up questions: 'Have we ever restored from them? Where are the bare-metal recovery media? Is there a written runbook?' The answers are: no, nowhere, and no.
scenarios.title: A Backup You Haven't Tested Is Not a Backup
scenarios.why: A backup's only job is to be restorable, and only a test restore proves that: corrupted VSS writers, missing bare-metal recovery media, wrong drivers, or encrypted-but-unreadable sets all hide behind 'Success' logs. The corrective action is a scheduled restore test (into an isolated environment so you don't clobber production), timed against your RTO, with the steps written into a DR runbook covering failover AND failback.

DNS (Domain Name System) and DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) failures look identical to users ('nothing works') but need completely different fixes — which is why you test them separately. This scenario runs the split diagnosis — Resolve-DnsName for names, DHCP scope and lease statistics for addresses — from the terminal...

A newly deployed app server (SRV-APP02, 10.20.5.44) can't be reached by hostname. nslookup fails, but Test-NetConnection 10.20.5.44 -Port 443 succeeds — so the box is up, DNS is the problem. You also suspect a DHCP scope is nearly exhausted because clients keep getting APIPA addresses.

Remoting — running commands on other computers via WinRM (Windows Remote Management) — turns one terminal into a fleet: Invoke-Command with a -ComputerName list runs your script block on every target and returns the results. The reasoning: logging into 50 servers one by one to check disk space is a week of work; fan-out remoting makes it one command, because the network carries the command instead of your feet. This scenario loops an inventory (OS version, free disk, uptime) across servers — and handles the real-world friction: unreachable hosts, credential prompts, and WinRM not enabled...

The asset audit needs OS version, last boot time, and free space on C: for 20 servers. RDP-ing into each is a non-starter. WinRM is enabled domain-wide. You want one script that fans out, collects the data, and writes a single CSV — and you want to know the difference between the two remoting approaches.
scenarios.title: Inventory 20 Servers Without Leaving Your Desk
scenarios.why: Invoke-Command -ComputerName fans out to MANY machines in parallel and returns unified objects — the right tool for fleet data collection. Enter-PSSession is interactive and 1:1: perfect for troubleshooting a single sick box, useless for 20. Inside the script block, $env:COMPUTERNAME identifies the source machine, Get-CimInstance reads OS facts, and Get-PSDrive C reads disk. Build a [pscustomobject] so Export-Csv gets clean columns. scenarios.situation:
PowerShell's execution policy is the safety switch deciding which .ps1 script files Windows will run — Restricted (nothing runs) is the default on clients, RemoteSigned (local scripts OK, downloads must be signed) the common server setting. The reasoning for the wall: it stops ACCIDENTAL and drive-by script execution (double-clicked malware, pasted scripts), not determined attackers — it's a seatbelt, not a vault door, which is why admins can legitimately change it. This scenario writes the first real script, hits the policy wall, and sets the policy correctly — understanding WHY the wall exists...

You wrote C:\Scripts\New-HireSetup.ps1: it creates the AD user, adds them to groups, and creates their home folder. Double-clicking runs it in Notepad. Running it in PowerShell throws: 'cannot be loaded because running scripts is disabled on this system.' The script came from your own keyboard, on a domain workstation.
scenarios.title: Your First .ps1 Won't Run — Execution Policy
scenarios.why: Restricted blocks ALL scripts — the default on Windows clients. RemoteSigned allows locally-authored scripts while requiring downloaded ones to be signed: the right least-privilege setting, scoped to CurrentUser so you don't change machine policy. Run .ps1 files with .\script.ps1 (PowerShell won't run scripts from the current directory by bare name — a security feature). Bypass/Unrestricted as a habit defeats the malware guardrail; interviewers want to hear you treat execution policy as a safety rail, not an annoyance.

scenarios.title: Think Aloud: 'Automate This' — Sweep 40 Servers for Stopped Automatic Services
scenarios.situation: The ops manager drops a recurring task on you: every Monday, someone RDPs into 40 servers and eyeballs the Services console for anything set to Automatic that is not Running. 'Automate this,' she says, 'and make it email-ready.' You have WinRM and domain admin.
scenarios.prompt: Narrate your thinking aloud as you work: what do you check first and why? Then: sketch the approach (discovery → query → filter → report) before writing a single line — what cmdlets, in what order, and why not RDP or a -ComputerName loop?
evidence: 40 Windows Servers (2019/2022), all domain-joined, WinRM enabled, PSRemoting tested from the admin jump box.
RDP → services.msc → sort by Startup Type → eyeball Automatic/Stopped → screenshot → email. ~3 hours, every Monday, errors included.
Must run unattended from the jump box, produce a CSV the manager can open, and finish in minutes not hours.

Loop Get-Service -ComputerName $server over all 40 names sequentially — simple, readable, uses a familiar parameter.

Fan out with remoting: $servers = Get-ADComputer -Filter "OperatingSystem -like '*Server*'" -Properties OperatingSystem | Select-Object -ExpandProperty Name; Invoke-Command -ComputerName $servers { Get-Service | Where-Object { $_.StartType -eq 'Automatic' -and $_.Status -ne 'Running' -and $_.Name -notin @('sppsvc') } } | Select-Object PSComputerName, Name, DisplayName, Status | Export-Csv C:\Reports\svc-sweep.csv -NoTypeInformation
Install an agent on all 40 servers that reports service state to a central dashboard — the enterprise solution.
scenarios.why: Narrate first: (1) DISCOVERY — get the server list from AD (Get-ADComputer), not from a stale spreadsheet; (2) QUERY — one Invoke-Command fans out to all 40 in parallel instead of 40 sequential RPC calls; (3) FILTER — StartType Automatic AND Status not Running, computed ON the remote end so only the hits cross the wire; (4) REPORT — PSComputerName tags each row, Export-Csv makes it manager-ready. Get-Service -ComputerName is legacy DCOM/RPC, sequential, and firewall-hostile; RDP-to-each is the 3-hour problem you were asked to kill; and deploying an agent fleet for a Monday report is a six-month project answering a one-line script. The -notin exclusion list is the professional touch: some Automatic services (like sppsvc) are SUPPOSED to be stopped, and your report should not cry wolf. Logic Check: automate the boring, report the interesting — and compute the filter where the data lives, so the network carries answers, not raw data.

scenarios.situation:
SMBv1 is the 1980s-era file-sharing protocol that WannaCry rode around the world — its flaws are in the design, not the code, so there is no patch, only removal. The reasoning it lingers: old printers, scanners, and legacy apps still speak SMBv1, so admins fear breaking them — which is why this scenario pairs removal with an AUDIT: prove what still needs it before you kill it, then verify it's actually gone, because 'we turned it off' without verification is how it survives for years...

A Nessus scan flagged SMBv1 as enabled on your file servers — a known vector for wormable ransomware. You push a GPO and hardening script to disable it across the domain. A week later, one legacy print appliance stops talking to a share.
scenarios.title: Disable SMBv1 and verify it stays off
scenarios.why: SMBv1 is deprecated and the EternalBlue-class attack surface; both server and client driver should be disabled via the MS Security Guide GPO baseline and verified per host. A legacy device needing SMBv1 gets a contained exception (isolated VLAN, host firewall, migration plan), never a rollback of the baseline — one exception host re-enabling SMBv1 domain-wide would re-expose everything.

objectives: Lateral movement prevention via unique credentials
scenarios.prompt: Which implementation is correct and most complete?
scenarios.situation:
LAPS (Local Administrator Password Solution) gives every computer its own unique, random, auto-rotating local admin password stored in Active Directory — so one compromised password no longer unlocks every machine in the building. The reasoning: the classic attack is pass-the-hash — steal ONE local admin hash, and because every PC shares the same local password, you own the fleet — unique passwords per machine break that skeleton key into 500 useless individual keys. This scenario deploys it and shows the retrieval workflow: authorized admin, AD lookup, audited access...

Every workstation image in your domain was built with the same local Administrator password — your helpdesk admits they use it 'all the time' for remote fixes. You decide to deploy LAPS (Windows Local Administrator Password Solution) so each machine gets a unique, rotated password stored in Active Directory.
scenarios.title: Roll out LAPS for local administrator accounts
scenarios.why: LAPS makes each machine's local admin password unique and rotates it on a schedule, with the password stored in the computer object's ms-Mcs-AdmPwd attribute. The correct rollout: schema extension, SELF write permissions on the computer objects, READ restricted to an authorized group (with an extended-rights read if needed), and the GPO client-side extension managing rotation. Renaming the account or sharing one strong password doesn't fix lateral movement — one compromised host's hash would still open every other machine.

choices: Enable Credential Guard (VBS, requires UEFI/Secure Boot/TPM) on supported hosts, eliminate reversible encryption for the legacy app or isolate it, enforce LAPS + gMSA so stolen hashes are useless, and require tiered admin model so no Domain Admin credentials touch member servers
Give every server a complex 30-character local admin password and rely on EDR alone — if EDR blocks Mimikatz, credentials are safe
Disable LSASS entirely on file servers since they don't need authentication
Move all admin work to RDP with saved credentials — RDP encrypts everything so hashes can't be stolen

Turn On Virtualization Based Security: Enabled, Secure Boot + Credential Guard with UEFI lock
scenarios.hint: EDR is detection, not architecture. Which layers make the credential itself worthless even if the attacker lands on the box?
objectives: Defense in depth against credential theft
scenarios.prompt: Which combination best reduces credential-theft risk in this environment?
scenarios.situation:
Windows once kept passwords (or their hashes) in memory where tools like Mimikatz could steal them out of the LSASS process — Credential Guard fixes this with virtualization-based isolation (the secrets live in a memory region even the OS kernel can't read). The reasoning: you can't patch human memory out of the equation (passwords must live in RAM to be used), so instead you move them somewhere theft tools can't reach — a smaller, isolated virtual machine whose only job is guarding secrets. This scenario explains the attack, the defense, and how to verify it's actually enabled — because Group Policy saying 'on' isn't proof...

Your EDR flagged a Mimikatz-style LSASS access attempt on a file server. Passwords in this domain are still reversibly synced for one legacy app, and some servers run without virtualization-based security. Leadership wants a plan, not panic.
scenarios.title: Credential theft defense: Credential Guard vs LSASS dumping
scenarios.why: Credential Guard isolates secrets in a VBS-protected enclave so LSASS memory no longer holds usable plaintext/hashes for pass-the-hash or Mimikatz-style extraction. But it's one layer: reversible encryption must go (it defeats the purpose), unique per-machine credentials (LAPS) and gMSA limit what a stolen credential can do, and the tiered admin model keeps high-value Domain Admin credentials off workstations and member servers entirely. RDP with saved credentials actually caches credentials and worsens the exposure.

choices: Wait for the normal Ring 2 day-14 deployment since the rings were already agreed with management

Compress the rings for this CVE: push to Ring 0 within 24h, validate the spooler-dependent app in the lab in parallel, Ring 1 at 48-72h, full fleet inside the 21-day KEV deadline; keep the normal rings for non-KEV updates

scenarios.hint: KEV changes the math on how long you can wait, but does active exploitation remove the need to verify the critical app still works?
scenarios.prompt: What is the right patch response?
scenarios.situation:
Patch rings are the rollout order: Ring 0 (test lab) → Ring 1 (IT staff canaries) → Ring 2 (general population) → Ring 3 (critical servers last) — so a bad patch breaks the lab, not payroll. Out-of-band patches are the emergency exceptions (active exploit in the wild — you don't wait for Patch Tuesday). The reasoning: every patch is a gamble (it fixes a vulnerability but might break a workload), and rings convert one big gamble into four small ones — but a KEV-listed (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) active exploit flips the math, because the attack is certain and the patch risk is only possible. This scenario runs both: the ring schedule and the 2 AM emergency patch...

It's the second Tuesday. Microsoft released a critical RCE in the print spooler with active exploitation, and CISA added it to the KEV catalog with a 21-day deadline. Your WSUS rings are: Ring 0 (IT pilot, day 2), Ring 1 (10% of servers, day 7), Ring 2 (rest, day 14). A business-critical app broke on last month's cumulative.
scenarios.title: Patch rings and an emergency out-of-band update
scenarios.why: Patch testing rings exist to catch app-breaking updates without leaving the fleet exposed — but actively exploited KEV vulnerabilities compress the timeline. Accelerated rings keep the pilot-lab validation (so the spooler-dependent app gets checked) while beating the KEV deadline. Skipping testing risks an outage; waiting for day 14 violates the federal exploitation deadline and common-sense exposure window. The WSUS-vs-WUfB tooling debate is separate from the ring strategy.

choices: Inventory each DA member, remove former employees' accounts and standing vendor access immediately, move the backup service account to a dedicated group with only backup rights, deploy a PAM/JIT workflow for time-bound elevation, and keep a monitored break-glass DA account sealed in a safe
Demote everyone and give all admins local admin on every server instead — that's basically the same thing
Keep the 47 members but require them all to use smart cards — membership count doesn't matter if auth is strong
Rename Domain Admins to something obscure so attackers can't find it, then leave the membership alone
evidence:
Request: DA-2026-1010-041 | Justification: DC promo rebuild
Start: 2026-10-10 14:00 | End: 2026-10-10 18:00 | Approved by: CISO
scenarios.hint: Count the real risk: every standing member is a 24/7 target. What replaces standing access for the people who genuinely need it sometimes?
scenarios.prompt: Which remediation plan is correct?
scenarios.situation:
Domain Admins is the keys-to-the-kingdom group — and in most companies it's full of people who needed it once, three years ago. The reasoning for the purge: every extra member multiplies the attack surface — an attacker who compromises ANY member's account owns the entire domain — while almost nobody needs domain-wide power for daily work (that's what separate, dedicated admin accounts are for). This scenario audits the group, identifies who actually needs it, and removes the sprawl without breaking anyone's real work...

An audit finds 47 members of Domain Admins — including two vendors, five former employees whose accounts are still enabled, and a backup service account. You need least privilege plus a JIT elevation workflow without breaking the nightly backup.
scenarios.title: Remove Domain Admins sprawl with just-in-time access
scenarios.why: Least privilege means Domain Admins holds almost nobody, standing. Former-employee accounts and vendor standing access are removed outright; service accounts get their own least-privilege groups (backups need backup rights, not domain keys). JIT/PAM replaces standing membership with time-bound, approved, logged elevation. The break-glass account is the exception — sealed, monitored, tested — for when PAM itself is down. Renaming the group or spreading local admin everywhere are theater; membership count is the actual attack surface.

choices: Disable the Domain profile firewall on that server — the developer needs to work and the perimeter firewall covers us
Add an Allow rule for 0.0.0.0/0 on the app's port — simplest fix, one rule
Delete the baseline block rule since the vendor installer clearly knows what the app needs

Explain that Block rules take precedence over Allow rules, scope the vendor allow rule to the app's exact executable/ports and authorized source subnets, keep the baseline block, and turn on firewall auditing so future blocks are logged — never disable the profile
evidence:
PS C:\> Get-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName '*VendorApp*' | ft DisplayName,Direction,Action,Profile

DisplayName        Direction Action Profile
VendorApp-In       Inbound   Allow  Any
Baseline-BlockApp  Inbound   Block  Domain

Event 5152: The Windows Filtering Platform has blocked a packet.
Application: C:\Vendor\app.exe | Direction: Inbound
scenarios.hint: Two rules conflict — one says allow, one says block. Which one wins in Windows Firewall, and what does that tell you about the fix?
scenarios.prompt: How do you diagnose and fix this correctly?
scenarios.situation:
Windows Firewall rules have a precedence order — like firewall ACLs (Access Control Lists), the first matching rule wins, with explicit BLOCK rules beating ALLOWs. Over years, rules accumulate: stale allows for dead apps, duplicate blocks, 'temporary' test rules from 2021. The reasoning for the audit: every unexplained ALLOW is a hole someone punched and forgot, and rule shadows (a broad rule above a specific one) mean the firewall isn't doing what anyone thinks — this scenario finds the shadows, the overly-broad allows, and the rules nobody can explain...

A developer says 'the firewall is blocking my app' on a member server and asks you to just disable the firewall profile. There's an allow rule for the app from the vendor's installer, but also a block rule from your baseline GPO. You need to resolve it without weakening the baseline.
scenarios.title: Windows Defender Firewall rule precedence and audit
scenarios.why: In Windows Defender Firewall, an explicit Block always beats Allow regardless of rule order — that's why the vendor's allow rule does nothing while the baseline block exists. The right fix is surgical: keep the baseline, narrow the allow rule to the app's real executable, ports, and source subnets (scoped, not 0.0.0.0/0). Disabling the profile removes host-level defense in depth that the perimeter firewall cannot replace, and deleting baseline rules weakens every server at once.

scenarios.title: The Firewall Log Shows the App's Packets Being Dropped
scenarios.situation: The new inventory app cannot reach the database on TCP 1433 from the app subnet. The firewall team shows you the allow rule — it exists, it is enabled, and it was 'working in testing'. The app team wants the host firewall disabled 'temporarily'.
scenarios.prompt: The pfirewall.log has a DROP line for the exact traffic. The rule exists. What single misconfiguration explains both facts?
evidence:
PS C:\> Get-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'Allow App DB' | Select-Object Enabled, Profile, Action
Enabled Profile Action
------- ------- ------
True    Private Allow
Connection profile on the DB server

PS C:\> Get-NetConnectionProfile | Select-Object Name, NetworkCategory
Name        NetworkCategory
----        ---------------
CORP-NET    Public   <-- NLA misclassified after Sunday's reboot
choices: Disable the Windows Firewall on the DB server temporarily so the app team can work while you investigate.
Widen the rule: change RemoteAddress to Any and add TCP 1433 to all profiles — the app needs to work now.

Fix the profile mismatch: the NIC is classified Public but the rule is scoped to Private. Either correct the NLA classification (Set-NetConnectionProfile -NetworkCategory Private) or scope the rule to the Public profile. The DROP line plus a correct-but-inactive-profile rule is the classic signature.
The app server's IP changed — update the rule's RemoteAddress to the new IP.
scenarios.why: The log is the witness: DROP on TCP 1433 from the app server means the packet arrived and a rule decision killed it. The allow rule is real and enabled — but scoped to the Private profile, while NLA classified the NIC as Public after the reboot (gateway unreachable at boot is the usual trigger). A rule on the wrong profile is a rule that does not exist for this traffic. Disabling the firewall 'temporarily' trades a 2-minute fix for an unprotected database server, and widening to Any/Any converts a misconfiguration into an exposure. Fix the classification (or the rule's profile scope), then re-test — and add 'verify NetworkCategory after every reboot' to the runbook, because NLA will do this again. Logic Check: when the log shows DROP and the rule shows ALLOW, stop reading the rule's ACTION and start reading its SCOPE — the rule is right, its audience is wrong.
scenarios.hint: The rule says Private. The NIC says Public. Which one does the firewall believe?

choices: Just the commands you ran, pasted from your terminal history — that's all anyone needs

What the procedure fixes and why, numbered steps in exact order with the commands, how to verify success (sync completes in console), the rollback (restore renamed folder / re-sync from upstream), and the date it was last validated
A paragraph describing the incident in prose — the on-call engineer can figure out the steps
A link to the Microsoft docs page for WSUS — the docs are maintained by Microsoft anyway
evidence:
# SOP-2026-041: WSUS sync failure recovery
## What / Why: ...
## Steps: 1...
## Verification: ...
## Rollback: ...
## Last validated: 2026-10-10
scenarios.hint: Imagine it's 2 AM and the on-call person has never seen this failure. What five things would keep them from waking you up?
scenarios.prompt: What must the SOP capture to be useful next month?
scenarios.situation:
An SOP (Standard Operating Procedure) is the written recipe for a repeatable task — and the best ones get written right after the task just bit someone, while the pain is fresh. The reasoning: tribal knowledge ('ask Dave, he knows') fails the day Dave is on vacation, and it fails YOU at 3 AM when you can't remember the exact flag — writing it down converts one person's memory into the team's capability. This scenario writes one from a real incident: the password-reset SOP that stops the next Monday-morning chaos — numbered steps, exact commands, expected outputs, zero tribal knowledge...

It's 6 PM on a Friday. You just fixed a failed WSUS sync that was blocking patch Tuesday, and the on-call engineer will face the same failure next month. You have 20 minutes before you leave. The fix involved: stopping services in order, renaming the SoftwareDistribution folder, re-running wsusutil reset, and verifying sync in the console.
scenarios.title: Write an SOP under time pressure
scenarios.why: A usable SOP under pressure needs five things: what/why (so the reader knows it's the right doc), steps in order (sequence matters — services must stop before the folder rename), verification (how you know it worked, not just that you ran commands), rollback (what to do if a step fails), and a validated date (so stale docs get caught). Terminal history alone lacks verification and rollback; prose buries the steps; an external link rots and doesn't capture your environment's specifics.

choices: A spreadsheet of IP addresses — diagrams are outdated the moment they're drawn, so a list is more honest
One high-level diagram with vendor logos and cloud shapes — executives like it and the NOC can ask questions if needed
Label only the firewalls and ISPs; the switches are 'standard config' and don't need documenting

Two diagrams: physical (device names, models, switch port numbers, uplink paths, cable IDs) and logical (VLAN IDs/names, subnets in CIDR, gateway IPs, firewall HA roles); every device labeled with hostname and management IP; legend, date, and owner on each revision
evidence:
L1 physical: device names, models, port numbers, uplinks, cable IDs
L2/L3 logical: VLAN IDs + names, subnets/CIDR, gateway IPs, SVI assignments
Legend + date + owner on every revision
scenarios.hint: At 3 AM the NOC needs to answer two questions fast: what's connected to what, and what IP do I type. What must be on the page for that?
scenarios.prompt: Which diagram standard makes this actually useful in an incident?
scenarios.situation:
A network diagram is useless if nobody can read it: standards — consistent icons (the same shape always means 'switch'), links labeled with port numbers and VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) IDs, a legend, and a 'last updated' date — are what make it a tool instead of wall art. The reasoning: a diagram is a shared mental model, and every inconsistency forces the reader to guess — during an outage, guessing wastes the minutes you don't have, and an outdated diagram is worse than none because it sends troubleshooters hunting ghosts. This scenario grades a diagram against the standard and fixes what's missing...

A new branch office goes live Monday. You must hand the NOC a network diagram they can actually troubleshoot from at 3 AM: two ISP uplinks, a firewall pair in HA, core and access switches, three VLANs (data, voice, guest), and the server subnet. The last diagram someone made was a Visio of unlabeled boxes.
scenarios.title: Network diagram must-haves for an incident
scenarios.why: A 3-AM-troubleshootable diagram separates physical (what's plugged into what, port numbers, cable IDs) from logical (VLANs, subnets, gateways) because incidents start at one layer and cross to the other. Hostnames plus management IPs let the NOC actually log in; HA roles matter because 'which firewall is active' decides the failover procedure. A date and owner make staleness visible instead of silent. Pretty vendor-logo diagrams and IP spreadsheets both fail the 'trace the path in 60 seconds' test.

choices: Before state (current 2016 scope config), after state (2022 failover pair, lease changes), step-by-step execution with verification after each step, a backout plan with the exact reversal steps and the 1 AM go/no-go decision point, risk assessment, and a test plan
Before/after only — backout plans are implied by having backups
A verbal walkthrough at the CAB meeting instead of written documentation — faster and everyone hears it
Just the after state and the window — the CAB trusts senior engineers to handle the details
evidence:
CR-2026-118: DHCP migration to 2022 failover pair
Before: single 2016 scope, 192.168.10.0/24, 4h lease
After: 2022 hot-standby pair, same scope, 8h lease
Backout: re-authorize 2016, deactivate pair, rollback deadline 01:00
scenarios.hint: The CAB's job is to approve risk they understand. What would you need to see, as an approver, to sign off on someone else's Saturday-night migration?
scenarios.prompt: What does the revised change record need to get approved?
scenarios.situation:
Every change gets a record: what, why, when, who — and the backout plan (exact steps to UNDO it if things go wrong). The reasoning: 'we'll figure out the rollback if we need it' is how 10-minute changes become 6-hour outages — under pressure, nobody remembers the previous value of the setting they just overwrote, so you write the undo steps BEFORE you need them, while you're calm. This scenario writes the change record for a firewall rule change, backout plan included, before the change happens...

You're scheduled to migrate the DHCP scopes from the old Windows Server 2016 box to the new 2022 DHCP failover pair this Saturday. The change advisory board rejected your first request: 'insufficient backout detail.' The maintenance window is 10 PM – 2 AM with a hard rollback deadline of 1 AM.
scenarios.title: Change documentation: before/after and backout plan
scenarios.why: A change record exists so someone other than you can judge risk and execute the backout at 1 AM. Before/after states define the delta; ordered steps with verification catch partial failures; the backout plan must be explicit (re-authorize the old server, deactivate the pair) with a decision deadline, because 'restore from backup' is not a plan at 12:45 AM with 15 minutes left. Risk and test plans let the CAB approve with eyes open. Verbal-only changes leave no record for the post-incident review.

choices: A dump of every ticket you worked this month — the on-call person can search for what's relevant

Dates of coverage, known issues with their workarounds AND what not to do (don't reboot Backup Server 2), time-critical jobs with deadlines, escalation contacts with contract numbers, things to leave alone, and where the runbooks live
Your cell number and 'call me if anything breaks' — fastest handover, zero writing
Only the critical alerts — known issues aren't alerts so they don't need documenting
evidence:
## Covering: 10/11 - 10/18 | Owner: on-call rotation
## Known issues: Tape drive 2 flaky (30% fail) -> retry job, do NOT reboot
## Must-complete: Veeam copy job before 06:00 daily
## Escalation: SAN vendor 1-800-XXX, contract #XXXXX
## Do not touch: ...
scenarios.hint: The covering engineer is smart but has zero context on your systems. What would you want handed to you on your first day covering someone else's backup infra?
scenarios.prompt: What makes handover notes effective here?
scenarios.situation:
