Handover notes are what the next on-call human needs to survive the night: what's currently broken or degraded, what changed today, what's scheduled overnight, and where the runbooks live. The reasoning: the night shift inherits your context gap — without notes they start every investigation from zero, and the 3 AM page goes to YOU instead — good handover is buying your own sleep. This scenario writes the handover after a messy day — complete enough that the night shift never has to call you, honest enough to flag what you DON'T know...

You're going on PTO for a week. The on-call engineer covering you has never touched the backup infrastructure. There's a known flaky tape drive on Backup Server 2 (job fails ~30% of the time, workaround is a retry), a Veeam backup copy job that must finish before 6 AM, and the vendor support contract number for the SAN.
scenarios.title: Handover notes for the on-call engineer
scenarios.why: Good handover notes assume the reader is competent but context-free: coverage dates set the boundary, known issues with workarounds prevent rediscovery, 'do not touch' items prevent well-meaning damage (rebooting the flaky backup server mid-job), time-critical jobs set priorities, and escalation contacts with contract numbers remove the 2 AM scramble. A ticket dump buries signal; 'call me on PTO' defeats the purpose of PTO; and known issues are exactly what bites the covering engineer.

choices: 10.10.0.0/16 carved into /24 blocks aligned to the third octet: VLAN 10 users 10.10.10.0/24, VLAN 20 servers 10.10.20.0/24, VLAN 30 management 10.10.30.0/24, VPN pool 10.10.100.0/24. Each block has 254 usable hosts; the third octet names the function.

10.10.0.0/16 carved into /25 blocks per function: users 10.10.10.0/25 (126 usable hosts), servers 10.10.10.128/25 (126 usable), management 10.10.11.0/25, VPN 10.10.11.128/25. Tight blocks waste no space.
Publicly routable 203.0.113.0/24 split across the VLANs — every host gets a real public IP, which removes all NAT complexity for remote access.
One flat 192.168.1.0/24 for everything — users, servers, printers, guests. 254 addresses covers 60 devices with room to spare, and a flat network is the simplest to manage.
evidence: 50 user PCs, 12 printers/phones, 10 servers today. Growth projection: ~100 users and ~20 servers within 3 years. Remote VPN users expected.
Many employees work from home on 192.168.1.0/24 home routers — the office plan must not overlap, or VPN routing breaks.
scenarios.hint: Count the usable hosts per block (2^host-bits minus 2), then ask which plan still fits after headcount doubles — twice.
scenarios.prompt: Which addressing plan do you adopt for Contoso Labs, and why does it survive the growth projection?
scenarios.situation: Contoso Labs is a fictional 50-person company: 50 users (each with a PC, plus printers and phones), 10 servers today, and the founders expect headcount to roughly double within 3 years. You are handed a blank sheet and asked for the IP addressing scheme the whole build will stand on. The wrong choice here means renumbering the entire company later — a weekend-destroying mistake.
scenarios.title: Designing the Address Plan for Contoso Labs
scenarios.why: A /24 gives 2^8 - 2 = 254 usable hosts. Fifty users sit at ~20% utilization; doubling twice (50 → 100 → 200) still fits inside one /24, so the plan survives the 3-year projection with zero renumbering. Aligning function to the third octet (10 = users, 20 = servers, 30 = management) makes firewall rules and troubleshooting human-readable at a glance, and the whole 10.10.0.0/16 supernet summarizes to one route for VPN and routing tables. 10.x.x.x also never collides with employees' 192.168.1.0/24 home routers. The flat /24 has no segmentation — one broadcast domain, no security boundary, and guests share a subnet with servers. The /25 plan fits today but breaks at ~126 users per function and its split boundaries are ugly to administer. Public IPs on the LAN burn scarce address space and expose every host directly. Logic Check: if the plan cannot absorb the stated growth without renumbering, it is not a plan — it is a future outage with a date on it.

choices: Access ports to every endpoint (switchport mode access, one VLAN per port); a single 802.1Q trunk to the router/firewall carrying VLANs 10/20/30 with SVIs as gateways; firewall rules at the inter-VLAN boundary — allow users to servers only on required ports (445, 443, DNS, DHCP), deny all server-to-user initiation, management VLAN reachable only from the admin jump box.
One VLAN for everything with the firewall only between the LAN and the internet — internal traffic is trusted, and segmentation adds complexity with no benefit at 50 users.
Trunk every port including user PCs, so any device can reach any VLAN without reconfiguring the switch — maximum flexibility and no per-port mistakes.
Keep the switch as a pure forwarder and enforce all policy on each PC's host firewall — defense happens at the endpoint, so the network stays simple.
evidence: One 48-port managed switch. Uplinks: 1x to the router/firewall. Endpoints: PCs, printers, 2 physical servers (Hyper-V hosts), APs.
Users need SMB (445) and HTTPS (443) to servers, DNS/DHCP everywhere. Servers must never initiate connections to user PCs. Management VLAN: admin jump box only.
scenarios.hint: Trace one packet from a user PC to a server: where does it cross a policy boundary? That choke point is where the rule must live.
objectives: VLAN design and trunk vs access
scenarios.prompt: Which ports become trunks vs access, where do the firewall rules live, and what does the rule set look like?
scenarios.situation: The address plan is approved. Now the switching and firewall design: three VLANs (10 users, 20 servers, 30 management), one router/firewall doing inter-VLAN routing, and 48 access ports to wire up. A junior tech proposes trunking every port 'for flexibility' and putting the firewall rules on each PC's host firewall instead.
scenarios.title: VLANs, Trunks, and Firewall Rules for Contoso Labs
scenarios.why: Access ports carry one untagged VLAN to endpoints — simple, and it blocks VLAN-hopping tricks that trunked endpoint ports invite. The single trunk to the router/firewall carries all three VLANs tagged (802.1Q), and its SVIs are the gateways — so every inter-VLAN packet physically crosses the firewall, which is exactly where policy belongs. Rules follow least privilege: users reach servers only on ports the business needs (445/443/DNS/DHCP), and the deny on server-to-user initiation kills the lateral-movement path malware uses after landing on a server. The management VLAN isolated to the jump box means stolen user credentials cannot reach switch/router admin interfaces. Trunking endpoints, endpoint-only firewalls, and flat trusted LANs all surrender the one choke point you actually control. Logic Check: if a compromised PC can reach a server on a port the business never uses, your segmentation is decoration — every allowed port must map to a stated requirement.

choices: Skip on-prem AD entirely — 50 users can share local accounts in a workgroup, so there is no DC to patch, protect, or pay for.
A separate OU and domain controller per department (HR-DC, Finance-DC, Engineering-DC) so each team is fully independent and an outage only hits one team.
One domain controller is enough for 50 users — simpler and cheaper. Put everyone in the default Users container and link GPOs at the domain root.

Two domain controllers (one per Hyper-V host), forest root corp.contoso.com, OU tree Contoso/Users, Contoso/Workstations, Contoso/Servers with accidental-deletion protection, GPOs linked at the Contoso OU, DNS forwarders to 1.1.1.1 and 8.8.8.8, DHCP scopes per VLAN with exclusions for static infrastructure.
evidence: Two physical Hyper-V hosts available. 50 users, one office, no branch sites. Line-of-business app authenticates against AD.
Authentication must survive any single server failure — Monday morning logons cannot depend on one box. Helpdesk needs password-reset rights without Domain Admin.
scenarios.hint: Count the single points of failure, then picture Monday 8 AM with that one box dead. Also: GPOs cannot link to the default Users/Computers containers.
scenarios.prompt: How many DCs, what OU structure, and which supporting services — and why?
scenarios.situation: Network is up. Now identity: Contoso Labs needs Active Directory for 50 users in one office. Decisions on the table: how many domain controllers, the forest/domain name, the OU tree, DNS forwarding, and DHCP per VLAN. The founder asks 'can't we just do one server and skip the complexity?'
scenarios.title: Domain Controllers and OU Design for Contoso Labs
scenarios.why: Two DCs on separate hosts means authentication, DNS, and DHCP survive any single hardware failure — and you can patch one DC while the other serves logons. The OU tree exists for two reasons: delegation (helpdesk gets password-reset rights on Contoso/Users only, not Domain Admin) and GPO targeting (policies link to OUs, never to the default containers, which reject GPO links). Accidental-deletion protection guards the tree itself. DNS forwarders let the DCs resolve corp.contoso.com authoritatively while forwarding internet queries upstream — and clients must use ONLY the DCs for DNS, or AD name resolution breaks. DHCP per VLAN with exclusions keeps static infrastructure (.1–.49) out of the dynamic pool. One DC is a company-wide outage waiting for a patch Tuesday; per-department DCs multiply cost and complexity for zero benefit at one site; a workgroup gives up central authentication, auditing, and policy — the LOB app and any compliance need die there. Logic Check: every design element must answer 'what breaks if this box dies?' — if the answer is 'the company stops logging in,' you need two of it.

choices: External virtual switch bound to the physical NIC with AllowManagementOS enabled (VMs get real LAN IPs, host stays manageable); Private switch reserved for the future isolated malware VM; DC and file server as separate VMs; production checkpoints allowed sparingly (VSS-aware) — never as backups, which go to separate storage.
External switch with AllowManagementOS disabled and no host management IP — if the host has no address on the network, attackers cannot reach it.
One VM running everything (DC + file services + SQL on a single guest) — fewer VMs to patch, and a checkpoint before every change replaces backups.
Private switch for all production VMs — complete isolation from the physical network is the most secure option available.
evidence: 2x Hyper-V hosts, 1 physical NIC each (for now). VMs need LAN IPs and internet. A malware-analysis VM is planned for next quarter — fully isolated.
Founder asks: 'checkpoints are free — why pay for backup software?'
scenarios.hint: A checkpoint is a differencing disk on the same storage as the VM. Ask what happens to the whole chain when that storage dies.
scenarios.prompt: Which virtual switch types, which VM layout, and what is the checkpoint policy?
scenarios.situation: The two physical hosts need Hyper-V. Planned VMs: CL-DC01 (domain controller) and CL-FS01 (file server) on host 1; CL-DC02 and an app server on host 2. One physical NIC per host for now. The junior admin asks which virtual switch type each VM gets, and whether nightly checkpoints can replace the backup software to save money.
scenarios.title: Hyper-V Design: Switches, VMs, and Checkpoint Policy
scenarios.why: An External switch bridges VMs onto the physical LAN — that is the only switch type that gives production servers real IPs clients can reach. AllowManagementOS keeps a virtual NIC on the host so you can still manage it (a host you cannot reach is a host you cannot patch). The Private switch carries VM-to-VM traffic only — perfect for the future malware lab, useless for servers that clients must reach. Separate VMs per role isolate failure domains and let you patch/reboot the file server without taking down authentication. Checkpoints are differencing-disk chains (AVHDX) on the SAME storage as the VM: they cost merge I/O, grow silently, and die with the disk they sit on — they are change-undo buttons, not backups. Backups must land on separate storage. The unmanageable host and the all-in-one VM both trade away the thing virtualization is for: isolation. Logic Check: ask of every protection mechanism 'does it survive the failure it protects against?' — a checkpoint on the same disk as the VM does not survive disk failure, so it is not a backup.

choices: Transaction log backups every 15 minutes with no FULL backups — the logs record every change, so a full backup is redundant.
SIMPLE recovery model with a FULL backup every night — one file to manage, one file to restore, simplest possible operation.
FULL backup every Sunday night only — backups consume storage and time, and the SAN already takes snapshots.

FULL recovery model; nightly FULL backup, DIFFERENTIAL every 6 hours, transaction LOG backup every 15 minutes — all to separate storage; monthly restore test. Worst-case loss is 15 minutes of logs (inside the 1-hour RPO); the short chain restores well inside the 4-hour RTO.
evidence: RPO 1 hour (max acceptable data loss), RTO 4 hours (max acceptable downtime). Database ~40 GB, grows ~2 GB/month. Orders table is append-heavy all day.
Database in SIMPLE recovery model, one FULL backup nightly to the same disk as the data files. Never restore-tested.
scenarios.hint: Translate RPO into 'how often must a backup run' and RTO into 'how many files must I restore, and how long does each take?'
scenarios.prompt: Which backup strategy meets the stated RPO and RTO?
scenarios.situation: Contoso Labs runs its orders on ContosoDB (SQL Server). The business states two numbers: losing more than 1 hour of orders is unacceptable (RPO = 1 hour), and the system must be back within 4 hours of a failure (RTO = 4 hours). Design the backup strategy — recovery model, schedule, and restore proof.
scenarios.title: SQL Backup Strategy for the Line-of-Business App
scenarios.why: RPO 1 hour dictates backup frequency: something must capture data at least hourly — 15-minute log backups cap worst-case loss at 15 minutes, comfortably inside the requirement. That requires the FULL recovery model (SIMPLE truncates the log and makes point-in-time recovery impossible — worst-case loss becomes 24 hours). RTO 4 hours dictates chain length: a nightly FULL plus 6-hour DIFFERENTIALs means a restore replays at most one diff and a handful of logs — minutes to tens of minutes, not hours. The log chain is anchored by the FULL: logs without a base full are un-restorable, and Sunday-only fulls allow up to 7 days of loss. Backups on the same disk as the data die with the disk — separate storage is non-negotiable — and an untested restore is a hope, not a plan. Logic Check: read the strategy backwards from the disaster — 'the DB is gone at 10:17 AM, what do I restore, in what order, how long does each step take?' If you cannot narrate the restore, the strategy is fiction.

choices: Disable every network service except HTTP/HTTPS for maximum lockdown, then re-enable whatever the business screams about on Monday.

1) Verify backups exist and restore-test one file — without recovery nothing else matters. 2) Patch critical vulnerabilities. 3) Disable SMBv1 and block inbound RDP/SMB at the firewall except via the jump box. 4) Host firewall default-deny, LAPS for unique local admin passwords, password/complexity GPO. Defer: SIEM tuning, packet capture, full 200-item checklist — scheduled for week two.
Work the 200-item benchmark checklist in order — completeness and auditability matter more than sequence.
Visibility first: deploy the SIEM and full packet capture before anything else — you cannot secure what you cannot see.
evidence: SMBv1 still enabled (legacy copier needs it — maybe), RDP open to the LAN, host firewalls on defaults, local admin passwords identical on all PCs, no backup restore test done, patches 60 days behind.
One day. The business must function Monday — anything you break must be fixable before then.
scenarios.hint: Rank by 'what kills the company fastest': no recoverable backups, remotely-exploitable unpatched RCE, or a missing dashboard?
scenarios.prompt: In what order do you harden, and what do you explicitly defer past go-live?
scenarios.situation: Go-live is Friday. You have one working day to harden Contoso Labs. The full benchmark checklist has 200 items and you will not finish it. Four proposals compete for the day: backups-first, visibility-first, checklist-order, and lockdown-everything. Choose the sequence — and defend what you deliberately defer.
scenarios.title: Hardening Priority: One Day Before Go-Live
scenarios.why: Sequencing is risk arithmetic. Backups first because every other control can fail and the company still survives — with no tested restore, one ransomware event is extinction. Patching kills known remote-code-execution; SMBv1 (EternalBlue-class worms) and LAN-wide RDP/SMB are the two most-exploited entry paths in real breaches, so they die before lunch. Default-deny host firewalls, unique local admin passwords via LAPS (one compromised hash must not equal every PC), and the password GPO close the cheap, high-yield gaps. The SIEM, packet capture, and the remaining checklist items are week-two work: visibility without basics just gives you high-fidelity alerts about breaches you could have prevented. Lockdown-everything breaks the business Monday and teaches the company that security equals outage. Logic Check: for each deferred item, name the specific attack it would have stopped this week — if you cannot name one, deferring it was correct.

choices: Delete it and start over — screenshots with no context are worse than nothing and will actively mislead.
Nothing — 40 screenshots of every settings page is thorough documentation; a competent new hire can reconstruct everything from them.
Just add the remaining passwords into the document and it is complete — everything else is visible in the screenshots.

The pack is missing: as-built network diagram with IPs/VLANs, credential inventory (where each credential lives — sealed, never passwords in the doc), SOP index with verification steps, backup/restore runbook, change log, and vendor/support contacts. Screenshots without procedures are archaeology, not documentation.
evidence: 40 screenshots (Settings pages, no captions), server name list (CL-DC01, CL-FS01, no IPs), Wi-Fi password on a sticky note. No procedures, no diagram, no backup info, no contacts.
File server down. You are new. The founder is standing behind your chair.
scenarios.hint: Monday 8:15 AM, file server down, founder watching: which page of the pack gets files serving again? If no page does, the pack failed its only test.
scenarios.prompt: What is missing from the pack, and what must a real handover contain?
scenarios.situation: The previous admin left a 'complete handover pack': 40 screenshots of settings pages, a list of server names, and a sticky note with the Wi-Fi password. You start Monday. At 8:15 AM the file server stops serving files. Judge the pack: what is missing, and what does a real handover contain?
scenarios.title: The Handover Pack: Would a New Hire Survive Monday?
scenarios.why: Documentation has exactly one test: can a competent stranger keep the business running with only this pack? That requires five things. What it is: the as-built diagram with IPs, VLANs, and roles — so you know CL-FS01 is 10.10.20.11 before you troubleshoot. How to fix it: runbooks with numbered steps AND verification ('run X — you should see Y') plus rollback. How to get in: a credential inventory naming where each credential lives (sealed envelope, vault) — passwords themselves never sit in a document. What changed: the change log, so you know Friday's 'quick fix' is today's outage. Who to call: vendor and support contacts. Screenshots rot (UIs change, and a screenshot never says why a setting is that value), and deleting the pack throws away the one true thing in it — the server names. Logic Check: for every document you write, ask 'does this page change what the on-call person does at 2 AM?' — if not, it is decoration.

choices: Tell her to rename the file to .xlsx so it opens, then re-enable macros manually. Renaming changes the hash so the block will not trigger again, and she can finish the deck before the board meeting.
Put the entire finance department into Learning Mode for the rest of the day so nobody else gets blocked, then switch everyone back to Secured tomorrow morning.
Approve all .xlsm files company-wide in the Approval Center so this never happens again, and disable macro blocking for the finance OU permanently.

Verify the file first: check its hash and digital signature in the Unified Audit deny entry, confirm it matches the known-good macro from before the laptop migration. Then approve that specific file (by hash/signer) in the Approval Center with scope limited to her machine or the finance policy, confirm it runs, and log the approval. Then explain to her that the block happened because the new laptop had never seen this file before — the old laptop's approval did not carry over.
evidence: 08:37:12 DENY | excel.exe attempted to load macro module | File: \\fileserver\finance\Q3_Board_Macro.xlsm | SHA256: 9f2c...a41d | Signer: (none — self-authored VBA) | Policy: FINANCE-SECURED | Reason: file not on Application Allowlist
Approval Center request from the CFO's machine
Request #4821 — 'Q3_Board_Macro.xlsm' requested by user via tray popup at 08:38. File hash matches the macro approved on her OLD laptop (retired 6 days ago). Requested scope: single machine.
scenarios.hint: What is the smallest permission that unblocks the CFO without unblocking everyone?
objectives: Verifying a file before approving it
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct way to get her working again without weakening the organization's security posture?
scenarios.situation: It is 8:40 AM and the CFO is building the board deck. She double-clicks her quarterly reporting macro — a .xlsm file she has used for two years — and ThreatLocker blocks it with an 'Application Not Permitted' popup. She calls the helpdesk, furious, saying the old antivirus never did this. The file lives on a network share, and last week IT migrated her to a new laptop with a fresh agent install.
scenarios.title: The CFO's Macro Won't Run
scenarios.why: Allowlisting blocks by identity (hash/signer), not by reputation — a file that was fine on the old laptop is unknown on the new one, and that is the system working as designed. The fix is verification plus a scoped approval: approve that exact file, for that user or policy, and nothing else. Blanket approvals ('all .xlsm files') and org-wide Learning Mode trade one blocked macro for an open door — the exact failure mode allowlisting exists to prevent. In a demo, this is your best story: 'the block fired, we verified in under a minute, the CFO was working before 9 AM, and the audit trail shows exactly who approved what.'

choices: Ringfence the browser with: no spawning child processes (blocks PowerShell, cmd, wscript launched from the browser), no registry writes, internet access limited to standard web ports, no access to other applications' memory or files outside its own profile. Downloads still save to disk, but downloaded installers cannot execute without approval. Expected breakage: 'click-to-run' installers from websites stop working, protocol handlers that launch local apps (e.g., a 'open in desktop app' link) get blocked, and browser-launched helper tools fail — and that is the containment doing its job.
Ringfence the browser but allow it to spawn child processes, because several internal web apps launch a local helper executable. Keep registry access open too, since the browser needs it for updates.

Do not Ringfence the browser at all — fencing breaks too many things. Instead rely on Application Allowlisting alone, since the PowerShell payload is not allowlisted and will be blocked when it tries to run.
Block the browser from the internet entirely inside the Ringfence. A browser with no network access cannot be exploited, which fully solves the watering-hole problem.
evidence: Application: chrome.exe / msedge.exe | Internet: allow (80/443 only) | Registry: deny write | Spawn child processes: deny | Interact with other processes: deny | File access: own profile + Downloads folder only
14:02:55 RINGFENCE BLOCK | msedge.exe attempted to spawn powershell.exe -enc <base64> | Action: denied, process terminated | User impact: none — tab kept rendering
scenarios.hint: A browser's job is rendering web pages — what else was it doing that it never needed to do?
scenarios.prompt: Which Ringfencing policy contains the browser correctly, and what breakage should you expect (and accept)?
scenarios.situation: Threat intel flags a watering-hole campaign targeting your industry: compromised legitimate websites are serving browser exploits that spawn PowerShell to download a second-stage payload. Your CISO asks you to contain the risk on all 400 endpoints today. The browsers must keep working — sales lives in web apps all day — but a compromised browser must not be able to move anywhere.
scenarios.title: Ringfence the Browser
scenarios.why: Ringfencing assumes the application WILL be compromised and limits the blast radius: the exploit can own the browser tab, but it cannot spawn PowerShell, touch the registry, or reach other processes — so the second stage never launches. The breakage (no click-to-run installers, no browser-launched helpers) is not a bug; it is the policy working. Choice 3's logic is half-right — allowlisting does block the unknown payload — but it misses fileless and living-off-the-land techniques where no new executable ever appears. The demo line: 'I let the exploit run, and all it got was a tab.'

choices: Walk the attack chain and show where it dies: (1) the ransomware payload is not on the Application Allowlist, so when it tries to execute — from email, download, or USB — it is denied and the user gets a popup, not an encryption event; (2) if it arrives through an allowed-but-compromised app, Ringfencing stops it from touching other processes, the registry, or mapped drives, so it cannot spread or persist; (3) Network Control blocks its callback to the attacker's server, so it cannot receive keys or exfiltrate data; (4) Storage Control blocks it from jumping to USB drives. Close honestly: no product is a force field, and backups still matter — but default-deny turns ransomware from a company-wide encryption event into a blocked popup with a full audit trail of exactly what was stopped.
Say the platform's detection engine identifies all ransomware strains, including zero-days, before they execute — no ransomware family has ever bypassed it.
Assure them it cannot happen: with default-deny in place, ransomware is 100% impossible on a protected machine, so they can stop worrying about it entirely.
Deflect: explain that ransomware recovery is really a backup problem, and pivot to talking about their backup vendor instead of answering about prevention.
evidence: Lab attack chain — simulated ransomware attempt

T+0: invoice.exe downloaded from phishing email → T+1: ALLOWLIST DENY on execute (hash unknown) → T+3s: user clicks 'Request approval' → T+40s: admin denies in Approval Center → T+41s: Unified Audit shows full chain: download source URL, deny, request, denial
Same payload via fenced application (assume-breach test)

Payload injected into allowed app's memory → RINGFENCE BLOCK on registry write → RINGFENCE BLOCK on spawning vssadmin (shadow-copy deletion) → NETWORK BLOCK on C2 callback → payload inert, machine clean
scenarios.hint: Answer the attack chain step by step — where does it die?
objectives: Layered product story (Allowlisting + Ringfencing + Network + Storage)
scenarios.prompt: What is the strongest honest answer, built from actual product capabilities?
scenarios.situation: You are five minutes into the product demo. The prospect — an IT director who lived through a ransomware incident last year — interrupts: 'Okay, but what if ransomware gets in anyway? Every vendor says they stop it. Walk me through what actually happens on one of my machines.' The room goes quiet. This is the moment the demo is won or lost.
scenarios.title: Demo Day: The Ransomware Question
scenarios.why: The prospect has heard 'we stop ransomware' from every vendor, so absolute claims trigger skepticism, not confidence. The winning move is assume-breach: grant that something malicious arrives, then walk each stage of the kill chain and name the control that kills it — Allowlisting at execution, Ringfencing at lateral movement and persistence (note the blocked vssadmin shadow-copy deletion, the classic ransomware setup step), Network Control at command-and-control. The honest close ('no force field, backups still matter') is what makes the rest believable. Never promise 100% — one overclaim torches your credibility for the whole demo.

choices: Add the backup software's executable to the Application Allowlist and reboot the server. The software needs to be allowlisted before Storage Control will let it write.

Diagnose before touching anything: open Unified Audit on the file server and filter for the backup window — look for a Storage Control deny on the USB device. The deny entry names the exact device serial number that was blocked. The fix is a scoped exception: add that specific drive's serial number to the file server's Storage Control policy (allow writes for that device only), leave the default-deny for all other removable media intact, re-run the backup, verify it completes, and document the exception with the rotation schedule. The junior admin's plan would leave every USB port on the file server wide open.
Assume the backup software is malfunctioning after the agent install. Reinstall the backup software, reformat the USB drive, and open a ticket with the backup vendor.
Agree with the junior admin: disable Storage Control on the file server, re-run the backup, and re-enable it later. Backups are more important than USB policy for one night.
evidence: 02:14:03 STORAGE DENY | backupsvc.exe attempted write to removable device | Device: USB-HDD Serial 8HG4-22TQ-9917 | Policy: SERVERS-STORAGE-DEFAULT | Reason: device serial not on approved list | Note: backupsvc.exe itself was permitted — the block was on the DEVICE, not the application
Removable storage: deny by default | Approved devices: (empty — rollout Friday never added the rotation drives) | Read-only mode: off
scenarios.hint: The log will tell you whether the software failed or the policy said no — check it first.
objectives: Unified Audit as the first troubleshooting step
scenarios.prompt: How do you diagnose this correctly, and what is the right fix?
scenarios.situation: Monday 6:00 AM: the weekend backup job on the file server failed. The backup software's log says 'destination not writable.' The destination is a USB hard drive rotated weekly for offsite storage. Nothing about the backup software changed — but last Friday, Storage Control was rolled out to all servers. The junior admin's plan is to 'just turn off Storage Control on the file server until backups work again.'
scenarios.title: Storage Control Blocks the Backup
scenarios.why: This is the classic policy-vs-malfunction fork, and the Unified Audit answers it in seconds: the software was allowed, the device was not. The root cause is a rollout gap — the rotation drives' serials were never added to the approved list — not a broken product. The scoped fix (approve by device serial, server policy only) keeps the security value of Storage Control — every other USB stick plugged into that server is still denied — while the backup runs. Disabling the control 'for one night' is how 'temporary' exceptions become permanent holes; the audit trail is exactly what lets you prove to an auditor that the exception was deliberate, narrow, and documented.

scenarios.title: The API Says No
scenarios.situation: Monday 7:40 AM. The overnight onboarding script that creates accounts in the company's cloud HR app through its REST API failed — 12 new hires start today with no accounts, no email, no badge access. The script worked Friday. Nobody changed the script. The API docs say: POST https://hr-api.corp.local/v2/users, authenticate with an Authorization header using the Bearer scheme, and send a JSON body with displayName, userPrincipalName, and department. The helpdesk wants to 'just create the accounts by hand.' You have one hour before the new-hire orientation.
scenarios.prompt: Decide whether the failure is the auth header, the endpoint, or the JSON body — then fix the script and prove it with a clean 201 Created.
evidence:
Invoke-RestMethod : The remote server returned an error: (401) Unauthorized.
At C:\Scripts\New-HireProvision.ps1:42
The script's own debug log (what it actually sent)

Send your API token in the Authorization header using the Bearer scheme:
  Authorization: Bearer <your-api-token>
Status codes: 401 = the server rejected your credentials (fix the header). 404 = no such endpoint (fix the URL). 400 = the server could not parse your request body (fix the JSON).
choices: The JSON body is malformed — rebuild the body hashtable field by field until the server accepts it.
The API server is down — page the vendor's on-call engineer and create the 12 accounts by hand in the meantime.
The endpoint is wrong — the API must have moved to /v1/users over the weekend. Change the URL in the script and re-run.

The auth header is wrong: the script sends 'Authorization: Token ...' but the API requires the 'Bearer' scheme — that is exactly what a 401 means. Change the header to 'Bearer <token>', re-run one provisioning call, and confirm a 201 Created with the new user's id in the response before running the remaining 11.
scenarios.why: Read the status code first: it tells you which part of the request the server objected to. 401 blames the credentials (the header), 404 blames the URL (the endpoint), 400 blames the payload (the body). Here the server answered 401, the URL matches the docs (/v2/users), and the body parses as valid JSON — so the only suspect left is the header, and the debug log confirms it: 'Token' instead of 'Bearer'. One-word fix, then prove it with a single 201 before bulk-running the rest. Changing the endpoint or rebuilding the body chases parts of the request the server never complained about, and paging the vendor wastes everyone's morning on a server that is demonstrably alive — it answered you, it just didn't like your credentials.
scenarios.hint: The server answered you — so it is not down. Match the 401 to the docs' status-code table, then compare the script's header to the docs' header line word by word.

scenarios.title: Pilot the New Backup Tool
scenarios.situation: The company is replacing its aging tape backup system. You shortlisted two products and ran a 30-day pilot of each on five real servers with the success criteria locked in before the pilot started. The pilot just ended. The CFO has seen the price tags and is leaning toward the cheaper one. Your written recommendation goes to the leadership meeting tomorrow.
scenarios.prompt: Score both products against the pre-agreed criteria, call out the tradeoff honestly, and make a recommendation.
evidence:
CRITERION (must-have)            | VaultGuard          | SnapSafe
Backup success, 30 days          | 150/150 (100%)      | 141/150 (94%, 9 missed)
Restore under 30 minutes        | 12 min, 3/3 passed  | 40 min, 1 of 3 restores FAILED
Immutable backup copies         | Yes (ransomware     | No — backups are writable
 (ransomware cannot alter)      | cannot alter)       | by any admin account
Supports Windows Server 2025    | Yes                 | No — agent crashed on 2 of 5 pilot servers
Support                         | 24/7 phone          | Email only, next-business-day
COST (200 agents, per year)      | $18,000             | $9,500
"SnapSafe saves us $8,500 a year. Unless there's a hard reason, let's go with SnapSafe. — CFO"
Pilot success criteria (signed off before the pilot)

A product passes only if it meets ALL must-haves: 100% backup success over 30 days, restore under 30 minutes, immutable copies, Server 2025 support. Price is a tiebreaker between products that pass — it does not override a failed must-have.
choices: Recommend extending the pilot 60 more days to give SnapSafe a chance to fix its agent and retry the failed restore.
Recommend keeping the tape system — neither new product is perfect, so change nothing.

Recommend VaultGuard: it is the only product that passed every pre-agreed must-have. State the tradeoff plainly — it costs $8,500/year more — and show the math: SnapSafe's writable backups plus a failed restore mean one ransomware incident would cost multiples of that difference, and the criteria were locked before pricing was discussed so the goalposts cannot move now.
Recommend SnapSafe — it is $8,500 cheaper per year and 'close enough' on the criteria; document the gaps as accepted risks.
scenarios.why: The entire point of locking success criteria before the pilot is to stop price from re-deciding the contest afterward. SnapSafe fails three must-haves outright: backups missed (94%, not 100%), a restore failed and took 40 minutes, copies are mutable (a ransomware attack encrypts the backups too — the one scenario backups exist for), and the agent crashes on Server 2025. 'Close enough' on a backup product means 'fails when you need it most.' VaultGuard passed everything; the honest tradeoff is the $8,500/year delta, which you state up front alongside the cost of a single unrecoverable incident. Extending the pilot rewards failure with more time, and keeping tape ignores why the project started.
scenarios.hint: Which rules were written before anyone saw the price tags? Price is a tiebreaker between products that passed — did both pass?
objectives: Writing an honest recommendation with the tradeoff stated

scenarios.title: Registry Edit Gone Wrong
scenarios.situation: Friday 4:30 PM. A junior admin followed a 'Windows hardening' blog post on the RDS session host and edited the registry. Now nobody can get a desktop: every logon authenticates, shows a black screen for about ten seconds, then drops back to the logon screen — for every user, including the junior admin. Fifty users are locked out of their sessions going into the weekend. The junior admin kept notes and, luckily, exported the registry key before changing it.
scenarios.prompt: Get logons working again with the smallest, safest change — and leave proof the system is back to its pre-change state.
evidence: "Changed HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon\Shell from 'explorer.exe' to 'C:\Tools\hardened-shell.exe' per the hardening blog. Exported the key first to C:\Backup\winlogon-backup.reg."

Logon authenticates fine (no bad-password errors). Black screen ~10 seconds, then back to the logon screen. Safe Mode with Command Prompt DOES work — it uses cmd.exe as the shell instead of the Winlogon Shell value.
"Once you've rebooted and confirmed the new shell loads, delete your .reg backup to keep things clean and secure."
choices: Rebuild the RDS host from the gold image — the registry is corrupted and a rebuild is the only trustworthy fix.

Boot into Safe Mode with Command Prompt, confirm the Shell value is the bogus path, restore the exported backup with 'reg import C:\Backup\winlogon-backup.reg', reboot normally, and verify a test logon reaches a full desktop. Then file the blog's 'delete your backup' advice under 'never do this.'
Delete the entire Winlogon registry key — Windows will recreate it with defaults on the next boot.
Run System Restore back to last week's restore point — it will undo the registry change along with everything else.
scenarios.why: Follow the symptom precisely: authentication succeeds, so accounts, passwords, and the security subsystem are fine — the failure is what Windows launches AFTER logon, which is exactly the Shell value he changed. C:\Tools\hardened-shell.exe does not exist, so the shell fails to start and Windows ends the session. Safe Mode works because it bypasses that value (it uses cmd.exe), which both confirms the diagnosis and gives you a working command prompt to fix it. The exported .reg is the surgical reversal — one command, zero collateral. Windows does NOT regenerate a deleted Winlogon key (that choice bricks logon permanently); System Restore would roll back a week of legitimate changes to fix a one-value mistake; and rebuilding the host turns a five-minute fix into a weekend outage. The deeper lesson: the backup he was told to delete is the only reason this is recoverable — always export before you edit, and never follow advice that tells you to destroy your way back.
scenarios.hint: Logon works — it is what happens AFTER logon that fails. What does Windows launch right after you authenticate, and what did he change about it?
objectives: Safe Mode recovery and .reg backup restore

scenarios.title: Which Layer Is It?
scenarios.situation: Monday morning helpdesk queue, three tickets, one you. The users all describe their problem as 'the network is down,' but the symptoms point at three different OSI layers. Your job: for each ticket, name the broken layer and the single command that proves it — before you touch anything.
scenarios.prompt: Map each ticket to its OSI layer and the diagnostic tool that proves it.
evidence: "Can't open any website by name — browser says the site can't be reached. But ping 8.8.8.8 replies fine."
"My PC can't reach the file server at all — ping fails. But 'arp -a' shows the gateway's MAC address, so the local network seems alive."
"No network at all since this morning — the link light on the back of the PC is dark."
choices: Ticket A is Layer 7 (DNS name resolution) — IP connectivity works (ping 8.8.8.8), so Layers 1–3 are fine and only names fail; prove it with nslookup or Resolve-DnsName. Ticket B is Layer 3 (IP) — ARP resolving the gateway MAC proves Layer 2 works, but ping (ICMP, Layer 3) fails, so the break is at or above IP; prove it with ping and tracert. Ticket C is Layer 1 (physical) — a dark link light means no signal on the wire; check with Get-NetAdapter status, then reseat or swap the cable and try another switch port.
Ticket A is Layer 3 (routing) — run tracert. Ticket B is Layer 2 (switching) — swap the cable. Ticket C is Layer 7 (application) — reinstall the browser.
Ticket A is Layer 2, Ticket B is Layer 7, Ticket C is Layer 3 — escalate all three to the network team since the layers don't match the symptoms.
All three are Layer 4 (TCP) problems — reboot each PC and retest before doing anything else.
scenarios.why: Work bottom-up: find the highest layer that still works, and the break is the layer just above it. Ticket A: ping to a raw IP works, so Layers 1–3 are healthy — only name resolution fails, and DNS is a Layer 7 service, proven with nslookup/Resolve-DnsName (never 'reinstall the browser' for a name problem). Ticket B: ARP is a Layer 2 protocol and it resolved the gateway's MAC, so the local link works — but ICMP ping, a Layer 3 protocol, fails, placing the fault at Layer 3 (IP forwarding/routing past the gateway), diagnosed with ping and tracert. Ticket C: no link light is the textbook Layer 1 symptom — no command fixes a dead wire; Get-NetAdapter confirms the OS sees 'Disconnected,' then it's hands-on: cable, port, NIC. The wrong answers either test the wrong layer for the symptom or give up and reboot/escalate without diagnosing.
scenarios.hint: For each ticket, find the HIGHEST layer that provably still works — the broken layer is the one just above it. What does a working ping prove? What does a resolved ARP entry prove?
objectives: Choosing the right diagnostic tool per layer

scenarios.title: Which Firewall Rule Fired?
scenarios.situation:
Monday 7:40 AM. The helpdesk queue is filling with the same ticket: 'Payroll web app is down — can't reach the payroll site.' The junior admin swears nothing changed, then remembers: during last night's incident response he added a temporary policy to the FortiGate 'to stop the bleeding' while they investigated a malware alert. He shows you the policy list:

policy 1: LAN → WAN, service ALL, action DENY, name 'incident-block-temp'
policy 2: LAN → WAN, service HTTPS, destination payroll vendor, action ACCEPT, name 'allow-payroll'

'But the allow rule is right there!' he says. 'Policy 2 explicitly allows it!'
scenarios.prompt: Why is the payroll traffic being blocked, and how do you prove which rule is responsible?
choices: Policy 2's service definition is wrong — HTTPS web traffic needs a custom service object for TCP 443, and the built-in HTTPS object doesn't cover it. Fix the service and the allow will work.
Source NAT isn't enabled on policy 2, so the payroll server's replies have no translation to return to. Enable NAT on the allow rule and the session will complete.
Policy 2 must be disabled — the implicit deny at the bottom of the list overrides explicit allow rules, so explicit allows never work. Delete policy 2 and rely on the implicit behavior.

Policy 1 matches the payroll traffic first and denies it — FortiGate evaluates top-down and stops at the first match, so policy 2 is never consulted. The diagnose hit counts on policy 1 will be climbing. Fix: move the allow above the deny (or remove the stale temp rule).
scenarios.why: Firewalls evaluate policies top-down and stop at the FIRST match — they never go looking for a 'better' rule below. Policy 1 (service ALL, action DENY) matches the payroll HTTPS traffic before policy 2 is ever evaluated, so the allow rule is decoration until the order is fixed. LOGIC CHECK: 'show' tells you what EXISTS; hit counts tell you what is FIRING. 'diagnose firewall policy list' shows policy 1's hits climbing with every blocked payroll attempt — that is your witness. The fix is ordering: specific allows above, general denies below, and temporary incident rules get removed or re-seated the moment the incident ends.
scenarios.hint: Which rule does the firewall read FIRST — and what does 'service ALL' match?
evidence:
config firewall policy
    edit 1
        set name "incident-block-temp"
        set srcintf "port1"
        set dstintf "port2"
        set action deny
        set service "ALL"
    next
    edit 2
        set name "allow-payroll"
        set srcintf "port1"
        set dstintf "port2"
        set action accept
        set service "HTTPS"
    next
end

id   name                 action   hits
1    incident-block-temp  deny     4821   <-- climbing every minute
2    allow-payroll        accept   0      <-- never fires

scenarios.title: The App That Wasn't a Port
scenarios.situation:
Your Palo Alto rulebase has a rule the previous admin was proud of: 'allow-web' — application ANY, service tcp/80 + tcp/443, action allow. 'Web browsing allowed, everything else blocked,' he said. This week two things happen:

1. The new internal dashboard (a web app served on TCP 8080) won't load for anyone. Helpdesk blames the server team; the server team blames the network.
2. The SOC finds an unsanctioned remote-access tool tunneled inside TLS on TCP 443, exfiltrating data — sailing straight through 'allow-web'.

One rule, two failures — in opposite directions.
scenarios.prompt: What single change fixes BOTH the broken dashboard and the tunneled exfiltration?
choices: Replace the port-based rule with an App-ID application-based rule: application 'web-browsing', service 'application-default', action allow — plus explicit denies for the unwanted applications by name. App-ID identifies WHAT the traffic is regardless of port, so the dashboard on 8080 is recognized as web-browsing and allowed, while the remote-access tool on 443 is recognized as what it really is and denied.
Move 'allow-web' below the deny rules so it gets evaluated last — order is the problem, not the matching method.
Add TCP 8080 to the allow-web service list and add a second rule denying the remote-access tool's destination IPs. Ports are the only thing a firewall can match, so you enumerate them.
Change the service to 'any' so all ports are allowed — the dashboard works, and you can sort out the exfiltration later with endpoint agents.
scenarios.why: Ports describe WHERE traffic goes; App-ID describes WHAT IT IS. The old rule matched the envelope (tcp/443), so anything stuffed into a 443 envelope — including the rogue tool — passed, while the legitimate dashboard on 8080 missed the port list and broke. LOGIC CHECK: application-based policy follows the application, not the port number it happened to use today. With application 'web-browsing' + service 'application-default', the firewall identifies real web traffic on ANY port (dashboard on 8080: allowed) and simultaneously sees through port-masquerading (rogue tool on 443: identified by behavior, denied by name). One matching method, both failures fixed — that is the entire business case for App-ID.
scenarios.hint: The rule matched the envelope, not the letter. What identifies the application itself?
evidence: src 10.0.1.44 -> dst 185.220.70.9, port 443, app 'proxy-avoidance', rule 'allow-web', action ALLOW — 2.1 GB uploaded
'New dashboard at https://dash.internal:8080 times out for all users since Monday.' Server team: 'The service is up — we can reach it from the server VLAN.'

scenarios.title: VPN or Bust
scenarios.situation:
Friday 4:00 PM — the worst possible time. The new site-to-site IPsec tunnel between HQ (FortiGate) and the Branch office is 'up' according to the project manager, but nobody at Branch can reach a single HQ server. You run diagnose vpn tunnel list:

gateway Branch-P1 -> 198.51.100.7 : up
   phase2 Branch-P2 : down (phase2 incomplete)

Phase 1 is UP — the two firewalls authenticated each other fine. Phase 2 is DOWN — no encrypted traffic is flowing.
scenarios.prompt: Phase 1 is up but phase 2 is down. What is the most likely cause, and where do you look?
choices: The pre-shared key is wrong — re-enter it on both ends and reboot both firewalls. Phase 1 can't really be up with a bad PSK.
The WAN interface is down — check the physical link before touching crypto configuration.
The firewall policy allowing Branch-to-HQ traffic is missing — add an allow policy and traffic will flow once phase 2 negotiates.

Phase 2 parameters don't agree — the proposals (encryption/hash) or the traffic selectors (local/remote subnets) differ between the two ends. Compare 'show vpn ipsec phase2-interface' on the FortiGate against the Branch side's IPsec settings; the subnets and crypto must mirror exactly.
scenarios.why: Phase 1 answers 'do we trust each other?' (peer authentication, IKE crypto) — and it's UP, so the PSK and phase-1 crypto are fine. Phase 2 answers 'WHAT traffic do we encrypt?' — it negotiates the IPsec crypto plus the traffic selectors (which local subnets may talk to which remote subnets). If one end says local 10.0.1.0/24 <-> remote 10.0.5.0/24 and the other end has a typo (10.0.9.0/24), phase 2 can never agree and stays down. LOGIC CHECK: up/down state is a diagnostic, not a verdict — Phase1-UP + Phase2-DOWN isolates the fault to the phase-2 proposal or selectors with near-certainty. Compare both ends line by line; crypto parameters and subnet pairs must MIRROR. (And yes, you'll still need firewall policies permitting the tunneled traffic — but policies can't fix a phase 2 that won't negotiate.)
scenarios.hint: Phase 1 = trust. Phase 2 = what gets encrypted. Which question is still unanswered?
evidence:
gateway Branch-P1 -> 198.51.100.7 : up
   phase2 Branch-P2 : down (phase2 incomplete)

edit "Branch-P2"
        set phase1name "Branch-P1"
        set proposal aes256-sha256
        set src-subnet 10.0.1.0 255.255.255.0
        set dst-subnet 10.0.9.0 255.255.255.0   <-- HQ thinks Branch is 10.0.9.0/24
    next
(Branch's real LAN: 10.0.5.0/24)

scenarios.title: Fortinet vs Palo Alto: Pick the Right Tool
scenarios.situation:
Two projects land on your desk the same week:

Project A — a 25-person branch office. Needs firewall, site-to-site VPN back to HQ, and basic web filtering. One box, tight budget, and it has to be running by end of month.

Project B — a hospital SOC. Must allow the electronic-health-record web app while blocking everything else that merely LOOKS like web traffic, with full per-application audit trails and a change-control board that approves every rule edit.

Finance will only fund one platform per project, and both teams ask: 'Which firewall should we buy?'
scenarios.prompt: Which platform fits each project — and what is the reasoning you'd defend in front of both teams?
choices: Palo Alto for both — it's the premium option, so it must be better at everything, including the branch's budget constraints.

FortiGate for Project A (all-in-one value: firewall + VPN + UTM web filtering on one box, fast to deploy, budget-friendly) and Palo Alto for Project B (App-ID precision to allow the EHR app while blocking look-alikes by application identity, plus commit-based change control and rich logging for the audit trail). Match the tool to the requirement, not the logo.
Generic port-based firewalls for both — applications don't matter as long as you get the port numbers right.
FortiGate for both — one platform means one skill set, and any firewall can do application control if you try hard enough.
scenarios.why: There is no 'best' firewall — there is only the best FIT. Project A is an all-in-one value play: one appliance doing firewall, VPN, and UTM web filtering, deployed fast on a branch budget — FortiGate's home turf. Project B is an application-identity and governance play: the requirement isn't 'allow port 443' (that allows everything wearing a 443 costume), it's 'allow THIS application and nothing else, provably, with audited changes' — Palo Alto's App-ID plus commit-based change control. LOGIC CHECK: when someone asks 'which is better,' translate it to 'better AT WHAT?' List the actual requirements (budget, speed, app precision, auditability), then score each platform against the list. The logo never wins the argument — the requirements do.
scenarios.hint: Project A is constrained by budget and speed; Project B is constrained by precision and proof. Which strength maps to which?
evidence: 'Single appliance, tight capex, firewall + site VPN + web filtering, live by the 30th. No dedicated firewall admin on site.'
'Must distinguish the EHR web application from all other TLS traffic; every rule change needs an auditable approval trail for the compliance review.'

scenarios.title: VM or Container?
scenarios.situation: You inherit a single Proxmox host (64 GB RAM) at a small company. The to-do list: deploy a Windows Server domain controller, plus 12 lightweight Linux services (internal DNS, a monitoring agent, a wiki, and nine small internal tools). A junior admin suggests putting everything in virtual machines 'for consistency'.
scenarios.prompt: How do you split the workloads between KVM virtual machines and LXC containers, and what is the technical reason for each choice?
choices: All 13 workloads as KVM virtual machines — uniform tooling (qm commands only) and maximum isolation everywhere. Containers are a shortcut that sacrifices reliability.
Skip Proxmox: install the 12 Linux services directly on the host OS and run only the Windows DC in a VM. Fewer moving parts beats virtualization for small shops.
Everything as LXC containers, including the domain controller — containers boot in 2 seconds and the Windows workload can run under Wine inside a container to save RAM.

Windows domain controller as a KVM virtual machine; the 12 Linux services as LXC containers. VMs provide the separate kernel Windows requires; containers share the host kernel, which Linux services don't need duplicated — each idles on ~50 MB RAM instead of 1-2 GB, so all 12 fit comfortably.
scenarios.hint: Ask what each workload fundamentally needs: its own kernel, or just an isolated slice of Linux?
objectives: Distinguish KVM virtualization (own kernel, own virtual hardware) from LXC (shared kernel)
Size RAM budgets: VM overhead vs container overhead
Apply the rule: Windows or custom kernel -> VM; lightweight Linux service -> container
scenarios.evidence: In the Proxmox simulator (sims/proxmox-sim.html, LXC vs VM tab): create a container with pct create and compare its 512 MB footprint against a 2048 MB VM in qm list.
scenarios.why: LOGIC CHECK: a container shares the host's Linux kernel, so it physically cannot boot Windows — that single fact decides the DC placement. The 12 Linux services gain nothing from 12 duplicate kernels, but each duplicate kernel costs 1-2 GB of idle RAM; 12 VMs would exhaust the 64 GB host while 12 containers (~50 MB idle each) leave headroom. What: KVM = virtual hardware + own kernel; LXC = OS-level isolation on the shared kernel. When: VM for Windows/custom-kernel/untrusted workloads; LXC for fleets of small Linux services.

scenarios.title: Permission Denied
scenarios.situation: Monday 8:12 AM. The deployment pipeline is red. The on-call admin ran /home/admin/deploy.sh and got 'permission denied'. You check: ls -l shows -rw-r--r-- (644), owner admin. The script must run as the admin user in 10 minutes for a client demo.
scenarios.prompt: What is the minimal correct fix, and why is it preferable to the alternatives?
choices: chmod 755 /home/admin/deploy.sh — adds owner execute (rwx) while keeping group/others at read+execute (r-x): the owner can run and modify it, everyone else can only run and read it. Minimal privilege that solves the problem.
chown root /home/admin/deploy.sh then run it with sudo — root ownership is the safest way to run deployment scripts.
Copy the script to /tmp and run bash /tmp/deploy.sh — bypasses the execute bit entirely and /tmp is world-writable by design.
chmod 777 /home/admin/deploy.sh — it guarantees the script runs no matter which user the pipeline uses, and you can tighten it later.
scenarios.hint: Read the ls -l string: which of rwx is missing, and for whom? Fix exactly that — nothing more.
objectives: Decode an ls -l permission string into owner/group/other triples
Convert rwx to octal (r=4, w=2, x=1) and choose 755 over 777
Explain why 777 is never the answer (any user could replace the script with malware)
scenarios.evidence: In the Terminal simulator (sims/terminal-mastery.html): run ls -l /home/admin/deploy.sh, apply chmod 755, verify with ls -l, and complete Challenge 2 'Fix the script permissions'.
scenarios.why: LOGIC CHECK: the failure is a missing execute bit for the owner (644 = rw-r--r--), not an ownership problem — so chown/sudo treats the wrong disease, and 777 treats it by removing all security (any local user could then rewrite a deployment script that touches production). What: x on a file = permission to execute. How: chmod 755 = 7 (4+2+1) for owner, 5 (4+1) for group and others. When: every 'permission denied' on a script you own — check ls -l first, fix the exact missing bit.

scenarios.title: Merge Conflict Monday
scenarios.situation: Two admins both fixed the VPN timeout on Friday — you set timeout = 90 on main, your colleague set timeout = 60 on branch fix/vpn. Monday morning you run git merge fix/vpn and Git stops: 'CONFLICT in vpn.md — automatic merge failed'. The change must ship today.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct resolution sequence, in order?
choices: Commit your side first with git commit --allow-empty, then merge — the empty commit forces Git to take your version automatically.
Delete vpn.md and re-create it with timeout = 90, then git add . and git push --force to overwrite the branch history.
Run git merge --abort, delete the fix/vpn branch, and re-type the colleague's change manually on main so history stays linear.

Open vpn.md, choose the correct timeout value (or combine both changes deliberately), remove the <<<<<<< ======= >>>>>>> markers, then git add vpn.md and git commit. The resulting merge commit has two parents, preserving both histories.
scenarios.hint: A conflict is Git asking a human a question it can't answer. The markers show you both answers — pick deliberately, then tell Git the file is resolved.
objectives: Explain what a merge conflict is (same lines changed on both sides since the branch split)
Resolve via edit -> git add -> git commit, and describe why the merge commit has two parents
scenarios.evidence: In the Git simulator (sims/git-simulator.html, Merge Conflicts tab): run the guided walkthrough — set up the conflict, resolve it, and inspect the two-parent merge commit in the graph.
scenarios.why: LOGIC CHECK: force-pushing or deleting the branch destroys the colleague's history and hides the decision — the opposite of what version control is for. The conflict markers are data, not damage: they show exactly which lines diverged so a human can decide (90? 60? a third value?). git add is how you tell Git 'I resolved this'; the merge commit's two parents permanently record that a human adjudicated. What: a conflict = divergent edits to the same lines. When: resolve calmly — it happens on every team, every week.

scenarios.title: Pick the Hypervisor
scenarios.situation: A 40-person company asks you to recommend their virtualization platform. Constraints: tight budget (no per-CPU enterprise licensing), a mix of Windows and Linux VMs, and they want HA failover, live migration, and built-in backups without buying add-ons. In the interview they ask: 'Why not just use what everyone else uses?'
scenarios.prompt: Which platform fits, and how do you frame the answer without disparaging alternatives?
choices: Recommend Proxmox VE: free and open-source with HA, live migration, replication, and backups built in; KVM handles the Windows and Linux VMs and LXC covers lightweight Linux services. Frame it as fit, not rivalry: the enterprise platforms dominate large licensed estates, Hyper-V is natural where Windows Server licensing already exists, and Proxmox gives small teams enterprise features at open-source cost.
Avoid hypervisors entirely: one big physical server per workload is more reliable than any virtualization layer.
Recommend a Type-2 hypervisor on top of a desktop OS — simplest install, and live migration can be scripted later if needed.
Recommend the most expensive enterprise hypervisor — price signals quality, and the company can grow into the licensing.
scenarios.hint: Match the constraints (budget, mixed OS, HA/migration/backups included) to the platform whose feature list and price contain all three — then frame competitors by fit.
objectives: Compare Proxmox VE vs Hyper-V vs ESXi on cost, VM tech, containers, management, and migration
Map concepts across vendors (bridge = virtual switch, storage pool = datastore, live migration = vMotion/Live Migration)
Give an interview-safe vendor framing that never trashes a product
scenarios.evidence: In the Proxmox simulator (sims/proxmox-sim.html, Compare tab): study the feature table, then practice the one-sentence mapping aloud: 'In Proxmox that's a Linux bridge; in Hyper-V you'd call it a virtual switch.'
scenarios.why: LOGIC CHECK: the constraints eliminate per-CPU licensed platforms on budget and Type-2 on capability (no real HA/live migration story) — Proxmox is the only option checking every box, and its concepts transfer: learn bridges, pools, and migration once, then translate vocabulary per employer. What: all three are Type-1 bare-metal hypervisors; they differ in price and ecosystem, not in kind. Interview rule: frame by fit ('dominates large VMware shops') — never trash a vendor's product in an interview.

scenarios.title: The Log Partition Is Full and the App Is Down
scenarios.situation: The Linux app server stopped taking orders at 11:20. df shows /var at 100%. The app team wants a bigger disk provisioned 'urgently'. One 38 GB file is sitting in /var/log.
scenarios.prompt: The disk is full because of one runaway log. What frees the space RIGHT NOW without losing data the app still needs, and what prevents the recurrence?
evidence: ls /etc/logrotate.d/  →  syslog, apt, dpkg — no entry for app.log. The app holds app.log open (lsof shows the handle).
choices: Truncate the open log with : > /var/log/app.log (frees the space while the app keeps its handle), then add an /etc/logrotate.d/app entry (size-based rotation, compress, keep 4). rm would NOT free the space until the app closes its handle — the classic trap.
rm /var/log/app.log — deleting the file frees 38 GB instantly and the app will recreate it.
Reboot the server — the reboot clears temp files and the app will restart cleanly.
Provision a bigger disk for /var immediately — the app team is right, running at 100% is the emergency.
scenarios.why: Deleting a file that a process holds open removes the directory entry but NOT the disk blocks — the space stays allocated until the last handle closes, so rm 'frees' exactly zero bytes while destroying your evidence. Truncating (: > file) empties the file THROUGH the open handle: the app keeps writing at offset zero, the blocks release immediately, and the log data you actually needed is... gone either way, but the service recovers in seconds instead of after a restart. The recurrence fix is logrotate — size-based (e.g., 500M, rotate 4, compress) so no single log can ever eat the partition again. A bigger disk without rotation just schedules the same outage with a larger number. Logic Check: on a full disk, find the biggest file FIRST (du), free it through the open handle (truncate, not rm), then fix the process (logrotate) — bigger hardware is never the answer to unbounded growth.
scenarios.hint: The app holds the file open — what does rm do to the disk blocks while a handle is still attached?
objectives: Truncate vs delete on open files

domains.name: ThreatLocker Platform: Zero Trust Endpoint Security

scenarios.title: Application Allowlisting: Default-Deny Execution
scenarios.situation: A user reports that a legitimate business application won't launch. The ThreatLocker agent blocked it. You need to understand why allowlisting blocked it and how to properly permit it without compromising security.
objectives: Identify why an app was blocked
scenarios.prompt: A user's custom inventory application (inventory.exe) is blocked by ThreatLocker Allowlisting. The app is legitimate but wasn't previously approved. What is the secure way to handle this?

choices.a: Disable Allowlisting temporarily so the user can work
choices.b: Add a temporary permit for the file hash, then submit for permanent approval review
choices.c: Tell the user to rename the file to match an allowed application
choices.d: Whitelist the entire folder to avoid future blocks

scenarios.hint: Think about Zero Trust: never trust, always verify. Temporary permits with review maintain security.
scenarios.why: Option B maintains the default-deny posture while enabling business continuity. The temporary permit is scoped to the specific file hash (not the folder), and the review ensures it's legitimate. Disabling protection (A) or whitelisting folders (D) creates security gaps. Renaming (C) is evasion, not administration.

scenarios.title: Ringfencing: Application Containment
scenarios.situation: A PDF reader was exploited via a malicious document. The attacker tried to use the PDF reader to launch PowerShell and access the network. ThreatLocker Ringfencing contained the attack.
objectives: Describe how Ringfencing limits app behavior
Identify what actions can be restricted
scenarios.prompt: Your PDF reader needs to open documents but should never launch PowerShell, access the registry, or make network connections. Which ThreatLocker control enforces this?

choices.a: Application Allowlisting - it blocks unauthorized apps
choices.b: Ringfencing - it controls what allowed apps can do
choices.c: Network Control - it only manages firewall rules
choices.d: Elevation Control - it only manages admin rights

scenarios.hint: Allowlisting decides WHAT can run. Something else decides what running apps can DO.
scenarios.why: Ringfencing is application containment - it defines boundaries for what an allowed application can do (block child processes, network access, registry writes, etc.). Allowlisting (A) only controls whether the app can launch at all. This is defense-in-depth: even if an app is exploited, Ringfencing contains the damage.

scenarios.title: Network Control: Host-Based Firewall Policy
scenarios.situation: You need to ensure that only approved applications can communicate over the network, and only to approved destinations. Traditional Windows Firewall rules are too broad.
scenarios.prompt: A workstation has a custom application that should only communicate with 10.0.1.50 on port 443. All other network access for this app should be blocked. Which approach provides application-aware network control?

choices.a: Windows Firewall with Advanced Security - create an outbound rule for the app
choices.b: ThreatLocker Network Control - define per-application network policies
choices.c: Network segmentation with VLANs - isolate the workstation
choices.d: Disable the network adapter when the app isn't in use

scenarios.hint: Windows Firewall can do this, but ThreatLocker provides centralized, application-aware policy management.
scenarios.why: ThreatLocker Network Control provides granular, centrally-managed per-application network policies. While Windows Firewall (A) can create app-specific rules, Network Control offers unified management, easier auditing, and integration with the broader Zero Trust policy. VLANs (C) are network-level, not app-level.

scenarios.title: Elevation Control: Privilege Management
scenarios.situation: Users need to run a specific application that requires administrative privileges, but you cannot grant them local admin rights. The application must elevate without exposing full admin access.
objectives: Describe privilege management vs admin rights
scenarios.prompt: A legacy application requires admin rights to update its database file in Program Files. Users are standard users. What is the most secure solution?

choices.b: Disable UAC so the app can elevate silently
choices.c: Use Elevation Control to permit elevation for only this specific application
choices.d: Move the database file to the user's Documents folder

scenarios.hint: Least privilege means giving the minimum access needed. Can you elevate just one app without making the user an admin?
scenarios.why: Elevation Control provides just-in-time, application-specific elevation without granting permanent admin rights. Option A violates least privilege catastrophically. Option B disables a security control. Option D might break the app and doesn't solve the elevation need. Elevation Control is the Zero Trust approach: elevate the specific action, not the user.

scenarios.title: Storage Control: Removable Media Policy
scenarios.situation: Your organization needs to prevent data exfiltration via USB drives while still allowing specific encrypted drives for authorized data transfer. You also need audit logs of all file movements.
scenarios.prompt: A user needs to transfer files using a company-issued encrypted USB drive. All other USB storage devices should be blocked. File transfers must be logged. Which control addresses this?

choices.a: Group Policy - disable USB ports entirely via registry
choices.b: ThreatLocker Storage Control - permit specific devices with auditing
choices.c: Physical security - remove USB ports from workstations
choices.d: User training - tell users not to use personal USB drives

scenarios.hint: You need granular control: allow specific devices, block others, and audit everything. Group Policy is all-or-nothing.
scenarios.why: Storage Control provides device-specific policies (allow by serial number, block by class), encryption requirements, and detailed audit logs of file operations. Group Policy (A) is too coarse - it can disable USB entirely but can't distinguish between authorized and unauthorized devices with auditing. Physical removal (C) is impractical. Training (D) isn't a control.

domains.name: Microsoft 365 & Entra ID: Cloud Identity and Productivity

scenarios.title: M365 License Management and Assignment
scenarios.situation: A new hire needs Microsoft 365 E3 license with Exchange, SharePoint, and Teams. You must assign the license and verify services are provisioned.
scenarios.prompt: A new user needs email, Teams, and OneDrive. Which PowerShell command assigns an M365 E3 license and what must you verify afterward?

choices.a: Set-MsolUserLicense; verify in M365 admin center that services show as provisioned
choices.b: Add-ADGroupMember; verify the user can log in to Windows

scenarios.hint: M365 licenses are assigned in Entra ID (Azure AD), not on-prem AD. The cmdlet starts with Msol or Mg.
scenarios.why: M365 licenses are managed through Entra ID. Set-MsolUserLicense (or Set-MgUserLicense with Graph) assigns the license. You must verify in the M365 admin center that Exchange, SharePoint, Teams, etc. show as provisioned - assignment doesn't guarantee immediate provisioning.

scenarios.title: Entra Connect: Hybrid Identity Synchronization
scenarios.situation: Your organization uses hybrid identity. On-prem AD users sync to Entra ID. A user changed their password on-prem but can't log in to M365 with the new password. Sync appears healthy.
scenarios.prompt: Password hash sync is enabled. On-prem password changed 30 minutes ago. M365 still accepts the old password. What do you check first?

choices.a: Force a full sync with Start-ADSyncSyncCycle -PolicyType Initial
choices.b: Check the Entra Connect Synchronization Service Manager for password sync errors
choices.c: Reset the user's password in Entra ID directly

scenarios.hint: Password sync is separate from object sync. Check the specific component.
scenarios.why: Password hash sync has its own status in the Synchronization Service Manager. A full sync (A) won't fix password sync issues and is disruptive. Resetting in Entra ID (C) breaks the hybrid model. Check the password sync status first - it may show errors or be disabled.

scenarios.title: Conditional Access: Zero Trust Policy Enforcement
scenarios.situation: You need to require MFA for all users accessing M365 from outside the corporate network, but allow seamless access from compliant devices on the LAN.
scenarios.prompt: Which Conditional Access configuration enforces MFA for external access while allowing internal seamless SSO?

choices.a: Block all external access - users must use VPN
choices.b: Require MFA for all cloud apps, exclude trusted locations (corporate IPs)

scenarios.hint: Conditional Access has Conditions (who, what, where) and Controls (require MFA, require compliant device, block).
scenarios.why: Conditional Access policies evaluate conditions (user, app, location, device) and enforce controls. Excluding trusted locations (your corporate public IPs) from the MFA requirement allows seamless internal access while protecting external access. This is Zero Trust: verify based on context, not just network location.

domains.name: Portfolio Projects: Build to Prove Your Skills

scenarios.title: Project 1: Complete AD Homelab with GPO Deployment
scenarios.situation: Build a virtualized Active Directory environment demonstrating enterprise administration skills. This is the #1 project to show on Tuesday - it proves you can do the core job.
objectives: Build a working AD domain from scratch
scenarios.prompt: You have 2 days to build a demo. What is the minimum viable AD homelab that proves enterprise competency?

choices.a: One VM with AD installed, no configuration - "it works"
choices.b: DC + client VM, OU structure, 10 test users via PowerShell, 3 GPOs (security baseline, mapped drives, software restriction), documented in a GitHub README with screenshots
choices.c: Full production replica with 50 servers - takes weeks to build
choices.d: Just watch YouTube videos about AD - no hands-on needed

scenarios.hint: Interviewers want to see you DID the work, not just read about it. Screenshots + code + documentation = proof.
scenarios.why: Option B is achievable in a weekend and demonstrates the full lifecycle: building, configuring, automating, and documenting. The GitHub README with screenshots is your proof. Option A is too trivial. Option C is unrealistic for the timeline. Option D provides zero evidence.

scenarios.title: Project 2: Zero Trust Policy Implementation Demo
scenarios.situation: Create a demonstration showing you understand Zero Trust principles by implementing application controls on a Windows workstation using built-in tools (AppLocker/WDAC concepts that map to ThreatLocker Allowlisting).
objectives: Map ThreatLocker concepts to Windows native tools
scenarios.prompt: How do you demonstrate ThreatLocker Allowlisting concepts without having ThreatLocker installed?

choices.b: Use Windows AppLocker to create default-deny policies, document the rules, show blocked vs allowed execution, and explain how this maps to ThreatLocker Allowlisting
choices.c: Just memorize the ThreatLocker product descriptions
choices.d: Install a cracked version of ThreatLocker

scenarios.hint: ThreatLocker Allowlisting ≈ AppLocker/WDAC concepts. Show you understand the PRINCIPLE, not just the product.
scenarios.why: Option B proves you understand the underlying security principle (default-deny application control) and can implement it with native tools. In the interview, you can say: "I implemented allowlisting using AppLocker - here's my policy, here's what it blocks, and this is how it maps to ThreatLocker's Allowlisting." That's powerful. It shows conceptual mastery, not just product memorization.

scenarios.title: Project 3: PowerShell Admin Toolkit (GitHub Repo)
scenarios.situation: Build a GitHub repository with PowerShell scripts that solve real admin problems. This is your "show me the code" project.
scenarios.prompt: Which scripts belong in a PowerShell admin toolkit that would impress a hiring manager?

choices.a: A single 1000-line script that does everything - "look how much code I wrote"
choices.b: 5-10 focused scripts: New-Hire Onboarding (creates AD user, mailbox, groups), Health Check (tests DC replication, DNS, DHCP), Backup Verification, Log Parser, each with comment-based help and examples
choices.c: Scripts copied from the internet with no modifications

scenarios.hint: Quality over quantity. Focused, documented, working scripts beat a massive unmaintainable mess.
scenarios.why: Option B shows you think like an admin: identify repetitive tasks, automate them, document them. Each script should have: .SYNOPSIS, .DESCRIPTION, .EXAMPLE, parameter validation, error handling. The New-Hire Onboarding script is gold - it touches AD, Exchange, groups, and shows you understand the full user lifecycle.

scenarios.title: Project 4: Network Troubleshooting Lab with Documentation
scenarios.situation: Document a network troubleshooting scenario you solved (or simulate one). Create a professional troubleshooting runbook that shows your methodology.
scenarios.prompt: What makes a troubleshooting runbook impressive to an interviewer?

choices.a: Just the solution - "I fixed it by rebooting"
choices.b: Full methodology: symptoms, hypothesis, tests performed (with commands and output), root cause, solution, prevention, timeline. Include actual command output and diagrams.
choices.c: A vague description - "network was down, I fixed it"
