Worked example: place 192.168.7.200 in its /27 subnet

Step 1: /27 mask = 255.255.255.224. Block size = 256 - 224 = 32.
Step 2: Network boundaries are multiples of 32: .0, .32, .64, .96, .128, .160, .192, .224.
        200 falls between 192 and 224  =>  network = 192.168.7.192/27
Step 3: Broadcast = one below next boundary = 192.168.7.223
Step 4: Usable range = .193 - .222  (62 addresses, 2^5 - 2 = 30 usable)

Verify with binary AND (last octet only):
  200 = 1 1 0 0 1 0 0 0
  224 = 1 1 1 0 0 0 0 0
  AND = 1 1 0 0 0 0 0 0 = 192   <-- matches block-size result

Subnetting a /24 into /27s: 2^(27-24) = 8 subnets, each /27 = 32 addresses,
30 usable. First three: 192.168.7.0/27 (.1-.30, bcast .31),
192.168.7.32/27 (.33-.62, bcast .63), 192.168.7.64/27 (.65-.94, bcast .95).
example.walkthrough: The block-size method (256 minus the interesting mask octet) gives subnet boundaries without binary. The -2 in the host formula reserves the network address (all host bits 0) and broadcast address (all host bits 1), which can never be assigned to a host. Cross-check with binary AND when stakes are high — both methods must agree.

pitfalls: Forgetting the -2: a /26 has 64 addresses but only 62 usable hosts
Using the subnet ID (.0) or broadcast (.63) as a host or gateway address
Off-by-one broadcast: broadcast is one BELOW the next network boundary, not the boundary itself

concepts: A VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) is like putting invisible walls inside one physical switch so different groups can't see each other's traffic — imagine one office building with keycard floors: same building, but finance can't wander into engineering. A trunk is the elevator shaft carrying all floors' traffic between switches (each frame tagged so it knows its floor), and inter-VLAN routing is the security desk in the lobby — a router or Layer-3 switch — deciding which cross-floor trips are allowed. This lesson teaches you to carve, tag, and route those invisible floors. Logic Check — here's the reasoning: VLANs exist because broadcasts don't scale — every broadcast hits every device, so a 5,000-device flat network drowns in noise; carving it into VLANs confines each broadcast to its neighborhood, and the router between them exists because total isolation would make shared resources (printers, servers) unreachable.

WHAT: A VLAN (virtual local area network) is a way to split one physical switch into multiple logical switches: devices on VLAN 10 cannot talk to devices on VLAN 20 unless a router deliberately forwards between them, even though they plug into the same hardware. A trunk is an uplink port that carries many VLANs at once by tagging each frame with a 4-byte 802.1Q header saying which VLAN it belongs to, except the native VLAN, which travels untagged. Think of a trunk as a highway with labeled lanes, and the native VLAN as the one lane with no signs.

HOW: An access port is assigned to exactly one VLAN and sends untagged frames; it is the port your PC or printer plugs into. When a frame needs to cross to another switch, the trunk port inserts the 802.1Q tag; the receiving switch reads the tag and drops the frame into the right VLAN. Because VLANs are separate broadcast domains, traffic between them needs Layer 3 routing. Router-on-a-stick uses one physical router interface split into subinterfaces (Gi0/0.10, Gi0/0.20), one per VLAN, each tagged. It works for small sites but every packet hairpins up and down one cable through a software-based router. The enterprise answer is a Layer 3 switch with SVIs (switched virtual interfaces: virtual router interfaces, one per VLAN, like interface Vlan10 with an IP address) plus 'ip routing' enabled, which forwards between VLANs in hardware ASICs (application-specific chips built for packet forwarding) at line rate instead of in software.

WHY: Without VLANs, a guest's laptop shares a broadcast domain with your domain controllers: one ARP storm or one compromised device away from chaos, and no way to write firewall rules that treat servers differently from printers. A native VLAN mismatch (one end says native 1, the other says 99) lets untagged frames leak into the wrong VLAN: a security hole plus CDP (Cisco Discovery Protocol) mismatch errors that confuse every troubleshooter. Funneling inter-VLAN traffic through a firewall as router-on-a-stick pegs the firewall CPU at 95% doing forwarding work it was never sized for. That is why the L3-switch SVI design exists: route where it is cheap, inspect where it matters.

WHEN: Create a VLAN per trust boundary and traffic type: servers, workstations, VoIP (voice over IP phones), guest, management, each with its own subnet and DHCP scope. Use router-on-a-stick only for tiny sites. The wrong way is keeping it at a 6-VLAN branch and wondering why the firewall melts at 9 AM when 780 Mbps of inter-VLAN traffic hairpins through it. Another wrong way is leaving trunk ports on auto/DTP negotiation (Dynamic Trunking Protocol). An attacker can negotiate a trunk from an access port and hop VLANs, so hard-set every port to access or trunk. The alternative to VLANs entirely is physically separate switches per segment: maximally secure, maximally expensive, and unmanageable at scale, which is why VLANs won.

CONNECTS: VLANs need subnets (the subnetting lesson) and DHCP scopes per VLAN (the DHCP lesson: each scope serves one VLAN's subnet). Inter-VLAN routing is the routing lesson in action (SVIs appear as connected routes), and the firewall ACL lesson governs what crosses between VLANs at the firewall. In the security lessons, isolating the legacy SMBv1 appliance or a compromised host means dropping it into a quarantine VLAN. Same mechanism, defensive purpose.

THEORY: Three pieces of math govern real networks. First, the bandwidth-delay product (BDP): bandwidth (bits/second) x round-trip time (seconds) = the number of bits that must be 'in flight' to keep the pipe full. TCP can only have one window's worth of unacknowledged data outstanding, so if the window is smaller than the BDP, the sender idles waiting for ACKs and throughput collapses — this is why a fat but high-latency link (satellite, intercontinental) feels slow even though the pipe is wide: the pipe's capacity is irrelevant if you cannot fill it. Second, VLAN (Virtual LAN) subnet sizing: each VLAN is its own broadcast domain and needs its own subnet, sized by hosts + 2 (network and broadcast), rounded UP to the next power of 2 — because host bits are whole bits, subnets only come in powers of 2. Third, longest-prefix match: when a router holds overlapping routes (a /8, a /16, and a /24 that all match a destination), it forwards via the LONGEST matching prefix — the most specific route — because more matching bits means a smaller, more precise destination set. It is a pure number comparison on prefix length, evaluated after the bitwise match.

WORKED EXAMPLE: Worked 1 — BDP. A 100 Mbps link with 100 ms RTT to a branch office. BDP = 100,000,000 bits/s x 0.10 s = 10,000,000 bits = 1,250,000 bytes = 1.25 MB. A TCP window of 64 KB (the classic default) allows only 65,536 bytes outstanding: throughput ceiling = window / RTT = 65,536 x 8 bits / 0.10 s = 5.24 Mbps — you bought 100 Mbps and get 5. The fix is window scaling (RFC 1323) raising the window past 1.25 MB, not a bigger pipe. Lesson: on high-latency paths, latency — not bandwidth — is the throughput limiter, and the BDP tells you exactly how big the window must be.

Worked 2 — VLAN subnet sizing. Three VLANs: 48 hosts (engineering), 200 hosts (floor Wi-Fi), 12 hosts (printers). Engineering: 48 + 2 = 50 -> next power of 2 is 64 = 2^6 -> 6 host bits -> /26 (62 usable; 14 spare for growth). Wi-Fi: 200 + 2 = 202 -> next power of 2 is 256 = 2^8 -> /24 (254 usable). Printers: 12 + 2 = 14 -> next power of 2 is 16 = 2^4 -> /28 (14 usable; 2 spare — tight, flag for growth). Carve from 10.10.0.0/22 (1024 addresses): Wi-Fi 10.10.0.0/24 (.0.0-.0.255), engineering 10.10.1.0/26 (.1.0-.1.63), printers 10.10.1.64/28 (.1.64-.1.79) — each starts on a multiple of its block size (256, 64, 16), so nothing overlaps.

Worked 3 — longest-prefix match. Routing table: 0.0.0.0/0 -> ISP, 10.0.0.0/8 -> core, 10.1.2.0/24 -> branch router. Packet for 10.1.2.5: compare the first N bits against each route. /8 matches the first 8 bits (10.x.x.x — yes). /24 matches the first 24 bits (10.1.2.x — yes). 0.0.0.0/0 matches everything. Longest match wins: /24 (24 > 8 > 0), so the packet goes to the branch router. The /8 is the less-specific summary; the default route is the last resort. This is also why a misconfigured more-specific route (e.g., a stray /24) can hijack traffic meant for the /8 — longest match always prefers it.

PRACTICE: A 1 Gbps link has a 50 ms RTT. Compute the bandwidth-delay product in MB, and explain what happens if the TCP window is only 256 KB. | You need VLANs for 90 hosts, 25 hosts, and 6 hosts. Give the CIDR prefix and usable count for each, then carve them (in order, largest first) out of 172.16.8.0/22 showing each subnet's range.

ANSWERS: BDP = 1,000,000,000 x 0.05 = 50,000,000 bits = 6,250,000 bytes = 6.25 MB. With a 256 KB window: max throughput = window/RTT = 262,144 x 8 / 0.05 = 41.9 Mbps — about 4% of the gigabit link. The pipe is 96% idle because the sender must stop and wait for ACKs; only a window >= 6.25 MB (via window scaling) fills it. WRONG WAY: 'upgrade to 10 Gbps' — bandwidth is not the constraint; 10 Gbps x 0.05 s = 62.5 MB BDP makes the mismatch ten times worse with the same 256 KB window. | 90 hosts: 92 needed -> next pow2 128 = 2^7 -> /25 (126 usable). 25 hosts: 27 -> next pow2 32 = 2^5 -> /27 (30 usable). 6 hosts: 8 -> next pow2 8 = 2^3 -> /29 (6 usable — exact fit, zero growth room). Carve from 172.16.8.0/22 (range .8.0-.11.255): /25 block 128 -> 172.16.8.0/25 (.8.0-.8.127). Next free .8.128; /27 block 32 -> 172.16.8.128/27 (.8.128-.8.159). Next free .8.160; /29 block 8 -> 172.16.8.160/29 (.8.160-.8.167). Check boundaries: 0, 128 multiples of block sizes 128/32/8 — all valid. WRONG WAY: carving smallest-first fragments the space and risks misalignment; and forgetting the +2 (sizing 90 hosts into a /26 = 62 usable) guarantees address exhaustion on day one.

example.code:
! Access port: untagged, one VLAN
interface Gi0/5
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 20

! Trunk port: tagged, many VLANs, native untagged
interface Gi0/1
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk native vlan 99
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,99

! Router-on-a-stick subinterface (one per VLAN)
interface Gi0/0.10
 encapsulation dot1Q 10
 ip address 10.10.10.1 255.255.255.0

! L3 switch SVI alternative (preferred at scale)
interface Vlan10
 ip address 10.10.10.1 255.255.255.0
ip routing
example.walkthrough: Access ports belong to exactly one VLAN and send untagged frames; trunk ports carry many VLANs with 4-byte 802.1Q tags, except the native VLAN which stays untagged. Inter-VLAN routing needs a Layer 3 device: router-on-a-stick uses one physical link with tagged subinterfaces (fine for small sites), while a Layer 3 switch routes between SVIs in hardware at line rate (the enterprise answer).

pitfalls: Native VLAN mismatch across a trunk: untagged traffic leaks into the wrong VLAN
Leaving trunk ports on auto/dynamic: an attacker can negotiate a trunk (VLAN hopping via DTP) — hard-set access or trunk
Forgetting 'switchport trunk allowed vlan': prunes nothing by default, but an incomplete list silently drops VLANs

concepts: A network switch is only useful until the moment it becomes a single point of failure — this lesson is about the three seatbelts. STP (Spanning Tree Protocol) prevents loops when you plug in redundant cables; without it, one broadcast frame multiplies forever and melts the network, like a microphone held too close to a speaker. Port security glues specific devices to specific switch ports so a rogue laptop can't just plug in, and EtherChannel bundles several physical cables into one fatter logical pipe for speed plus failover. Together: no loops, no strangers, no single cable deciding your uptime. Logic Check — here's the reasoning: each seatbelt answers a specific failure — redundant links without STP create infinite broadcast loops (a frame circles forever, multiplying), open ports without port security invite rogue devices, single cables without EtherChannel are single points of failure — redundancy without discipline is just a faster way to fail.

WHAT: STP (Spanning Tree Protocol) is the loop-prevention protocol for switches: if you cable two switches together twice for redundancy, STP blocks one of the paths so broadcast frames do not loop forever and melt the network. Port security is a per-port bouncer: it limits which MAC addresses (media access control addresses, the hardware addresses burned into every network card) may use a port, and punishes violators. EtherChannel (LACP: Link Aggregation Control Protocol, the 802.3ad standard) bundles up to 8 physical links into one logical pipe for more bandwidth and redundancy. Together they answer: how do I make the switching layer survive cables, loops, and rogue devices?

HOW: STP elects the switch with the lowest bridge ID (priority plus MAC address) as the root bridge, then every other switch blocks the redundant ports that would create loops. Ports move through Blocking to Listening to Learning to Forwarding, taking 30 to 50 seconds total, unless PortFast is enabled on edge ports (ports facing end devices, never other switches), which skips straight to Forwarding. Port security learns MACs on a port, with sticky mode writing dynamically learned MACs into the config, caps the count (switchport port-security maximum 2), and reacts to violations with protect (silently drop the extra frames), restrict (drop and log), or shutdown (err-disable the port until a human intervenes). LACP bundles links: both ends set channel-group mode active, the switches negotiate, and traffic hashes across member links. If one cable dies, the channel keeps working on the survivors.

WHY: Without STP, one accidental loop, a user plugging both ends of a cable into wall jacks, creates a broadcast storm that takes down the entire VLAN in seconds. It is the most common cause of 'the whole network just died' in flat networks. Without port security, anyone can unplug a printer, plug in a laptop, and join your server VLAN, or plug in a rogue DHCP server and hijack address assignment for the segment. Without EtherChannel, your uplink is a single cable and a single point of failure. With it misconfigured (active on one end, ON on the other, where ON means no negotiation), the channel silently never forms and you are back to one link without knowing it.

WHEN: Enable STP everywhere by default and never disable it; use PortFast only on ports facing single end-devices, never on uplinks or trunk ports. The wrong way is PortFast on a trunk: a loop there has zero STP protection and the network dies before anyone can react. Use port security on user-facing access ports. The wrong way is violation mode shutdown on a busy conference-room port, where one visitor's phone err-disables the port and generates a ticket. Bundle uplinks with LACP when you need bandwidth or redundancy. The alternative is multiple independent uplinks with STP blocking one: simpler, but you waste half your bandwidth on a blocked link.

CONNECTS: STP's root election and the native VLAN lesson both live on trunk links: misconfigured trunks break both. Port security's MAC limiting is the switch-level cousin of DHCP snooping and the 802.1X story in the hardening lesson. EtherChannel uplinks carry the trunked VLANs from the VLAN lesson, and the SVIs doing inter-VLAN routing from that lesson ride on top of this resilient switching fabric. If STP or the channel fails, every VLAN on that link fails with it.

example.code:
! STP: lowest bridge ID (priority + MAC) becomes root
spanning-tree vlan 10 priority 4096     ! make this switch root
show spanning-tree vlan 10              ! check Root ID vs Bridge ID

! Port states a port moves through:
!   Blocking -> Listening -> Learning -> Forwarding  (30-50s total)
! PortFast skips straight to Forwarding (edge ports ONLY)
interface Gi0/5
 spanning-tree portfast

! Port security: learn MACs, cap them, act on violation
interface Gi0/5
 switchport port-security
 switchport port-security maximum 2
 switchport port-security mac-address sticky
 switchport port-security violation restrict   ! protect | restrict | shutdown

! EtherChannel with LACP (802.3ad): bundle links, one logical pipe
interface range Gi0/1-2
 channel-group 1 mode active              ! active = LACP
interface Port-channel1
 switchport mode trunk
example.walkthrough: STP prevents switching loops by electing the lowest bridge-ID switch as root and blocking redundant ports; ports transition Blocking->Listening->Learning->Forwarding, with PortFast shortcutting edge ports. Port security binds MACs to a port (sticky learns them dynamically) and reacts to violations with protect (drop), restrict (drop + log), or shutdown (err-disable). LACP bundles up to 8 active links into one logical channel for bandwidth and redundancy.

pitfalls: Enabling PortFast on a trunk/uplink port: a loop there has no STP protection and melts the network
Port security violation 'shutdown' on a user port: one rogue device err-disables the port until manual recovery
LACP mode mismatch (active vs passive is fine; active vs ON is not): channel never forms — match modes on both ends

lessons.try_it: Enable STP debugging on a lab switch, disconnect/reconnect a redundant link, and watch the port states transition; then configure sticky port security and plug in a second device to trigger a violation.

concepts: IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) is the armored tunnel companies build between offices over the public internet — your data drives through it encrypted where eavesdroppers can't see in. Building the tunnel takes two handshakes: IKE (Internet Key Exchange) Phase 1 is the two gateways verifying each other's identity and agreeing HOW to talk securely (the diplomatic meeting), and Phase 2 negotiates the actual encryption for the data (signing the trade deal). Most VPN failures are Phase 1 (we never agreed how to talk) versus Phase 2 (we agreed, but disagree on WHAT to protect) — this lesson teaches you to tell them apart from the logs. Logic Check — here's the reasoning: the two phases are sequential by design — you cannot negotiate WHAT to protect until both sides agree HOW to talk and prove who they are — which is why Phase 1 failures mean 'we never authenticated' and Phase 2 failures mean 'we authenticated but disagree on the traffic,' and the logs tell you exactly which.

WHAT: IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) is the standard for encrypted site-to-site VPN tunnels: it makes two office networks behave like one private network across the public internet. The tunnel is built in two phases. IKE Phase 1 (Internet Key Exchange) creates a secure management channel between the two gateways, and IKE Phase 2 uses that channel to negotiate the actual data-encryption terms. ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload, IP protocol 50) is the part that encrypts and authenticates the data; AH (Authentication Header, IP protocol 51) only authenticates without encrypting, which is why security questionnaires demand ESP for confidentiality.

HOW: Phase 1 (the ISAKMP SA: Internet Security Association and Key Management Protocol security association) is two gateways agreeing on a codebook. They negotiate encryption (AES-256), hash (SHA256), Diffie-Hellman group (the math that lets them derive a shared secret over an insecure channel; group 14 is 2048-bit and the current sane minimum), lifetime (86400 seconds, i.e. 24 hours, after which they renegotiate), and authentication (pre-shared key or certificates). Phase 1 must fully succeed before Phase 2 is even attempted. Phase 2 (quick mode) negotiates the IPsec SA: the transform set (ESP encryption plus authentication for the data itself) and the proxy IDs, the mirrored subnet pairs. Local says 10.1.0.0/16 to 10.2.0.0/16, so remote must say 10.2.0.0/16 to 10.1.0.0/16. Tunnel mode wraps the entire original IP packet including its header, hiding internal addressing from anyone watching the internet path. Transport mode only protects the payload and is for host-to-host, not gateways.

WHY: Without Phase 1, there is no authenticated channel, so nothing about Phase 2 can be trusted. The protocol deliberately refuses to negotiate data encryption with a stranger. A single wrong element (a PSK typo nobody can see in the proposal, a DH group mismatch) kills Phase 1 with 'no matching proposal found,' and because the failure is binary the tunnel just never comes up. Phase 2 fails when proxy IDs do not mirror: each side encrypts different traffic, so quick mode cannot agree and no data flows even though Phase 1 is green. This is the classic 'Phase 1 up, Phase 2 down' that wastes hours if you do not know the two-phase split. Behind NAT, ESP (IP protocol 50) has no ports for the NAT device to translate, so it gets dropped unless NAT-T (NAT Traversal) wraps it in UDP port 4500.

WHEN: Use IPsec site-to-site for permanent office-to-office and office-to-cloud connectivity with gateways on both ends. The wrong way is troubleshooting a Phase 2 symptom (no traffic) by re-checking Phase 1 proposals for the fifth time. Phase 1 UP on the status screen means move on to proxy IDs. Another wrong way is using transport mode gateway-to-gateway, which leaves original IP headers visible on the internet path. Always tunnel mode for site-to-site. The alternative for cloud connectivity in some designs is TLS-based tunnels, but for gateway-to-gateway carrying mixed internal traffic, IPsec in tunnel mode is the standard.

CONNECTS: IPsec tunnels ride on the routing lesson: the interesting-traffic ACLs are effectively static routes into the tunnel, and longest-prefix-match decides what enters it. NAT-T connects to the firewall lesson, because UDP 500 and UDP 4500 must be permitted. The branch-office firewall rules and the client VPN lesson (IKEv2 uses the same IKE machinery for remote users) are the sibling topics. Same crypto, different endpoint type.
IKE Phase 1 (ISAKMP SA)
IKE Phase 2 (IPsec SA / quick mode)
ESP vs AH
Tunnel vs transport mode
PSK vs certificates
Proxy IDs

THEORY: IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) encrypts packets between sites by wrapping each original packet inside a new encrypted packet — ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) in tunnel mode. That wrapper is not free: it adds a new outer IP header (20 bytes, so the tunnel endpoints can route it across the internet), an ESP header (SPI — Security Parameter Index — 4 bytes + sequence number 4 bytes = 8), an IV (initialization vector, 8-16 bytes so identical plaintexts encrypt differently), padding (0-15 bytes to round up to the cipher's block size), and an ICV (integrity check value, 12-16 bytes proving nobody tampered with it). Typical total: ~50-70 bytes per packet. MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit) is the largest packet a link accepts — 1500 bytes on Ethernet, because the original Ethernet spec fixed the max frame at 1518 bytes (1500 payload + 14 header + 4 FCS frame check), a compromise between per-packet overhead efficiency and serialization delay on shared media. If a 1500-byte packet enters a tunnel that adds 70 bytes, the result is 1570 bytes — too big — so the router must fragment it into two packets, doubling header overhead and per-packet CPU cost, and some firewalls drop fragments entirely. MSS (Maximum Segment Size) clamping fixes this at the source: MSS is the largest TCP payload a host will send, negotiated during the TCP handshake, so if the router rewrites it downward (typically to ~1360 on IPsec tunnels), hosts simply never build packets big enough to need fragmentation.

WORKED EXAMPLE: Worked — sizing MSS for an IPsec tunnel. Assume ESP overhead of 70 bytes (worst-case-ish: 20 outer IP + 8 ESP header + 16 IV + 10 padding + 16 ICV = 70).

Step 1 — Effective tunnel MTU = 1500 - 70 = 1430 bytes. Any inner packet larger than 1430 bytes will fragment after encapsulation. (This is why 'the VPN is up but large transfers stall or crawl' is the classic MTU symptom: small packets like pings flow, full-size data packets fragment or get dropped.)

Step 2 — Normal MSS on Ethernet: MSS = MTU - IP header - TCP header = 1500 - 20 - 20 = 1460 bytes. The 20-byte IP header and 20-byte TCP header are fixed protocol overhead on every packet — MSS counts only the TCP payload, the actual application data.

Step 3 — Tunnel MSS ceiling = 1430 - 20 - 20 = 1390 bytes. A host sending 1390-byte segments produces 1430-byte IP packets, which encapsulate to exactly 1500 — no fragmentation.

Step 4 — Operators clamp to 1360, not 1390. Why the extra 30 bytes of margin? Padding varies per packet (0-15 bytes depending on alignment), IV sizes differ by cipher, and some paths add their own small headers (e.g., GRE or NAT-T UDP encapsulation adds 8 more). 1360 is a conventional safe value comfortably under the 1390 ceiling with headroom for all of that, and it is a multiple of common block sizes. The rule: compute your ceiling, then round DOWN to a standard conservative value — never up.

Throughput impact: a full 1500-byte packet carries 1500 - 70 = 1430 bytes of real payload through the tunnel, so per-packet efficiency = 1430/1500 = 95.3%. The bigger cost is not the 4.7% byte overhead but per-packet CPU: encryption cost scales with packet count, and fragmentation (if you skip MSS clamping) turns one packet into two, roughly doubling that cost while adding latency. This is why 'VPN throughput is lower than line rate' even on fast links.

PRACTICE: An IPsec tunnel adds 62 bytes of ESP overhead to every packet on a 1500-byte-MTU path. What is the largest inner IP packet that avoids fragmentation, and what is the per-packet payload efficiency for a full-size packet? | Explain in your own words why a site-to-site VPN can show 'connected' with working pings but file transfers hang or crawl — and name the two-part fix.

ANSWERS: Largest unfragmented inner packet = 1500 - 62 = 1438 bytes. Efficiency = payload / total = 1438 / 1500 = 95.9%. Working shown: the 62 bytes are pure overhead (outer IP header + ESP header + IV + padding + ICV), so only 1438 of the 1500 bytes on the wire carry the original packet. WRONG WAY: answering 1500 - 62 = 1438 as the MSS — MSS is the TCP payload only, so you must also subtract the 20-byte IP and 20-byte TCP headers: MSS ceiling = 1438 - 40 = 1398, clamped down to ~1360 in practice. | Pings are tiny (typically 32-64 bytes) — they fit inside the tunnel with overhead to spare, so IKE (Internet Key Exchange) and basic connectivity look fine. Full-size 1500-byte data packets become ~1560+ bytes after ESP encapsulation, exceeding the path MTU: the router fragments them (extra latency, double CPU, some fragments dropped by firewalls) or, if the DF (Don't Fragment) bit is set, drops them and sends ICMP 'fragmentation needed' — which many firewalls block, so the sender never learns and keeps retransmitting: the hang. Two-part fix: (1) MSS clamping on the tunnel interface (rewrite TCP MSS to ~1360 in the handshake so hosts never send packets that need fragmenting), and (2) verify ICMP Path MTU Discovery is not being filtered so legitimate 'packet too big' messages get through.

example.code:
Phase 1 — builds the secure management channel (ISAKMP SA):
  1. Peers agree on policy: AES-256 + SHA256 + DH group 14 + 86400s lifetime
  2. DH exchange creates shared secret; peers authenticate (PSK or certs)
  3. Result: encrypted channel for Phase 2. (Main mode = 6 msgs, Aggressive = 3)

Phase 2 — negotiates the DATA channel (IPsec SA) via quick mode:
  1. Peers agree on transform set: ESP-AES-256 + ESP-SHA256 (AH = auth only, no encrypt)
  2. Proxy IDs must mirror: local 10.1.0.0/16 <-> 10.2.0.0/16
                            remote 10.2.0.0/16 <-> 10.1.0.0/16
  3. Tunnel mode wraps the ENTIRE original packet (gateway-to-gateway standard)
  4. SAs have short lifetimes -> rekey often; PFS adds fresh DH per rekey

Diagnosis cheat sheet:
  'no matching proposal' / stuck at MM_NO_STATE -> Phase 1: cipher/DH/lifetime/PSK mismatch
  Phase 1 UP (QM_IDLE) but no IPsec SA   -> Phase 2: proxy-ID or transform-set mismatch
  Works, then breaks behind new NAT       -> enable NAT-T (UDP 4500 wraps ESP proto 50)
example.walkthrough: Think of Phase 1 as two spies verifying identities and agreeing on a codebook over 6 messages; Phase 2 is them using that codebook to agree on how each actual message gets sealed. Phase 1 failures are always about the five proposal elements (encryption, hash, DH group, lifetime, authentication). Phase 2 failures are about what gets encrypted: the transform set and the mirrored proxy IDs.

pitfalls: PSK typo: proposals match on paper but the invisible PSK differs — most common Phase 1 failure
Proxy IDs not mirrored: local 10.1->10.2 vs remote 10.2->10.9 kills Phase 2 every time
Forgetting NAT-T: ESP (IP proto 50) has no ports, so NAT drops it unless wrapped in UDP 4500
lessons.title: IPsec Site-to-Site: IKE Phase 1 vs Phase 2
lessons.try_it: On a lab firewall pair, intentionally mismatch the DH group, watch Phase 1 fail, then fix it; next mismatch the interesting-traffic ACL and confirm Phase 1 succeeds while Phase 2 fails.

concepts: A client VPN connects one traveling laptop to the office network over the internet — a long encrypted hallway back to your desk — but not all hallways are built the same. This lesson compares the protocols (the construction methods): IKEv2/IPsec, SSTP, SSL-style VPNs, and WireGuard on the modern side, versus legacy PPTP/L2TP which you must recognize so you can refuse them (their encryption is broken). It also covers tunnel policy: split tunnel (only office traffic uses the hallway; YouTube goes direct) versus full tunnel (everything goes through the office — slower, but inspectable). Logic Check — here's the reasoning: every protocol is a different answer to 'hostile network between the laptop and the office' — SSTP wins where firewalls block everything but HTTPS (port 443), IKEv2 wins where phones roam between networks (it re-establishes in seconds), and PPTP loses everywhere because its encryption was broken years ago and 'encrypted with broken crypto' is worse than knowing you're exposed.

WHAT: Client VPN protocols connect individual remote devices (laptops on hotel Wi-Fi) back to the corporate network, unlike site-to-site tunnels that connect whole offices. The main options: SSTP (Secure Socket Tunneling Protocol: VPN traffic wrapped in HTTPS on TCP port 443), IKEv2 (Internet Key Exchange version 2, with MOBIKE for seamless Wi-Fi-to-cellular handoffs), L2TP/IPsec (Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol inside IPsec: needs UDP 500, UDP 4500, UDP 1701, plus ESP), and OpenVPN (flexible, but needs a third-party client install). Tunnel policy is the separate decision of what goes through the tunnel: full tunnel sends everything, split tunnel sends only corporate subnets.

HOW: SSTP encapsulates PPP frames inside TLS on TCP 443, so to any firewall or captive portal it looks like ordinary HTTPS web traffic. Port 443 is the one port virtually every network leaves open outbound, which is why SSTP connects from hotels and airports where everything else fails. IKEv2 re-establishes its security association in milliseconds when the network changes (MOBIKE: Mobility and Multihoming Protocol), so the VPN survives walking from Wi-Fi to cellular. L2TP/IPsec double-encapsulates (L2TP inside IPsec inside UDP) and needs four separate things to survive NAT and egress filtering: UDP 500 for IKE, UDP 4500 for NAT-T, UDP 1701 for L2TP, and ESP protocol 50. That is why it fails about 60% of the time on hostile networks. Full tunnel routes 0.0.0.0/0 (the default route, meaning 'everything') through the VPN; split tunnel routes only corporate prefixes like 10.0.0.0/8 plus internal DNS, and the rest goes direct to the internet.

WHY: Pick the wrong protocol and your road warriors simply cannot work from hotels. L2TP's four-port requirement is a connectivity tax paid in helpdesk tickets. PPTP (Point-to-Point Tunneling Protocol) must never be deployed at all: its MS-CHAPv2 authentication is cryptographically broken, so 'temporary PPTP' is permanent insecurity. The tunnel-policy decision is a genuine trade-off, not a right answer. Full tunnel lets the corporate firewall inspect everything but backhauls all traffic (180ms Zoom calls, gateway scaling costs). Split tunnel performs beautifully but makes the laptop a dual-homed bridge: malware arriving via the direct internet path can pivot across the VPN into the LAN. That is why split tunnel demands enforced EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) and host firewall posture on the endpoint.

WHEN: Default to IKEv2 for managed fleets (native on Windows and macOS, MOBIKE resilience) and SSTP as the fallback for hostile networks: Windows-native, no extra client. The wrong way is standardizing on L2TP/IPsec for travelers because 'we have always used it,' then acting surprised at the hotel-Wi-Fi failure reports. The wrong way on policy is enabling split tunnel for performance with zero endpoint controls: you have traded latency for a pivot path into the datacenter. The alternative is always-on VPN (the tunnel establishes before logon, so Group Policy and security tools work remotely) combined with full tunnel for high-risk users and split tunnel for everyone else. Policy can be per-group, not one-size-fits-all.

CONNECTS: Client VPNs authenticate against Active Directory (the FSMO/AD lessons: a dead PDC Emulator breaks VPN logons) and rely on DNS to resolve internal names once connected (the DNS troubleshooting lesson). The firewall ACL lesson governs what VPN clients may reach once inside, and the hardening lesson's endpoint controls (Defender, Credential Guard) are what make split tunnel defensible. Site-to-site IPsec from the previous lesson is the same crypto family applied to gateways instead of laptops.
SSTP (TCP 443)
IKEv2/MOBIKE
L2TP/IPsec ports
OpenVPN
Split vs full tunnel
Always-on VPN
