Protocol            Ports needed              Notes
-----------------   ------------------------  --------------------------------
SSTP              TCP 443                 PPP over TLS; looks like HTTPS,
                                              built into Windows, best for
                                              hostile hotel/airport networks
IKEv2             UDP 500, UDP 4500,      MOBIKE = seamless Wi-Fi/cellular
                  ESP proto 50            handoff; Windows/macOS native
L2TP/IPsec        UDP 500, 4500, 1701,    Double encapsulation overhead;
                  ESP proto 50            fragile behind strict NAT/firewalls
OpenVPN           UDP 1194 (or TCP 443)   Very flexible; needs client install

Tunnel policy decision:
  Full tunnel:  0.0.0.0/0 -> VPN. All traffic inspected by corp firewall.
                Cost: backhaul latency, gateway scaling.
  Split tunnel: 10.0.0.0/8 + corp DNS -> VPN; internet direct.
                Cost: endpoint bridges untrusted internet + LAN (pivot risk).
                Mitigate: always-on VPN + enforced EDR/host firewall posture.
example.walkthrough: Pick the client protocol by the network it must survive: SSTP over TCP 443 passes almost anywhere because it looks like HTTPS, while L2TP/IPsec needs four different UDP ports plus ESP and dies on hotel Wi-Fi. IKEv2 is the modern default for managed fleets thanks to MOBIKE reconnection. Tunnel policy is a risk call: full tunnel centralizes inspection at the cost of performance; split tunnel performs but makes the laptop a bridge — compensate with endpoint posture enforcement.

pitfalls: Deploying L2TP/IPsec for road warriors: UDP 500/4500/1701 + ESP rarely all survive hotel NAT
PPTP for anything: MS-CHAPv2 is broken — never deploy, even for 'temporary' access
Split tunnel without endpoint controls: the pivot risk is real, not theoretical
lessons.title: Client VPN Protocols and Tunnel Policy
lessons.try_it: From a phone hotspot, connect with SSTP and with L2TP/IPsec; note which succeeds. Then run tracert to an internal host and an internet host with split tunnel on and off, and compare paths.

lessons.title: Virtual switches: External, Internal, Private
concepts: In Hyper-V (Microsoft's hypervisor), virtual machines don't plug into real cables — they plug into virtual switches, software imitations of network switches that decide who each VM can talk to. External bridges to a physical NIC (Network Interface Card), so the VM joins the real network and the internet; Internal lets VMs talk to each other AND the host, but never the outside world (a lab with a door to the host); Private seals VMs off so they talk only to each other — a terrarium. Picking the wrong one is the #1 reason a new VM 'has no network,' so this lesson makes the choice mechanical. Logic Check — here's the reasoning: the switch type IS the VM's network boundary decision made before any firewall rule is considered — External says 'this VM is a citizen of the real network,' Internal says 'lab machines that may talk to the host,' Private says 'quarantine: these VMs must never touch anything real' — pick the boundary first, then configure within it.

WHAT: A Hyper-V virtual switch is a software switch inside the host that connects virtual machines to networks: the virtual equivalent of the physical switch on your rack. There are three types. External binds to a physical NIC (network interface card) and gives VMs real LAN and internet access. Internal creates a network shared between the host and its VMs only. Private creates a network for VM-to-VM traffic that the host itself cannot touch. The malware-analysis VM gets Private, production VMs get External, and the host stays reachable through management OS sharing.

HOW: When you create an External switch (New-VMSwitch bound to the physical NIC), Hyper-V inserts itself between the NIC and the host's TCP/IP stack: the physical NIC becomes the switch's uplink, and the host gets a virtual NIC (vEthernet) on the switch instead. The -AllowManagementOS flag (management operating system: the host OS itself) set to true keeps that host vNIC alive so you can still RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) to the host. Set it false and the host loses its network the moment the switch is created. An Internal switch creates a vEthernet adapter on the host plus virtual ports for VMs: host and VMs ping each other, but nothing reaches the physical LAN. A Private switch creates virtual ports only, with no host vNIC at all: VMs talk to each other and the host is blind to them, which is true isolation.

WHY: One physical NIC can host only one External switch. Try to bind a second and Hyper-V refuses, because the NIC is already consumed as an uplink. Forgetting -AllowManagementOS strands the host with no management path, turning a remote host into a box that needs a datacenter visit. Choosing Internal for the malware VM is the dangerous almost-right answer: Internal still lets the VM reach the host OS, so a VM-escape or a misconfigured share bridges your malware lab straight into the hypervisor. Only Private gives the guarantee that no host traffic exists.

WHEN: External for anything needing the LAN or internet; Internal for host-to-VM lab networks (a domain controller and a client that only the host touches); Private for malware analysis, forensics, or any workload that must not see the host. The wrong way is putting the malware VM on Internal 'because it is not External.' That is isolation theater that still exposes the host. The wrong way at the other end is giving every VM an External switch port when only some need LAN access: you have widened the blast radius for no reason. The alternative is VLAN tagging on the virtual switch port (Set-VMNetworkAdapterVlan) to trunk multiple VLANs into VMs through one External switch. That is how the VLAN lesson meets virtualization.

CONNECTS: Virtual switches are where the VLAN lesson goes virtual: trunk ports and access VLANs exist on vSwitches too. VM network adapters ride on these switches, so the migration lesson's live migrations carry the VM's switch attachments with them to the destination host. The firewall and hardening lessons apply at the host vNIC: the host's virtual adapter needs the same Defender Firewall profiles as any server, because it is a network interface like any other.
External switch
Internal switch
Private switch
Management OS sharing
One NIC, one external switch

example.code:
New-VMSwitch -Name "ExternalLAN" -NetAdapterName "Ethernet" -AllowManagementOS $true
Get-VMSwitch | Select-Object Name, SwitchType
example.walkthrough: This creates an External switch bound to the physical NIC named Ethernet. Virtual machines attached to it get real LAN and internet access, and -AllowManagementOS $true keeps the host reachable through a virtual NIC on the same switch. Dropping that flag would cut the host off the network the moment the switch is created.

pitfalls: Binding a second External switch to the same physical NIC — one NIC supports one external switch
Forgetting -AllowManagementOS $true and stranding the host with no management network
Using an Internal switch for a VM that must be isolated from the host (Internal still allows host-to-VM traffic — that is what Private is for)
lessons.try_it: On a lab host, create an Internal switch with New-VMSwitch, attach a VM, assign both sides IPs on the same subnet, and ping the host's vEthernet adapter. Then move the VM to a Private switch and watch the ping fail — that is isolation you can see.

lessons.title: Checkpoints done right: types, chains, and merging
concepts: A Hyper-V checkpoint is a save point for a virtual machine — like a video-game save before a boss fight: if the patch goes wrong, you reload. But checkpoints are NOT backups (they live on the same disk as the VM, so a dead disk kills both), and they form chains — each checkpoint freezes a differencing disk, and long chains slow the VM while devouring disk space. This lesson covers the two types (Standard checkpoints freeze memory state; Production checkpoints are application-consistent and backup-safe), why chains must be merged (folded back into the main disk), and the checkpoint sprawl that fills host disks at 2 AM. Logic Check — here's the reasoning: a checkpoint is cheap to create (just start a differencing disk) and expensive to keep (every write doubles into the chain, reads traverse the whole chain) — which is why the correct lifecycle is create → test → merge-or-delete within hours, and why 'checkpoint as backup' fails: it shares the disk, the host, and the fate of the VM.

WHAT: A Hyper-V checkpoint is a point-in-time snapshot of a VM: Hyper-V freezes the parent VHDX (virtual hard disk) and starts writing all new changes to a differencing disk (an AVHDX file), while optionally saving the VM's memory state. A standard checkpoint captures crash-consistent state, like yanking the power cord and rebooting. A production checkpoint uses VSS (Volume Shadow Copy Service, Windows' application-aware snapshot API) inside the guest so SQL Server and Active Directory flush their buffers first. It is an undo button for changes, not a backup: it lives on the same storage as the VM.

HOW: Checkpoint-VM creates the checkpoint: the current VHDX becomes read-only, a new AVHDX differencing disk captures every subsequent write, and for production checkpoints the Hyper-V integration services trigger VSS inside the guest so applications quiesce (settle into a consistent state) before the capture. Restore-VMCheckpoint discards the AVHDX changes and reverts to the frozen parent: the file you created after the checkpoint vanishes, because those writes lived only in the differencing disk. Remove-VMCheckpoint deletes the checkpoint and merges the AVHDX data back into the parent VHDX. The merge copies every changed block, takes time proportional to the AVHDX size, and needs free disk space to complete. A chain of twelve checkpoints is twelve nested AVHDX files, each differencing off the last, and every read may walk the chain.

WHY: Treating checkpoints as backups is the classic junior-admin disaster: the AVHDX chain sits on the same disks as the parent VHDX, so when the host's RAID dies, every 'backup' dies with it. A backup must be on separate storage to be a backup. Letting chains grow for weeks bloats storage (twelve 15 to 40 GB AVHDX files), slows the VM (every read may walk the chain), and turns the eventual merge into a hours-long, space-hungry operation. Resizing a VHDX or running out of disk with an unmerged chain can corrupt the chain outright, which is why the resize operation demands a clean chain first. Standard checkpoints on a domain controller can cause USN rollback (Update Sequence Number: AD's replication watermark going backwards, which breaks replication); production checkpoints with VSS exist for exactly this.

WHEN: Take a checkpoint before patches, upgrades, and config changes: the 30-second undo button that makes change windows safe. Merge or delete checkpoints within days, never weeks. The wrong way is the 'nightly checkpoint as backup strategy': a month of AVHDX files, critical disk space, and zero actual recoverability if the host dies. The wrong way on type is standard checkpoints on a domain controller or SQL Server: use production checkpoints with VSS for application-consistent captures. The alternative for real protection is actual backups (the SQL backup and 3-2-1 lessons). Checkpoints are change management, backups are disaster recovery, and they are not interchangeable.

CONNECTS: Checkpoints interact with the VHDX resize lesson (no resize with an open chain) and the replica lesson (replication and checkpoints are separate mechanisms: Replica copies to another host, checkpoints stay local). The backup strategy lesson is the philosophical twin: 3-2-1 and test restores are what checkpoints pretend to be. And the change-record lesson's rollback section is where you document 'checkpoint taken, merge after validation' as the formal backout plan.
Standard checkpoint
Production checkpoint (VSS)
AVHDX differencing chain
Merging on delete
Checkpoints are not backups

example.code:
Checkpoint-VM -Name "WEB01" -SnapshotName "PrePatch" -CheckpointType Production
# ... test the patch, then either roll back or clean up:
Restore-VMCheckpoint -VMName "WEB01" -Name "PrePatch" -Confirm:$false
Remove-VMCheckpoint -VMName "WEB01" -Name "PrePatch"
example.walkthrough: The first line takes a production checkpoint, which uses Volume Shadow Copy inside the guest for an application-consistent capture instead of just saving memory state. Restore-VMCheckpoint rolls the VM back to that point. Remove-VMCheckpoint deletes the checkpoint and merges its AVHDX differencing disk back into the parent VHDX — the merge takes time and needs free disk space.

pitfalls: Treating checkpoints as backups — they live on the same storage as the VM, so host loss kills them too
Letting checkpoint chains grow for weeks: AVHDX bloat, slower VMs, and long painful merges
Resizing a VHDX or running out of disk space with an unmerged chain in place
lessons.try_it: Checkpoint a lab VM, create a file inside the guest, restore the checkpoint, and confirm the file is gone. Then delete the checkpoint and watch the AVHDX file merge away in the VM's folder.

lessons.title: Replica, clustering, and moving running VMs
concepts: One physical host is a single point of failure for every VM on it — this lesson is the three answers to 'the host died, now what?' Hyper-V Replica keeps a scheduled copy of a VM on a second host, like a stunt double rehearsing offstage; you fail over manually when disaster strikes. Failover clustering groups hosts so VMs automatically restart on a surviving node — the understudy steps onstage without being asked. Live migration moves a RUNNING VM between hosts with zero downtime — the actor walks to a new stage mid-performance — and the exam-relevant distinction is which mechanism is automatic versus manual, and which needs shared storage. Logic Check — here's the reasoning: each answers a different failure with a different cost — Replica (cheap, manual, minutes behind) answers 'the building is gone,' clustering (expensive, automatic, seconds of downtime) answers 'a host died,' live migration (zero downtime) answers 'I need to service this host Tuesday' — match the mechanism to the failure, not the marketing.

WHAT: Hyper-V Replica is asynchronous VM replication to a second host: every 30 seconds, 5 minutes, or 15 minutes, the primary sends changed blocks to the replica, which keeps a crash-consistent copy ready to boot. A failover cluster is a group of Hyper-V hosts sharing storage (Cluster Shared Volumes, called CSVs: disks visible to all nodes at once) that can run each other's VMs; quorum (the voting system, usually a witness disk or file share) decides who stays authoritative if nodes lose contact. Live Migration moves a running VM between hosts with no downtime; Storage Migration moves its disks between storage while it runs; Quick Migration pauses it briefly. Together: how VMs survive host failures and maintenance.

HOW: Replica works at the VHDX block level: the primary tracks changed blocks, and on each interval ships them to the replica host, which applies them to its copy. The interval you choose (300 seconds = 5 minutes) IS your RPO (Recovery Point Objective, the maximum data age you will lose), because an unplanned failover boots the replica as of the last successful replication. Failover itself is Start-VMFailover on the replica side. A planned failover from a live primary uses -Prepare for zero loss; you cannot plan a failover from a dead host. Live Migration copies the VM's memory pages to the destination host while it keeps running, then transfers the last dirty pages in a sub-second stun. The VM never stops, which requires the hosts to share storage via CSVs or use shared-nothing SMB 3 migration. Failback after the primary recovers is Reverse-VMReplication, flipping the direction.

WHY: Without Replica, a dead host means restoring from backup: hours of RTO (Recovery Time Objective, how long until service returns) versus minutes to boot a replica. Expecting zero data loss from Replica is the dangerous misunderstanding: asynchronous means the replica is always one interval behind, so a 5-minute interval can lose 5 minutes of transactions. If the business needs zero loss, it needs synchronous storage replication, not Hyper-V Replica. Quick Migration's brief pause is fine for file servers and fatal for a latency-sensitive app; knowing which migration keeps memory running uninterrupted is the difference between a maintenance window and an outage.

WHEN: Use Live Migration to evacuate a host for firmware updates with zero downtime; use Storage Migration to move VHDX files off a dying SAN (storage area network) LUN (logical unit number, a slice of SAN storage) while the VM serves users. The wrong way is 'live migrating' by shutting VMs down and copying VHDX files manually: hours of outage for what takes seconds. The wrong way on Replica is setting a 15-minute interval on a database and promising the business 'we will not lose anything.' The RPO is 15 minutes; say it out loud. The alternative to Replica for zero-loss is guest-level clustering (SQL Always On availability groups) or storage-level synchronous replication: more complex, genuinely zero data loss, and the right answer when the RPO must be zero.

CONNECTS: Replica's RPO/RTO vocabulary is the backup strategy lesson's language applied to VMs: same concepts, different mechanism. Live Migration depends on the virtual switch lesson (the VM's network attachments must exist on the destination) and the storage lesson (CSVs live on shared RAID). The SQL backup lesson covers the application-consistent alternative: for databases, log shipping plus Replica is belt and suspenders, because Replica alone gives you a crash-consistent VM, not a transactionally clean database.
Hyper-V Replica intervals (30s/5m/15m)
Primary / Replica / Extended replica
Live Migration
Quick vs Storage Migration
Quorum and Cluster Shared Volumes

example.code:
Get-VMReplication -VMName "APP01" | Select-Object State, Health, FrequencySec
Move-VM -Name "APP01" -DestinationHost "HOST03"
example.walkthrough: Get-VMReplication shows the replica state, health, and FrequencySec — the replication interval in seconds, which is your recovery point objective (300 = up to 5 minutes of data loss). Move-VM performs a live migration of the running VM to another host with no downtime, provided the hosts are clustered with shared storage (or SMB 3 shared-nothing migration).

pitfalls: Expecting zero data loss from Hyper-V Replica — the RPO equals the replication interval
Using Quick Migration (save/pause, brief outage) when the task requires zero downtime
Attempting Live Migration without cluster validation, quorum, or reachable shared storage
lessons.try_it: Run Get-VMReplication on a lab replica pair, read FrequencySec, and convert it to an RPO in minutes. Then live-migrate a running lab VM between two hosts and keep a continuous ping running to prove zero packet loss.

lessons.title: Backup, restore, and recovery models
concepts: SQL Server is Microsoft's database engine — the vault where applications keep their data — and this lesson is about the only question that matters at 3 AM: 'can we get the data back, and how much will we lose?' The recovery model is the database's promise about the future: Simple (lose everything since the last backup — fine for throwaway data), Full (every transaction logged, so you can restore to any second — the price is log maintenance), Bulk-logged (the middle child). You'll learn backup chains (full + differential + log, applied IN ORDER like stacking transparencies) and the point-in-time restore that rewinds to 'two minutes before the intern deleted the table.' Logic Check — here's the reasoning: the recovery model is a contract about the future written in the present — Full says 'I promise you can rewind to any second, and I pay for it with log maintenance forever,' Simple says 'I promise nothing between backups, and I pay nothing' — pick the model by asking the business how much data loss is acceptable, then engineer to that number.

WHAT: SQL Server backup is a chain: a FULL backup copies the whole database, a DIFFERENTIAL copies everything changed since the last full, and a LOG backup copies the transaction log (the sequential record of every committed change) since the last log backup. The recovery model decides what chains are possible. FULL allows log backups and point-in-time restore. SIMPLE truncates the log automatically and allows only full and differential restores (no point-in-time). BULK-LOGGED is FULL with minimal logging for bulk operations. Point-in-time restore replays the chain forward to an exact moment: 'recover to 10:16, one minute before the bad DELETE.'

HOW: The restore replays backups in LSN order (Log Sequence Number: the log's internal ordering stamp, which guarantees every change applies exactly once in the right sequence). Restore the FULL with WITH NORECOVERY (leaves the database in the 'restoring' state, ready for the next backup in the chain), then the most recent DIFFERENTIAL with NORECOVERY, then each LOG backup in order with NORECOVERY, and the final log backup with WITH RECOVERY plus STOPAT = '2026-10-07 10:16'. STOPAT tells SQL Server to roll forward only to that timestamp, then RECOVERY brings the database online and discards the uncommitted tail. The 15-minute log backup interval is why you can hit 10:16: your recovery granularity is never finer than your log backup frequency. SIMPLE model breaks this entirely: no log backups exist, so the only restore points are the full and differential times.

WHY: Without chain discipline, the Wednesday 10:17 DELETE with no WHERE clause is permanent data loss: the most common real-world restore scenario, caused by a human, not hardware. Restoring WITH RECOVERY too early closes the chain: the database comes online and the remaining log backups can never be applied, so your 10:16 target becomes unreachable and you are stuck at the full-backup time. Leaving a production database in SIMPLE 'because the log was growing' trades a disk-space annoyance for the inability to recover to any point between backups. When the bad delete happens at 10:17 and your last full was 02:00, you have lost eight hours of orders.

WHEN: Run FULL recovery on any database where point-in-time matters (orders, finance, ticketing); schedule log backups at the interval matching your RPO: 15-minute logs for a 15-minute data-loss tolerance. The wrong way is FULL recovery model with no log backup job. The log grows forever until the disk fills and the database stops, which is worse than SIMPLE. The wrong way reversed is SIMPLE on the orders database because 'backups are simpler,' then explaining to the business why Wednesday's orders are gone. The alternative: for read-only or easily rebuilt databases (a data warehouse reloaded nightly from source), SIMPLE is genuinely correct. Match the model to the data's value, not to habit.

CONNECTS: This is the database-flavored twin of the 3-2-1 backup strategy lesson: same RPO/RTO thinking, applied to transaction logs instead of files. The RAID lesson decides what storage the database lives on (RAID 10 for the log volume, because log writes are sequential and parity penalties hurt). The SQL security lesson's service accounts matter here too: the backup job runs as a service account, and a password change that breaks the SQL Server service (that lesson's scenario) also breaks the backup chain silently.
FULL / DIFFERENTIAL / LOG backups
Simple vs Full vs Bulk-Logged
Backup chain in LSN order
WITH NORECOVERY vs WITH RECOVERY
STOPAT point-in-time restore

example.walkthrough: The first two statements take a full backup and then a transaction log backup — only possible because Orders is in the FULL recovery model. The restore replays them in chain order: the full goes down WITH NORECOVERY so the database stays in the restoring state, and the log backup applies on top with STOPAT rolling forward to exactly 10:16 before WITH RECOVERY brings the database online.

pitfalls: Leaving a database in SIMPLE recovery and then expecting point-in-time restores — SIMPLE cannot take log backups
Restoring WITH RECOVERY too early, which breaks the chain and blocks the remaining log backups
Skipping the differential in the chain and trying to apply log backups straight onto an older full
lessons.try_it: On a test database in FULL recovery: take a full backup, insert a row, take a log backup, delete the row, then restore the chain with STOPAT set to just before the delete. Verify the row is back.

lessons.title: Security: logins, users, and roles
concepts: SQL Server has two doors and beginners confuse them: a login is permission to ENTER the server building (authenticated at the server level), while a user is permission to enter a specific ROOM — a database — inside it (mapped from a login). Roles are bundles of permissions ('db_datareader can read everything in this database') so you grant the bundle instead of hand-picking 200 checkboxes per person. This lesson teaches the login → user → role chain, the principle of least privilege (nobody gets more access than the job needs — the #1 audit finding in the industry), and how to diagnose the infamous 'Login failed for user' error 18456. Logic Check — here's the reasoning: separating login (who are you) from user (what can you touch in THIS database) means one identity maps to different permissions per database — and roles exist because granting 200 individual permissions per person guarantees mistakes, while granting one tested bundle ('db_datareader') makes access reviewable — least privilege isn't philosophy, it's error reduction.

WHAT: SQL Server security has two layers: a LOGIN is a server-level principal, the credential that gets you through the front door of the SQL Server instance; a USER is a database-level principal, the identity that decides what you can touch inside one specific database. Authentication is either Windows auth (your Active Directory account, no separate password) or SQL auth (a username and password stored in SQL Server, requiring mixed mode). Permissions are granted through ROLES: server roles like sysadmin open the whole instance, database roles like db_datareader and db_datawriter open one database. Least privilege means granting the smallest role that covers the job.

HOW: You create the front door first: CREATE LOGIN [DOMAIN\ana] FROM WINDOWS registers her AD account at the server level. At this point she can connect but sees nothing. Then inside the Reporting database you run CREATE USER [ana] FOR LOGIN [DOMAIN\ana], mapping the login to a database identity: now she exists inside Reporting but has no permissions. Then ALTER ROLE db_datareader ADD MEMBER [ana] and ALTER ROLE db_datawriter ADD MEMBER [ana] grant read and write within Reporting only; she still cannot see or touch any other database, and she has no server roles beyond public. Hardening the instance means disabling sa (ALTER LOGIN sa DISABLE): sa is the built-in superuser every attacker tries first. Error 18456 state codes diagnose failures: state 5 is a bad username, state 8 is a bad password (the classic post-rotation mismatch when the app's connection string still holds the old password).

WHY: Without the login/user split, every permission would be instance-wide: there would be no way to say 'read Reporting but not Finance,' and the only options would be 'everything' or 'nothing.' Granting sysadmin 'to make it work' hands one developer the keys to every database on the instance, including the ability to read payroll and drop production: a breach or a mistake with blast radius equal to the whole server. Leaving sa enabled with a weak password is leaving the master key under the doormat: it is the first account in every brute-force dictionary, and a compromised sa bypasses every database-level permission you have carefully built.

WHEN: Default to Windows auth: no passwords to rotate, no connection-string secrets, and disabling the AD account instantly kills database access. Use SQL auth only when the client cannot do Windows auth (non-domain apps, some third-party tools). The wrong way is SQL auth everywhere 'for consistency': you have just created dozens of passwords to rotate and leak. The wrong way on roles is db_owner 'because she might need to create a table someday.' db_owner can drop the database; grant db_ddladmin if she needs schema changes, and revisit. The alternative for cross-database needs is contained database users or application roles, but start with the login to user to role chain. It is the model interviewers expect you to draw from memory.

CONNECTS: This is Active Directory security thinking applied to SQL: the least-privilege principle is identical to the Domain Admins sprawl lesson (47 members is the same sin as sysadmin for everyone). Service accounts here connect to the hardening lesson's gMSA guidance (group Managed Service Accounts: AD-managed, auto-rotated, no human-known password), so password rotations never break the SQL Server service again. And the backup lesson's backup jobs run under these logins: least privilege applies to service accounts too, not just humans.
Login (server) vs User (database)
Windows auth vs SQL auth (mixed mode)
Server roles vs database roles
sa hardening
Least privilege

example.walkthrough: CREATE LOGIN registers the Windows account at the server level so it can connect. Inside the Reporting database, CREATE USER maps that login to a database principal, and the two ALTER ROLE statements grant reader and writer rights scoped to Reporting only. Disabling sa removes the most attacked account on the instance — a key hardening step alongside strong passwords and mixed-mode-only-when-needed.

pitfalls: Granting sysadmin when a database role would do — sysadmin owns the whole instance
Leaving sa enabled with a weak or default password
Creating the login but forgetting CREATE USER, then wondering why the database is inaccessible
lessons.try_it: Create a test SQL login, map it to a user in exactly one database with db_datareader, log in as that user, and prove a SELECT works there but fails in another database.

concepts: RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks) is the art of combining several physical disks so they behave as one — trading some capacity for speed, survival, or both. Think of it as teamwork strategies: RAID 0 stripes data across disks for pure speed with ZERO safety net (one disk dies, everything dies); RAID 1 mirrors two disks (every byte written twice — half the capacity, survives one failure); RAID 5 stripes data plus parity math so ANY one disk can die and be rebuilt (you lose one disk's worth of capacity); RAID 6 survives TWO dead disks; RAID 10 mirrors then stripes (fast AND safe, at half capacity). This lesson is the capacity math behind how many terabytes you actually get, and which level fits databases versus archives. Logic Check — here's the reasoning: every RAID level answers which failure you are willing to pay for: RAID 0 pays nothing and survives nothing (speed only), RAID 1 pays half its capacity to survive one disk, RAID 5 pays one disk to survive one disk with better capacity, RAID 6 pays two disks because rebuilds on huge modern disks take so long a second failure during rebuild is likely — the level is a bet on which failure you'll meet.

WHAT: RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks) combines multiple physical disks into one logical volume for speed, redundancy, or both. RAID 0 stripes data across disks (fast, zero redundancy: one disk dies, everything dies). RAID 1 mirrors two disks (simple, 50% capacity overhead). RAID 5 stripes data with distributed parity (usable capacity = (n minus 1) times the smallest disk, survives any 1 failure). RAID 6 uses double parity (usable = (n minus 2) times the smallest disk, survives any 2). RAID 10 is a stripe of mirrors (usable = (n/2) times the smallest disk, best write performance of any redundant level). Parity is the clever bit: extra data computed from the stripe with XOR math that lets the controller reconstruct a dead disk's contents.

HOW: On every write to a RAID 5 stripe, the controller must read the old data, read the old parity, write the new data, and write the new parity: four I/Os for one write, the famous write penalty (RAID 6 does six: double parity means double the penalty). RAID 10 has no parity math: a write goes to both mirrors simultaneously, so it delivers the best write throughput of any redundant level, and a rebuild is just copying the surviving mirror: fast and low-risk. When a disk dies in RAID 5, the controller reconstructs each missing block on the fly by XORing the surviving data with parity. If disks hold A, B, and A-XOR-B, losing A means A = B XOR (A-XOR-B). That reconstruction reads every surviving disk end-to-end, which is why rebuild windows on multi-terabyte disks stretch for days, and why a second failure or an unreadable sector (URE: Unrecoverable Read Error, a bad spot the disk cannot read) during those days kills a RAID 5 array.

WHY: Without redundancy, a single disk failure is total data loss. RAID exists because disks are the most failure-prone component in a server and 'restore from backup' takes hours the business does not have. RAID 5 on large disks is the trap: the parity math that saves you on 500 GB disks becomes a multi-day rebuild on 12 TB disks, and the chance of hitting a URE during a full-array read grows with disk size. The array most likely to need its redundancy is the least likely to survive using it. RAID 0 for production data is not a trade-off, it is an absence of a plan: it doubles your failure rate (two disks, either can kill you) for speed you could get from SSDs.

WHEN: RAID 10 for write-heavy and latency-sensitive workloads: database data and log volumes, virtualization hosts. The lab's SQL log-ingestion VM on 8 SSDs wants RAID 10 (4 TB usable, no write penalty, fast rebuilds). RAID 6 for bulk capacity where writes are light: file archives, backup targets (12 TB usable on 5x4TB, survives 2). RAID 1 for simple two-disk OS volumes. The wrong way is RAID 5 for the database because 'it gives 7 TB instead of 4.' The DBA gets capacity and pays in write latency and rebuild risk. The wrong way reversed is RAID 10 for a write-once media archive: you have burned half your disks for write performance nobody uses. The alternative is skipping RAID for the OS and using it only for data, or using Storage Spaces or VSAN, but the parity-versus-mirror math is identical whatever the brand.

CONNECTS: RAID is the physical foundation the whole course stands on: Hyper-V hosts need RAID 10 under their Cluster Shared Volumes (the clustering lesson) because VM performance dies on parity write penalties; SQL Server log volumes demand RAID 10 for the same reason (the backup chain lesson's log backups are only as fast as the log disk); and the 3-2-1 backup lesson exists because RAID is not a backup. RAID survives disk failure, not ransomware, fire, or accidental deletion. The monitoring story closes the loop: a RAID controller that emails nobody about a dead disk is redundancy you cannot see degrading.
RAID 0 striping (speed, no redundancy)
RAID 1 mirroring (simple, 50% overhead)
RAID 5 parity (n-1 capacity, 1-disk survival)
RAID 6 double parity (n-2 capacity, 2-disk survival)
RAID 10 stripe-of-mirrors (best performance + redundancy)
Rebuild windows and URE risk on large disks

THEORY: RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks) spreads data across disks so you get more speed, more usable space, or survival of disk failures. Parity is the clever part: instead of mirroring every byte (100% overhead), RAID 5 computes one parity block per stripe using XOR (exclusive-or) — a bitwise operation where the output bit is 1 if an odd number of input bits are 1. XOR has a magical property: if you know the parity and all surviving data blocks, you can reconstruct the missing block (P = D1 XOR D2 XOR D3, so D3 = D1 XOR D2 XOR P). That is why one disk's worth of capacity buys survival of any ONE disk failure — the parity is distributed across all disks so no single disk is a bottleneck. The write penalty exists because parity must stay consistent: changing one data block means the old parity is now wrong, and the controller cannot recompute it without knowing the old values — hence read old data + read old parity + write new data + write new parity = 4 disk I/Os per single write (RAID 5). RAID 6 keeps two independent parities (P and Q, computed with different math) so any TWO disks can die; updating both parities costs 6 I/Os. RAID 10 just mirrors stripes, so a write goes to two disks = penalty 2, and RAID 0 stripes with no redundancy = penalty 1.

WORKED EXAMPLE: Worked 1 — capacity: 4 x 2 TB disks in RAID 5. RAID 5 usable = (n - 1) x disk size, because the distributed parity consumes the equivalent of exactly one disk. (4 - 1) x 2 TB = 3 x 2 = 6 TB usable. Parity overhead = 1/4 = 25%. WRONG WAY: answering 8 TB (n x size) forgets the parity disk entirely; answering 4 TB confuses RAID 5 with RAID 10 mirroring. Check against RAID 6 on the same disks: (4 - 2) x 2 = 4 TB, overhead 2/4 = 50% — the second parity disk costs you another 2 TB but buys survival of two simultaneous failures.

Worked 2 — write penalty in IOPS. An 8-disk array of 15,000-RPM SAS drives, each ~180 IOPS (IOPS = input/output operations per second; a 15K drive does one random seek in ~2 ms plus transfer, so roughly 1/0.0055 s ≈ 180). Raw array IOPS = 8 x 180 = 1440. But every application WRITE costs penalty I/Os on the disks. RAID 5 effective write IOPS = 1440 / 4 = 360. RAID 10 effective write IOPS = 1440 / 2 = 720. So for a write-heavy database, RAID 10 delivers literally double the write throughput from identical disks — the math is why DBAs insist on RAID 10 for transaction logs. Reads are penalty-free on both (penalty 1), so this only governs writes.

Worked 3 — rebuild time estimate. A 2 TB disk fails in the RAID 5 array above and is replaced. The controller must read every surviving disk end-to-end and XOR-reconstruct the missing 2 TB onto the new disk. At a sustained 150 MB/s rebuild read speed: 2 TB = 2,000,000 MB (using decimal TB as drive vendors do). 2,000,000 / 150 = 13,333 seconds. 13,333 / 3600 = 3.7 hours — and that is the theoretical minimum with zero contention; with the array still serving production I/O, real rebuilds run 2-3x longer. This is the deep reason RAID 5 fell out of favor for large disks: during those 4-10 hours the array has zero redundancy left, and a second failure (or an unreadable sector — URE — on a surviving disk during the full-stripe read) kills the array. Bigger disks = longer rebuild window = higher risk, which is the mathematical argument for RAID 6 on anything above ~4 TB per disk.

PRACTICE: Six 4 TB disks in RAID 6: what is the usable capacity, how many disk failures can it survive, and what is the parity overhead percentage? | You have 8 disks at 180 IOPS each. Compare effective write IOPS for RAID 5 vs RAID 10 and explain which you would choose for a write-heavy SQL transaction log and why.

ANSWERS: Usable = (n - 2) x size = (6 - 2) x 4 TB = 4 x 4 = 16 TB. RAID 6 survives any TWO simultaneous disk failures (dual distributed parity). Parity overhead = 2/6 = 33.3%. WRONG WAY: (6 - 1) x 4 = 20 TB is the RAID 5 formula — RAID 6 always subtracts 2. Also note 16 TB here is less than the 20 TB RAID 5 would give on the same disks; the 4 TB difference is the price of the second parity disk. | Raw IOPS = 8 x 180 = 1440. RAID 5 write penalty is 4 (read old data, read old parity, write new data, write new parity — the parity cannot be recomputed without the old values), so effective write IOPS = 1440 / 4 = 360. RAID 10 write penalty is 2 (write to both mirrors), so 1440 / 2 = 720. Choose RAID 10 for the transaction log: identical disks, double the write throughput (720 vs 360), and faster rebuilds (copy a mirror vs XOR-reconstruct every stripe). The cost is capacity: RAID 10 usable = (8/2) x size vs RAID 5's (8-1) x size — you trade disk space for write speed and safety.

example.code:
# RAID capacity cheat-sheet computed in PowerShell
$n = 5; $diskTB = 4
"RAID 5  : {0} TB usable, survives 1 failure" -f (($n-1)*$diskTB)
"RAID 6  : {0} TB usable, survives 2 failures" -f (($n-2)*$diskTB)
"RAID 10 : {0} TB usable, survives 1 failure per mirror pair" -f (($n/2)*$diskTB)
# RAID 10 needs an even disk count n: usable = (n/2) * smallest disk
example.walkthrough: This snippet encodes the three parity/mirror formulas so you can sanity-check any interview whiteboard question: RAID 5 costs one disk, RAID 6 costs two, RAID 10 costs half your disks. Run it with different $n and $diskTB values until the formulas are muscle memory — interviewers love asking '8x2TB in RAID 6?' (answer: 12 TB, survives 2).

pitfalls: Saying RAID 5 'can lose 2 disks' — it cannot; a second failure during rebuild is fatal
Forgetting RAID 10 needs an EVEN number of disks and gives only 50% usable capacity
Recommending RAID 0 for anything production — striping has zero redundancy
lessons.title: RAID Levels: Capacity Math and When to Use Each
lessons.try_it: On paper: a NAS has 6x3TB drives. Compute usable capacity and failure survival for RAID 5, RAID 6, and RAID 10. Then verify with the PowerShell snippet above. (Answers: RAID 5 = 15 TB/1 disk; RAID 6 = 12 TB/2 disks; RAID 10 = 9 TB/1 per pair.)

concepts: Backups are worthless until proven restorable — this lesson is the strategy layer above the 'click backup' button. The 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies of data, on 2 different media types, with 1 copy offsite (because fire doesn't care about your RAID). RTO (Recovery Time Objective) = how LONG you may be down ('we must be back in 4 hours'); RPO (Recovery Point Objective) = how MUCH data you may lose ('we can lose at most 1 hour of transactions') — every backup schedule is just math serving these two numbers. You'll also learn backup chains (full → differential → incremental, and why restore order matters) and the uncomfortable truth the assessment loves: an untested backup is a rumor, not a recovery plan. Logic Check — here's the reasoning: 3-2-1 exists because failures are independent — disks die, buildings burn, regions flood, and one disaster must never take all copies — while RTO/RPO exist because 'back up everything constantly' is unaffordable, so the business states its pain tolerance in hours of downtime and minutes of data lost, and engineering converts it into a schedule with a price tag.

WHAT: The 3-2-1 rule: keep 3 copies of your data, on 2 different media types, with 1 copy offsite. Backup chains come in flavors: FULL copies everything; DIFFERENTIAL copies everything changed since the last full (restore needs full plus latest differential); INCREMENTAL copies everything changed since the last backup of any type (restore needs full plus every incremental in order: one corrupt middle link breaks the chain). RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is how much data loss you tolerate: '1 hour' means backups at least hourly. RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is how fast service must return: '4 hours' means your restore procedure must complete in 4 hours. The final rule: a backup you have never restored from is not a backup, it is a hope.

HOW: RPO drives backup frequency: a 1-hour RPO on a changing database means hourly transaction-log or incremental backups. Nightly fulls allow up to 24 hours of loss and fail the requirement outright. RTO drives restore speed and readiness: a 4-hour RTO means tested restore procedures, staged media, and hardware that can actually absorb the restore in 4 hours. You prove it by timing a real restore, not by estimating. The differential advantage: Friday's differential plus Sunday's full is a complete two-media restore, while incremental would need Sunday plus Monday plus Tuesday plus Wednesday plus Thursday plus Friday chained in order. The offsite copy must be genuinely separate: ransomware encrypts the NAS (network attached storage) too, so 'offsite' means offline, air-gapped, or immutable cloud storage the attacker cannot reach with your domain credentials. The proof step is a scheduled test restore into an isolated environment (so you do not clobber production), timed against the RTO, with the steps written into a DR (disaster recovery) runbook covering failover AND failback.

WHY: Without 3-2-1, one event takes everything: the cryptolocker that encrypts the primary NAS also encrypts the 'backup' on the same NAS. Two copies, one fate. Nightly fulls against a 1-hour RPO fail silently for months until the day you need them, when you discover the business lost 23 hours of ticketing data it was contractually promised to keep. Green backup logs prove the backup job ran, not that the data is recoverable: corrupted VSS writers, missing bare-metal recovery media, encrypted-but-unreadable sets, and wrong drivers all hide behind 'Success.' The senior admin's three questions (have we restored, where are the recovery media, where is the runbook) exist because every one of those has bitten someone.

WHEN: Design from RPO/RTO backwards: get the numbers from the business continuity plan first, then choose frequency and media. Never buy the backup product before knowing the objectives. The wrong way is 'more backups = safer': hourly fulls that nobody ever test-restores are expensive theater; frequency without verification is the trap. The wrong way on 3-2-1 is NAS plus tapes in the same building counted as 'offsite because the tapes go to the safe.' A fire takes both; offsite means a different facility. The alternative to differentials is incrementals for tight backup windows (smaller nightly transfers), but accept the longer, more fragile restore chain. There is no free lunch, only trade-offs you choose deliberately.

CONNECTS: This is the strategy layer above the SQL backup chain lesson: same RPO/RTO vocabulary, file-level instead of transaction-level. The RAID lesson is the 'why not just RAID' answer: RAID survives disk failure, 3-2-1 survives everything else. Hyper-V Replica (the clustering lesson) is a fourth copy with a 5-minute RPO, not a replacement for the rule. And the documentation lesson is where the runbook lives: the DR runbook with failover and failback steps is the deliverable that turns 'we have backups' into 'we can recover in 4 hours, proven last quarter.'
3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, 2 media, 1 offsite
Full vs incremental vs differential restore chains
GFS rotation for long-term retention
RPO = data-loss tolerance (drives backup frequency)
RTO = downtime tolerance (drives restore speed)
Untested backups are not backups: restore drills + runbooks

THEORY: Three numbers govern storage performance. IOPS (input/output operations per second) counts how many read/write operations complete per second. Throughput (usually MB/s) measures how much data moves per second. Latency is how long one operation takes. They relate by a simple identity: throughput = IOPS x average I/O size. That identity is why quoting IOPS alone is meaningless — 5,000 IOPS of 4 KB database reads is 20 MB/s, while 5,000 IOPS of 128 KB backup writes is 640 MB/s; same IOPS, 32x the throughput. Latency sets the IOPS ceiling for a single outstanding operation (IOPS <= 1/latency), which is why a hard drive with ~8 ms seek latency caps around 120 IOPS while an SSD at ~0.1 ms can do tens of thousands. RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is the maximum data loss you accept, expressed as a time: RPO of 1 hour means backups must run at least hourly, because everything since the last backup is losable. RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is the maximum acceptable downtime: RTO of 4 hours means your restore procedure must complete within 4 hours or you breach the objective. The 3-2-1 rule — 3 copies of data, on 2 different media types, with 1 copy offsite — is probability arithmetic: if one copy fails with probability p per year, two independent copies fail together with probability p x p. At p = 3% per drive-year, two copies = 0.09% — but 'independent' is doing heavy lifting, which is exactly why the offsite copy exists: fire, flood, and ransomware break the independence assumption for everything in the same building.

WORKED EXAMPLE: Worked 1 — backup window. You must back up 500 GB over a link that sustains 100 MB/s. Step 1: convert to common units — 500 GB = 500,000 MB (decimal GB, as backup tools report). Step 2: time = data / rate = 500,000 MB / 100 MB/s = 5,000 seconds. Step 3: 5,000 / 60 = 83.3 minutes, about 1 hour 23 minutes. So a 2-hour overnight window fits — barely, with no headroom for growth. WRONG WAY (the classic): the link is '100 Mb/s' — lowercase b means megabits. 100 Mb/s = 100/8 = 12.5 MB/s. Then 500,000 / 12.5 = 40,000 seconds = 666.7 minutes = 11.1 hours — the backup blows through the whole night and into the workday. Bits vs bytes is a factor-of-8 error and the single most common backup-window mistake; always check the case of the 'b'.

Worked 2 — RTO vs RPO as numbers. The business sets RPO = 15 minutes and RTO = 4 hours for the order database. RPO 15 min means the most data you may ever lose is 15 minutes' worth — so backups (or log shipping) must capture changes at least every 15 minutes; a nightly backup alone violates RPO by design. RTO 4 h means from 'database is down' to 'orders flowing again' must be <= 4 hours: that budget has to cover detecting the failure, provisioning/restoring (a 2 TB restore at 250 MB/s = 2,000, 000/250 = 8,000 s = 133 min ≈ 2 h 13 min — fits), replaying 15 minutes of logs, and validating. If the restore alone took 5 hours, the RTO is unachievable and you must change the architecture (standby replica, faster storage), not just hope.

Worked 3 — 3-2-1 numerically. One external drive, annual failure probability ~3% (0.03). Two drives in different places: 0.03 x 0.03 = 0.0009 = 0.09% chance both die in the same year — 33x safer. But if both sit on the same desk, one ransomware event or office fire kills both at once: the failures are correlated, so the real probability is far worse than 0.09%. The offsite copy restores the independence the multiplication assumes. That is the entire mathematical justification for the '1' in 3-2-1.

PRACTICE: A full backup of 2 TB must finish inside a 3-hour window. The backup target sustains 250 MB/s. Does it fit? Show the math, including the headroom or shortfall. | Your SLA states RPO = 1 hour and RTO = 30 minutes for a file server. A colleague proposes nightly backups and restoring from last night's tape 'which only takes 20 minutes.' Identify every violation and explain what each number actually demands.

ANSWERS: 2 TB = 2,000,000 MB. Time = 2,000,000 / 250 = 8,000 seconds = 133.3 minutes = 2 hours 13 minutes. The 3-hour (180-minute) window fits with 180 - 133.3 = 46.7 minutes of headroom (~26% margin). Caveat: that assumes the full 250 MB/s sustained — real throughput dips with small files and competing I/O, so 26% headroom is thin; plan for growth. WRONG WAY: 2,000,000/250 = 8,000 and calling it '8,000 minutes' (unit error — the division MB/(MB/s) yields seconds), or using 2 TB = 2,000 GB but then dividing by 250 GB/s — keep units consistent: MB divided by MB/s gives seconds. | Two violations. (1) RPO = 1 hour means at most 1 hour of data may be lost, so backups must run at least hourly — nightly backups expose up to 24 hours of loss, violating RPO by design; hourly (or continuous) protection is required. (2) RTO = 30 minutes vs the proposed 20-minute restore: the 20-minute figure only covers the copy phase — the full RTO budget must also include detecting the outage, deciding to fail over, mounting/presenting storage, and validating services, which routinely exceeds the extra 10 minutes. The proposal is wrong on RPO (fix: hourly backups) and optimistic on RTO (fix: actually time a full drill end-to-end, then compare to 30 minutes).

# Check Windows Server Backup versions and last success
wbadmin get versions
wbadmin get status
# Start a one-time bare-metal-capable backup to a dedicated disk
wbadmin start backup -backupTarget:E: -include:C:,D: -allCritical -systemState -quiet
example.walkthrough: wbadmin get versions lists every recoverable backup version on the target — your first check when someone says 'the backups are fine.' get status shows the currently running job. The start backup line performs a bare-metal-capable backup (-allCritical grabs boot/system volumes, -systemState grabs AD/registry) to drive E:. In an interview, pair this with the rule: schedule it, then prove it with a test restore.

pitfalls: Confusing RTO and RPO — RPO is about data AGE (how much loss), RTO is about CLOCK time (how fast you're back)
Keeping all 3 copies in the same building — offsite means OFFSITE (ransomware encrypts the NAS too)
Incremental chains: one corrupt middle backup breaks every restore after it — know the trade-off vs differentials

concepts: PowerShell's pipeline (|) is its superpower: the output of one command becomes the input of the next, like an assembly line where each station does one job — Get-Service finds services, Where-Object filters them, Select-Object picks columns. This lesson introduces the three discovery cmdlets (pronounced 'command-lets,' PowerShell's built-in commands) that make the terminal self-teaching: Get-Help (the manual — including -Examples, the fastest way to learn any command), Get-Command (finds commands by verb or noun when you know what you want but not its name), and Get-Member (reveals what properties an object actually has, so you stop guessing column names). Learn these three and you can teach yourself any cmdlet under pressure — which is exactly what Tuesday demands. Logic Check — here's the reasoning: the pipeline works because every PowerShell command passes OBJECTS (with named properties), not text — that's why Select-Object can pick columns reliably while Unix text-parsing breaks when output formatting changes — and the discovery cmdlets exist because no human memorizes 10,000 commands, so the shell was designed to be self-teaching under pressure.

WHAT: PowerShell's pipeline passes .NET objects between commands, not text: Get-Service emits service objects with .Name, .Status, .StartType properties, and the next command acts on those properties directly. Three discovery cmdlets make you self-sufficient: Get-Command finds cmdlets by verb or noun ('what touches AD users?'), Get-Help -Examples shows real usage, and Get-Member lists an object's properties and methods ('what can I actually read off this thing?'). Where-Object filters rows, Select-Object picks columns, Sort-Object orders, Format-Table displays for eyeballs, Export-Csv writes data for files. This is the grammar of all Windows administration.

HOW: The canonical shape is verb-noun with parameters, composed left to right: Get-Service | Where-Object {$_.Status -eq 'Running'} | Select-Object Name, DisplayName, StartType | Export-Csv report.csv -NoTypeInformation. Each stage transforms objects: Where-Object keeps only objects whose Status property equals 'Running' (-eq is the comparison operator; = is assignment and silently breaks the filter), Select-Object projects just the three properties you need, Export-Csv serializes to CSV - with -NoTypeInformation stripping the junk #TYPE header line PowerShell otherwise emits. The discovery loop before you build: Get-Command -Noun ADUser to find the cmdlets, Get-Help Get-ADUser -Examples to learn the patterns, Get-ADUser -Filter * -ResultSetSize 1 | Get-Member to see the real property names on one sample object (never guess property names - Get-Member is the source of truth). Format-* cmdlets are terminal: they convert objects into display formatting, so piping Format-Table into Export-Csv exports formatting garbage instead of data - always Export BEFORE formatting.

WHY: Designer reasoning: the pipeline passes objects instead of text because PowerShell's designers watched Unix admins lose data at every pipe - 'ps aux | grep' gives you strings, and the moment you need the third column you re-parse text that was already structured. Objects preserve types (dates stay dates, numbers stay numbers), so Sort-Object on a date actually sorts chronologically instead of alphabetically. Without the pipeline mental model, every admin task becomes manual GUI clicking or fragile text parsing: the difference between managing 5 servers and managing 500. Guessing property names instead of using Get-Member produces the classic failure: the script 'runs fine' but the CSV is empty because the property was LastLogonDate and you filtered on LastLogon. Logic Check: the Format-before-Export mistake is insidious because it looks successful - a CSV gets created, full of formatting objects, and nobody notices until the auditor opens it. The pipeline exists so that discovery, filtering, shaping, and output are composable primitives instead of one-off scripts.

WHEN: Decision matrix: live in the pipeline for everything - reporting, auditing, bulk changes; if you are doing it more than twice, pipe it. Wrong way 1: Get-ADUser -Filter * | Select-Object * - dumping every attribute including binary ones across the network for 800 users, then filtering client-side; filter at the source (-Filter) and project only needed properties (-Properties) instead, because the domain controller can filter 800 objects faster than your workstation can download them. Wrong way 2: memorizing cmdlet names from blog posts instead of Get-Command - in the assessment you will face cmdlets you have never seen, and the interviewers are testing whether you can discover them cold. Tradeoff: -Filter is fast but limited to the provider's query language; Where-Object is expressive but downloads everything first - use -Filter for the coarse cut, Where-Object for the fine cut. Alternative: for one-off interactive exploration, Format-Table is fine and Out-GridView is lovely - just never let display cmdlets touch a data pipeline.

CONNECTS: The pipeline is the tool behind every other PowerShell lesson: the AD/DNS/DHCP one-liners are pipelines (Get-ADUser | Where-Object | Export-Csv), the remoting lesson fans pipelines out across 20 servers with Invoke-Command, and the Hyper-V lesson's Get-VM | Where-Object {$_.State -eq 'Running'} is the canonical filter pattern. Cross-layer constraint: the pipeline's filter-at-source principle directly determines network load - a Get-ADUser -Filter * across a WAN link to a branch DC pulls every attribute of every user through the same link the replication traffic uses, so a lazy pipeline can starve AD replication of bandwidth; the cmdlet you choose shapes the network, not just the output. It also powers the operational lessons: repadmin and dcdiag output get parsed, DHCP scope statistics get exported, and the hardening baseline checks (Get-SmbServerConfiguration, Get-LocalGroupMember) become audit reports - all through this same grammar.
Get-Command: discover cmdlets by verb/noun
Get-Help -Examples: learn by example
Get-Member: see an object's properties/methods
Pipeline: objects flow, not text
Where-Object / Select-Object: filter and shape
Format-Table vs Export-Csv: display vs data

THEORY: In classic shells (cmd.exe, bash), commands pass TEXT to each other: 'ipconfig | findstr IPv4' works by one program printing characters and the next program scanning those characters with string matching — fragile, because a column shift or a translated OS language breaks the parse. PowerShell does something fundamentally different: cmdlets pass .NET OBJECTS. When you run Get-Service, each service is a ServiceController object carrying typed properties (.Name as a string, .Status as an enum, .StartType, methods like .Stop()). Get-Member is the X-ray: pipe anything into it and it lists every property and method the object exposes, which is how you discover what you can filter and act on. The pipeline (|) hands these live objects — not their screen text — to the next cmdlet, so Where-Object tests real properties ($_.Status -eq 'Running' compares the actual status value, not the letters on screen) and Stop-Process receives genuine process handles. Formatting (the table you see) happens only at the very end, when output reaches the console — it is a display layer, never the data. That is why 'everything is an object' matters practically: you filter on meaning, not on text layout.

WORKED EXAMPLE: Worked — stopping runaway processes without text parsing. Goal: stop every process using more than 60 seconds of CPU time.

Step 1 — Inspect the object: Get-Process | Get-Member. In the output you find CPU as a property of type double (seconds of processor time) — now you know the exact property name and that it is numeric, so numeric comparison is valid.

Step 2 — Filter on the property: Get-Process | Where-Object { $_.CPU -gt 60 }. $_ is the current pipeline object (one process at a time); .CPU reads its numeric property; -gt 60 is a numeric comparison. No string parsing, no column counting — if Microsoft renames a display column tomorrow, this still works, because you never touched the display.

Step 3 — Act on the objects: Get-Process | Where-Object { $_.CPU -gt 60 } | Stop-Process. Stop-Process receives live Process objects with real handles and terminates them. Compare the old text way: tasklist output piped to findstr, then for /f tokenizing columns to extract a PID, then taskkill /PID — every step re-parses text and breaks if spacing changes.

The 'wrong way' demonstration: Get-Service | Out-String | Where-Object { $_.Status -eq 'Running' }. Out-String converts the rich objects into one flat block of text FIRST — after that, .Status no longer exists (a string has no Status property), the filter silently matches nothing, and you have destroyed the very data you wanted to query. Rule: format cmdlets (Format-Table, Out-String) go LAST, only for human eyes; never put them mid-pipeline.

PRACTICE: Explain in two sentences why Get-Service | Where-Object { $_.Status -eq 'Running' } keeps working even if Microsoft changes the column layout of the Get-Service display table. | A script contains: Get-Process | Format-Table Name, CPU | Where-Object { $_.CPU -gt 60 } | Stop-Process. Predict what happens and explain the mechanism behind the failure.

ANSWERS: Because Where-Object never looks at the display table at all: the pipeline carries ServiceController objects, and $_.Status reads the object's real Status property (a typed value), while the table layout is just a last-moment formatting view applied when results reach the console. Changing the display changes cosmetics; the object's properties are untouched, so the filter keeps working. (This is the core difference from text pipelines, where the display IS the data.) | Nothing gets stopped — and worse, it fails silently-ish. Format-Table converts the Process objects into formatting objects (Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Internal.Format.*) that describe how to draw a table; those formatting objects have no CPU property, so $_.CPU is $null for every row, $null -gt 60 is false for every row, Where-Object passes nothing through, and Stop-Process receives no input. Mechanism: formatting cmdlets destroy the original objects and replace them with display instructions — they are terminal cmdlets for human eyes only, never for further processing.

example.code:
# The discovery loop every admin lives in:
Get-Command -Noun ADUser            # what cmdlets touch AD users?
Get-Help Get-ADUser -Examples       # show me real usage
Get-ADUser -Filter * -ResultSetSize 1 | Get-Member  # what properties exist?
# Then build the pipeline: filter -> shape -> output
Get-Service | Where-Object {$_.Status -eq 'Running'} |
  Select-Object Name, DisplayName, StartType |
  Sort-Object Name | Format-Table -AutoSize
example.walkthrough: This is the universal PowerShell workflow: discover the cmdlet (Get-Command), learn it (Get-Help -Examples), inspect what it returns (Get-Member — note -ResultSetSize 1 so you only pull one object), then compose. The service pipeline shows the canonical shape: Where-Object filters rows, Select-Object picks columns, Sort-Object orders, Format-Table displays. Swap Format-Table for Export-Csv when the output must be data, not eyeballs.

pitfalls: Piping Format-Table into Export-Csv — Format-* cmdlets produce display objects, destroying your data; always Export BEFORE formatting
Using = instead of -eq in Where-Object script blocks — = is assignment and silently breaks the filter
Forgetting -Properties on Get-ADUser for attributes like LastLogonDate that aren't returned by default
lessons.title: The Pipeline: Get-Help, Get-Command, Get-Member and Friends
lessons.try_it: Without looking: use only Get-Command, Get-Help, and Get-Member to discover how to list all stopped services, then build a one-liner that exports their Name and DisplayName to C:\temp\stopped.csv. Time yourself — this is the muscle interviewers probe.

concepts: Active Directory (AD), DNS (Domain Name System), and DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) are the trio that makes a Windows network function — user logins, name translation, and automatic addressing — and administrators manage all three from PowerShell one-liners instead of clicking through consoles. This lesson collects the highest-yield commands: finding stale AD accounts, unlocking users and resetting passwords, testing DNS with Resolve-DnsName, and auditing DHCP scopes — each a single pipeline you can memorize as a pattern. The assessment tests whether you can DO the admin task from the terminal, not whether you can find the right GUI (graphical interface) tab. Logic Check — here's the reasoning: one-liners beat GUIs for administration because they're repeatable (the same pipeline runs on 500 users without drift), auditable (the command IS the documentation of what you did), and composable (find → filter → act chains in one line) — the GUI is for learning, the pipeline is for doing at scale.

WHAT: This is the working vocabulary of daily Windows administration: the AD cmdlets (New-ADUser, Unlock-ADAccount, Set-ADAccountPassword, Get-ADComputer, Get-ADGroupMember) for the user lifecycle, the DNS cmdlets (Add-DnsServerResourceRecordA, Resolve-DnsName) for name records, and the DHCP cmdlets (Get-DhcpServerv4Scope, Get-DhcpServerv4Lease) for address management, plus Test-NetConnection and Resolve-DnsName for triage. Each one-liner follows the pipeline grammar: discover the object, filter it, act on it, verify the change with a read. If the pipeline lesson is grammar, this is vocabulary.

HOW: Triage first, fix second. Test-NetConnection 10.20.5.44 -Port 443 proves the host is reachable at layers 3 and 4 (like ping plus a port check), while Resolve-DnsName SRV-APP02 failing proves name resolution is the gap: two commands that separate 'server down' from 'DNS broken' in ten seconds. The fix uses the real cmdlet names with their real required parameters: Add-DnsServerResourceRecordA -ZoneName corp.local -Name SRV-APP02 -IPv4Address 10.20.5.44 (-ZoneName is mandatory and there is no -IP parameter, which is exactly the kind of detail the assessment tests). For the user lifecycle: Unlock-ADAccount clears the lockout flag; Set-ADAccountPassword -Reset changes the password administratively (pipe -PassThru into Set-ADUser -ChangePasswordAtLogon $true to force a change at next logon); New-ADUser -Enabled $true -AccountPassword (Read-Host -AsSecureString) creates an immediately usable account with no plaintext password anywhere. DHCP investigation is Get-DhcpServerv4Scope (utilization percent per scope) then Get-DhcpServerv4Lease (who holds what): data before action, because APIPA addresses (169.254.x.x, the automatic fallback when DHCP fails) mean scope exhaustion until proven otherwise.

WHY: Designer reasoning: these cmdlets exist because the GUI tools (ADUC, DNS Manager, DHCP console) were built for one-off changes, and Microsoft's own operations teams needed scriptable, repeatable, auditable equivalents - every admin GUI since Server 2008 is literally a wrapper over these same cmdlets, so the cmdlet IS the real interface and the GUI is the skin. Without this vocabulary, every common task becomes a GUI treasure hunt or a web search, and in a 3-hour assessment there is no time for either. Invented cmdlet names are the classic interview trap: Remove-ADAccountLockout and Reset-ADAccountPassword do not exist, and writing them proves you memorized blog posts instead of using Get-Command. Plaintext passwords in scripts (the -NewPassword 'Temp123!' anti-pattern) do not just fail the assessment: in production they land in script history, backups, and ticket attachments, becoming a credential leak with your name on it. Logic Check: AD writes can fail silently on replication delays or permission denials, so 'I ran the command' is not 'it worked' - the verify-with-a-read habit (Get-ADUser after every write) exists because the directory is eventually consistent, not instantly consistent.

WHEN: Decision matrix: reach for one-liners for targeted daily work - unlocks, resets, record adds, scope checks; the 8:05 AM lockout triage is three cmdlets, not a project. Wrong way 1: RDPing into the DC and clicking through ADUC (Active Directory Users and Computers, the GUI) for 20 password resets: slow, unlogged, and unverifiable. Wrong way 2: writing a 200-line script for a one-time unlock: the pipeline one-liner IS the tool for single actions. When the job crosses into bulk (500 new hires from HR's CSV) or repetition (same unlock flow weekly), graduate to Import-Csv piped into New-ADUser in a proper script: that is the remoting/scripting lesson's territory. Tradeoff: one-liners optimize for speed of execution; scripts optimize for repeatability and audit trail. Knowing when a one-liner has grown into a script is itself the skill.

CONNECTS: These one-liners operate the systems from the AD lessons: Unlock-ADAccount and Set-ADAccountPassword are the daily face of the FSMO/OU infrastructure; Add-DnsServerResourceRecordA maintains the zones from the DNS troubleshooting lesson; the DHCP cmdlets manage the scopes from the DHCP exhaustion scenario. Cross-layer constraint: a wrong -ZoneName on the DNS cmdlet does not just fail the command - it can create the record in the wrong zone, and then every client resolving that name gets the wrong IP, which breaks Kerberos (which demands name-to-IP consistency), which breaks AD authentication downstream. The hardening lesson's LAPS rollout and the Group Policy lesson's deployments are both verified with these same Get-* reads, and the pipeline lesson is the grammar every one of these sentences is written in.
Get-ADUser -Filter with -Properties
New-ADUser / Unlock-ADAccount / Set-ADAccountPassword
Get-ADComputer and Get-ADGroupMember
Add-DnsServerResourceRecordA (-ZoneName, -IPv4Address)
Get-DhcpServerv4Scope / Get-DhcpServerv4Lease
Test-NetConnection and Resolve-DnsName for triage

THEORY: DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) exists so addresses are leased, not owned: a scope defines the pool, and math decides how big it must be. A /24 scope holds 2^8 = 256 addresses, but the .0 network and .255 broadcast are unusable, leaving 254 — then you subtract exclusions (ranges reserved for static assignment, e.g., printers and servers) and reservations (specific IPs tied to MAC addresses) to get the true leasable pool. Lease timing runs on two fractions of the lease length T: at T/2 (T1) the client tries to RENEW with its original server (unicast — quiet, polite), and at T x 0.875 (T2) it starts REBINDING via broadcast to ANY server. The 50% mark is early enough that renewal almost always succeeds before expiry; the 87.5% mark gives the original server one last long window (37.5% of the lease) before the client desperately shouts to the whole network. Windows Server's default lease is 8 days — not a protocol law, just a default balancing act: long enough that stable networks barely generate DHCP traffic, short enough that a laptop that left the building frees its address within a week. When no DHCP server answers at all, Windows assigns itself an APIPA (Automatic Private IP Addressing) address from 169.254.0.0/16 — a /16 (65,536 addresses) so randomly self-picked addresses rarely collide; the first and last /24 (169.254.0.x and 169.254.255.x) are reserved, leaving 169.254.1.0-169.254.254.255 (65,024 usable). An APIPA address is a diagnostic signal, not a configuration: it means 'DHCP failed,' and the machine can only talk to other APIPA machines on the same wire. DNS (Domain Name System) is the phone book: TTL (Time To Live) on each record is how many seconds resolvers may cache it, which is why DNS changes are not instant — a record with TTL 3600 can take up to an hour to stop being served stale from caches worldwide. A recursive resolver does the walking for the client (root -> TLD -> authoritative servers); an authoritative server owns the zone data and gives final answers. Record types in one line each: A = hostname to IPv4 address; AAAA = hostname to IPv6 address; CNAME = alias pointing one name at another name; MX = which server handles mail for the domain; PTR = reverse lookup, IP back to hostname (used by spam filters); SRV = service location with port/priority (how AD clients find domain controllers via _ldap._tcp SRV records); NS = which servers are authoritative for the zone; SOA = the zone's metadata record (primary server, serial, refresh timers). Protocol design reasoning you must be able to explain: DNS queries use UDP (User Datagram Protocol) because a typical query and response each fit in one small packet — UDP has no handshake, no connection state, and minimal header overhead (8 bytes), so a lookup costs one packet each way with minimum latency; the query is idempotent (safe to retry), so if a UDP packet is lost the resolver simply asks again. Zone transfers (AXFR/IXFR, full or incremental copies of an entire DNS zone between primary and secondary servers) use TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) because they move megabytes that MUST arrive complete and in order — TCP's sequencing, retransmission, and flow control guarantee that, which UDP cannot. The two meet in the middle: if a UDP response would exceed the size limit (historically 512 bytes; EDNS0 raises it, commonly to 4096), the server sets the TC (truncated) flag and the client retries over TCP. So: UDP = small, fast, retryable lookups; TCP = large, must-be-perfect transfers — each transport matched to the job's requirements.

WORKED EXAMPLE: Worked — sizing a DHCP scope. The 3rd floor needs addresses for 200 DHCP clients on 192.168.50.0/24, plus: .1 is the gateway (static), printers take .10-.19 (10 addresses, excluded), and 12 conference-room PCs get reservations.

Step 1 — Start from the /24: 256 total addresses. Subtract the 2 reserved (network .0, broadcast .255): 256 - 2 = 254 usable.

Step 2 — Subtract exclusions and reservations: the gateway .1, printers .10-.19 (10 addresses), and 12 reservations are all unavailable to the dynamic pool: 254 - 1 - 10 - 12 = 231 leasable addresses.

Step 3 — Compare to demand: 200 clients need 200 addresses; 231 >= 200, so the scope fits with 31 spare (~13% headroom). If demand were 240, the /24 would NOT fit and you would need a /23 (510 usable) — you cannot just 'squeeze' because each address can only be leased once.

Step 4 — Lease timeline with the 8-day Windows default: T1 renewal at day 4 (client unicasts 'may I keep 192.168.50.87?' to the original server), T2 rebinding at day 7 (0.875 x 8 = 7; client broadcasts to any server), expiry at day 8 (address returns to the pool if never renewed). A laptop that leaves on Friday and returns Monday renews quietly at T1 without anyone noticing.

Step 5 — Failure mode: the DHCP server dies. New arrivals get no answer and self-assign APIPA, e.g., 169.254.10.20. They can ping other 169.254.x.x machines on the same switch but reach nothing else — no gateway (APIPA assigns no gateway), no DNS. Seeing 169.254.x.x on a client is therefore never 'a weird address to work around'; it is the symptom that DHCP is down or unreachable (check the server, the relay agent on the router, and the switch path).

PRACTICE: A scope on 10.20.30.0/24 must serve 220 DHCP clients. Exclusions: .1-.30 (30 addresses) for static infrastructure; 10 reservations for printers. What is the leasable pool size, and does the scope fit? If not, what is the smallest change that fixes it? | With an 8-day lease, on which day does a client first attempt renewal, on which day does it start rebinding, and what is the practical difference between the two? A client shows 169.254.44.12 — what does that tell you, and what are the first three things you check?

ANSWERS: Usable from the /24: 256 - 2 = 254. Subtract 30 exclusions and 10 reservations: 254 - 30 - 10 = 214 leasable. Demand is 220 > 214 — the scope does NOT fit; you are 6 addresses short. Smallest fix: shrink the exclusion range (e.g., .1-.24 frees 6, giving exactly 220 — zero headroom, risky) or, properly, expand to a /23 (10.20.30.0/23 = 512 total, 510 usable, minus 40 = 470 pool). WRONG WAY: counting 256 as the pool (forgetting .0/.255) gives 216 — still short, but the arithmetic error hides the real margin; and 'just shorten the lease' does not create addresses, it only recycles them faster. | Renewal (T1) at 50% of 8 days = day 4; rebinding (T2) at 87.5% = day 7. Difference: renewal is a unicast to the ORIGINAL server ('may I keep my address?'), quiet and preferred; rebinding is a broadcast to ANY DHCP server, used only when the original server never answered renewals — it is the client's last resort before the lease expires on day 8. 169.254.44.12 is APIPA: the client got NO DHCP response. Check in order: (1) is the DHCP server service running and authorized, (2) is there a path — can the client reach the server (same VLAN? relay agent configured on the router if different subnet?), (3) is the scope exhausted or out of leases (event log / scope statistics) — an exhausted pool also yields APIPA for new clients.

example.code:
# New-hire provisioning: user + groups + home folder, verified
$pw = Read-Host "Temp password" -AsSecureString
New-ADUser -Name "Ava Reyes" -SamAccountName areyes -Enabled $true `
  -AccountPassword $pw -ChangePasswordAtLogon $true -PassThru |
  ForEach-Object { Add-ADGroupMember -Identity "SG_Helpdesk" -Members $_.SamAccountName }
New-Item -Path "\\files\home$\areyes" -ItemType Directory
Get-ADUser areyes -Properties Enabled, PasswordLastSet | Format-List Name, Enabled, PasswordLastSet
example.walkthrough: Read-Host -AsSecureString keeps the temp password out of plain text and out of history. New-ADUser -PassThru emits the new object so ForEach-Object can immediately add it to groups — no second lookup. -ChangePasswordAtLogon forces the user to set their own password on first sign-in. The final Get-ADUser re-reads the account: never trust a write you haven't verified with a read.

pitfalls: Putting passwords in plain text in scripts — always SecureString via Read-Host or a vault
Add-DnsServerResourceRecordA without -ZoneName — the cmdlet requires it; there is no -IP parameter
Inventing cmdlet names under pressure (Remove-ADAccountLockout doesn't exist — it's Unlock-ADAccount)
