lessons.try_it: In a lab VM: create a test user with New-ADUser, lock the account by failing logons (or simulate with Search-ADAccount -LockedOut), unlock it with Unlock-ADAccount, reset the password with Set-ADAccountPassword -Reset, and verify each step with Get-ADUser.

concepts: Remoting is PowerShell's ability to run commands on OTHER computers from your terminal — you sit at your desk while the commands execute on the server across the building, via WinRM (Windows Remote Management), the behind-the-scenes messenger. This lesson connects remoting to Hyper-V management (querying and controlling VMs on a remote host without logging into it) and then crosses the final bridge: saving commands into a .ps1 script file so a 20-line task becomes one double-click — including execution policy, the safety switch deciding which scripts Windows will run (and the #1 reason a perfect script 'does nothing' when you try it). Logic Check — here's the reasoning: remoting inverts the admin's travel — instead of your session going to 50 servers, the command goes to 50 servers and only results come back — and scripts exist because any task you'll do twice should be captured once: the script doesn't forget steps at 3 AM, doesn't typo the third server, and IS the documentation of what was done.

WHAT: PowerShell remoting lets you run commands on remote machines over WinRM (Windows Remote Management, the HTTP-based management protocol - usually TCP 5985/5986): Invoke-Command fans a script block out to MANY machines in parallel and returns unified objects, while Enter-PSSession opens an interactive 1:1 session for poking at a single sick box. A .ps1 script packages commands with structure: a param() block for input, functions for reusable jobs, foreach loops, and if/else branches. Execution policy (Restricted blocks all scripts, RemoteSigned allows locally-authored ones while requiring downloaded scripts to be signed) is the safety rail that decides what may run.

HOW: Invoke-Command -ComputerName $servers -ScriptBlock { ... } serializes the script block, runs it on every target simultaneously, and streams the resulting objects back - inside the block, $env:COMPUTERNAME identifies which machine each result came from, so you build [pscustomobject] rows (custom objects with named properties) and Export-Csv once at the end for a single clean report. Enter-PSSession is the opposite shape: one persistent interactive shell on one machine, perfect for troubleshooting, useless for twenty. A well-formed script declares #requires -Modules Hyper-V up front (fail fast if the module is missing), takes a param([string[]]$ComputerName) instead of hard-coding names, wraps one job per function, and uses -eq/-gt comparisons (PowerShell even understands 8GB as a number natively: 8GB is 8589934592 bytes without you doing the math). Execution policy fix is Set-ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser - the least-privilege change, affecting only your account - and scripts run as .\script.ps1 because the current directory is deliberately not in PATH (a security feature, not an annoyance). Persistent sessions must be closed with Remove-PSSession; orphans leak memory on both ends.

WHY: Designer reasoning: Invoke-Command fans out in parallel rather than looping serially because the designers measured the actual admin workload - 20 servers at 30 seconds each is 10 minutes serial versus about 35 seconds parallel, and the difference between 'I will check the fleet' and 'checking the fleet is not worth it' is exactly that latency. Without remoting, a 20-server audit is 20 RDP sessions: a full day of clicking versus one script and one CSV. Without the Invoke-Command/Enter-PSSession distinction, admins either RDP everywhere (slow) or try to Enter-PSSession twenty machines (absurd) - using the wrong shape for the job is the most common remoting failure. Execution policy exists because scripts are the malware delivery vehicle of choice on Windows: Restricted-by-default on clients means a double-clicked attachment cannot execute, and treating Bypass as a habit ('just bypass it, it is faster') trains exactly the muscle memory attackers rely on. Logic Check: the .\ requirement feels like pedantry until you realize it is the thing stopping a malicious script named 'notepad.ps1' in your Downloads folder from executing when you type a command - PATH exclusion is a trust boundary, and trust boundaries always feel annoying right up until they save you.

WHEN: Decision matrix: Invoke-Command for fleet data collection and fleet changes (patch verification, service restarts across servers); Enter-PSSession for interactive diagnosis of one machine ('let me look around inside this sick box'). Wrong way 1: Enter-PSSession into each of 20 servers for the audit - you have rebuilt RDP with extra steps. Wrong way 2: Stop-Computer when you meant Stop-VM - one reboots the HOST, and in a script fanned out to 20 hosts that is a datacenter-wide outage from a noun typo; always double-check the noun. Tradeoff: fan-out is fast but gives you one combined result stream - when you need interactive back-and-forth ('it is broken, let me poke'), the 1:1 session wins despite being slower. Alternative to WinRM remoting: SSH-based remoting for cross-platform, or configuration management tools - but for Windows-to-Windows in an AD domain, WinRM + Invoke-Command is the native answer, and Kerberos handles the authentication silently.

CONNECTS: Remoting is the delivery mechanism for the hardening lesson: the baseline checks (Get-SmbServerConfiguration, Get-MpComputerStatus) become a fleet audit when fanned out via Invoke-Command. The Hyper-V cmdlets from the virtualization lessons (Get-VM, Checkpoint-VM, Get-VMReplication) are the payload in the health-check script, and the AD/DNS/DHCP one-liners run remotely against DCs the same way. Cross-layer constraint: WinRM itself is a network service with firewall and authentication dependencies - if the hardening baseline's host firewall blocks TCP 5985, or if Kerberos is broken because DNS is wrong (the DNS lesson again), remoting fails with access-denied errors that look like credential problems but are really name-resolution problems; the network layer constrains the automation layer. The pipeline lesson's grammar composes with remoting's fan-out: filter-shape-export locally, execute everywhere.
Invoke-Command: fan out to many machines at once
Enter-PSSession: interactive 1:1 troubleshooting
Get-VM | Where-Object State filtering
Checkpoint-VM / Stop-VM for VM lifecycle
Execution policy: Restricted vs RemoteSigned
Script anatomy: param, functions, foreach, if/else

example.walkthrough: A complete mini-script showing professional structure: #requires declares the Hyper-V module up front, param() accepts input instead of hard-coding, the function wraps one job (VM health), foreach loops over hosts, if/else branches on state and memory. Invoke-Command runs Get-VM remotely and returns objects you loop locally. Note -gt 8GB — PowerShell understands KB/MB/GB suffixes natively. Save as .ps1, set execution policy RemoteSigned, run with .\script.ps1.

pitfalls: Running scripts by bare name (.\script.ps1 is required — current directory is not in PATH by design)
Leaving New-PSSession sessions open — always Remove-PSSession; orphans leak memory
Stop-Computer vs Stop-VM mix-up — one reboots the HOST, know which noun you're targeting

concepts: Hardening is the systematic removal of everything an attacker could use: if a service isn't needed, it's disabled; if a port isn't required, it's closed; if a default password exists, it's changed. Think of it as moving into a new house and changing every lock, barring the windows you never open, and disconnecting the landline you don't use — the house works the same for you and offers nothing to a burglar. This lesson is the baseline checklist in priority order: disable SMBv1 (the ancient file-sharing protocol behind WannaCry), deploy LAPS (Local Administrator Password Solution — unique random passwords for each machine's local admin), enable Credential Guard, and strip local admin rights. Logic Check — here's the reasoning: hardening is subtraction because every running service, open port, and default credential is a thing an attacker can use but you don't need — the math is asymmetric (removing SMBv1 costs you nothing if nothing uses it, but removes an entire wormable attack class), so the baseline is ordered by 'most risk removed per least breakage.'

WHAT: Hardening is the systematic reduction of a server's attack surface before adding defenses: disable or remove unused roles, features, and legacy protocols, then enforce secure baselines. The concrete controls: SMBv1 (Server Message Block version 1, the 1980s file-sharing protocol behind wormable ransomware like WannaCry) disabled on both server and client; LAPS (Local Administrator Password Solution - unique, auto-rotated local admin passwords per machine, stored in Active Directory) replacing shared passwords; Credential Guard (VBS - Virtualization-Based Security - isolating secrets in a hypervisor-protected enclave so LSASS memory holds nothing stealable) on capable hardware; Microsoft Security Baselines applied via GPO (Group Policy Object); Defender AV with cloud-delivered and tamper protection; host firewall on all profiles. Hardening answers: how do I make this server a bad target before the attacker arrives?

HOW: You work in layers, and order matters: first inventory with the four checks (Get-SmbServerConfiguration for SMBv1, the Win32_DeviceGuard WMI class for Credential Guard - value 2 means running, Get-MpComputerStatus for Defender real-time and tamper protection, Get-LocalGroupMember for admin sprawl), because you cannot harden what you have not measured. Then disable SMBv1 via the MS Security Guide GPO baseline (server AND client driver - disabling only one leaves the other half of the attack surface), deploy LAPS via schema extension plus the GPO client-side extension (each machine's password becomes unique and rotated, readable only by an authorized group), and enable Credential Guard via GPO - but only on hardware with UEFI, Secure Boot, and TPM 2.0 (Trusted Platform Module, the hardware security chip), because without those VBS never activates and the GPO gives a false sense of protection. Service accounts move to gMSA (group Managed Service Accounts - AD-managed, auto-rotated, no human-known password) so a password rotation never breaks the SQL Server service again. Patch discipline closes the loop: tiered testing rings (pilot, then 10%, then fleet) for normal updates, compressed rings for KEV-listed CVEs (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities - CISA's catalog with a 21-day federal remediation deadline, because 21 days is the window CISA judged as the maximum tolerable exposure for actively exploited flaws).

WHY: Designer reasoning: hardening works in the order it does (remove, then configure, then monitor) because every control you add sits on top of the attack surface beneath it - there is no point deploying EDR on a server still running SMBv1, since the worm does not care about your detection when the vulnerability is the front door. An unhardened server is a server trusting its defaults, and defaults are chosen for compatibility, not security - SMBv1 enabled, identical local admin passwords on every workstation image, reversible password encryption for one legacy app. One compromised host with a shared local admin password gives the attacker every host: they dump the hash once and pass-the-hash (reusing the stolen hash to authenticate without cracking it) across the fleet - LAPS exists specifically to break that lateral movement by making every password unique. Logic Check: EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) without hardening is detection without architecture - it may catch the Mimikatz-style LSASS access, but Credential Guard makes the theft fail in the first place, and prevention that works while you sleep beats detection that pages you at 3 AM. And a baseline that is not verified (Credential Guard GPO applied to non-VBS hardware) is worse than no baseline - it is confidence without protection.

WHEN: Decision matrix: harden every server at build time from a baseline image or GPO; retrofitting hardening onto 200 production servers is ten times the work and ten times the breakage. Wrong way 1: disabling SMBv1 domain-wide on a Friday without inventorying legacy dependencies - Monday brings the dead print appliance and the old NAS, and the panicked rollback re-exposes everything; isolate the legacy devices on a segmented VLAN (the VLAN lesson) with compensating controls instead. Wrong way 2: pushing the KEV emergency update to the whole fleet untested because 'speed matters' - the spooler-dependent app breaks and you have traded a vulnerability for an outage; compress the rings, do not skip them. Tradeoff: aggressive hardening (disable everything unused) risks breaking unknown dependencies; timid hardening (change nothing) preserves the attack surface - the inventory-first workflow is how you resolve it, finding the dependencies before the change instead of after the outage. Alternative to GPO baselines: DSC (Desired State Configuration) or MDM for non-domain machines - but the control set (disable legacy, unique creds, protect secrets, patch fast) is identical whatever the delivery truck.

CONNECTS: The hardening baseline is deployed and enforced by Group Policy (the GPO lesson) and aimed at the OU structure (the OU design lesson) - policy without targeting is spam. LAPS and Credential Guard are the credential-theft defenses from the incident-response lesson's world: hardening is what makes the IR team's job rare. Cross-layer constraint: the tiered admin model (no Domain Admin credentials on member servers) directly limits what a compromised SQL Server service account can reach - the SQL security lesson's least-privilege logins and this lesson's credential hygiene are the same principle at different layers, and a gMSA service account compromised on one box cannot be replayed elsewhere because there is no password to steal. The firewall rule-precedence lesson lives here too - the host firewall on all profiles is a baseline control - and the PowerShell remoting lesson turns these four checks into a fleet-wide audit.
Attack surface reduction: disable or remove unused roles, features, and legacy protocols (SMBv1, LLMNR, NetBIOS) before adding controls
Credential hygiene: LAPS for unique local admin passwords, gMSA for service accounts (no human-managed passwords), Credential Guard with VBS on capable hardware
Baseline enforcement: Microsoft Security Baselines via GPO, Defender AV with cloud-delivered protection and tamper protection, host firewall on all profiles
Patch discipline: tiered testing rings, accelerated timelines for KEV-listed CVEs, out-of-band process for active exploitation

example.code:
# 1. Verify SMBv1 is disabled on the server role
Get-SmbServerConfiguration | Select EnableSMB1Protocol

# 2. Check Credential Guard status (2 = running)
(Get-CimInstance Win32_DeviceGuard).SecurityServicesConfigured

# 3. Confirm Defender real-time protection and tamper protection
Get-MpComputerStatus | Select RealTimeProtectionEnabled, TamperProtectionSource

# 4. List local admins to spot sprawl
Get-LocalGroupMember -Group 'Administrators'
example.walkthrough: Run these four checks on any server you inherit. SMBv1 disabled closes the wormable-protocol hole; Credential Guard running means LSASS secrets sit in a VBS enclave; Defender real-time plus tamper protection stops both malware and 'helpful' disabling of AV; and the local Administrators list reveals sprawl (vendors, old accounts) before you audit Domain Admins. Each check maps to one baseline control — together they tell you whether the server was hardened or just installed.

pitfalls: Disabling SMBv1 without checking for legacy dependencies first — find the print appliances and old NAS boxes that still need it, then isolate them rather than rolling back the baseline
Enabling Credential Guard on hardware without UEFI/Secure Boot/TPM 2.0 — the GPO applies but VBS never activates, giving a false sense of protection; verify with the DeviceGuard WMI class
Hardening the OS but leaving service accounts as domain admins with non-expiring passwords — the service account becomes the weakest link; move to gMSA

concepts: Incident response is what you do in the first 30 minutes when something is actively wrong — ransomware encrypting the file server, a breached account, malware beaconing out. It's fire-drill discipline: contain FIRST (isolate the host from the network — pull the virtual cable before you 'investigate'), then eradicate, then recover — and NEVER reboot or 'clean' a compromised machine before preserving evidence (logs and memory are the crime scene; rebooting destroys them). This lesson gives you the sysadmin's playbook: the order of operations, what to capture, who to call, and the two career-ending mistakes (destroying evidence, and hiding the incident). Logic Check — here's the reasoning: contain-before-investigate exists because the incident is ACTIVE — every minute of connectivity is another minute of spread and another encrypted share — while preserve-before-reboot exists because logs and memory are the only witnesses, and rebooting destroys them — order of operations isn't bureaucracy, it's triage under fire.

WHAT: Incident response is the six-phase discipline for handling security events: Preparation, Detection and Analysis, Containment, Eradication, Recovery, and Lessons Learned - in that order, each producing something the next needs. For sysadmins the critical insight is containment before eradication: isolate the host from the network but keep it powered on, because volatile memory and logs are evidence. Short containment is immediate (disable the switch port, move to a quarantine VLAN); long containment is forensic (full disk and memory imaging for confirmed breaches). You are the first responder, not the forensics lab: your job is to stop the bleeding and preserve the evidence.

HOW: The first five actions on 'suspected ransomware on FILE-02': declare the incident and start a timestamped timeline log (without timestamps you can never determine dwell time - how long the attacker was inside); isolate the host via quarantine VLAN or switch-port shutdown while keeping it powered on (pulling the plug destroys memory evidence: running processes, network connections, encryption keys); preserve volatile evidence first - process list, then Security and System event logs exported with wevtutil to a write-protected evidence share with documented chain of custody (who handled the evidence, when - the legal record that it was not tampered with); determine blast radius (which hosts and backup jobs touched FILE-02 in the last 24 hours, and whether the backup repository is isolated from the domain so the ransomware cannot reach it); then escalate to the security team or IR retainer with specifics - hostname, user, indicators - so they act instead of re-investigating. Recovery comes from the isolated backup tier: rebuild from known-good media, restore data, reset credentials for affected accounts - and only then the lessons-learned review that updates the runbook.

WHY: Designer reasoning: the phase order exists because each phase's output is the next phase's input, and skipping one corrupts everything downstream - containment without detection means you isolate the wrong host; eradication without containment means the attacker re-infects during cleanup; recovery without eradication means you restore onto a still-compromised network. Reimaging immediately feels productive and destroys everything: volatile memory with the attacker's processes, logs showing lateral movement, the ransom note's metadata - you 'fix' one box and never learn the blast radius, so the attacker still owns three others. Containing too slowly because you are 'still investigating' is how one encrypted file server becomes fifty: ransomware spreads in minutes, and every minute of 'let me just check one more thing' is lateral movement you are allowing. Logic Check: keep-it-powered-on feels wrong (the instinct is to kill it), but power state IS evidence state - RAM holds the decryption keys, the C2 connections, and the process tree, and all of it evaporates on shutdown while the disk image survives; that is why isolation (network) and preservation (power) are separate controls. Without the timeline, the post-incident review cannot answer the two questions leadership always asks: how long were they in, and did our response work - which means the same incident recurs because nothing was actually learned.

WHEN: Decision matrix: invoke the runbook for ransomware behavior, domain controller involvement, data exfiltration indicators, or anything beyond your authority to wipe - those are the escalation triggers, and 'I can handle it' is not a trigger. Wrong way 1: treating every malware alert as a full incident - you burn the IR retainer's hours on adware; match the response to the indicators (adware = reimage and move on; ransomware behavior = full runbook). Wrong way 2: treating a DC compromise as 'just reimage it' - a compromised domain controller means the entire AD forest is suspect (golden ticket territory: forged Kerberos tickets granting persistent domain admin), and that escalates past sysadmin authority immediately. Tradeoff: aggressive containment (isolate first, ask later) risks brief business disruption of a host that turns out clean; slow containment risks enterprise-wide encryption. For ransomware indicators, the math always favors isolate-first. Alternative to building this alone: an IR retainer contract - but the first five actions are yours regardless; the retainer cannot teleport to your datacenter.

CONNECTS: IR is the reason the hardening lesson exists: every baseline control (Credential Guard, LAPS, SMBv1 off, tiered admin model) is designed to make this day rare and small - hardening is prevention, IR is the plan for when prevention fails, and the tiered admin model directly limits blast radius by keeping Domain Admin credentials off member servers. The backup strategy lesson provides the recovery mechanism: the isolated backup tier you restore from is the 3-2-1 offsite copy, and the DR runbook's failover/failback steps are the recovery phase written down. Cross-layer constraint: if the backup repository is domain-joined and reachable with the same credentials the ransomware stole, your 'isolated' recovery tier is already encrypted - the backup lesson's isolation requirement is what makes the IR lesson's recovery phase possible. Quarantine VLANs come from the VLAN lesson, and the whole response gets documented in the SOP format from the documentation lesson: the IR runbook IS an SOP, written before you need it at 2 AM.
The six phases: Preparation, Detection & Analysis, Containment, Eradication, Recovery, Lessons Learned — know them in order and what each produces
Containment first, evidence always: isolate the host from the network (but keep it powered on) before wiping — volatile memory and logs are evidence
Short vs long containment: disable the switch port or quarantine VLAN for immediate isolation; full forensic imaging for confirmed breaches

Escalation triggers: ransomware behavior, domain controller involvement, data exfiltration indicators, or anything beyond your authority to wipe — escalate to the security team/IR retainer immediately

example.code:
# Suspected compromised workstation WS-SALES-114
# 1. QUARANTINE: move to isolation VLAN (do NOT power off)
# 2. Preserve volatile evidence before anything else
Get-Date | Out-File \\nas\ir\WS-SALES-114\timeline.txt -Append
Get-Process | Out-File \\nas\ir\WS-SALES-114\processes.txt
# 3. Capture event logs to the evidence share
wevtutil epl Security \\nas\ir\WS-SALES-114\security.evtx
wevtutil epl System   \\nas\ir\WS-SALES-114\system.evtx
# 4. THEN escalate: page security with host, user, indicators
example.walkthrough: The order is the lesson: isolate first (VLAN quarantine keeps it on for memory forensics while cutting lateral movement), then preserve volatile data (process list, timestamps) and event logs to a write-protected evidence share with a documented chain of custody. Only after containment and evidence do you escalate with specifics — hostname, user, indicators — so the security team can act instead of re-investigating. Reimaging before these steps destroys the evidence you need to answer 'how far did it spread.'

pitfalls: Reimaging the machine immediately — it feels productive but destroys volatile evidence and you never learn the blast radius
Containing too slowly because you're 'still investigating' — if ransomware behavior is suspected, isolate first and investigate from the evidence copies
Not documenting timestamps and actions — without a timeline, the post-incident review can't determine dwell time or what worked

concepts: An SOP (Standard Operating Procedure) is a written recipe for a repeatable task — 'how we reset a password, every time, the same way' — and a runbook is its emergency cousin: the step-by-step for a specific incident ('file server down: do exactly this'). The test of a good runbook is brutal: could a competent stranger follow it successfully at 3 AM while stressed? That means numbered steps, exact commands with expected output, decision points ('if X, go to step 7'), and a backout plan. This lesson teaches you to write procedures that survive contact with a tired on-call human — because on Tuesday, that human is you, and the examiner is grading your trail. Logic Check — here's the reasoning: the 3 AM test is the real spec — a stressed, tired human has narrow working memory, so numbered steps, exact commands, and expected outputs exist to remove every decision the reader shouldn't have to make — and the backout plan exists because the person executing may need to abort, and aborting without a plan is how incidents get worse.

WHAT: An SOP (Standard Operating Procedure) is a procedure document written for the 2 AM reader: a competent engineer with zero context on your systems. The five-section structure: What/Why (is this the right doc for my error?), Steps (numbered, in exact order, with exact commands), Verification (how I know it worked - a concrete pass/fail signal), Rollback (the exact reversal if a step fails), and Last validated date (so staleness is visible). A runbook is the incident-flavored SOP: the ordered response for a specific failure. One procedure per document: if it covers three scenarios, it is three SOPs, because findability beats comprehensiveness.

HOW: Write it under time pressure using the structure as scaffolding: What/Why names the error code and root cause (WSUS console 0x80072EE2, corrupted content metadata) so the reader can confirm the match in seconds. Steps are numbered with the exact commands in the exact order - 'stop services BEFORE renaming the folder' is load-bearing sequence, and prose hides sequence, which is where outages come from. Verification is a specific observable outcome (WSUS console shows sync Success within 30 minutes), not 'it should work now.' Rollback is the precise reversal (rename WsusContent.old back, restart services, re-sync upstream) - because a failed fix without a rollback becomes a second incident. The validated date turns the SOP into a living document: every incident that uses it either validates it (update the date) or breaks it (fix the steps that day). Twenty minutes on a Friday with this structure beats two hours of prose.

WHY: Designer reasoning: the five sections map to the five questions a context-free engineer actually asks at 2 AM, in order - 'is this my problem?' (What/Why), 'what do I type?' (Steps), 'did it work?' (Verification), 'how do I undo it?' (Rollback), 'can I trust this?' (date). Miss any one and the engineer escalates to you, which is the failure mode the SOP exists to prevent. Without the five sections, the on-call engineer gets terminal history ('the commands I ran') - which lacks verification and rollback - or a prose paragraph they must reverse-engineer into steps at 2 AM, or a link to vendor docs that rotted three versions ago and never captured your environment's specifics. Skipping verification leaves the engineer guessing whether the fix worked, so they either wake you up anyway (defeating the SOP's purpose) or declare victory prematurely. Logic Check: a dateless SOP is a rumor because procedures decay - software updates change commands, servers get renamed, workarounds get fixed - and without a date there is no signal distinguishing a validated procedure from a fossil; the date is the cheapest trust mechanism in documentation.

WHEN: Decision matrix: write the SOP immediately after fixing something novel - the 20-minute Friday window, while the commands are still in your terminal history and the pain is fresh. Wrong way 1: 'I will document it next week' - next week the details are gone and the SOP never gets written; the second occurrence costs another full investigation. Wrong way 2: one mega-document covering every WSUS failure - the 2 AM reader cannot find their error in it; split by scenario, because findability beats comprehensiveness. Tradeoff: writing SOPs costs the 20 minutes you do not have on a Friday; not writing them costs the 3 AM page you will definitely get. The math favors writing. Alternative: video walkthroughs or wiki pages - fine as supplements, but the five-section text doc is the thing that works over a phone SSH session at 2 AM when the wiki is down (and the wiki being down is itself an incident).

CONNECTS: SOPs are where the whole course's procedures go to live: the WSUS recovery SOP, the DHCP migration change record, the ransomware IR runbook from the incident-response lesson, the backup restore procedure timed against the RTO from the backup strategy lesson. The assessment blueprint lesson depends on SOP thinking: narrating steps into a notes file is a live SOP. Cross-layer constraint: an SOP's verification section is only as good as the monitoring it references - 'verify sync completes in the console' assumes the WSUS console is reachable, which assumes the network path from the admin workstation works, which is the diagrams lesson's territory; the SOP, the diagram, and the monitoring form one operational unit. And the network diagrams lesson pairs with this one: the diagram shows the territory, the SOP describes the route through it.
The five-section SOP: What/Why, Steps (numbered, in order), Verification (how you know it worked), Rollback (exact reversal), Last validated date
Write for the 2 AM reader: assume competence, zero context — no tribal knowledge, no 'you know the drill'
One procedure per document: if the SOP covers three scenarios, it's three SOPs — findability beats comprehensiveness
Living documents: every incident that uses an SOP either validates it (update the date) or breaks it (fix the steps that day)

example.code:
# SOP-2026-041: WSUS sync failure recovery

## What / Why
Fixes WSUS console error 0x80072EE2 (sync timeout) that blocks
Patch Tuesday approvals. Root cause: corrupted content metadata.

## Steps
1. Stop services IN ORDER: `Stop-Service WsusService, W3SVC`
2. Rename: `Rename-Item 'C:\WSUS\WsusContent' 'WsusContent.old'`
3. Reset content: `wsusutil.exe reset`
4. Start services: `Start-Service WsusService, W3SVC`

## Verification
WSUS console > Synchronizations shows Success within 30 min.

## Rollback
Rename WsusContent.old back; restart services; re-sync upstream.

## Last validated: 2026-10-10
example.walkthrough: Notice what each section does for the 2 AM reader: What/Why confirms this is the right doc for their error code; numbered steps with exact commands remove sequencing mistakes (stopping services before the rename is load-bearing); Verification gives a concrete pass/fail signal instead of 'it should work now'; Rollback is the exact reversal so a failed fix doesn't become a second incident; the date tells the reader whether to trust it. This SOP was written in 20 minutes on a Friday — completeness comes from structure, not length.

pitfalls: Writing prose instead of steps — paragraphs hide sequence, and sequence is where outages come from
Skipping the verification section — 'run these commands' without a success signal leaves the engineer guessing whether it worked
Letting SOPs go stale silently — an SOP without a validated date is a rumor; tie updates to the incidents that use them

lessons.try_it: Take a fix you performed this week and rewrite it as a five-section SOP. Time yourself — aim for under 30 minutes.

concepts: A network diagram is the map of the territory: every device, connection, IP address, and VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) drawn so anyone can understand the network without tracing cables. Standards matter — consistent icons, links labeled with port numbers, a legend, and a 'last updated' date — because an outdated diagram is worse than none (it sends troubleshooters hunting ghosts). Paired with it is the change record: who changed what, when, why, and how to undo it — the backout plan. This lesson covers diagram types (physical vs logical), what must be labeled, and why the assessment grades your documentation as evidence, not decoration. Logic Check — here's the reasoning: a diagram is a shared mental model, and troubleshooting is hypothesis testing against that model — if the model is wrong (outdated diagram), every hypothesis is wrong and you hunt ghosts — while the change record exists because the most common cause of a new outage is the most recent change, and identifying what changed is always the first question.

WHAT: Two diagrams, two jobs: the physical diagram shows what is plugged into what (device names, models, switch port numbers, uplink paths, cable IDs) for hands-on work; the logical diagram shows how traffic flows (VLAN IDs with names, subnets in CIDR notation, gateway IPs, SVI assignments, firewall HA roles) for troubleshooting paths. A change record is the CAB's (Change Advisory Board - the group that approves risky changes) decision document: before/after state, ordered steps with verification after each, an explicit backout plan with a go/no-go deadline, risk assessment, and test plan. Handover notes are the human version: coverage dates, known issues with workarounds, 'do not touch' items, time-critical jobs, escalation contacts with contract numbers.

HOW: Build the logical diagram from the VLAN and subnetting lessons: every VLAN gets its ID, name, and subnet in CIDR (VLAN 10 data 192.168.10.0/24), every gateway IP is labeled, every SVI noted - because at 3 AM the NOC (network operations center) needs to answer 'what IP do I type' in 60 seconds. The physical diagram gets port numbers and cable IDs because 'unplug the uplink' is meaningless without knowing which cable. The change record's backout plan must be explicit actions with a decision deadline - 're-authorize the 2016 DHCP server, deactivate the 2022 pair, rollback deadline 01:00' - not 'restore from backup,' which at 12:45 AM with 15 minutes left is a wish, not a plan. Verification gates after each step (client renews and gets a 192.168.10.x address with an 8-hour lease) catch partial failures before they become outages. Every page gets legend, date, and owner: the date makes staleness visible instead of silent, so the NOC never trusts a 2019 diagram for a 2026 network.

WHY: Designer reasoning: the two-diagram split exists because incidents cross layers - they start as 'users cannot reach the app' (logical: which VLAN, which subnet, which gateway) and become 'go unplug the right cable' (physical: which switch, which port). One diagram cannot serve both without becoming unreadable, so the standard separates them the way the OSI model separates concerns. Without diagrams, every incident starts with discovery: the NOC burns the first hour mapping the network instead of fixing it, and 'which firewall is active' becomes a guessing game during a failover. An after-state-only change record cannot be verified ('did the change do what was intended?') and cannot be rolled back by anyone but the author - which is exactly why the CAB rejected the first DHCP migration request. Handover notes without 'do not touch' items invite well-meaning damage: the covering engineer reboots the flaky backup server mid-job because nobody wrote down that the workaround is a retry, not a reboot. Logic Check: undated diagrams are landmines because they look authoritative while describing a network that no longer exists - the date is the cheapest staleness detector ever invented, and its absence is why engineers learn to distrust all diagrams.

WHEN: Decision matrix: diagram every new site before go-live (the branch office handover pack: two diagrams, one SOP, handover notes, single PDF); update diagrams as part of every change, not as a separate project, because a separate documentation project never gets scheduled. Wrong way 1: 'diagrams are outdated the moment they are drawn, so a spreadsheet of IPs is more honest' - a spreadsheet cannot show the path a packet takes, and path is what troubleshooting needs. Wrong way 2: verbal walkthrough at the CAB instead of written documentation - faster, and leaves zero record for the post-incident review when the change causes the outage. Tradeoff: exhaustive diagrams cost maintenance time; the standard answers it with 'minimum viable labels' (hostname, mgmt IP, VLAN/subnet, date, owner) rather than all-or-nothing. Alternative: auto-generated diagrams from monitoring tools - excellent as a starting point, but they show what is there, not what it means; the human-added labels (HA roles, cable IDs, owners) are what make them troubleshooting tools.

CONNECTS: Diagrams visualize the VLAN, subnetting, and routing lessons: the logical diagram IS those three lessons drawn on one page. Change records govern the risky operations from across the course: DHCP migrations (the DHCP lesson), firewall rule changes (the ACL lesson - remember the firewall change that broke AD replication), FSMO role moves (the FSMO lesson). Cross-layer constraint: the change record for a firewall rule change must reference the logical diagram's inter-VLAN paths, because a rule that looks safe on paper ('block 10.10.40.0 to the web server') breaks AD replication if the diagram shows the branch DC's replication traffic crossing that same path - the diagram is what reveals the hidden dependency. Handover notes carry the backup job deadlines (the 3-2-1 lesson's 6 AM copy job) and known issues (the flaky tape drive), and the SOP lesson's five-section structure is the format the handover's procedures borrow.
Two diagrams, two jobs: physical (cabling, ports, device models) for hands-on work; logical (VLANs, subnets, gateways, HA roles) for troubleshooting paths
Label everything a stranger needs: hostname, management IP, VLAN IDs with names, subnets in CIDR, uplink paths — plus legend, date, owner on every revision
Change records need before/after state, ordered steps with verification, explicit backout plan with a go/no-go deadline, risk, and test plan
Handover notes: coverage dates, known issues with workarounds, 'do not touch' list, time-critical jobs, escalation contacts with contract numbers

example.code:
## CR-2026-118: DHCP migration to 2022 failover pair
**Window:** Sat 22:00 - 02:00 | **Rollback deadline:** 01:00

**Before:** Single WS2016 DHCP, 192.168.10.0/24, 4h leases
**After:** WS2022 hot-standby pair, same scope, 8h leases

**Steps:**
1. Export config: `netsh dhcp server export C:\dhcp\backup.dat all`
2. Build pair, import, verify scope options match
3. Deactivate 2016 scope; authorize 2022 pair
4. Verify: client renew gets 192.168.10.x, 8h lease

**Backout (by 01:00):** re-authorize 2016, deactivate pair,
restore backup.dat if scope corrupted.

**Risk:** Medium — DHCP outage = no new leases. **Test:** lab clone first.
example.walkthrough: This change record would pass a CAB because every question is pre-answered: the window and hard rollback deadline bound the blast radius; before/after defines the delta precisely; steps are ordered with a verification gate (client actually gets the right lease); the backout is explicit actions, not 'restore from backup'; risk is stated honestly; and a lab test is committed. The netsh export line is the kind of concrete detail that turns a backout plan from a wish into a procedure.

pitfalls: Documenting only the after state — without the before state, nobody can verify the change did what was intended or roll it back
Backout plans that say 'restore from backup' with no steps, no deadline, and no decision owner — at 12:45 AM that sentence is useless
Diagrams without dates or owners — the NOC can't tell a current diagram from a 2019 artifact, and will trust the wrong one
lessons.title: Network Diagrams and Change Records
lessons.try_it: Diagram your home lab (or a branch office you know): one physical view and one logical view, fully labeled, with legend, date, and your name as owner.

concepts: Hop 1 - DHCP: the laptop gets an address. What: when the laptop's Wi-Fi connects it has no IP address, so it shouts a DHCPDISCOVER broadcast asking 'is there a DHCP server?' How: the server answers with a DHCPOFFER (here is 10.10.20.44, mask /24, gateway 10.10.20.1, DNS 10.10.20.11, lease 8 hours), the laptop replies DHCPREQUEST ('I'll take it'), and the server confirms with DHCPACK - DORA: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge. Why: without this handshake the laptop falls back to an APIPA address (169.254.x.x, the automatic address when DHCP fails), which can talk to nobody - every hop after this one silently never happens.

Hop 2 - DNS: the name becomes an address. What: the user types app.corp.local, which is meaningless to IP routing, so the laptop asks its DNS server (10.10.20.11, learned from DHCP) to resolve it. How: the resolver sends a recursive query to the domain controller's DNS service; the controller checks its AD-integrated zone (zone data that replicates with Active Directory itself, so every DC is also a DNS server) and answers 10.10.10.50; the laptop caches it for the TTL (time to live). Why: without DNS the user is typing raw IPs, and worse, Kerberos authentication (hop 5) demands that names resolve consistently forward and backward - a DNS lie breaks authentication even when the network is fine.

Hop 3 - VLAN and firewall: the packet is segmented and filtered. What: the laptop's access port tags its frames into VLAN 20 (workstations); the app server lives on VLAN 10 (servers), so the packet must cross a trust boundary. How: the Layer 3 switch routes between the VLANs via SVIs (switched virtual interfaces, one virtual router interface per VLAN), but the firewall ACL between them is evaluated top-down with first match winning and an implicit deny at the bottom - the permit for workstation-to-app traffic must sit ABOVE the deny or it never fires. Why: without segmentation every device shares one broadcast domain with the domain controllers (one compromised laptop away from the crown jewels); without the firewall's ordered rules, segmentation is just addressing with no enforcement.

Hop 4 - Switching and routing: the packet finds its path. What: inside each VLAN, switches forward frames by MAC address (hardware address); between VLANs, the router forwards packets by IP address using longest-prefix-match (the most specific matching route wins). How: the switch learns which MAC lives on which port and forwards only there (unknown destinations get flooded once, then learned); the L3 switch checks its routing table for the most specific route to 10.10.10.50 - the connected 10.10.10.0/24 beats any summary route - and STP (Spanning Tree Protocol) has already blocked the redundant looped port so the frame does not circle forever. Why: without MAC learning every frame is a broadcast and the network collapses under its own chatter; without longest-prefix-match the router cannot choose between overlapping routes; without STP one miscabled loop takes down both VLANs in seconds.

Hop 5 - Active Directory: the user proves who they are. What: the app asks 'who are you?' and the laptop answers with Kerberos, AD's authentication protocol - no passwords cross the network. How: the laptop already got a Ticket Granting Ticket at logon from the domain controller (which is why logon needs the DC reachable); now it requests a service ticket for the app server, the DC encrypts it with a key derived from the server's account, and the server decrypts it - proving the user is who they claim without ever seeing a password. Why: without this hop there is no identity - every app would need its own password database - and a dead PDC Emulator (the FSMO role that arbitrates password changes and lockouts) means nobody can change passwords anywhere.

Hop 6 - Group Policy: the machine becomes compliant. What: at logon and every ~90 minutes after, the laptop pulls its GPOs and applies them in LSDOU order (Local, Site, Domain, OU - later wins). How: Local policy applies first, then Site, Domain, OU, each overwriting the last; the OU-linked baseline (firewall on, SMBv1 off, Defender configured, LAPS rotating the local admin password) lands last and wins, unless an Enforced parent GPO punches through. Why: without this hop every laptop drifts toward its user's preferences and away from the security baseline - the hardening lesson's controls only exist on machines because Group Policy put them there and keeps putting them there.

Hop 7 - SQL Server: the data is served with least privilege. What: the app queries SQL Server for the user's dashboard, authenticating with a service account. How: the login (server-level: allowed to connect) maps to a user (database-level: exists inside the AppDB database) which sits in db_datareader - read-only, one database, nothing else; the query executes, the transaction commits to the log, and the log backup every 15 minutes captures it into the restore chain. Why: without the login/user/role split the app's account would need sysadmin or nothing - and a compromised app with sysadmin owns every database; without the FULL recovery model and log chain, a bad DELETE at 10:17 is permanent.

Hop 8 - Backup and watch: the system protects itself and someone is watching. What: tonight's differential backup plus Sunday's full give a two-media restore; the 3-2-1 copies (production, NAS, offsite immutable) mean ransomware cannot take all three; and the morning routine - repadmin /replsummary, dcdiag, wbadmin get versions, Get-VMReplication health - verifies it all. How: RPO (Recovery Point Objective, the data-loss tolerance: 1 hour) drives the hourly log backups; RTO (Recovery Time Objective, the downtime tolerance: 4 hours) was proven by timing last quarter's test restore; monitoring is just these checks run on a schedule with alerts, because a RAID controller that emails nobody about a dead disk is redundancy you cannot see degrading. Why: without the backup chain every hop above is one disaster away from irrelevance, and without the watching routine the first sign of failure is the outage - the difference between an admin who hopes and an admin who knows.

example.code:
08:00  Ana opens her laptop. The Wi-Fi associates; the laptop broadcasts DHCPDISCOVER.
08:00  DHCP server answers: DHCPOFFER 10.10.20.44/24, gateway 10.10.20.1,
       DNS 10.10.20.11, lease 8h. Laptop: DHCPREQUEST. Server: DHCPACK.
       (Hop 1 - DHCP. Without it: 169.254.x.x and nothing works.)
08:01  Ana opens https://app.corp.local. Laptop asks 10.10.20.11: 'app.corp.local?'
       DC's DNS checks the AD-integrated zone: 10.10.10.50. Cached for the TTL.
       (Hop 2 - DNS. Without it: names are dead, Kerberos breaks.)
08:01  The first packet leaves Ana's access port tagged VLAN 20 (workstations).
       The L3 switch routes it via its VLAN 20 SVI toward VLAN 10 (servers).
       The firewall ACL is read top-down: rule 20 permits 10.10.20.0/24 to
       10.10.10.50:443 BEFORE the deny - first match wins, packet passes.
       (Hop 3 - VLAN + firewall. A permit below the deny would silently fail.)
08:01  Inside VLAN 20 the switch forwards by MAC (learned port table).
       The L3 switch picks the connected 10.10.10.0/24 route - longest prefix
       match beats the summary. STP has the redundant link blocked: no loop.
       (Hop 4 - switching + routing. Every table was built before Ana arrived.)
08:01  The app challenges Ana. Her laptop presents its Kerberos service ticket
       (granted at logon by the DC - no password on the wire). The app server
       decrypts it with its own account key: identity proven.
       (Hop 5 - Active Directory. Without the DC: no logon, no tickets.)
08:01  At logon Ana's laptop applied GPOs in LSDOU order: the OU baseline won -
       host firewall on, SMBv1 off, Defender real-time on, LAPS rotated the
       local admin password last night. The laptop is compliant by construction.
       (Hop 6 - Group Policy. The baseline is not a hope; it is enforced.)
08:02  The app queries SQL01 as svc_app. Login (server) -> user (AppDB) ->
       db_datareader: read-only, one database. The dashboard renders.
       The SELECT's transaction committed to the log; the 15-min log backup
       will capture it. (Hop 7 - SQL Server. Least privilege, chained backups.)
02:00  Tonight: differential backup runs (changes since Sunday's full).
       3-2-1 holds: production copy, NAS copy, immutable offsite copy.
       07:00  The morning routine: repadmin /replsummary clean, dcdiag passes,
       wbadmin get versions lists the new backup, replica health Normal.
       (Hop 8 - backup + watch. Proven recoverable, not merely 'backed up.')
example.walkthrough: Follow the packet, not the diagram. Ana's single click touches eight infrastructure systems in about two seconds, and every one of them was configured, secured, and verified BEFORE she arrived - DHCP scopes sized by the subnetting math, VLANs trunked with matching native VLANs, firewall rules ordered permit-before-deny, AD replicating cleanly (repadmin said so this morning), GPOs applying in LSDOU order, SQL Server running least-privilege with a log chain, and backups that were test-restored last quarter. The walkthrough names the failure each hop prevents: no DHCP means APIPA; no DNS means Kerberos dies; a misordered ACL means silent denies; a dead PDC Emulator means no password changes; a missing log chain means the bad DELETE is forever. Read it again and cover the parentheticals: if you can narrate each hop's mechanism from memory, you understand the system, not just the pieces.

pitfalls: Troubleshooting DNS when it is DHCP: the app 'can't resolve names' but ipconfig shows 169.254.x.x - the laptop never got an address, so no DNS server was ever learned. Check ipconfig before nslookup; the name layer cannot work when the address layer never happened.

Forgetting the firewall between VLANs: the app works for the server team (same VLAN, no firewall in path) but times out for workstations. The permit rule was added BELOW the deny - ACLs stop at first match, so the fix never fires. Always read ACLs top-down like the firewall does.

Blaming the app when it is AD replication: Ana changed her password at HQ, but the branch app rejects it hours later. The app is fine; repadmin /replsummary shows 1722 (RPC unavailable) from the branch DC - the firewall change last week blocked TCP 135. Identity problems are often replication problems wearing a costume.

Treating the VM backup as the database backup: the VM was restored from last night's image and SQL Server starts - but the database is crash-consistent, not transactionally clean, and the 10:17 DELETE is still gone. VM images protect the server; only the SQL log chain (FULL recovery + log backups + STOPAT) protects the data. Different layers, different tools.

lessons.try_it: Draw the full stack from memory on paper, then explain each hop aloud as if teaching a new hire

lessons.title: Numbers for Networkers: Binary, Decimal, and Hex
concepts: Why binary: computers store everything as bits (binary digits, 0 or 1) because a transistor has two stable states — on or off. Eight bits make one byte, and every number a computer handles is a pile of bytes. Networking math is binary math with a decimal costume.

Place values: in decimal, each position leftward is x10 (1s, 10s, 100s). In binary, each position leftward is x2: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. An 8-bit byte's places are 128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1, and the value is the sum of the 'switched on' places. This is the single skill everything else rests on.

Decimal to binary (the subtraction method): take the number, subtract the largest place value that fits, write 1, keep the remainder; for each smaller place, write 1 if it fits in the remainder (subtracting it) else 0. Example: 192 -> 192-128=64 -> 1; 64-64=0 -> 1; 0 fits nowhere else -> 0 0 0 0 0 0. Result: 11000000.

Binary to decimal (the addition method): write the place values over the bits and add the ones that are switched on. Example: 10101000 -> 128 + 32 + 8 = 168. Always verify by converting back the other way.

Why octets: an IPv4 address is 32 bits, but nobody reads 32 bits at once, so it is split into four 8-bit groups (octets) written in decimal: 192.168.1.1. Each octet holds 2^8 = 256 values (0-255). Dotted decimal is a human-readability convention, not a computer reality — the wire sees 32 bits.

The five octets you must know cold: 0 = 00000000, 128 = 10000000, 192 = 11000000, 224 = 11100000, 255 = 11111111. And 168 = 10101000 (128+32+8). These appear in nearly every subnet mask and private address; memorizing them removes half the conversion work in exams and on the job.

Hexadecimal (hex, base 16): digits 0-9 then A=10, B=11, C=12, D=13, E=14, F=15. One hex digit = exactly 4 bits (a nibble), so one byte = exactly two hex digits. That exact mapping is why hex is the language of MAC addresses (48 bits = 6 bytes = 12 hex digits, e.g., 00:1B:44:11:3A:B7) and IPv6 (128 bits = 8 groups of 4 hex digits, e.g., 2001:0db8:...). Hex digit to 4-bit table: 0=0000, 1=0001, 2=0010, 3=0011, 4=0100, 5=0101, 6=0110, 7=0111, 8=1000, 9=1001, A=1010, B=1011, C=1100, D=1101, E=1110, F=1111.

Hex conversions: hex to decimal = (high digit x 16) + low digit — e.g., 0xC0 = 12x16 + 0 = 192. Hex to binary = expand each digit to its 4 bits — e.g., 0xA8 = 1010 1000 = 10101000 = 168. Binary to hex = regroup bits into fours from the right — e.g., 11000000 -> 1100 0000 -> C 0 -> 0xC0.

Bitwise AND (the operation subnetting is built on): compare two bits; the result is 1 only if BOTH are 1, else 0. Truth table: 1&1=1, 1&0=0, 0&1=0, 0&0=0. Applied column by column across 8 bits. Example: 130 (10000010) AND 192 (11000000): 1&1=1, 0&1=0, 0&1=0, rest 0&0=0 -> 10000000 = 128.

Logic Check — the whole number-system chain: transistors have two states -> bits -> 8 bits = 1 byte = the unit computers move -> 32-bit IPv4 addresses -> humans cannot read 32 bits -> split into four 8-bit octets in decimal (dotted decimal) -> but masks and AND operate on BITS, so you convert back to binary for the interesting octet -> hex exists because 4 bits = 1 digit exactly, keeping bit structure visible in MAC/IPv6 notation. Every notation is a human interface over the same bits; subnetting is the skill of moving between the interfaces without losing the bits.

Logic Check — why 2^8 = 256 values per octet, not 255: 8 bits count from 00000000 (0) to 11111111 (255) — that is 256 distinct patterns INCLUDING zero. Forgetting zero is the root of every off-by-one in networking ('a /24 has 255 addresses' — no: 256 total, 254 usable). Zero is a value, not the absence of one.

example.walkthrough: The example converts 172.16.254.1 octet by octet using the subtraction method, verifying each octet by adding its place values back. It deliberately includes 254 to teach the 'all ones minus the last bit' pattern, and cross-checks the first octet via hex (0xAC -> 10101100) to show hex and binary are two views of the same bits. Key takeaway: never trust a conversion you have not verified by converting back.

pitfalls: Reading binary right-to-left: the 128s place is on the LEFT. Reading 10110100 backwards as if the leftmost bit were the 1s place gives 45 instead of 180. Always label place values before adding.
Forgetting the 0 octet: 0 = 00000000, all eight bits written out. Writing '0' as a single 0 breaks column alignment in AND operations.
Hex F = 15, not 16: a single hex digit maxes at F (like decimal maxes at 9, not 10). 0xF0 = 15x16 = 240, not 256.

Memorizing conversions instead of the method: under pressure you will face numbers you have not memorized (like 172). The subtraction method works on every number; memorize only the five mask octets (0, 128, 192, 224, 255) plus 168.
Treating dotted decimal as four independent numbers: 192.168.1.1 is one 32-bit number wearing a costume. Subnet math operates on the bits; the dots are just punctuation for humans.
lessons.try_it: Convert 10.0.0.255 to full 32-bit binary (all four octets, 8 bits each). Then convert the MAC byte 0xB7 to decimal and to 8-bit binary. Answers: 10 = 00001010 (8+2), 0 = 00000000, 255 = 11111111 (all ones — the 'broadcast' pattern), so 00001010.00000000.00000000.11111111. 0xB7 = 11x16 + 7 = 176 + 7 = 183 = 10110111 (128+32+16+4+2+1 = 183).

lessons.title: Math You'll Use Every Day: Subnets, Scopes, and Capacity
concepts: The two formulas that run infrastructure: addresses per subnet = 2^(host bits), usable hosts = 2^(host bits) - 2. Host bits = 32 - prefix length. The -2 removes the network address (all host bits 0, means 'this network') and the broadcast address (all host bits 1, means 'everyone here') — both reserved by convention, never assigned to a host.

The block-size method, proven: in the interesting octet, block size = 256 - mask octet. Why it works: the mask octet's 1-bits sum to 256 minus the smallest counting unit of the host bits in that octet. A /26 leaves 6 host bits total, 2 in the last octet's share... more precisely, for a /26 the last octet has 2 network bits (value 128+64 = 192 = 256 - 64), and the host portion counts in units of 2^6 = 64. 256 - 192 = 64 is not a trick; it is the same number computed from the other side.

Finding the network address: bitwise AND the address with the mask (interesting octet to binary, AND column by column). Finding the broadcast: network address + block size - 1 (in the interesting octet). Usable range: everything between. Always sanity-check: the given address must fall between network and broadcast.

Sizing a subnet for N hosts: required addresses = N + 2, round UP to the next power of 2, host bits = log2 of that, prefix = 32 - host bits. Powers of 2 to memorize: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024. A /24 (254 usable) is the default LAN size because 8 host bits is the largest block where the interesting octet is the last one — the simplest possible mental math.

DHCP scope math: leasable pool = 2^(host bits) - 2 - exclusions - reservations. Exclusions are ranges withheld from dynamic assignment (static infrastructure); reservations pin specific IPs to MAC addresses (printers, servers that should keep an address but stay centrally managed). Size the scope from measured demand plus growth headroom, typically 20-30%.

DHCP lease timeline: with lease length T, renewal (T1) at T/2, rebinding (T2) at T x 0.875, expiry at T. Windows default T = 8 days, so T1 = day 4 (unicast renewal to the original server), T2 = day 7 (broadcast rebind to any server). Short leases (hours) suit guest Wi-Fi with high churn; long leases (days) suit stable offices — the lease length trades address recycling speed against DHCP chatter.

Capacity planning formulas: RAID 5 usable = (n-1) x disk; RAID 6 = (n-2) x disk; RAID 10 = (n/2) x disk; RAID 1 = 1 x disk. Write penalty (disk I/Os per application write): RAID 0 = 1, RAID 1/10 = 2, RAID 5 = 4, RAID 6 = 6. Effective write IOPS = raw IOPS / penalty. Rebuild time ≈ disk size / sustained rebuild speed — the window during which a RAID 5 has no redundancy left.

Backup window math: time = data / sustained throughput, in consistent units. The bits-vs-bytes trap: network links are quoted in bits (100 Mb/s = 12.5 MB/s) while backup tools report bytes — a factor-of-8 error if you mix them. RPO sets backup frequency (RPO 1 h -> back up at least hourly); RTO sets the restore deadline (the whole recovery procedure, not just the copy phase, must fit inside it).

Logic Check — the daily-math causal chain: business need (N hosts) -> +2 reserved -> round UP to power of 2 (whole host bits only) -> prefix length -> carve largest-first on block boundaries (multiples of block size, else misalignment) -> DHCP pool = usable - exclusions - reservations -> lease T sets renewal at T/2 and rebind at 0.875T -> capacity: usable = f(RAID level), write speed = raw IOPS / penalty -> backup window = bytes / bytes-per-second with units checked. Each step's output is the next step's input; an error anywhere compounds downstream — which is why every step gets verified before moving on.

example.code:
Scenario: a new office needs 3 subnets (90, 40, and 15 hosts), a DHCP scope for the 90-host subnet, and a backup window check.

PART A — size the subnets from 192.168.10.0/24.
  90 hosts: need 92 addresses -> next power of 2 is 128 = 2^7 -> /25 (126 usable).
    Block 128 -> 192.168.10.0/25 (range .0 - .127).
  40 hosts: need 42 -> next power of 2 is 64 = 2^6 -> /26 (62 usable).
    Next free: .128; block 64 -> 192.168.10.128/26 (range .128 - .191).
  15 hosts: need 17 -> next power of 2 is 32 = 2^5 -> /27 (30 usable).
    Next free: .192; block 32 -> 192.168.10.192/27 (range .192 - .223).
  Leftover: 192.168.10.224/27 free for growth. All starts are multiples of their block sizes.

PART B — DHCP scope on 192.168.10.0/25.
  Usable: 128 - 2 = 126. Exclusions: .1 (gateway), .2-.9 (8 switches/printers) = 9 total.
  Reservations: 6 lab PCs. Leasable pool = 126 - 9 - 6 = 111.
  Demand: 90 hosts -> 111 >= 90 fits, 21 spare (~19% headroom).

PART C — backup window: 400 GB nightly to a target sustaining 120 MB/s.
  400 GB = 400,000 MB. 400,000 / 120 = 3,333 s = 55.6 min. Fits a 2-hour window with margin.
  If the link were '120 Mb/s' (megabits): 120/8 = 15 MB/s -> 400,000/15 = 26,667 s = 7.4 h. MISSES the window — the bits/bytes trap.
example.walkthrough: One scenario chains all three skills: subnet sizing (N+2, round to power of 2, carve largest-first on block boundaries), DHCP scope math (usable minus exclusions minus reservations vs demand), and a backup window with the bits-vs-bytes trap sprung deliberately to show the factor-of-8 consequence. Each part verifies its answer against the next (the /25 from Part A feeds Part B's pool).

pitfalls: Forgetting the -2: a /26 has 64 addresses but 62 usable hosts. Answering '64 hosts' is the single most common subnetting error.
Sizing for N instead of N+2: 30 hosts need 32 addresses (/27), not a /28 (14 usable). The network and broadcast addresses are not optional.
Carving smallest-first: always carve the largest subnet first. Smallest-first fragments the space and causes block-boundary misalignment.
Counting exclusions but forgetting reservations (or vice versa) in the DHCP pool: leasable = usable - exclusions - reservations. Both reduce the pool.
Bits vs bytes in throughput: 100 Mb/s (megabits, networks) vs 100 MB/s (megabytes, storage tools). Dividing bytes by bits-per-second without converting inflates or deflates the answer 8x.
Treating RTO as 'copy time': RTO covers detection, decision, restore, replay, and validation. A 20-minute copy inside a 30-minute RTO leaves almost no budget for everything else.
lessons.try_it: You have 10.20.0.0/22 and need subnets for 400, 100, and 20 hosts. Give each subnet's CIDR, range, and usable count, carved largest-first. Answers: 400 hosts -> need 402 -> next pow2 512 -> /23 (510 usable): 10.20.0.0/23 (.0.0-.1.255). 100 hosts -> need 102 -> 128 -> /25 (126 usable): next free 10.20.2.0/25 (.2.0-.2.127). 20 hosts -> need 22 -> 32 -> /27 (30 usable): next free 10.20.2.128/27 (.2.128-.2.159). Remainder of the /22 free. Boundary check: .0.0, .2.0, .2.128 are multiples of block sizes 512, 128, 32 — valid.

lessons.title: How Authentication Really Works: Kerberos and LDAP
concepts: The problem Kerberos solves: proving identity without sending the password. Every password sent over a wire can be captured; Kerberos never sends it. Instead, both sides derive the same secret key from the password (via a hash), and the client proves knowledge by encrypting something with that key — knowledge demonstrated, password untransmitted.

The KDC (Key Distribution Center): a service on every domain controller that knows every principal's secret (users' password hashes, servers' long-term keys). It is the trusted third party: clients and servers never share secrets directly; both trust the KDC, so a ticket the KDC sealed is proof of identity to anyone.

Leg 1 — AS exchange (Authentication Service): AS-REQ = client sends username plus a timestamp encrypted with its password-derived key. AS-REP = the KDC decrypts it (proving the client knows the password), checks the timestamp is fresh (replay protection), and returns a TGT (Ticket-Granting Ticket): a blob encrypted with the KDC's own secret containing the user identity, validity window, and a session key. The client cannot read the TGT — it just carries it.

Leg 2 — TGS exchange (Ticket-Granting Service): the client presents the TGT plus the name of the service it wants (file server, LDAP, SYSVOL for Group Policy) in TGS-REQ. The KDC verifies the TGT (it can decrypt it — it sealed it), and returns TGS-REP: a service ticket encrypted with the TARGET SERVER's secret, containing the user identity, the client's network address, validity window, and a fresh session key for client-server talk.

Leg 3 — AP exchange (Application): AP-REQ = the client hands the service ticket to the server. The server decrypts it with its own secret, sees a KDC-sealed identity, optionally verifies a fresh authenticator timestamp, and grants access. The server never talked to the KDC during this — that is the point of tickets: offline-verifiable, KDC-signed identity assertions.

The two constants, explained: ticket lifetime 10 hours (Default Domain Policy 'Maximum lifetime for user ticket') — about one workday, bounding how long a stolen ticket is useful, renewable up to 7 days so long sessions are unaffected; clock skew tolerance 5 minutes ('Maximum tolerance for computer clock synchronization') — every authenticator carries a timestamp, and anything older than 5 minutes is rejected as a possible replay, which is why an 8-minute clock drift breaks logons with cryptic errors while the cryptography is perfectly fine.

LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol): the query language of Active Directory — how clients READ the directory (find users, groups, computers, SRV records locating domain controllers). LDAP binds traditionally used simple username/password (sent, ideally over TLS on port 636 / LDAPS); modern AD authentication uses Kerberos for the actual logon and LDAP for directory lookups. Port 389 = LDAP, 636 = LDAP over TLS, 3268 = Global Catalog LDAP.

Why Group Policy depends on all of this: at boot/logon the machine authenticates via Kerberos (legs 1-3 against the DC), then reads policy files from SYSVOL using the service tickets — a broken clock, an expired machine password, or a failed TGS exchange means policies silently stop applying. 'Check time sync, then check the secure channel' is Kerberos troubleshooting in one sentence.

Logic Check — the authentication causal chain: password must never cross the wire -> prove knowledge via encrypted timestamp instead -> need a trusted party holding everyone's secrets -> the KDC -> proving identity once per logon is enough; per-service access uses short-lived scoped tickets (TGT -> service tickets) -> servers verify tickets offline using their own KDC-shared secret -> timestamps bound every step -> clocks must agree within 5 minutes or freshness checks fail -> Group Policy rides on top of all of it (machine authenticates, then reads SYSVOL). Break any link — wrong password, drifty clock, broken secure channel — and everything above it fails with misleading symptoms.

Logic Check — Kerberos vs LDAP roles (why both exist): authentication ('who are you?') and directory lookup ('what groups is she in? where is the nearest DC?') are different problems. Kerberos solves authentication with tickets and cryptography; LDAP solves directory queries with a query protocol. AD uses Kerberos to prove identity, then LDAP (often with the Kerberos identity attached) to read the directory. One protocol doing both would couple security credentials to every directory read — separation keeps each mechanism matched to its job.

example.code:
Timeline: user alice@corp logs on at 08:00, opens \\files\share at 08:05, still working at 19:00.

08:00:00  AS-REQ:  workstation -> KDC: 'I am alice' + [timestamp 08:00:00 encrypted with alice's password-derived key].
08:00:01  KDC: decrypts with stored hash of alice's password -> success (password proven, never sent).
            Timestamp 08:00:00 vs KDC clock 08:00:01 -> 1 s skew, within 5 min -> fresh, not a replay.
08:00:01  AS-REP:  KDC -> workstation: TGT (sealed with KDC secret; workstation cannot read it)
            valid 08:00-18:00 + session key K1 (workstation CAN read this).
08:00:02  Group Policy: workstation -> KDC in TGS-REQ: [TGT] + 'I need the file service (SYSVOL)'.
08:00:03  TGS-REP:  KDC -> workstation: service ticket for the DC's file service (sealed with the DC's secret) + session key K2.
08:00:04  AP-REQ:   workstation -> DC: service ticket. DC decrypts with its own secret,
            sees KDC-sealed 'alice, valid till 18:00', serves Group Policy files. Logon completes.
08:05     \\files\share: TGS-REQ/TGS-REP again for the file server's service, then AP-REQ to it.
            Note: NO new AS exchange — the TGT from 08:00 is reused. One logon, many service tickets.
18:00     TGT expires. Nothing visible happens — tickets gate NEW authentications only.
19:00     Alice opens a new share: workstation transparently does a fresh AS exchange
            (cached credentials, no prompt; renewable up to 7 days) and carries on.
example.walkthrough: The timeline shows all three Kerberos legs in order with the cryptographic role of each message: AS proves password knowledge, TGS trades the TGT for service-specific tickets, AP presents the ticket to the server. It demonstrates TGT reuse across services (one logon, many tickets), the 10-hour expiry as a non-event for the session, and transparent renewal — the three behaviors learners most often misunderstand.

pitfalls: Thinking the password crosses the network: it never does — only a timestamp encrypted with the password-derived key. Packet captures of Kerberos show ciphertext, not credentials.

Confusing the TGT with a service ticket: the TGT (from the AS exchange) only gets you MORE tickets; the service ticket (from the TGS exchange) is what the file server actually accepts. 'I have a TGT' does not mean 'I can access the share'.
Expecting a kickoff at ticket expiry: tickets are checked at authentication time, not continuously. Expiry at 18:00 does not end the session; the next new resource transparently re-authenticates.
Resetting passwords for clock-skew failures: an 8-minute drift fails the 5-minute freshness check (KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW) with misleading errors. Fix time sync (w32tm), not the account.
Treating LDAP as the logon protocol: in AD, Kerberos authenticates and LDAP queries the directory. An LDAP bind succeeding does not mean Kerberos is healthy, and vice versa.

Forgetting the machine account: computers are Kerberos principals too, with their own passwords rotated every 30 days. A broken secure channel (machine password mismatch) breaks Kerberos for the whole machine — rejoin or reset the machine account, not the user.
lessons.try_it: At 14:00 a user authenticates and gets a TGT. (a) When does it expire? (b) At 15:00 they access a file server — which Kerberos exchanges occur, and is a new AS exchange needed? (c) The user's PC clock is 12 minutes behind the DC and logon fails — name the failing check, the error concept, and the fix. Answers: (a) 14:00 + 10 h = 24:00 (midnight). (b) TGS-REQ/TGS-REP for the file server's service ticket, then AP-REQ to the server. No new AS exchange — the 14:00 TGT is presented to the TGS; AS only happens at initial logon/renewal. (c) The authenticator freshness check: 12 min exceeds the 5-minute clock-skew tolerance, so the KDC rejects the timestamp as a possible replay (KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW). Fix: synchronize time (w32tm /resync against the domain hierarchy); investigate the drift source so it does not recur.

lessons.title: PowerShell From Zero: Variables, Objects, and the Pipeline
concepts: A cmdlet (pronounced 'command-let') is PowerShell's single-purpose command, always named Verb-Noun: the VERB says what it does, the NOUN says what it acts on. Get-Process reads processes, Stop-Service stops a service. Memorize the verbs and you can guess commands you have never seen.

The four verbs that unlock 80% of infrastructure work: Get (read/inspect — never changes anything, always safe to run), Set (modify something that already exists), New (create something), Remove (delete something). Add Start/Stop/Restart for services and VMs and you can navigate almost any module.

Variables always start with $ and need no declaration: $name = 'Orlando'. The $ is part of the name — forget it and PowerShell reads 'name' as literal text. Assign with a single = ; PowerShell has no == operator, and = inside a comparison silently assigns instead of comparing.

Everything in PowerShell is an OBJECT, not text. Get-Process does not return lines of text — it returns Process objects, each carrying properties (Name, CPU, Id, WorkingSet) and methods (Kill(), Refresh()). The table you see on screen is just one rendering of those objects.

Get-Member is your X-ray: pipe anything into it (Get-Process | Get-Member) to list every property and method an object exposes. When you do not know what you can grab from a cmdlet's output, Get-Member tells you. Run it before you guess property names.

The pipeline character | passes whole OBJECTS — properties and all — from one cmdlet to the next, not just screen text. That is why Where-Object can filter on .CPU two steps later: the property traveled inside the object. CMD pipes pass text; PowerShell pipes pass data.

Select-Object picks WHICH properties to keep (columns), Where-Object filters WHICH objects pass through (rows), Sort-Object orders them. All three operate on objects, so they can sit anywhere in the pipeline — but Format-Table and Format-List are display-only and must go LAST, because they destroy the objects and replace them with screen-layout instructions. Logic Check: WHY filter (Where) before select (Select)? Two reasons. (1) Performance: fewer objects travel downstream. (2) Correctness: Where-Object needs properties that an early Select-Object may have already dropped. The pipeline is a one-way street — each stage only sees what the previous stage passed on, so order your stages by what each one needs to still be there.

example.code: Get-Process | Where-Object CPU -gt 100 | Select-Object Name, CPU
example.walkthrough: Read left to right. (1) Get-Process emits one Process object per running process — each carrying Name, CPU, Id, and dozens more properties. (2) The pipe hands every object to Where-Object, which keeps only rows where the CPU property is -gt (greater than) 100 seconds of processor time. This is the simplified syntax: 'Where-Object CPU -gt 100' means property CPU, operator -gt, value 100 — no curly braces or $_ needed for a single comparison. (3) Select-Object keeps only the Name and CPU properties and drops the rest, producing the clean two-column view. Why this order? Filter FIRST (fewer objects travel downstream, so it runs faster), select AFTER (the filter needed the CPU property, which Select-Object would have thrown away). Swap steps 2 and 3 and the filter fails — once Select-Object drops CPU, Where-Object has nothing left to compare.

pitfalls: Piping Format-Table before Where-Object: Format-Table converts your objects into formatting records (screen-layout instructions). Everything after it sees formatting objects, not your data — so Where-Object CPU -gt 100 silently matches nothing and you get an empty table with no error. Format-* cmdlets are for human eyes only and always go LAST. Logic Check: ask 'does the next cmdlet need DATA or a PICTURE of data?' Where-Object needs data — objects with properties. Format-Table outputs formatting records, which are instructions for the screen renderer, not data. Once you format, there is no data left to filter — that is WHY format goes last, always.

Forgetting the quotes on -Filter: Get-ADUser -Filter Enabled -eq $false fails because PowerShell tries to evaluate the expression itself before the AD provider ever sees it. The filter is a STRING the provider parses: -Filter 'Enabled -eq $false' with single quotes so $false is not expanded early. Logic Check: TWO parsers touch this command — PowerShell parses the command line FIRST, then the AD provider parses the -Filter string. Unquoted, PowerShell consumes 'Enabled -eq $false' as its own expression and the provider receives garbage. The quotes are not decoration; they are a boundary marker telling PowerShell 'hands off — this string belongs to the provider.'

Using = or == in comparisons: if ($x = 5) ASSIGNS 5 to $x and is always true; == is not a PowerShell operator at all. Comparisons are -eq (equal), -ne (not equal), -gt, -lt, -ge, -le, -like (wildcard match), -match (regex match).

Treating output as text: Select-Object Name shows a Name column, but the objects downstream still carry every other property until you narrow them. That richness is the point — do not flatten to text (Out-String) mid-pipeline or you lose the ability to filter and sort.
lessons.try_it: In a PowerShell console run: Get-Service | Where-Object Status -eq 'Running' | Select-Object Name, Status | Sort-Object Name. Then run Get-Process | Get-Member and find three properties you did not know a process object had. Finally, deliberately run Get-Process | Format-Table | Where-Object CPU -gt 100 and observe the silent empty result — then fix the order.

lessons.title: PowerShell Scripting: Loops, Conditionals, Functions
concepts: A .ps1 file is just saved PowerShell commands that run top to bottom. Write it in any editor, save with the .ps1 extension, and run it with .\myscript.ps1 — the .\ is mandatory because PowerShell deliberately refuses to run scripts from the current directory by bare name (a safety design borrowed from Unix shells). Logic Check: WHY the .\ rule? Windows searches PATH before the current directory — without this rule, a malicious script named 'notepad.ps1' sitting in some folder could hijack your innocent 'notepad' command. The .\ prefix is you explicitly declaring 'I mean THIS file, in THIS folder.'

Execution policy is PowerShell's seatbelt: it controls which scripts are allowed to run. Restricted (the default on Windows clients) runs NO scripts at all. RemoteSigned — the standard for admin workstations — runs your own local scripts freely but requires scripts downloaded from the internet to carry a digital signature. Logic Check: WHY the local-vs-internet split? The threat model is 'a script you were tricked into downloading,' not 'a script you wrote.'
