A signature proves the file came from an identified publisher and has not changed since signing. Your own local scripts need no signature because YOU are the trust boundary — you wrote them, on this machine.

Set-ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser changes the policy for YOUR account only: no admin rights needed, no machine-wide change. -Scope Process changes it for just the current console window and evaporates when you close it — handy on a locked-down assessment VM where you cannot persist settings.

foreach ($item in $collection) { ... } runs the block once per item; inside the block, $item is the current object. Use the foreach STATEMENT for readable scripts; the ForEach-Object cmdlet (alias %) is the one-liner pipeline version of the same idea.

if (condition) { } elseif (condition) { } else { } — conditions use -eq/-ne/-gt/-lt (never ==), every condition sits in PARENTHESES, every action block in CURLY BRACES. PowerShell evaluates top to bottom and runs the first branch whose condition is true.

Functions wrap reusable logic: function Get-StaleUsers { param([string]$OU) ... }. The param() block declares inputs with types ([string], [int], [switch]) — typed parameters reject bad input immediately instead of corrupting data silently three steps later. Name functions Verb-Noun like cmdlets so they feel native.

example.walkthrough: Line by line. (1) Import-Module ActiveDirectory loads the AD cmdlets — on a member server without RSAT this errors, which is your cue to install the management tools. (2) Get-ADUser -Filter 'Enabled -eq $false': the filter is a QUOTED string because the AD provider parses it, not PowerShell — single quotes stop PowerShell from expanding $false first. -Properties LastLogonDate is mandatory because Get-ADUser returns only about ten default properties and LastLogonDate is not one of them. (3) foreach walks each returned user object; $user holds the FULL object with all requested properties. (4) The if compares $user.LastLogonDate against (Get-Date).AddDays(-90): Get-Date returns right now, .AddDays(-90) rewinds 90 days, and -lt means 'older than'. (5) Write-Host prints progress; $($...) is a subexpression — required inside double quotes to evaluate an expression. Without it, "$user.SamAccountName" would print the literal text. (6) $disabled.Count works because Get-ADUser returned an ARRAY of objects. Save as Find-DisabledUsers.ps1 and run .\Find-DisabledUsers.ps1 — bare 'Find-DisabledUsers.ps1' without .\ will fail by design.

pitfalls: The script will not run at all: 'cannot be loaded because running scripts is disabled on this system.' That is the execution policy (Restricted), not a broken script. Fix: Set-ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser, then re-run. Do not reach for -ExecutionPolicy Bypass in a real environment without understanding why the policy exists.

Forgetting the -Filter quotes: Get-ADUser -Filter Enabled -eq $false throws a parser error before anything runs. The AD provider needs the whole expression as one string: -Filter 'Enabled -eq $false'.
Using == or = in conditions: if ($user.Enabled == $false) is a syntax error; if ($user.Enabled = $false) silently ASSIGNS false and the branch always runs. Always -eq, -ne, -gt, -lt.

Forgetting -Properties: $user.LastLogonDate comes back EMPTY (no error, just blank) if you did not request it. Blank is not the same as 'never logged on' — verify what you actually fetched with Get-Member before drawing conclusions.
lessons.try_it: Save the example as Find-DisabledUsers.ps1, check your current policy with Get-ExecutionPolicy -List, set RemoteSigned for your user scope, and run it with .\Find-DisabledUsers.ps1. Then extend it: add an elseif branch that flags disabled accounts where PasswordNeverExpires is true (request it via -Properties).

lessons.title: Every AD/DNS/DHCP/Hyper-V Cmdlet You'll Need
concepts: I need to CREATE a user → New-ADUser. -Name (REQUIRED: display name, 'Jane Doe'). -SamAccountName (REQUIRED: the pre-Windows-2000 logon name, max 20 characters, 'jdoe'). -Path (the OU distinguished name — technically optional, but omit it and the account lands in the default CN=Users container where OU-linked GPOs can never target it). -AccountPassword (a SecureString, never plain text — build it with (Read-Host -AsSecureString 'Password') so it is never on screen or in history). -Enabled $true (new accounts are DISABLED by default; forget this and the user cannot log on). -UserPrincipalName ('jdoe@corp.lab': the modern username@domain logon format). -GivenName/-Surname fill the name fields properly instead of leaving them blank.

I need to FIND users → Get-ADUser. -Filter (a quoted query string — effectively MANDATORY: the cmdlet refuses to run with neither -Filter nor -Identity; use -Filter * for 'everything' or -Filter 'Enabled -eq $false'). -Identity (one specific user; accepts four formats: SamAccountName, DistinguishedName, GUID, or SID — 'jdoe' just works). -SearchBase (limits the search to one OU — faster and scoped: -SearchBase 'OU=Users,OU=Orlando,DC=corp,DC=lab'). -Properties (extra attributes to return; the DEFAULT set is only ~10 properties, so LastLogonDate, PasswordLastSet, and MemberOf each need an explicit -Properties request).

I need to RESET a password → Set-ADAccountPassword. -Identity (who — SamAccountName works). -NewPassword (SecureString, same Read-Host pattern). -Reset $true (REQUIRED for admin resets: it marks the operation as an administrative reset, which skips the 'must know the old password' requirement. Without -Reset it behaves like a user changing their own password and fails). Example: Set-ADAccountPassword -Identity jdoe -NewPassword (Read-Host -AsSecureString 'New password') -Reset $true

I need to UNLOCK a locked account → Unlock-ADAccount -Identity jdoe. This clears the lockout flag after too many bad passwords — it changes NO password. If the account re-locks immediately, check the Account Lockout Threshold GPO: the user is still typing the wrong password and every attempt re-arms the lockout.

I need to DISABLE or RE-ENABLE an account → Disable-ADAccount -Identity jdoe / Enable-ADAccount -Identity jdoe. Disable for terminations and suspensions: it preserves the account, its group memberships, and its SID history for audit — deleting instead destroys that forensic trail. Enable reverses it; the password and memberships are untouched.

I need to CREATE an OU → New-ADOrganizationalUnit. -Name (REQUIRED). -Path (the PARENT distinguished name — default is the domain root, so always specify it deliberately). -ProtectedFromAccidentalDeletion $true (STRONGLY recommended: blocks casual deletes in the GUI; when you later genuinely need to delete the OU, flip it to $false first — 'the OU will not delete' is this flag doing its job). Example: New-ADOrganizationalUnit -Name 'Orlando' -Path 'DC=corp,DC=lab' -ProtectedFromAccidentalDeletion $true

I need to CREATE and LINK a GPO → New-GPO -Name 'Baseline-Hardening' creates the (initially empty, unlinked) policy object; New-GPLink -Name 'Baseline-Hardening' -Target 'OU=Workstations,OU=Orlando,DC=corp,DC=lab' attaches it. -Target is the OU/domain/site distinguished name the GPO links to. -LinkEnabled Yes/No toggles the link without deleting it. -Enforced Yes sets 'No Override' — the GPO wins every precedence battle beneath it. Link order: when several GPOs link to one OU they process bottom-up by link order; rearrange with Set-GPLink -Order.

I need to CREATE a DNS host record → Add-DnsServerResourceRecordA. -ZoneName 'corp.lab' (the forward lookup zone — it MUST already exist; the cmdlet will not create zones). -Name 'web01' (the HOST portion only, not the FQDN). -IPv4Address '10.1.10.50'. -AllowUpdateAny permits insecure dynamic updates — fine in a lab, never in production (use secure updates there). To delete: Remove-DnsServerResourceRecord -ZoneName 'corp.lab' -Name 'web01' -RRType 'A' — -RRType picks which record type to delete when one name holds several records.

I need to CREATE a DHCP scope → Add-DhcpServerv4Scope -Name 'Orlando-LAN' -StartRange 10.1.10.100 -EndRange 10.1.10.200 -SubnetMask 255.255.255.0 -State Active. -State Active is the gotcha: scopes are created INACTIVE unless you say Active, and an inactive scope leases NOTHING — 'DHCP is not working' with a healthy service is usually this. Logic Check: WHY inactive by default? So you can build the scope, exclusions, and options FIRST, then activate when ready — activating a half-built scope would hand out wrong gateways and DNS to real clients. Inactive-default is a safety catch; -State Active is you declaring 'this scope is complete, go live.' Reserve addresses for statics with Add-DhcpServerv4ExclusionRange -ScopeId 10.1.10.0 -StartRange 10.1.10.1 -EndRange 10.1.10.20. Inspect leases with Get-DhcpServerv4Lease -ScopeId 10.1.10.0 (the -ScopeId is the network ID, 10.1.10.0, not a range address).

I need to MANAGE Hyper-V → Get-VM lists guests (pipe to Where-Object State -eq 'Running' for the running set). New-VM -Name 'WEB01' -MemoryStartupBytes 4GB -NewVHDPath 'C:\VMs\WEB01.vhdx' -NewVHDSizeBytes 60GB -SwitchName 'External-vSwitch' -Generation 2: -Generation 2 means UEFI/Secure Boot with no IDE controllers — required for modern Windows and Linux; pick Generation 1 only for legacy operating systems. New-VMSwitch -Name 'External-vSwitch' -NetAdapterName 'Ethernet' -SwitchType External: External binds a physical NIC and gives VMs LAN access; Internal reaches host + VMs only; Private is VM-to-VM only. Checkpoint-VM -Name 'WEB01' -SnapshotName 'PrePatch' snapshots a VM — production checkpoints for servers (application-consistent), standard checkpoints for dev/test.

The -WhatIf safety net: almost every New-/Set-/Remove- cmdlet accepts -WhatIf, which prints WHAT WOULD HAPPEN without doing it. Before a Remove-ADUser or a bulk Set-, run it with -WhatIf first, read the preview, then run it for real. In a timed assessment this ten-second habit prevents the disasters that cost thirty minutes. Logic Check: WHY does -WhatIf exist on destructive cmdlets? Because in systems like AD there is no undo — -WhatIf runs the cmdlet's full targeting and parameter-binding logic but skips the commit, showing you exactly which objects WOULD be touched. It answers 'what will this hit?' before anything is hit.

example.code:
New-ADUser -Name 'Jane Doe' `
  -SamAccountName 'jdoe' `
  -UserPrincipalName 'jdoe@corp.lab' `
  -GivenName 'Jane' -Surname 'Doe' `
  -Path 'OU=Users,OU=Orlando,DC=corp,DC=lab' `
  -AccountPassword (Read-Host -AsSecureString 'Password') `
  -Enabled $true
example.walkthrough: Parameter by parameter. -Name 'Jane Doe' is the display name shown in address books. -SamAccountName 'jdoe' is the legacy DOMAIN\jdoe logon name (20-character limit — longer names get silently truncated and then nothing matches). -UserPrincipalName 'jdoe@corp.lab' is the modern jdoe@corp.lab logon format users actually type. -Path pins the account into the Orlando Users OU as a full distinguished name — read right-to-left: DC=corp,DC=lab is the domain, OU=Orlando is inside it, OU=Users inside that. Skip -Path and the user lands in CN=Users, invisible to every OU-linked GPO. -AccountPassword takes a SecureString: (Read-Host -AsSecureString 'Password') prompts with masked input, so the password never appears on screen or in command history — never pass plain text here. -Enabled $true activates the account immediately; the default is disabled, and a disabled new hire generates a 'my login does not work' ticket. The backtick ` at each line end is PowerShell's line-continuation character — it must be the LAST character on the line (a trailing space after it breaks the continuation silently).

pitfalls: Unquoted -Filter is the #1 AD cmdlet error: Get-ADUser -Filter Enabled -eq $false dies in the parser. The filter belongs to the AD provider as a single string: -Filter 'Enabled -eq $false'. Use DOUBLE quotes only when you need a variable expanded inside, e.g. -Filter "Name -like '$name'".

Get-ADUser returns ~10 properties by default. $user.LastLogonDate is blank — not an error, just unrequested — unless you added -Properties LastLogonDate. Blank-looking output after a correct query almost always means a missing -Properties, not missing data.

Set-ADAccountPassword without -Reset $true fails asking for the old password, because without -Reset it behaves as a user-initiated change. Administrative resets REQUIRE -Reset $true. Logic Check: the cmdlet has TWO code paths — user-change (must prove the old password) versus admin-reset (authority overrides the old password). -Reset $true selects the admin path. Without it you are asking for a user-style change on someone else's account, which correctly fails.
New DHCP scopes are born INACTIVE. Add-DhcpServerv4Scope without -State Active creates a scope that leases nothing — always verify with Get-DhcpServerv4Scope | Select Name, State.

New-ADUser without -Enabled $true creates a DISABLED account (secure default). New-ADOrganizationalUnit without -ProtectedFromAccidentalDeletion $true leaves the OU one careless right-click from deletion.

-Identity is flexible (SamAccountName, DN, GUID, SID) but -Filter is not: -Filter 'SamAccountName -eq jdoe' needs the value unquoted-inside-quotes exactly so; when in doubt use -Identity for single objects and -Filter for searches.
lessons.try_it: Chain the full lifecycle on one test account: New-ADUser (Enabled $true) → verify with Get-ADUser -Identity tuser1 -Properties Enabled → Set-ADAccountPassword -Reset $true → Disable-ADAccount → confirm Enabled is False → Enable-ADAccount → Unlock-ADAccount. Run each Get- with -WhatIf first on the destructive steps, then for real.

lessons.title: CMD Survival Kit: ipconfig, ping, tracert, nslookup, netstat, netsh
concepts: ipconfig shows the machine's IP configuration. ipconfig /all is the full picture: IPv4 address, subnet mask, default gateway, DNS servers, DHCP server, lease obtained/expires times, and the MAC (Physical Address). /release drops the DHCP lease and /renew requests a fresh one — the first fix for 'suddenly no network' (a corrupt or expired lease). /flushdns empties the DNS resolver cache (fixes 'the record changed but I still get the old IP'); /displaydns shows what is currently cached so you can see the stale entry before you flush it.

ping sends ICMP Echo Requests and reports replies. -n 4 sets the count (default is already 4). -t pings FOREVER until Ctrl+C — use it to watch for intermittent drops over time ('is this link flapping?'). -l 1472 sets the packet SIZE in bytes — 1472 is the largest payload that fits an unfragmented standard Ethernet frame, so failures at -l 1472 with success at default size point at MTU/fragmentation problems. Diagnose in OSI order: ping 127.0.0.1 (is my own TCP/IP stack alive?) → ping <default gateway> (is the local link up?) → ping 8.8.8.8 (does routing leave my network?) → ping fileserver.corp.lab (does NAME resolution work?). The first step that fails names the broken layer. Logic Check: WHY this exact order? Each step ADDS exactly one dependency: loopback proves the local stack with zero network involved; the gateway adds the local link; 8.8.8.8 adds routing beyond your LAN; the hostname adds DNS. Ping the hostname first and a failure tells you nothing — any of four layers could be broken. Ordered testing converts one ambiguous failure into one named layer.

Reading ping output: 'Reply from 10.1.10.1: bytes=32 time=2ms TTL=64' is success (time= latency, TTL= hops remaining before the packet dies). 'Request timed out' is SILENCE — the packet vanished (firewall drop, dead host, blackhole route). 'Destination host unreachable' is a ROUTER telling you it has no path — arguably more informative, because something answered. 'Ping request could not find host' is DNS failing before any packet was ever sent.

tracert maps the PATH, hop by hop, by sending packets with increasing TTLs. tracert -d skips reverse-DNS lookups on every hop — dramatically faster and the output is just as useful for fault-finding. Read it like a story: each line is one router; the three times are three probes. '* * *' means that hop did not answer ICMP — usually a firewall filtering ICMP, NOT a dead router (if the NEXT hop answers, the starred hop forwarded fine). A sudden latency jump at one hop = congestion or a slow link there; the trace DYING at the same hop every time = a routing loop, an ACL, or a dead next-hop at that point.

nslookup queries DNS directly. nslookup fileserver.corp.lab asks your CONFIGURED resolver. nslookup fileserver.corp.lab 10.1.10.10 asks THAT SPECIFIC SERVER — this distinction is the whole diagnostic: if the specific server answers but your default does not, the record is fine and your client's resolver config (or its cache) is the problem. Inside nslookup's interactive prompt, 'server 10.1.10.10' switches the default server for follow-up queries. 'Non-authoritative answer' just means the answer came from cache rather than the zone owner — normal, not an error.

netstat shows connections and listening ports. netstat -ano is the muscle-memory form: -a shows ALL connections plus LISTENING ports, -n shows NUMERIC addresses (skips slow reverse-DNS so output appears instantly), -o shows the OWNING PID (process ID — match it in Task Manager or with tasklist). States: LISTENING = a service waiting for connections (0.0.0.0:3389 LISTENING means RDP is up on all interfaces); ESTABLISHED = a live connection; TIME_WAIT = a recently closed connection draining. -anb adds the executable name but needs an elevated prompt. 'Port 443 not listening' vs 'listening but connection refused from remote' are two different faults — netstat tells you which.

netsh is CMD's configuration Swiss-army knife, organized as nested CONTEXTS you navigate like folders: netsh > interface > ipv4 > show config. The pattern is netsh <context> <subcontext> <verb>: 'show' verbs inspect, 'set/add/delete' verbs change. You can also run it one-shot without entering contexts: netsh interface ipv4 show config. Set a static IP: netsh interface ipv4 set address name="Ethernet" static 10.1.10.50 255.255.255.0 10.1.10.1 (name, then static, then IP, mask, gateway — in that fixed order). Set DNS: netsh interface ipv4 set dnsservers name="Ethernet" static 10.1.10.10 primary. Quote interface names containing spaces ("Ethernet 2"). Back to DHCP: netsh interface ipv4 set address name="Ethernet" source=dhcp and netsh interface ipv4 set dnsservers name="Ethernet" source=dhcp. Logic Check: WHY the rigid argument order (name, static, IP, mask, gateway)? netsh is POSITIONAL on these verbs — it has no named-parameter parser, so position IS the meaning. Swap the mask and gateway and you get a valid-looking command that configures garbage with no error. Whenever a command is positional, slow down and count positions out loud.

example.code:
C:\> ipconfig /all
   IPv4 Address. . . . . . . . . . . : 10.1.10.45
   Default Gateway . . . . . . . . . : 10.1.10.1
   DNS Servers . . . . . . . . . . . : 10.1.10.10
C:\> ping 10.1.10.1
   Reply from 10.1.10.1: bytes=32 time=1ms TTL=64
C:\> ping 8.8.8.8
   Reply from 8.8.8.8: bytes=32 time=18ms TTL=115
C:\> nslookup fileserver.corp.lab
   *** Request to 10.1.10.10 timed-out
C:\> nslookup fileserver.corp.lab 10.1.10.10
   Name:    fileserver.corp.lab
   Address:  10.1.10.60
example.walkthrough: The ticket says 'cannot reach the file server'. (1) ipconfig /all shows a healthy 10.1.10.45 with gateway 10.1.10.1 and DNS 10.1.10.10 — no APIPA address (169.254.x.x would have meant DHCP failed), so layer 1–3 local config is fine. (2) ping 10.1.10.1 replies in 1ms — the local link and gateway are up. (3) ping 8.8.8.8 replies — routing past the gateway works, so this is not a routing fault. (4) nslookup fileserver.corp.lab against the DEFAULT resolver times out — but (5) the SAME query aimed directly at 10.1.10.10 answers instantly with 10.1.10.60. Verdict: the DNS RECORD is healthy; the client's configured resolver path is broken (service down on the client's usual server, a firewall blocking UDP 53 from this host, or a poisoned cache — ipconfig /flushdns is the 10-second test). Fix the resolver path, not the zone. Notice the method: each command ruled out one layer before moving up the stack.

pitfalls: Ping success does NOT mean the application works. Ping uses ICMP; your app uses TCP/UDP ports. A server can answer ping all day while its firewall blocks TCP 445 (SMB) or 3389 (RDP). When ping works but the app fails, the next tool is Test-NetConnection <host> -Port <port> (PowerShell) or telnet — you have proven layer 3, now test layer 4.

Panicking at tracert '* * *'. Starred hops are usually routers configured not to answer ICMP, and the trace continuing PAST them proves they forwarded fine. Only worry when the trace STOPS at the stars and never recovers.

nslookup without a server argument tests YOUR resolver, not the zone. 'The DNS record is broken' is unproven until you query the authoritative server directly: nslookup name <authoritative-server-IP>.

netsh interface names with spaces must be quoted: name="Ethernet 2". Unquoted, netsh parses 'Ethernet' and '2' as separate tokens and errors. When unsure of the exact name, run netsh interface show interface first.

ipconfig /release + /renew on a STATICALLY configured NIC does nothing (there is no lease to release) — and /release without a following /renew leaves a DHCP machine with NO address. Always pair them.
lessons.try_it: On your machine, run the full ladder right now: ipconfig /all → ping 127.0.0.1 → ping <your gateway> → ping 8.8.8.8 → nslookup <your machine name> → netstat -ano | findstr LISTENING. Write down which layer each step proves, and identify one listening port you did not expect — then find its PID's process with tasklist | findstr <PID>.

lessons.title: T-SQL Basics: Query and Protect Data
concepts: SELECT reads data: SELECT FirstName, LastName FROM dbo.Employees. List the COLUMNS you want (never SELECT * in production — it drags every column including future ones, breaks when the schema changes, and wastes I/O). FROM names schema.table — dbo is the default schema; always qualify it so you never accidentally hit the wrong schema's table. WHERE filters ROWS: WHERE Department = 'IT' AND Active = 1. ORDER BY LastName sorts the result; without it, row order is undefined and can change between runs.

INSERT adds rows: INSERT INTO dbo.Employees (FirstName, LastName, Department) VALUES ('Jane', 'Doe', 'IT'). The column list is mandatory hygiene — without it, your VALUES must match the table's physical column order exactly, and any future schema change silently corrupts your inserts. One VALUES tuple = one row; stack multiple tuples to insert many rows in one statement.

UPDATE modifies rows: UPDATE dbo.Employees SET Department = 'Security' WHERE EmployeeID = 42. The WHERE clause is the difference between a targeted fix and a resume-generating event — without it, EVERY row gets the new value. Discipline: write the SELECT version of your WHERE first (SELECT * FROM dbo.Employees WHERE EmployeeID = 42), confirm it returns exactly the intended rows, then convert it to the UPDATE.

DELETE removes rows: DELETE FROM dbo.Employees WHERE EmployeeID = 42 — same WHERE discipline as UPDATE. TRUNCATE TABLE dbo.Employees is the fast alternative: it empties the whole table with minimal logging and resets identity columns, but it takes no WHERE (all or nothing), cannot be filtered, and will not fire DELETE triggers. In an assessment, DELETE with a verified WHERE is the safe, scorable choice.

BACKUP DATABASE takes the full copy: BACKUP DATABASE Orders TO DISK = 'E:\Backups\Orders_Full.bak' WITH INIT, COMPRESSION, STATS = 10. TO DISK = 'path' is the destination FILE (SQL Server writes it; the service account needs write permission on that folder). WITH INIT OVERWRITES any existing backup sets in that file — the default is NOINIT, which APPENDS. COMPRESSION shrinks the backup at CPU cost (almost always worth it). STATS = 10 prints a progress message every 10% — your only feedback on a long backup. A DIFFERENTIAL captures only changes since the last FULL: BACKUP DATABASE Orders TO DISK = 'E:\Backups\Orders_Diff.bak' WITH DIFFERENTIAL — smaller, faster, and the reason restores do not always need the whole chain of logs. Logic Check: WHY INIT versus NOINIT? A backup FILE can hold multiple backup SETS (like a tape). INIT means 'this file is mine — overwrite,' giving one set per file and zero-ambiguity restores. NOINIT means 'append,' stacking many sets in one file that you must then address by POSITION at restore time. In an assessment, INIT plus timestamped filenames is the safe habit.

RESTORE DATABASE replays the chain in order: RESTORE DATABASE Orders FROM DISK = 'E:\Backups\Orders_Full.bak' WITH NORECOVERY, REPLACE. WITH NORECOVERY leaves the database in the 'restoring' state so further backups can be applied — this is what KEEPS THE CHAIN ALIVE. Then RESTORE DATABASE Orders FROM DISK = 'E:\Backups\Orders_Diff.bak' WITH RECOVERY — WITH RECOVERY (the default on the final step) brings the database online. Apply RECOVERY too early and the chain is broken: the differential has nothing to attach to and you start over. Logic Check: WHY NORECOVERY? A multi-file restore is one transaction: SQL Server must hold the database in 'restoring' limbo while it stacks full, differential, and logs. WITH RECOVERY means 'commit the transaction, bring it online.' Committing early ends the transaction — later files cannot join a committed restore. So EVERY file except the last gets NORECOVERY ('not done yet'); only the FINAL file gets RECOVERY ('commit now'). REPLACE allows overwriting the existing database — without it, a restore onto an existing DB is refused. Before trusting any backup file: RESTORE VERIFYONLY FROM DISK = '...' (readable and complete?), RESTORE HEADERONLY (what backup sets live in this file?), RESTORE FILELISTONLY (logical-to-physical file mapping — essential when restoring to a server with different drive letters).

Check backup HISTORY with: SELECT database_name, backup_start_date, type, physical_device_name FROM msdb.dbo.backupset bs JOIN msdb.dbo.backupmediafamily bmf ON bs.media_set_id = bmf.media_set_id WHERE database_name = 'Orders' ORDER BY backup_start_date DESC. The type column is the key: D = full database backup, I = differential, L = transaction log. Every table lives in the msdb system database — backup history survives even if the user database is gone, which is exactly when you need it.

example.walkthrough: Keyword by keyword. BACKUP DATABASE Orders names the source database. TO DISK = 'E:\Backups\Orders_Full.bak' is the destination FILE — SQL Server's service account (not your user account) must have write access to E:\Backups, the classic 'backup fails with access denied' cause. WITH INIT means overwrite whatever backup sets already live in that file — without INIT the default NOINIT would APPEND, and a month of appends turns one file into an unmanageable chain. COMPRESSION shrinks the output (CPU cost, almost always worth it; verify the edition supports it). STATS = 10 prints '10 percent processed' style progress messages — on a multi-GB backup this is your only sign of life. The semicolons terminate statements (required by some tools, good hygiene everywhere). Then VERIFYONLY reads the whole file and checks checksums WITHOUT restoring anything — a backup you have never verified is a hope, not a backup. HEADERONLY lists the backup sets inside the file (position, type D/I/L, dates) so you know exactly what you are holding before a restore.

pitfalls: UPDATE or DELETE without a WHERE clause: UPDATE dbo.Employees SET Salary = Salary * 1.1 touches EVERY row. There is no undo short of a restore. Write the SELECT first, count the rows, then convert to UPDATE/DELETE. Logic Check: WHY the SELECT-first ritual? The WHERE clause is the only thing standing between you and a table-wide change, and you cannot SEE a WHERE clause's effect until it runs. The SELECT is a dry run of the exact same filter — it shows you the blast radius before anything is modified. SELECT-first in T-SQL and -WhatIf in PowerShell are the same safety pattern in two languages.

Restoring the full backup WITH RECOVERY and THEN trying to apply the differential: RECOVERY brings the database online and closes the restore sequence — the differential apply fails and you must redo the full restore with NORECOVERY. The chain is FULL (NORECOVERY) → DIFF (NORECOVERY if more steps follow, RECOVERY only on the LAST file).

WITH INIT on the wrong file: INIT overwrites ALL backup sets in the destination file. Pointing a fresh backup at the file holding last night's only good full destroys it. When in doubt, back up to a NEW timestamped filename and use NOINIT semantics deliberately.

A differential with no base full is useless: WITH DIFFERENTIAL is relative to the most recent FULL. If that full is missing or corrupt, the differential cannot restore alone — which is why VERIFYONLY on the full matters.

Backing up to C: (or any system drive): a large backup fills the OS disk and crashes the server. Backups go to a dedicated data/drive or network share — E:\Backups in this course's convention — and the SQL Server SERVICE account needs write rights there.
lessons.try_it: Write the complete restore chain for a 2 AM full (Orders_Full.bak) plus a noon differential (Orders_Diff.bak) after an accidental 1 PM DELETE without WHERE: the two RESTORE statements with correct NORECOVERY/RECOVERY placement, then the verification SELECT proving the deleted rows are back, then the msdb history query confirming both backups exist. Say out loud what each WITH option does as you write it.

lessons.title: Switch & Router Config: IOS-Style Syntax
concepts: IOS speaks in MODES — a hierarchy of command contexts, and every command only works in its mode. User EXEC (Switch>) is the lobby: look around, almost no power. Type enable to reach Privileged EXEC (Switch#): all show commands, reloads, and dangerous operations live here. configure terminal (or conf t) drops into Global Configuration (Switch(config)#): system-wide settings like hostname. From there, interface GigabitEthernet1/0/5 enters Interface Configuration (Switch(config-if)#): settings for that port only. exit steps back ONE level; end (or Ctrl+Z) jumps straight back to privileged EXEC (#). The #1 IOS syntax error in assessments is typing a config command at the wrong prompt — the switch rejects it and beginners assume the command is wrong.

Start every session the same way: enable, then configure terminal, then hostname SW-ORLANDO-01. The hostname is not cosmetic — the prompt BECOMES the hostname, so every later prompt tells you which device and which mode you are in (SW-ORLANDO-01(config-if)# reads as: this switch, interface config mode). On a multi-device assessment this prevents configuring the wrong box.

Create a VLAN in the VLAN database: vlan 10, then name SERVERS, then exit. The VLAN now EXISTS on the switch, but nothing uses it yet — creation and assignment are separate steps, and a VLAN with no member ports carries no traffic. Verify with show vlan brief: you should see 10 SERVERS active with no ports listed.

ACCESS port (end devices — PCs, printers, servers): interface gi1/0/5, then switchport mode access, then switchport access vlan 10. Access means ONE VLAN, UNTAGGED — the connected device sends normal frames and the switch internally associates them with VLAN 10. Use interface range gi1/0/1 - 10 to configure many ports at once instead of repeating yourself ten times.

TRUNK port (switch-to-switch or switch-to-router links): interface gi1/0/24, then switchport mode trunk, then switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20. Trunk means MANY VLANs, TAGGED with 802.1Q headers so the far switch can sort them. The allowed vlan list is a FILTER — any VLAN you omit is silently dropped on that trunk, so 'VLAN 20 works locally but not across the trunk' is almost always a missing entry here. Untagged traffic on a trunk rides the NATIVE vlan (default 1); both ends must agree on it or you get subtle, maddening behavior. Logic Check: WHY do trunks tag frames while access ports do not? An access port serves ONE VLAN, so the switch knows the frame's VLAN by which PORT it arrived on — no tag needed. A trunk multiplexes MANY VLANs over ONE cable, so each frame must carry its VLAN ID in an 802.1Q tag or the far switch cannot sort them. Tagging is the price of multiplexing.

SVI — the switch's own IP address in a VLAN: interface vlan 10, then ip address 10.1.10.2 255.255.255.0, then no shutdown. The SVI gives the switch a management address reachable in VLAN 10, and on a Layer-3 switch it becomes the default gateway / inter-VLAN routing interface for that subnet. no shutdown is mandatory: IOS interfaces are ADMINISTRATIVELY DOWN by default, and a configured-but-shutdown SVI shows 'down/down' in show ip interface brief while you wonder why nothing pings. Logic Check: WHY down by default? So a half-configured interface never starts forwarding traffic — imagine an SVI with a typo'd IP coming up and hijacking the gateway address. IOS makes you finish the config, THEN explicitly say 'no shutdown' = 'I have reviewed this, bring it up.' Shutdown-default is a safety catch — the same family as DHCP scopes being born inactive.

Prove everything with show commands (privileged EXEC, # prompt): show vlan brief (VLANs and their member ports), show interfaces trunk (which ports are trunking and which VLANs are allowed/forwarding), show ip interface brief (every interface/SVI with up/up or down/down status — the fastest health scan on the box), show ip route (routing table, on L3 devices — look for the C directly-connected entries for your SVIs), show running-config (the LIVE config; pipe it: show running-config | section vlan).

Nothing is saved until you save it: every change lives in the RUNNING config (RAM) and VANISHES on reboot. copy running-config startup-config (or the classic wr mem) writes it to NVRAM. In an assessment, configure, VERIFY with show commands, then SAVE — an unsaved perfect config scores zero after the power cycle in the next task.

example.code:
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW-LAB-01
SW-LAB-01(config)# vlan 10
SW-LAB-01(config-vlan)# name SERVERS
SW-LAB-01(config-vlan)# exit
SW-LAB-01(config)# interface range gi1/0/1 - 4
SW-LAB-01(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW-LAB-01(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 10
SW-LAB-01(config-if-range)# exit
SW-LAB-01(config)# interface gi1/0/24
SW-LAB-01(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW-LAB-01(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20
SW-LAB-01(config-if)# end
SW-LAB-01# show vlan brief
SW-LAB-01# show interfaces trunk
SW-LAB-01# copy running-config startup-config
example.walkthrough: Follow the prompts — they narrate the mode changes. Switch> to Switch# via enable (user EXEC → privileged). configure terminal → (config)# (global config). hostname renames the prompt itself so you always know where you are. vlan 10 → (config-vlan)# is a SUB-mode for that VLAN; name SERVERS labels it; exit returns to (config)#. interface range gi1/0/1 - 4 → (config-if-range)# configures four ports at once — switchport mode access locks them to access mode (never leave the default 'dynamic auto', which negotiates trunking unpredictably), switchport access vlan 10 assigns them. interface gi1/0/24 → (config-if)# for the uplink: switchport mode trunk plus an EXPLICIT allowed vlan list (10,20) — explicit beats the default 'allow all', which leaks every VLAN everywhere. end jumps back to # (faster than three exits). Then the proof: show vlan brief should list VLAN 10 SERVERS with Gi1/0/1–4; show interfaces trunk should show Gi1/0/24 trunking with 10,20 allowed. Only after the show output is correct: copy running-config startup-config — RAM to NVRAM, or the next reboot erases it all.

pitfalls: Forgetting no shutdown on SVIs and physical interfaces: IOS defaults to administratively down. A perfectly addressed interface shows down/down in show ip interface brief and passes nothing. When 'the config looks right but nothing works', check status first.

switchport trunk allowed vlan omitting a VLAN: the trunk comes up, the allowed VLANs work, and the missing one is silently dropped. 'VLAN 20 works on each switch but not between them' is this command missing ',20' — check with show interfaces trunk.

Putting switchport mode trunk on a port facing a PC: the PC sends untagged frames and cannot read 802.1Q tags — connectivity dies in a confusing way (link is up, nothing passes). Trunks face switches/routers/firewalls; end devices get access ports.

Typing config commands at the wrong prompt: interface gi1/0/5 at Switch> is rejected with an error that looks like a syntax problem. Read the prompt: > means user EXEC (enable first), # means privileged (configure terminal next), (config)# means global, (config-if)# means interface. The prompt IS the documentation.

Forgetting copy running-config startup-config: the assessment's next task power-cycles the switch (or the grader reads startup-config), and your unsaved work evaporates. Configure → show-verify → save, every time. Logic Check: WHY two configs? running-config lives in RAM (fast, editable, volatile); startup-config lives in NVRAM (slow, persistent). Every change lands in RAM first so you can test and back out; NOTHING is durable until you copy it to NVRAM. A grader reading startup-config is checking 'what survives a reboot' — the only config that matters.
lessons.try_it: From memory, write the full command sequence for: hostname SW-TEST, VLAN 30 named GUEST, ports gi1/0/5-8 as access in VLAN 30, gi1/0/24 as trunk allowing 10,20,30, SVI for VLAN 30 at 10.1.30.2/24 (enabled), then the three show commands that prove it and the save. Compare against the example's pattern line by line — mode by mode.

lessons.title: Writing PowerShell Functions From Scratch
concepts: What a function is: a named, reusable block of code — you write it once, then call it by name with different inputs instead of retyping logic
Why functions beat one-liners for repeated work: parameters replace editing, help text replaces tribal knowledge, and a function can be tested and shared — a chat paste cannot
When to write one: a human will run this more than twice, with variations. Fewer than that — a one-liner is the honest answer (see the granularity scenario)

The name contract: Verb-Noun using an approved verb (run Get-Verb to see the list) — why: Get-Command discovers commands by verb, so 'Do-Stuff' is invisible to the next admin while 'Get-StaleADUser' is findable

param(): the function's front door — typed parameters ([int], [string]), defaults (= 90), [Parameter(Mandatory)] — why types: bad input is rejected at the door before your code runs, not halfway through
BEGIN runs ONCE before any input arrives: setup work — compute the cutoff date once, open connections once. Why not per-item: doing setup per object is slow and sometimes wrong

PROCESS runs once PER PIPELINE OBJECT: the per-item work lives here. Why it exists: without a PROCESS block, your code behaves as the END block — it runs once after ALL pipeline input arrives, and per-object logic never fires per object
END runs ONCE after all input: summaries, totals, closing connections, cleanup

Return values: PowerShell returns OBJECTS, not text. Anything your code does not assign or suppress goes to the output stream — that is why you can pipe a function into Export-Csv. Use 'return' only to exit early, not to 'send back' a value

try/catch: catches TERMINATING errors. Why -ErrorAction Stop matters: most cmdlets emit non-terminating errors by default, which sail right past your catch block — -ErrorAction Stop converts them so catch actually fires
Comment-based help (<# .SYNOPSIS ... #>): Get-Help reads it. Why: at 2 AM the on-call tech reads your help text, not your source code — the help IS the documentation

example.walkthrough: Line by line. 'function Get-StaleADUser' declares the name — approved verb Get, noun describing the output. The <# ... #> block is comment-based help: .SYNOPSIS is the one-line summary Get-Help shows, .DESCRIPTION the detail, .PARAMETER documents each parameter, .EXAMPLE shows real usage — this is the documentation the next admin reads. [CmdletBinding()] promotes it to an 'advanced function': you get -Verbose, -WhatIf, and -ErrorAction for free, which is why Write-Verbose works later. param() is the front door: [int]$DaysInactive = 90 types the input (passing 'banana' is rejected immediately) and gives a named default instead of a magic number; [Parameter(ValueFromPipeline = $true)] on $SamAccountName is what lets 'jdoe' | Get-StaleADUser work — without it, piped input is ignored. BEGIN runs once: $cutoff is computed a single time, not once per user — efficiency. PROCESS runs once per piped username: the foreach handles each name, Get-ADUser -Identity fetches that one account, -ErrorAction Stop makes a 'DC unreachable' failure terminating so catch fires. The if ($user.Enabled -and $user.LastLogonDate -lt $cutoff) is the actual business rule. The output is a PSCustomObject via Select-Object — objects, not text — with a calculated property DaysInactive, so the result pipes cleanly into Export-Csv or Where-Object. catch { Write-Error ... } reports the failure and continues with the next user instead of dying mid-list; $_ is the error itself. END runs once: a verbose 'done' marker. Prerequisites: run on a domain-joined machine with the ActiveDirectory module (RSAT) — the structure is the lesson, the AD calls are the example workload.

pitfalls: Skipping the PROCESS block: 'jdoe','asmith' | Get-StaleADUser then silently processes nothing per-user — code outside named blocks runs once as END, after all pipeline input has already arrived

Write-Host for output: it prints to the console but NOT to the pipeline — a downstream Export-Csv receives nothing. Emit objects; reserve Write-Host for interactive-only messages (or better, Write-Verbose)
catch without -ErrorAction Stop: Get-ADUser failing to reach a DC is non-terminating by default, so catch never fires and the function reports success on a failed query
Untyped parameters: -DaysInactive 'banana' is accepted at the door and explodes deep inside .AddDays() — types move the failure to the front where it belongs
Per-item work in BEGIN: BEGIN runs once before any input arrives, so a loop there sees zero objects and cheerfully reports 'all clear'
Using 'return $x' inside PROCESS to skip one item: return exits the ENTIRE function, not just the current item — the remaining pipeline input is abandoned
lessons.try_it: Take a one-liner you actually use and convert it: wrap it in function Verb-Noun, add a param() block, move per-object work into PROCESS, add a .SYNOPSIS, then run Get-Help on your own function. If Get-Help shows your synopsis, you did it right.

lessons.title: Bash Functions and Script Basics
concepts: What a bash function is: a named command you define in a script — same reuse idea as PowerShell, simpler machinery, no param() block
Syntax: backup_file() { commands; } — you call it by name; $1, $2 are positional arguments, $@ is all of them, $0 is the script's own name
local: functions share GLOBAL scope by default — why 'local src' matters: without it, your function's variable overwrites the caller's variable of the same name three functions up
if with [[ ]]: [[ -f $file ]] tests that a file exists — why double brackets: [[ ]] is a bash built-in with no word-splitting surprises, unlike the older [ ]
for loops: for conf in /etc/ssh/sshd_config /etc/fstab — why: the shell expands globs and lists before your code runs, so the loop just iterates

The shebang #!/bin/bash: tells the KERNEL which interpreter runs this file — why it matters: without it the script executes in whatever shell the user happens to run, and on many servers that is /bin/sh (dash), where bash syntax like [[ ]] is a syntax error
chmod +x: sets the execute bit — why: the kernel refuses to run a file without it ('Permission denied'). The bit is the operating system's consent flag, separate from read/write
set -euo pipefail: exit on any error, treat unset variables as errors, propagate failures inside pipes — why: a backup script that half-runs and reports success is worse than one that crashes loudly
>&2 and return: warnings go to stderr so stdout stays clean and pipeable; 'return 1' sets the function's exit code, which callers test with $?

example.code:
#!/bin/bash
# backup_configs.sh - copy critical config files to a timestamped folder

set -euo pipefail

backup_dir="/backup/configs/$(date +%F)"
mkdir -p "$backup_dir"

backup_file() {
    local src="$1"
    if [[ -f "$src" ]]; then
        cp "$src" "$backup_dir/"
        echo "Backed up: $src"
    else
        echo "WARNING: not found: $src" >&2
        return 1
    fi
}

for conf in /etc/ssh/sshd_config /etc/fstab /etc/hosts; do
    backup_file "$conf"
done

echo "Backup complete: $backup_dir"
example.walkthrough: Line by line. #!/bin/bash is the shebang — the kernel reads these exact bytes to choose the interpreter; delete it and the script inherits the caller's shell. set -euo pipefail is the safety net: -e aborts on the first failed command (no silent half-backups), -u turns a typo'd variable into an immediate error instead of an empty string, -o pipefail makes a failure inside a pipeline fail the whole line. backup_dir uses $(date +%F) — command substitution producing 2026-10-10 — so every run lands in its own folder; the quotes around the assignment guard against spaces. mkdir -p creates the folder and does not complain if it exists. backup_file() defines the function; local src=$1 copies the first argument into a function-scoped variable — without 'local', src would leak into (or clobber) the global scope. [[ -f $src ]] tests file existence the safe bash way. The WARNING goes to >&2 (stderr) — why: stdout stays machine-readable for piping while humans still see the warning. return 1 signals failure to the caller without killing the whole script (contrast: 'exit 1' would abort everything). The for loop iterates a literal list — one function call per config file, so adding a fourth file is one word, not new logic. Run it with: chmod +x backup_configs.sh (sets the execute bit — without this, ./backup_configs.sh dies with 'Permission denied') then ./backup_configs.sh — or 'bash backup_configs.sh', which works without +x because then bash, not the kernel, is doing the executing.

pitfalls: Unquoted variables: cp $src $dest breaks on paths with spaces ('My Documents') — quote every expansion: "$src", always
Forgetting 'local': your loop counter 'i' silently overwrites the caller's 'i' — functions share global scope unless you say local
No shebang plus bashisms: the script runs under dash/sh on the server and [[ ]] dies as a syntax error at 2 AM
Parsing 'ls' output: filenames with spaces or newlines break 'for f in $(ls)' — glob instead: for f in *.log
lessons.try_it: Write backup_one.sh: a function that takes a directory as $1, creates a timestamped tar.gz of it, prints a usage message to stderr and exits 1 when $1 is missing. Include the shebang, set -euo pipefail, and local variables. chmod +x it and run it against /etc/ssh.

lessons.title: UML for Infrastructure People
concepts: What UML is: the Unified Modeling Language — a standardized visual vocabulary where each box, arrow, and label has an agreed meaning
Why it exists: so a diagram drawn by a contractor you never met is readable by you — without a shared language, every diagram needs its author standing next to it explaining what the arrows mean

When UML earns its place in infra work: authentication flows, runbooks/SOPs, and infrastructure maps. When it does not: a simple labeled box diagram beats a forced, incorrect UML diagram — use the right amount of ceremony
Sequence diagrams — WHAT: each participant gets a vertical dashed lifeline, time flows top to bottom, messages are horizontal arrows between lifelines

Sequence diagrams — WHY for auth flows: authentication IS a story about who talks to whom, in what order, and what comes back. The diagram makes ordering, round-trips, and 'who knows what when' visible at a glance

Why NOT a class diagram for auth: class diagrams show static structure (what fields a User object has, what inherits from what) — they cannot show time, order, or message flow, which is the entire question in an auth flow

Reading a sequence diagram: lifeline (dashed vertical line = one participant over time), message arrow (solid horizontal, labeled with exactly what is sent), activation bar (thin rectangle on a lifeline = this participant is busy processing), return messages (often dashed arrows back)
Activity diagrams — WHAT: rounded rectangles for actions, diamonds for decisions, thick bars for parallel (fork/join) flows

Activity diagrams — WHY for runbooks and SOPs: they show branches and parallel paths ('if locked, do X; else do Y') as the primary visual — a sequence diagram buries decisions, an activity diagram foregrounds them
Swimlanes: vertical columns showing WHO performs each step — why: an SOP step is useless if nobody knows whose job it is; swimlanes assign ownership visually
Deployment diagrams — WHAT: nodes (servers, VMs, devices — drawn as 3D boxes) holding artifacts (the software deployed on them), connected by communication paths labeled with protocol

Deployment diagrams — WHY for infrastructure: they answer 'where does this software physically run, and how do the pieces talk to each other' — the physical-vs-logical mapping question no other diagram type asks directly
The universal drawing rule: label every arrow — what is sent, over which protocol, on which port. An unlabeled arrow is decoration, not documentation

example.code:
SEQUENCE DIAGRAM: User logon to the domain

    User          Workstation            Domain Controller
     |                |                        |
     | 1. types       |                        |
     |    username    |                        |
     |    + password  |                        |
     |--------------->|                        |
     |                | 2. AuthRequest         |
     |                |    (username +        |
     |                |     password hash)    |
     |                |----------------------->|
     |                |                        | 3. validates
     |                |                        |--+ credentials
     |                |                        |  | against AD
     |                |                        |<-+
     |                | 4. AuthResponse        |
     |                |    (success +          |
     |                |     session ticket)    |
     |                |<-----------------------|
     | 5. desktop     |                        |
     |    appears     |                        |
     |<---------------|                        |

ACTIVITY DIAGRAM: Password-reset runbook (excerpt)

        (*) --> [Verify caller identity] --> {ID verified?}
                                                  | yes        | no
                                                  v            v
                                         [Unlock account]  [Escalate to
                                                  |         team lead]
                                                  v            |
                                         [Force password       |
                                          change at logon]     |
                                                  |            |
                                                  v            v
                                                 (*)<----------*

DEPLOYMENT DIAGRAM: Ticketing app (excerpt)

   +------------------+                    +------------------+
   | <<device>>       |   HTTPS :443       | <<device>>        |
   | Office firewall  |------------------->| Cloud VM web-01  |
   +------------------+                    | <<artifact>>     |
                                           | ticketing.war    |
                                           +------------------+
example.walkthrough: Read the sequence diagram top to bottom — time flows downward, and that ordering is the whole point. Each vertical dashed line is a lifeline: one participant's existence over time. Message 1 (User to Workstation) is the human typing credentials — note the arrow is labeled with WHAT travels, not just 'sends stuff'. Message 2 (Workstation to Domain Controller) carries the username plus password hash — never the plaintext password, and the label says so; this is where a security reviewer looks first. At the Domain Controller, the thin activation bar during step 3 means 'this participant is busy processing' — the credential check against AD happens inside that bar. Message 4 is the dashed return arrow: success plus a session ticket — what comes back is often the sensitive part (a ticket an attacker would love to steal), which is why the diagram shows returns explicitly. Message 5 closes the loop to the user. Why a sequence diagram and not the alternatives: a class diagram would show that a User 'has-a' Credential — true and useless, because it says nothing about order or who talks to whom. An activity diagram could show the logon steps but would hide which party performs each step. Only the sequence diagram answers 'who talks to whom, in what order, carrying what' — which is precisely the question every auth flow asks. The activity diagram excerpt shows the complementary strength: the password-reset runbook is a DECISION problem (verified? unlock vs escalate), and the diamond makes the branch the visual centerpiece — try drawing that branch as a sequence diagram and it becomes spaghetti. The deployment diagram answers the third question: the ticketing app (artifact: ticketing.war) runs on a specific node (Cloud VM web-01), reached over a labeled path (HTTPS :443) through the office firewall — software mapped onto hardware with the protocol on the wire. Three diagram types, three different questions; picking the type IS the analysis.

pitfalls: Arrows without labels: 'Workstation -> DC' tells the reader nothing — label WHAT travels ('AuthRequest: username + hash'), or the arrow is decoration
Using a class diagram for a login flow: structurally correct boxes, zero information about order — the wrong tool for any time-based question
Timelines that do not align: drawing message 4 above message 3 teaches the wrong sequence — time flows DOWN, strictly, no exceptions
Showing the request but not the return: the response (ticket, token, session) is often the security-sensitive half — omitting it hides what an attacker actually wants
Activity diagrams with no end state: every branch must terminate at (*) — a path that just stops is an unfinished procedure
lessons.try_it: On paper, draw the account-unlock flow twice: once as an activity diagram (verify identity? -> unlock vs escalate -> verify -> end) and once as a sequence diagram (Tech -> AD -> Tech). Notice which questions each answers better — that felt difference is how you choose the type on the job.

lessons.title: How to Write a System Design Document
concepts: What a design doc is: the written argument for HOW you will build something — written BEFORE building, read by everyone who pays for it, builds it, operates it, or secures it

1. Overview (one paragraph): the shared 30-second understanding of what is being built and for whom — why: if stakeholders cannot agree on one paragraph, they will never agree on the build; skip it and meetings argue past each other for weeks

2. Functional requirements (what it must DO): central login, shared files, VPN for remote staff — why: this is the checklist the design is graded against; skip it and you build the wrong thing confidently

3. Non-functional requirements (how WELL): RPO/RTO numbers, uptime target, performance, compliance — why: these decide the architecture and the budget; skip them and 'it works on my laptop' ships to production
4. Architecture diagram: the one-page map of the whole system — why: humans reason about pictures faster than paragraphs; skip it and every reader builds a different mental model of the same design

5. Components: each piece, its purpose, and WHY THIS ONE — including rejected alternatives — why: six months later 'why did we pick this?' is the most expensive question in the building; a decision record answers it for free
6. Data flow: how data moves between components — why: firewall rules, backup scope, and breach blast-radius all derive from this section; skip it and the security review stalls on question one

7. Security: authentication, encryption in transit and at rest, patching, least privilege — why: 'we will secure it later' is how breaches happen; skip it and the design is a vulnerability with a budget
8. Monitoring: what is watched, alert thresholds, who gets paged — why: an unmonitored system fails silently; skip it and you learn about outages from angry users
9. Disaster recovery: backup method, RPO/RTO numbers, and TESTED restores — why: an untested backup is a hope, not a plan; skip the restore test and the RTO number is fiction
10. Cost estimate: itemized, year 1 plus ongoing — why: management approves money, not diagrams; skip it and the design dies in finance, or finance cuts the wrong 20 percent blind
11. Risks and open questions: what could kill this design — why: naming risks early is cheap; discovering them during the outage is not
Decision matrices: for every real choice, a small table — options as rows, criteria as columns — why: turns 'I feel like option A' into an auditable decision the team can revisit without relitigating

example.code:
DESIGN DOC (condensed): 20-person company, Orlando office

1. OVERVIEW
   Replace the single aging server with a resilient core: two domain
   controllers, a dedicated file server, tested backups, and VPN for
   5 remote workers. Budget ceiling: $25,000 year 1.

2. FUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS
   F1 Central authentication for 20 users (join/leave in <30 min).
   F2 Shared drives with per-department permissions.
   F3 Secure remote access for 5 workers.
   F4 Nightly backup of all business data.

3. NON-FUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS
   NF1 RPO <= 24h, RTO <= 4h. NF2 Survive any single server failure.
   NF3 99% availability during business hours.

4. ARCHITECTURE
       Internet
          |
     [FW-ORL-01 + FW-ORL-02 HA pair]
          |
   +------+------+------+
   |      |      |      |
 DC-01  DC-02  FILE-01 NAS-BAK
 .11    .12    .20     .30
   10.10.0.0/16, VLAN 10 (servers), VLAN 20 (users)

5. COMPONENTS (with decisions)
   - 2x domain controllers (DC-01 physical, DC-02 as VM on FILE-01).
     WHY TWO: one DC is a single point of failure for ALL logins.
   - Business firewall HA pair with VPN. WHY NOT the $89 consumer
     router: no VPN audit trail, no support contract, dies = no
     internet and no remote access.

   DECISION MATRIX: second domain controller
   | Option            | Cost  | Survives 1 server dead? | RTO met? |
   |-------------------|-------|-------------------------|----------|
   | A: single DC      | $8k   | NO                      | NO       |
   | B: two DCs        | $14k  | YES                     | YES      |
   Chosen: B. Requirement NF2 is non-negotiable; A fails it.

6. DATA FLOW
   Logon: workstation -> DC-01/.11 (Kerberos :88, LDAP :389).
   Files: workstation -> FILE-01/.20 (SMB :445).
   Backup: all servers -> NAS-BAK/.30 nightly 01:00 (RPO 24h).

7. SECURITY
   BitLocker on all servers; firewall default-deny with logged
   rules; MFA required on VPN; patches monthly via maintenance
   window; domain admins limited to 2 accounts (least privilege).

8. MONITORING
   Watch: DC replication health, disk <15% free, backup job
   success, firewall failover events. Alerts -> on-call phone.

9. DISASTER RECOVERY
   3-2-1: nightly to NAS + weekly copy offsite (cloud).
   Restore drill QUARTERLY, timed — the RTO of 4h is only real
   if a drill has hit it. Last drill result recorded here.

10. COST ESTIMATE (year 1)
    Servers/firewalls/NAS: $16,500 | Licenses: $4,000
    Offsite backup: $1,200/yr | Labor/contingency: $3,300
    TOTAL: $25,000 (at ceiling, itemized so cuts are surgical).

11. RISKS / OPEN QUESTIONS
    R1 Single ISP (accepted: dual ISP quoted at +$400/mo, deferred
       to year 2 — documented, not forgotten).
    Q1 Cloud file sync later? Out of scope for year 1.
example.walkthrough: Notice how every section earns its place by serving a reader. The overview lets the owner verify in 30 seconds that this is the project they asked for — without it, the functional requirements get debated forever. F1–F4 are the grading rubric: the decision matrix in section 5 is scored against NF2 ('survive any single server failure'), which is exactly why option A loses despite being cheaper — requirements decide, price does not. The architecture diagram is the map every later section points at: data flow references the same hostnames and IPs, so the firewall engineer can write rules straight from section 6 (protocol and port on every flow — Kerberos :88, LDAP :389, SMB :445). Security is not a paragraph of good intentions: each control maps to a real threat (MFA on VPN because stolen passwords are the common breach path; two domain admins because standing admin sprawl is how ransomware spreads). Monitoring names WHO gets paged — an alert with no recipient is a log entry. Disaster recovery carries the two numbers (RPO 24h from nightly backups, RTO 4h) plus the sentence that makes them real: quarterly timed restore drills, with the last result recorded in the doc. The cost table is itemized so that when finance says 'cut 10 percent', the cut lands on something chosen — not on the backup nobody understood. And section 11 does something most docs skip: it writes down the accepted risk (single ISP) with its price tag, so next year's budget conversation starts from a documented decision instead of a surprise.

pitfalls: Requirements written AFTER the design: then they are justification, not requirements — write them first and grade the design against them, or the doc is marketing
RPO/RTO numbers with no restore test: 'RTO 4 hours' from an untested USB drive is fiction — the number is only real if a drill has hit it, on the record
Single points of failure you never named: one DC, one ISP, one admin holding all the passwords — if the doc does not list SPOFs explicitly, the design has them
Cost as a lump sum: '$11,000 total' hides what is inside — itemize, or finance will cut the wrong 20 percent and you will discover it during the outage
Decision without rejected alternatives: 'we chose X' with no matrix means the next hire re-litigates the choice from zero — record why the losers lost
lessons.try_it: Take the contractor proposal from the design-review scenario and rewrite it as a one-page design doc: fill every section, add the DC-count decision matrix, and write down the RPO/RTO numbers that proposal can honestly hit. The gaps you cannot fill ARE the rejection letter.

lessons.title: SOPs, Incident Reports, and Root Cause Analysis
concepts: What an SOP is: a Standard Operating Procedure — the exact steps to perform a task correctly, written so someone qualified but unfamiliar can execute it at 2 AM without calling you
SOP section — Purpose: WHEN to use this SOP and when NOT to — why: the wrong procedure applied confidently is worse than no procedure; skip it and someone runs the VPN SOP against a DNS outage
SOP section — Prerequisites: access, tools, permissions, lead time — why: discovering mid-procedure that you lack admin rights is where the incident gets longer; skip it and step 4 is a dead end

SOP section — Steps: numbered, ONE action per step, each with the exact command or click path AND the expected result — why: 'configure the server' means five different things to five techs; expected results turn 'did it work?' from a guess into a check
SOP section — Verification: how you PROVE it worked — why: 'looks done' is how half-fixed incidents get closed; skip it and the ticket reopens at the worst possible moment
SOP section — Rollback: how to UNDO the change — why: every change can fail; skip it and a bad change at 2 AM becomes a 6 AM outage with no exit
SOP header — version, date, owner: why: a 3-year-old SOP with no owner is a rumor; the header tells the reader whether to trust it before step 1

Incident report structure: timeline (what happened when — why: reconstruction beats recollection), impact (who and what was affected — why: drives priority and communication), root cause, remediation (what actually fixed it), action items
Action items need an OWNER and a DATE — why: 'improve monitoring' with no owner happens never; 'Priya enables cert-expiry alerts by Friday' happens
Root cause vs proximate cause: 'the tunnel dropped' is the symptom, not the cause — keep asking why until you reach something you can FIX: a process, a config, a missing owner

The 5 Whys: ask 'why?' five times, each answer moving one level from symptom toward system — why it works: it forces past the first comfortable answer; stop when the answer is a correctable process gap, not a person to blame
Blameless RCA — why: if the report punishes, the next incident goes unreported and you learn nothing; fix systems, not people, or the system never improves

example.code:
SOP-014: New Hire Onboarding — IT Account Setup
Version 1.3 | 2026-09-15 | Owner: IT Operations

PURPOSE
  Use for every new employee on/before day 1. Do NOT use for
  contractors (see SOP-015) or rehires (see SOP-016) — account
  naming and access differ.

PREREQUISITES
  - HR ticket with legal name, start date, department, manager.
  - You hold Account Operator rights in AD (request 2 days ahead).
  - Laptop imaged with standard build 2026.09 (see SOP-002).

STEPS
  1. Create AD account: New-ADUser -Name "Ana Reyes"
     -SamAccountName areyes -Path "OU=Users,OU=Orlando,DC=corp,DC=lab"
     EXPECTED: command returns no error.
  2. Add to department group: Add-ADGroupMember -Identity
     "Dept-Sales" -Members areyes
     EXPECTED: Get-ADGroupMember Dept-Sales lists areyes.
  3. Assign laptop asset tag in inventory; record in ticket.
     EXPECTED: ticket shows asset tag LTP-0447.
  4. Send credentials to manager via sealed envelope, never email.
     EXPECTED: manager acknowledges receipt in ticket.

VERIFICATION
  - Log on as areyes to a test workstation: must succeed.
  - Confirm access to the department share: must open.
  - HR ticket updated with account name + asset tag.

ROLLBACK
  - Before day 1: Disable-ADAccount -Identity areyes; reclaim
    laptop; note ticket 'onboarding cancelled'.
  - After day 1: do NOT delete — follow SOP-021 (termination).

REVISION HISTORY
  1.3 added sealed-envelope rule after Sep incident (see IR-088).

--- BAD SOP (same task, how NOT to write it) ---
  "Step 1: Set up the laptop. Step 2: Give them access.
   If stuck, ask Dave."
  WHY IT FAILS: which image? what access? how do you know it
  worked? Dave is on a plane. Every vague step is a future
  8 AM 'the new hire can't work' ticket.
example.walkthrough: Read the good SOP as a machine would execute it. The purpose draws a boundary — contractors and rehires are excluded BY NAME, because the wrong procedure applied confidently is worse than none. Prerequisites front-load every dependency: the HR ticket, the AD rights (with the 2-day lead time that prevents a day-1 scramble), the imaged laptop. Each step is one action with the exact command and the expected result — step 2 does not just say 'add to group', it gives the command and the verification query, so 'did it work?' is answered by output, not feeling. Verification is a separate section on purpose: it is the definition of done, checked by logging on AS the new user — the only test that proves the account works. Rollback covers both directions of failure (before/after day 1) because undoing a change is a different procedure from never making it. The revision history ties the doc to a real incident (IR-088) — the doc learns. Then the bad SOP: four lines that contain zero executable information. 'Set up the laptop' — with which image? 'Give them access' — to what? 'Ask Dave' — Dave left in March. Every vague step in that bad version is a future ticket; the good version's specificity is what makes a stranger successful at 2 AM.

pitfalls: BAD: 'Step 3: Configure the server.' — which settings? what values? expected result? Unverifiable steps produce unverifiable outcomes
BAD: 'If stuck, ask Dave.' — tribal knowledge inside an SOP is an admission the SOP is incomplete, and Dave is on a plane
Action items without owners and dates: 'improve monitoring' happened never — 'Priya enables cert-expiry alerts by Friday' happens
Root cause named as a person: 'root cause: Dave forgot' teaches nothing fixable — 'no checklist owned cert renewals' hands you something to fix
SOP with no rollback section: the change that breaks logins at 2 AM with no undo path is exactly how incidents become outages
Verification skipped 'to save time': the 30 seconds you saved becomes the reopened ticket at the worst moment — 'looks done' is not done
lessons.try_it: Take the 2 AM VPN incident: write the 5 Whys (tunnel down -> certificate expired -> no renewal alert -> monitoring gap -> nobody owned the cert lifecycle), then turn your incident notes into a 1-page SOP using this template. If a stranger could run it, it is done.

lessons.title: Network and Architecture Diagrams That People Can Read
concepts: What a good diagram is FOR: answering questions under pressure — 'what is the DMZ web server's IP?' — in under 30 seconds. If it cannot do that, it is wall art, not documentation

Standard symbols — why standards exist: a reader should not need the author in the room. Routers, switches, firewalls, servers, and clouds each have conventional shapes — use your org's legend, but be consistent on every page
The legend box: every symbol and color defined ON the diagram — why: colors mean nothing across monitors, printers, and colorblind readers without it; a legend makes the diagram self-contained

Physical vs logical views: physical = what plugs into what (cables, ports, racks) for the hands-on tech; logical = subnets, VLANs, zones, traffic flows for design and troubleshooting — why two views: one diagram carrying both is unreadable; draw both, link them by hostname

Labeling conventions: every device gets a hostname (FW-HQ-01 = type-site-number), its management IP, and its role; every link gets subnet/VLAN and interface names — why: an unlabeled diagram cannot drive a firewall migration or an incident call

Data-flow arrows: direction + protocol + port on EVERY arrow ('HTTPS :443 ->') — why: firewall rules are literally written from these arrows; a bare line between 'web' and 'db' authorizes nothing and migrates nothing
Layering: one concern per view — L1 cabling, L2/L3 topology, application flows each get their own sheet — why: mixing layers is the number-one cause of unreadable diagrams

Reference architecture — 3-tier web/app/db: why the tiers are separated: blast radius (web tier compromised does not equal database compromised), independent scaling, and firewall policy enforced at each tier boundary

Reference architecture — HA firewall pair: active/passive with a heartbeat link and state sync — why: a single firewall is a single point of failure for ALL traffic; the heartbeat is what makes failover automatic instead of a 2 AM drive to the office

Reference architecture — hub-and-spoke VPN: branches tunnel to HQ instead of meshing with each other — why: O(n) tunnels instead of O(n-squared), one place to enforce policy; the tradeoff is the hub as a single point of failure and hairpinned branch-to-branch traffic (see the matrix in the example)

example.code:
HUB-AND-SPOKE VPN — logical view (with legend + labels)

  LEGEND: [FW] = firewall  [R] = router  ---> = IPsec tunnel
          solid | = LAN link   dashed = VPN over internet

                        [HQ - Orlando]
                   FW-HQ-01 / FW-HQ-02 (HA pair)
                   heartbeat link between them (failover <60s)
                   LAN 10.10.0.0/16 | VLAN 10 mgmt, 20 users, 30 DMZ
                         |           |           |
        IPsec VPN        |  IPsec VPN|  IPsec VPN|        IPsec VPN
                         |           |           |
                  [Branch-Miami] [Branch-Tampa] [Branch-Jax]
                   R-MIA-01       R-TPA-01       R-JAX-01
                   10.20.0.0/16   10.30.0.0/16   10.40.0.0/16

  Traffic: Miami -> Tampa hairpins through HQ (see matrix).

  3-TIER WEB/APP/DB (reference pattern)
       Internet
          |
     [FW pair] -- DMZ: WEB-01, WEB-02 (10.10.30.0/24)
          |   HTTPS :443 in, nothing else
     [internal FW] -- APP-01, APP-02 (10.10.31.0/24)
          |   HTTPS :8443 from web tier only
        DB-01 (10.10.32.10) -- SQL :1433 from app tier only
     WHY: web tier breach cannot reach the database directly;
     each tier scales and patches independently.

  DECISION MATRIX: hub-and-spoke vs full mesh (6 branches)
  | Criterion              | Hub-and-spoke | Full mesh        |
  |------------------------|---------------|------------------|
  | Tunnel count           | 5 (O(n))      | 15 (O(n-squared))|
  | Single point of fail   | HQ hub        | none             |
  | Branch-to-branch path  | hairpin via HQ| direct           |
  | Config complexity      | low           | high             |
  | Verdict                | wins at 3-10  | wins past ~10 or |
  |                        | branches      | with SD-WAN      |
example.walkthrough: Read the hub-and-spoke diagram the way a firewall engineer would. The legend comes first — symbol definitions on the page, so no author is required. Every device follows the naming convention (FW-HQ-01: type-site-number) and carries its subnet; every tunnel is labeled IPsec VPN, and the HA pair notes its heartbeat link with the failover time (<60s) — because 'HA pair' without a heartbeat is just two firewalls. The branch routers each show their LAN subnet (10.20.0.0/16), so overlapping address space — the classic VPN killer — is visible at a glance. The hairpin note is honest documentation of the tradeoff: Miami-to-Tampa traffic goes up to HQ and back down, adding latency; the decision matrix below quantifies exactly when that tradeoff stops being worth it. Compare with full mesh: 15 tunnels for 6 branches (n times n-minus-1, divided by 2), no single point of failure, direct branch paths — but configuration complexity explodes, which is why the verdict row exists: hub-and-spoke wins at 3–10 branches, mesh (or SD-WAN, which automates the mesh) wins past that. The 3-tier pattern shows layering in action: each tier is its own subnet, each boundary lists the single allowed protocol and port, and the WHY paragraph states the security argument (blast radius) so the next engineer does not 'simplify' the tiers into one flat network. A diagram that carries labels, legend, flows with ports, and its own tradeoff matrix answers questions instead of raising them.

pitfalls: BAD: 23 unlabeled rectangles, double-headed arrows, no legend — fails the 30-second test: it answers zero questions without its author in the room
BAD: color-only meaning ('red = important') — meaningless printed in black-and-white and to colorblind readers; always pair color with text labels
BAD: physical cabling, VLANs, and firewall rules on one page — the mega-diagram: technically complete, practically unreadable; split into layered views
BAD: arrows with no protocol or port — 'web -> db' could be anything; the firewall engineer cannot write a single rule from it
BAD: no heartbeat/failover detail on an 'HA' pair — two firewalls with no state sync is not high availability, it is two single points of failure
lessons.try_it: Redraw a network you know (home lab counts) as a logical diagram: standard shapes, a legend, hostname + IP on every device, protocol:port on every arrow. Then time yourself answering 'what is the DNS server's IP?' — over 30 seconds means relabel.

concepts: Zero Trust, plainly stated: never trust, always verify — no application, file, or script runs just because it happens to be on the machine
Default-deny vs default-allow: traditional tools try to recognize bad things (blocklisting) and allow everything else; allowlisting flips it — everything is denied unless it is explicitly permitted

Why allowlisting beats blocklisting against novel attacks: a blocklist can only stop threats it has seen before; a brand-new ransomware variant has no signature yet, so the blocklist waves it through — allowlisting does not care whether the file is known malware or not, because 'unknown' means 'does not run'
What the agent evaluates: executables (.exe), DLLs, scripts (PowerShell, batch, JavaScript), installers, and drivers — every piece of code that tries to run is checked against the allowlist

Learning Mode vs Secured: Learning Mode is the onboarding phase — the agent watches what normally runs in the environment and builds the baseline allowlist without blocking anyone; Secured is enforcement — default-deny is live and anything not approved is blocked

The built-in trusted application list: thousands of known-good applications are pre-approved so day one is not a block-everything disaster — custom and in-house software gets approved through the Approval Center

example.code:
# Demo narration script — 'the block in action' (practice this verbatim)
# 1. "This is a fresh laptop. I'm going to download a utility the user asked for."
# 2. Double-click the installer -> BLOCKED popup: 'Application Not Permitted'
# 3. "Nothing executed. Not quarantined after running — it never ran."
# 4. Open the portal -> Unified Audit -> show the DENY entry with hash, path, timestamp
# 5. Click the tray popup's 'Request Approval' -> request lands in the Approval Center
# 6. Approve it -> "About a minute later, it runs. Every step is in the audit trail."
Get-FileHash .\unapproved-tool.exe -Algorithm SHA256  # the identity the allowlist checks
example.walkthrough: The demo that sells allowlisting is thirty seconds long: try to run something unapproved, watch it get blocked before it executes, then show the deny in Unified Audit and walk the approval. Hammer the contrast the prospect feels in their gut — their current tool would have let that file run and then tried to decide if it was bad; here, unknown simply does not run. Two landmines to avoid on stage: never call this 'antivirus' (it is a control plane, not a scanner), and never say it 'detects malware' — it does not detect anything, it denies everything not approved, which is stronger and simpler to explain. Also be honest that Learning Mode is not protection — it is observation. Protection starts when you flip to Secured.

pitfalls: Calling allowlisting 'antivirus' or saying it 'detects malware' — it denies by default; detection is a different product category
Forgetting that Learning Mode observes but does not block — a machine in Learning Mode is not yet protected
Approving files by name alone instead of by hash or publisher signature — filenames are trivially spoofed
lessons.title: Zero Trust and Application Allowlisting
lessons.try_it: Stand up and narrate the 30-second block demo out loud, twice: download, double-click, blocked popup, audit deny entry, approval request, approval, runs. Time yourself — if it takes more than a minute, you are over-explaining.
