concepts: What Ringfencing is: a policy cage around an application — the app keeps running and doing its job, but it is fenced off from everything it does not need

The four restriction dimensions: (1) internet access — which hosts and ports the app may reach; (2) registry access — whether it can read or write registry keys; (3) spawning child processes — whether it can launch other programs like PowerShell or cmd; (4) interacting with other processes and files — whether it can touch other applications' memory or data outside its own lane

WHY it exists — the attack it stops: assume-breach. Browsers, Office, PDF readers, and email clients get exploited constantly. Ringfencing assumes the app WILL be compromised and makes sure the compromise goes nowhere: the exploit owns a tab, but it cannot spawn a payload, cannot write persistence to the registry, cannot read other apps' data

Why this matters even WITH allowlisting: fileless attacks and living-off-the-land techniques never drop a new executable — there is nothing for the allowlist to block. Ringfencing catches what allowlisting cannot see, because it restricts behavior, not identity
Ringfencing is not blocking: a fenced browser still browses, a fenced Word still edits documents — the user experience is intact, which is why customers accept it

example.code:
# Demo narration script — 'the fenced browser' (the assume-breach moment)
# 1. "This browser is Ringfenced. Watch it work normally — web apps, tabs, downloads."
# 2. Simulate the exploit: a page tries to spawn powershell.exe from the browser.
# 3. RINGFENCE BLOCK popup -> show Unified Audit: 'msedge.exe attempted to spawn powershell.exe — denied'
# 4. "The exploit succeeded — and got nothing. The tab still renders. The payload never launched."
# 5. Show the fence policy pane: no child processes, no registry writes, web ports only.
# Key line: "I let the attacker in, and all they got was a tab."
example.walkthrough: Ringfencing is the product's most demo-able idea because it is visual: the attack visibly fails while the app visibly keeps working. Structure the story as assume-breach — 'let's say the browser is already exploited' — because every IT director has lived through a drive-by or malicious ad. Show the fence policy first (the four dimensions), then trigger the blocked behavior, then show the audit entry. The prospect's objection will be 'what breaks?' — answer it before they ask: click-to-run installers, browser-launched helper apps, and protocol handlers get blocked, and that is the containment working, not a misconfiguration. Never over-fence on stage: fencing an app from its own data directory breaks it and makes the product look fragile.

pitfalls: Over-fencing a legitimate workflow (e.g., fencing Outlook from the file system breaks attachments) and blaming the product instead of the policy
Presenting Ringfencing as a replacement for allowlisting — they are layers; allowlisting stops unknown code from running, Ringfencing contains allowed code that misbehaves
Forgetting to mention what breaks — the prospect WILL ask, and a rehearsed honest answer builds more trust than a surprise
lessons.title: Ringfencing™: Containing Applications
lessons.try_it: Pick three apps (browser, PDF reader, email client) and write down exactly which of the four restriction dimensions you would lock down on each — and one legitimate thing that would break on each. If you cannot name the breakage, you do not understand the fence yet.

concepts: Network Control — what it controls: which applications may use the network at all, and which destinations and ports they may reach. It is an allowlist firewall: deny by default, permit explicitly. WHY it exists: malware needs to phone home — command-and-control callbacks, data exfiltration, downloading stage two. If the app is not permitted to reach the attacker's server, the attack stalls even if code is running. Demo moment: show an unapproved app's outbound connection denied in Unified Audit.

Elevation Control — what it controls: who can run things as administrator. It replaces the habit of handing out local admin rights: instead of making the user an admin, the admin grants time-scoped elevation to a specific application. WHY it exists: most ransomware and persistence techniques need admin rights; users with permanent local admin can also disable security agents. The attack it stops is privilege escalation — malware and misbehaving installers hitting a wall where admin rights used to be free. Demo moment: request elevation from a standard user account, approve it in the portal, watch it expire.

Storage Control — what it controls: removable storage — USB sticks, external drives. Policy per device: block entirely, allow read-only, or allow fully, matchable by specific device serial number. WHY it exists: two attacks — data theft (someone walks out with the customer database on a thumb drive) and inbound infection (the classic dropped-USB attack, and ransomware hopping machine to machine via removable drives). Demo moment: plug in an unapproved USB stick and show the block popup; then approve that exact serial and show it mounting.

How the three fit together: Allowlisting decides WHAT runs, Ringfencing decides what a running app MAY DO, and these three decide what it may REACH — the network, admin privileges, and removable media. One sentence each is all a demo needs.

example.code:
# Demo narration — the 90-second 'three controls' tour
# NETWORK: "This unknown app tries to call out to its server." -> DENY in audit. "No callback, no exfiltration, no stage two."
# ELEVATION: "Standard user, no local admin. The installer needs elevation — request, approve, it runs, elevation expires."
#  -> "Nobody walks around with permanent admin anymore."
# STORAGE: Plug in USB -> BLOCKED popup. "Unapproved stick. Now I approve this serial number only..." -> mounts.
#  -> "Every other USB stick in the building is still denied."
# Close: "What runs, what it may do, what it may reach — three questions, all answered deny-by-default."
example.walkthrough: Do not demo these three as three separate products — demo them as one idea: 'what a running application is allowed to reach.' Ninety seconds, one beat each, each ending in a blocked-something moment. The prospect takeaway is the pattern repeating: deny by default, approve narrowly, everything logged. Two traps: do not grant permanent elevation on stage 'to stop the tickets' — it contradicts the entire story; and do not confuse Storage Control with backup software — it governs the device, not the application (that confusion is literally scenario 4 in this module, so learn it cold).

pitfalls: Treating Elevation Control as 'UAC with extra steps' — the point is eliminating standing local admin, not just adding a prettier prompt
Approving USB devices by 'any device' instead of by serial number — one scoped approval per drive is the whole security value
Demoing the three controls as disconnected features instead of one 'what may it reach' story — the pattern is the message
lessons.title: Network Control, Elevation Control, Storage Control
lessons.try_it: For each of the three controls, write one sentence saying what it controls and one demo line you would say while the block popup is on screen. Nine lines total. Memorize them.

concepts: The workflow, end to end: a user double-clicks an unapproved application → the agent blocks it and shows a popup with 'Request Approval' → the request lands in the Approval Center with the file's hash, path, publisher signature, and which machine asked → the admin reviews and approves or denies → approval typically lands in about a minute → the application runs

WHY this workflow is the product's answer to its own hardest problem: default-deny is only viable if legitimate work is not stuck waiting. Every allowlisting deployment in history died on helpdesk friction — users could not work, so someone turned the protection off. The 60-second approval loop is what makes deny-by-default survivable in a real company: security stays on because unblocking someone takes a minute, not a ticket queue

What the admin checks before approving: the file hash (is this the known-good version?), the publisher signature (is it signed by the expected vendor?), the source path (did it come from the vendor's site or a temp folder?), and the request context (does this user's job need this tool?) — approve the narrowest scope that solves it: one file, one machine or one policy

Unified Audit — what it is: a single searchable log of every security decision the platform makes — every allow, every deny, every approval, every elevation, every ringfence block — with who, what, when, and which policy fired

WHY the audit matters to customers: incident response ('show me everything this machine did Tuesday'), compliance reporting (auditors asking 'who approved this software?'), and troubleshooting (the Storage Control backup scenario is solved in the audit in seconds). It turns 'trust us, we're secure' into receipts

example.code:
# Demo narration — 'the 60-second approval' (the friction-killer moment)
# 1. Block an app on the demo machine -> user clicks 'Request Approval' in the popup.
# 2. Flip to the portal: "There's the request — hash, path, signer, machine, user."
# 3. Verify out loud: "Signed by the expected vendor, hash matches the release — approving for this policy."
# 4. Approve -> back on the machine, the app launches. "About a minute, door to door."
# 5. Open Unified Audit -> filter the machine -> "Block, request, approval, launch — one timeline."
# Key line: "This is why customers don't turn it off. Getting unblocked is faster than filing a ticket."
example.walkthrough: This lesson is the business case disguised as a workflow demo. Prospects do not fear the technology — they fear the helpdesk tickets. So narrate the approval flow as the answer to unspoken dread: show the request carrying real evidence (hash, signer), show the decision taking a minute, then show Unified Audit turning the whole thing into a compliance artifact. The auditor in the room just became your champion. Critical honesty point: users cannot approve their own applications — the admin approves. If you imply self-approval on stage, a technical evaluator will catch it and your credibility is done.

pitfalls: Implying users can approve their own apps — approval is an admin action in the Approval Center, always
Approving by filename instead of hash or signature — filenames lie, signatures do not
Letting the request queue pile up un-triaged — a slow approval loop recreates the exact friction the product was built to eliminate
lessons.title: The Approval Center and Unified Audit
lessons.try_it: Explain the full request-to-approval flow to someone non-technical in 30 seconds, then show them where the audit entry lives. If they ask 'but what stops someone approving malware?' — answer with hash plus signer verification, out loud, without hesitating.

concepts: The 10-minute structure — HOOK (0–2 min): open with ransomware blocked live. Do not open with slides or the portal dashboard. Run the unapproved payload, show the block popup, show the deny in Unified Audit. You now have the room's attention for the next eight minutes.

TOUR (2–8 min): three beats, each a block with a story. Beat 1 — Allowlisting: the approval flow, 'unknown does not run.' Beat 2 — Ringfencing: the fenced browser, 'I let the attacker in and all they got was a tab.' Beat 3 — the controls trio: one USB block, one elevation request, 'what it may reach.' End every beat in Unified Audit — the pattern of receipts is the product's signature.

CLOSE (8–10 min): business value in their language — fewer incidents because the attack surface is deny-by-default; audit-ready compliance without extra tooling; users stay productive because approvals take about a minute. Then stop. A demo that ends clean beats one that sprawls.

Talking points that land: 'unknown does not run' (allowlisting in four words); 'assume the browser is already hacked' (ringfencing framing); 'every decision is a receipt' (audit); 'faster than a ticket' (approval loop)

Landmines to avoid: never promise 100% protection — one absolute claim destroys credibility; never trash-talk the tool they currently use — the prospect in the room probably bought it; never run real malware on anyone's network — lab VM only, simulated payloads; never fumble portal navigation — rehearse every click, dead air kills demos; never get dragged into pricing or licensing weeds — 'I can get you that after' and move on

Questions to ask THEM (demos are conversations): 'How do software requests work here today — and how long does approval take?' / 'What was the entry point of your last real incident — email attachment, download, USB?' / 'Who approves new software right now?' / 'What does compliance reporting look like for you today?' — their answers tell you which beat to emphasize

example.code:
# Minute-by-minute run sheet (tape this to the monitor, then rehearse until you don't need it)
# 0:00 HOOK — "Let me show you what happens when ransomware hits this laptop." Run payload -> BLOCKED.
# 0:45     -> Unified Audit deny entry. "It never executed. Not quarantined — never ran."
# 2:00 TOUR — Beat 1: request approval from the popup, approve in portal, app launches. "About a minute."
# 4:00     -> Beat 2: fenced browser exploit attempt -> ringfence block. "All they got was a tab."
# 6:00     -> Beat 3: USB stick blocked; elevation requested and approved with expiry.
# 7:30     -> Unified Audit filtered to the demo machine: "Block, request, approval, fence, USB — one timeline."
# 8:30 CLOSE — "Deny by default, approvals in a minute, receipts for everything. Questions?"
# 10:00    -> STOP. Answer questions; do not start a second tour.
example.walkthrough: ThreatLocker University is free and open to anyone — use it before the interview to learn the real portal layout, the real popup wording, and the real policy names, so nothing on demo day is a surprise. Rehearse the full ten minutes out loud at least three times; demos die in transitions, so practice the sentence that moves you from beat to beat ('approvals keep users moving — now let's talk about what happens when the app itself is the problem'). If something fails live — a popup does not appear, a page loads slowly — narrate it instead of freezing: 'the audit entry will land in a moment; here's what it will show.' Composure is being graded alongside product knowledge.

pitfalls: Opening with slides or the dashboard instead of the live block — you get one chance at a first impression, spend it on the hook
Reading the portal UI aloud instead of narrating the attack each control stops — features without a story are forgettable
Running past ten minutes — a tight demo signals mastery; a sprawling one signals you do not know what matters
lessons.title: Demoing Like a Pro: The Product Demo Playbook
lessons.try_it: Record yourself delivering the full 10-minute demo on your phone. Watch it back and cut every sentence that does not either show a block or answer 'so what?' for the customer. Do it three times.

concepts: The honest one-paragraph version: traditional antivirus is a blocklist — it recognizes threats it has seen before and stops them, and it does that job well. Its gap is the unknown: a brand-new variant, a fileless attack, or a legitimate tool used maliciously has no signature yet, so the blocklist waves it through. Allowlisting attacks from the other side: instead of trying to recognize bad, it only permits known-good — so the novel attack fails at step one, not because it was detected, but because it was never approved.

Why signatures fail against novel malware, concretely: a signature is a fingerprint of a file someone has already caught and analyzed. Attackers repackage payloads automatically — new hash every build — so the fingerprint is stale on arrival. Fileless techniques skip files entirely. None of this is a scandal; it is just what a recognition-based approach cannot do.

The non-disparaging framing (memorize this): 'Signature-based tools do solid work against known threats — most of our customers keep theirs. We are the layer that catches what signatures cannot: the thing nobody has seen before. Unknown does not run.' You are selling a complement, not a replacement — and you are respecting the purchase the prospect already made.

Where the products genuinely differ in daily life: the AV conversation is about detections, quarantines, and threat feeds; the allowlisting conversation is about approvals, audit trails, and policy. Different jobs, different metrics — incidents prevented vs incidents caught.
The question that reframes the room: 'What stopped your last novel incident — the thing nobody had a signature for?' If the answer is 'nothing, it ran,' the allowlisting story tells itself.

example.code:
# The 60-second elevator version (practice until it sounds unrehearsed)
# "Traditional antivirus keeps a list of known-bad things and blocks them — great against
#  yesterday's malware. The problem is tomorrow's: a brand-new variant has no signature yet,
#  so it walks right past. We flip it around. Instead of trying to recognize bad, we only
#  allow known-good. The CFO's macro runs because we approved it. The ransomware doesn't
#  run because nobody approved it — and it doesn't matter that no one has ever seen it
#  before. Unknown doesn't run. Most of our customers keep their existing antivirus —
#  we're the layer underneath it that catches what signatures can't."
example.walkthrough: This conversation is a trust exercise, not a technical debate. The prospect's team chose their current tools, and anyone who calls those tools useless is calling the prospect foolish — so never say 'antivirus is dead,' never name a competing vendor, and never claim the platform stops everything. Lead with respect for what signatures do well, name the gap precisely (the unknown), and position allowlisting as the layer that covers it. If they press — 'so you're saying we should rip out our AV?' — the answer is no: defense in depth, each layer doing what it is good at. Confidence without contempt is the whole game.

pitfalls: Saying 'antivirus is dead' or naming competing vendors — you insult the prospect's past decisions and pick a fight you do not need
Claiming the platform stops 100% of threats — one absolute claim hands the skeptic in the room a weapon for the rest of the demo
Framing it as rip-and-replace — the winning frame is 'an additional layer that covers the gap,' which is also the honest one
lessons.title: ThreatLocker vs Traditional AV: The Conversation
lessons.try_it: Deliver the 60-second version to a friend with zero security background. If they can repeat back the difference between 'recognizing bad' and 'permitting good,' you nailed it. Do it without naming any vendor or product.

lessons.title: M365 & Entra ID for the On-Prem Admin
concepts: Microsoft 365 (M365) is a per-user, per-month subscription bundle, not a server you install: Exchange Online replaces your on-prem mail server, SharePoint Online and OneDrive replace file shares, Teams replaces the phone-and-chat stack. You stop patching those servers because Microsoft runs them — but you now manage licenses, one per user, and a user without the right license simply does not get the service.

Entra ID (renamed from Azure AD in 2023) is Microsoft's cloud directory — it is NOT 'Active Directory in the cloud.' It is a separate product with its own database, its own authentication, and no Group Policy. Get-ADUser does not talk to it; the Microsoft Graph API does. Interviewers love this distinction, so say it plainly: same company, different directory.

Entra Connect (the sync engine, formerly Azure AD Connect) is the bridge: it copies identity data — usernames, and password hashes, not plaintext passwords — from your on-prem AD up to Entra ID on a schedule (every 30 minutes by default). That is why one password works for both the office PC and the cloud mailbox. The sync server is usually a small dedicated VM; if it stops syncing, password changes made on-prem never reach the cloud.

Conditional Access is Entra ID's policy engine and the cloud answer to 'who can log in from where.' It works as IF-THEN rules: IF the user is in Finance AND signing in from outside the corporate IP range, THEN require MFA — or block the sign-in entirely. It evaluates every sign-in in real time; there is no GPO refresh interval to wait for.

Why hybrid exists: almost nobody rips out on-prem AD overnight. Hybrid is the staged reality — some mailboxes on Exchange Online while the old mail server still runs, some users synced while service accounts stay on-prem only, file servers local while SharePoint grows beside them. Entra Connect and Conditional Access are the tools that make the two halves feel like one company during the years-long transition.

The mental model to carry: on-prem AD is the system of record you own; Entra ID is the cloud copy your users actually sign into for M365; Entra Connect keeps them in agreement; Conditional Access guards the front door. Licensing (M365) pays for the services, identity (Entra ID) controls who reaches them.

example.code:
# 1. Install the module that talks to Entra ID / M365 (once per machine, per user)
Install-Module Microsoft.Graph -Scope CurrentUser -Force

# 2. Sign in. -Scopes declares the permissions you are REQUESTING.
#    The login window will show exactly these, and the admin must consent.
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes 'User.Read.All'

# 3. List users from the CLOUD directory (compare with Get-ADUser for on-prem)
Get-MgUser -Top 3 | Select-Object DisplayName, UserPrincipalName, AccountEnabled

# 4. On the Entra Connect sync server, check the sync engine itself
Get-ADSyncScheduler | Select-Object SyncCycleEnabled, NextSyncCyclePolicyType
example.walkthrough: Step 1 installs Microsoft.Graph, the official PowerShell module for the Graph API — the single API behind M365 and Entra ID. -Scope CurrentUser installs it just for you, no admin rights needed. Step 2's Connect-MgGraph opens a login window; -Scopes is you declaring up front which permissions you want (User.Read.All = read every user's profile), and nothing more — least privilege, stated explicitly. Step 3's Get-MgUser is the cloud twin of Get-ADUser: -Top 3 keeps it to three users so you don't dump the whole directory while learning. Step 4 runs only on the sync server: Get-ADSyncScheduler shows whether the 30-minute sync cycle is enabled and when it runs next — the first place to look when 'I changed the password on-prem but the cloud still has the old one.'

pitfalls: Saying 'Entra ID is just AD in the cloud' in an interview — it signals you don't know the product. They are separate directories: no GPOs, no OUs, no trusts in Entra ID. The sync (Entra Connect) is what relates them.

Assuming a user with an M365 license automatically gets everything — each workload needs its license assigned (Exchange Online for mail, for example). 'Licensed but no mailbox' is almost always a missing Exchange Online license, not a broken server.

Turning on Entra Connect sync without matching the on-prem UPN suffix to a verified cloud domain — users end up signing into M365 with an unroutable @corp.local name and nothing lines up. Verify the domain in the M365 admin center first, then sync.
lessons.try_it: If you have access to any M365 tenant (even a trial): run Connect-MgGraph and Get-MgUser -Top 3, then compare one user's UserPrincipalName with the same person's on-prem AD account — note which attributes match (synced) and which exist only in the cloud.

lessons.title: API Integrations with PowerShell
concepts: A REST API is a web server that returns data (usually JSON) instead of web pages. Where a browser GETs a page for a human, your script GETs /api/users for a list of users. Same HTTP, different audience. If you can use a browser's address bar, you already understand the transport — the API just speaks JSON.

Four verbs cover nearly everything: GET reads (list users), POST creates (add a user), PUT/PATCH updates (change a department), DELETE removes. The URL you call is the endpoint — /api/users means 'the users collection.' Wrong verb or wrong endpoint is the most common beginner failure, and the server tells you with a 404.

Headers are metadata about your request, sent alongside it. The important one is Authorization: it carries your credential, usually as 'Bearer <token>'. Think of the header as showing your badge at the door — the endpoint is which room you want, the badge is why they let you in.

The body is the payload you send with POST/PUT — the new user's details, formatted as JSON. Status codes are the server's reply in three digits: 2xx means success (200 OK, 201 Created), 4xx means YOUR request was wrong (401 bad credentials, 404 wrong URL, 400 bad body), 5xx means THEIR server broke. Learn this table; it is how you triage every API failure.

Invoke-RestMethod is PowerShell's API cmdlet, and its killer feature is automatic JSON conversion: the JSON response arrives as a real PowerShell object, so $users[0].displayName just works — no parsing code. Its parameters map one-to-one to the concepts above: -Uri (the endpoint), -Method (the verb), -Headers (your badge), -Body (your payload), -ContentType (telling the server the body is JSON).

Never hand-build JSON with string concatenation — one unescaped quote breaks the whole body silently. Build a hashtable and pipe it to ConvertTo-Json; PowerShell escapes everything correctly. And never paste a real token into a script file — keep it in a variable (or a secret vault), because scripts get copied, emailed, and committed.

example.code:
# --- The mock API lives in the lab; here is the client side, every parameter explained ---

# 1. The badge: a hashtable of headers. 'Bearer <token>' is the scheme most APIs expect.
$headers = @{ Authorization = 'Bearer demo-token-123' }

# 2. GET: read the user list. -Uri = endpoint, -Method = verb, -UseBasicParsing
#    avoids the old Internet Explorer dependency on Windows PowerShell 5.1.
$users = Invoke-RestMethod -Uri 'http://localhost:8080/api/users' `
                           -Method GET `
                           -Headers $headers `
                           -UseBasicParsing
$users.Count              # 2 — Invoke-RestMethod already turned JSON into objects
$users[0].displayName     # 'Ava Rivera' — dot-notation on the parsed response

# 3. POST: create a user. Build a HASHTABLE, convert with ConvertTo-Json
#    (never concatenate JSON strings by hand), declare -ContentType so the
#    server knows the body is JSON and not form data.
$newUser = @{
    displayName       = 'Noah Patel'
    userPrincipalName = 'noah.patel@corp.local'
    department        = 'IT'
}
$result = Invoke-RestMethod -Uri 'http://localhost:8080/api/users' `
                            -Method POST `
                            -Headers $headers `
                            -Body ($newUser | ConvertTo-Json) `
                            -ContentType 'application/json' `
                            -UseBasicParsing
$result.status   # 'created' — the server's confirmation, parsed for you
$result.id       # 3

# 4. Error handling: a bad token gets a 401. Catch it, READ the status code,
#    and let the code tell you which part of the request was wrong.
try {
    Invoke-RestMethod -Uri 'http://localhost:8080/api/users' -Method POST `
        -Headers @{ Authorization = 'Bearer wrong-token' } `
        -Body ($newUser | ConvertTo-Json) -ContentType 'application/json' `
        -UseBasicParsing
}
catch {
    $_.Exception.Message   # 'The remote server returned an error: (401) Unauthorized.'
    # 401 = credentials rejected -> fix the HEADER, not the URL or the body.
}
example.walkthrough: The GET call shows the happy path: -Uri names the endpoint, -Method GET says 'read,' -Headers presents the bearer token, and the returned JSON is already a PowerShell object — $users.Count and $users[0].displayName work with zero parsing code. The POST call adds -Body and -ContentType: the body is the hashtable piped through ConvertTo-Json (PowerShell handles all quoting/escaping; string-concatenated JSON is the classic way to produce a 400), and -ContentType 'application/json' tells the server how to interpret those bytes — skip it and many APIs reject the body or misread it as form data. The try/catch block is the professional habit: APIs fail, and $_.Exception.Message hands you the status code — 401 here means the header was wrong, so you fix the header instead of guessing at the URL or rebuilding the body. The full mock server this talks to is built step by step in the lab.

pitfalls: Concatenating JSON by hand ('{"name":"' + $name + '"}') — one apostrophe in a display name (O'Brien) breaks the body and produces a baffling 400. Hashtables plus ConvertTo-Json exist precisely to prevent this.

Catching API errors with an empty catch {} or no try/catch at all — the script dies with a red wall of text and you learn nothing. Always catch, always read the status code: it tells you whether to fix the header (401), the URL (404), or the body (400).

Hardcoding the bearer token in the script — the moment that file is shared, the credential is shared. Keep tokens in variables loaded at runtime (Read-Host -AsSecureString at minimum, a secret vault in production).
lessons.try_it: In the lab's mock API: POST a user, then GET the list and filter it in PowerShell — ($users | Where-Object department -eq 'IT').displayName — to prove the response is a real object you can query, not text you must parse.

lessons.title: Test Scripts with Pester
concepts: Pester is PowerShell's testing framework — the same idea as unit tests for developers, but pointed at infrastructure. Instead of 'does this function return 4,' you assert 'is the DHCP scope present,' 'is the service running,' 'does the backup file exist.' The test is a machine-readable definition of 'healthy.'

The syntax is four nested keywords that read like English. Describe names the thing under test ('File Server Baseline'). Context groups related tests under one scenario ('Services,' 'DHCP'). It states one expectation ('Print Spooler is running'). Should is the assertion — the actual check ('| Should -Be 'Running'').

Should has a family of matchers: -Be (equals), -BeTrue/-BeFalse (boolean), -Not -BeNullOrEmpty (something was returned). You pipe the real state into Should and Pester reports pass or fail. A failing test prints what it expected versus what it got — which is often the diagnosis handed to you.

Tests must be read-only. A test observes state; it never changes it. The moment a test creates users or restarts services, it is not a test — it is a script wearing a costume, and running it twice gives different results. Assert, don't act.

The workflow that makes Pester valuable: write the test BEFORE a change window describing the healthy state, make your change, re-run the test. Green means your change didn't break the baseline; red names exactly what did. This is how you prove 'nothing else broke' instead of asserting it.

Pester 5 is the modern version (Install-Module Pester); test files must end in .Tests.ps1 for Invoke-Pester to discover them. Run a file with Invoke-Pester -Path .\Lab.Tests.ps1 — it finds every Describe block, runs every It, and prints the pass/fail summary.

example.walkthrough: Describe opens the suite and names the system under test — one Describe per server or role keeps results readable. Each Context groups one aspect (Services, DHCP, Backups) so a failure tells you which area broke. Each It is a single assertion: Get-Service Spooler returns the real service object, .Status extracts its state, and Should -Be 'Running' fails loudly if it says anything else. The DHCP test uses Should -Not -BeNullOrEmpty because the assertion is existence — if the scope is missing the cmdlet returns nothing and the test goes red with a clear message. Test-Path returns $true/$false, so Should -BeTrue is the natural matcher. Invoke-Pester -Path runs the file; -Output Detailed shows every It with its pass/fail instead of just the summary. Run this before a change window, make your change, run it again — any new red is something your change broke, named precisely.

pitfalls: Writing a test that passes when the server is broken — e.g. testing that Get-Service doesn't throw instead of testing that the status is 'Running.' A test must assert the DESIRED state, not merely the absence of an error.

Letting tests change state (New-ADUser inside an It block) — the second run behaves differently from the first, failures cascade, and you can no longer trust green. Tests observe; scripts act. Keep them separate.

Mixing Pester 3 and Pester 5 syntax from old blog posts — discovery rules and some assertion forms changed. If a snippet doesn't run, check which version it was written for (Get-Module Pester -ListAvailable) before assuming your test is wrong.
lessons.try_it: Write one Describe block for your own machine: assert the EventLog service is running and that C:\Windows\System32\notepad.exe exists. Run it with Invoke-Pester — then deliberately break one assertion (test for a nonsense service name) and watch it go red, so you trust the green.

lessons.title: Product Research & Pilots
concepts: Requirements come before vendors — always. Write must-haves (the product fails without them) versus nice-to-haves (tiebreakers) BEFORE any demo, because the moment a salesperson is in the room, your requirements start bending toward their feature list. A requirement written after the demo is a justification, not a requirement.

Shortlist two or three products, not ten. Research widely (docs, admin forums, peer references), then cut ruthlessly to the two or three that plausibly meet the must-haves. Piloting more than three means none of them gets a real evaluation — you run out of time and pick by gut.

The scorecard is the evaluation made honest: the same criteria, the same weights, scored DURING the pilot for every product. Columns are criteria (features, cost, support, security); rows are products; every cell needs evidence ('restore took 40 min on 2026-10-03'), not vibes. Score as you go — scoring after you've decided is theater.

The pilot is a bounded experiment, not an early deployment. Scope it small (a handful of real servers, real workload), lock success criteria IN ADVANCE with a signature, and define the rollback plan before you start — how you get OUT if the product fails. A pilot with no exit criteria and no rollback is just a deployment you haven't admitted to.

The recommendation is one page: the winner, the scores that prove it, the tradeoff stated honestly (usually cost — 'Product A costs $8,500/yr more and here is what that buys'), and the pilot evidence behind each claim. Never let the vendor write it, never let price re-decide after the criteria were locked, and never recommend a product that failed a must-have because it was cheaper.

Run the pilot yourself on your workload. Vendor-led 'proofs of concept' demo the happy path on the vendor's hardware. Your pilot runs your backups, your restores, your failure modes — the unglamorous operations that decide whether the product survives contact with your environment.

example.code:
# PRODUCT EVALUATION — Backup replacement pilot (template: copy and fill per product)

## Requirements (written BEFORE vendor contact)
Must-have: 100% backup success over 30 days | restore < 30 min | immutable copies
           | supports Windows Server 2025 | 24/7 support
Nice-to-have: cloud tiering | single-pane dashboard

## Scorecard (scored DURING the pilot — every cell needs dated evidence)
| Criterion              | Weight | VaultGuard (score/5, evidence)              | SnapSafe (score/5, evidence)                |
|------------------------|--------|---------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| Backup reliability     | 30%    | 5 — 150/150 OK (2026-09-10..10-09)          | 2 — 141/150, 9 missed (pilot log 10-09)     |
| Restore speed/success  | 25%    | 5 — 12 min, 3/3 passed                      | 1 — 40 min, 1 of 3 FAILED                   |
| Security (immutability)| 25%    | 5 — immutable copies verified               | 1 — backups writable by any admin           |
| Platform support       | 10%    | 5 — Server 2025 agent stable                | 2 — agent crashed on 2/5 servers            |
| Support quality        | 10%    | 4 — 24/7 phone, <15 min pickup              | 2 — email only, next business day           |
| Cost (200 agents / yr) | tiebreak| $18,000                                    | $9,500                                      |

## Pilot scope & rollback
Scope: 5 production-adjacent servers, real nightly jobs, 30 days.
Rollback: uninstall agent, re-enable previous backup jobs (documented runbook §3).

## Recommendation
VaultGuard — the only product that met every must-have. Tradeoff stated plainly:
costs $8,500/yr more than SnapSafe; that delta buys immutable backups and verified
restores, i.e. the difference between 'we have backups' and 'we can actually recover.'
example.walkthrough: The Requirements section is dated before vendor contact for a reason — it is your defense when the CFO asks why the cheaper product lost. Must-haves are pass/fail; nice-to-haves only break ties. The scorecard's weights encode what the business actually values (reliability and restore matter more than the dashboard), and every score carries dated evidence so nobody can re-litigate the pilot from memory. Cost sits OUTSIDE the weighted score as a tiebreaker — that single layout decision prevents '$8,500 cheaper' from silently overriding three failed must-haves. The rollback paragraph proves the pilot was an experiment, not a commitment. The recommendation names the winner, quotes the scores, and states the cost tradeoff in one honest sentence — leadership can disagree with your judgment, but they cannot say you hid the price.

pitfalls: Letting the vendor run the pilot — they will demo the happy path on tuned hardware and call it a proof of concept. Your pilot, your servers, your failure modes, or the results describe their lab, not your environment.
Scoring after deciding — writing the scorecard to justify the product you already picked. Score during the pilot, cell by cell, with dated evidence; the scorecard should be able to surprise you.

Skipping the rollback plan because 'the pilot is small' — a failed pilot without an exit becomes a zombie deployment nobody owns. Write the way out before you go in: uninstall steps, re-enable steps, who does them.
lessons.try_it: Pick any tool you already use daily. Write five must-have requirements for it, score it 1–5 on each with one line of evidence per score, and note the final honest sentence — 'keep it because...' or 'replace it because...'. Notice how fast gut feel becomes a defensible number.

lessons.title: The OSI Model: The Map of Networking
concepts: The OSI model is seven layers that describe, bottom to top, everything between 'electricity on a wire' and 'the web page you see.' Layer 1 Physical (cables, link lights), Layer 2 Data Link (Ethernet, MAC addresses, switches), Layer 3 Network (IP addresses, routers, ping), Layer 4 Transport (TCP/UDP, ports), Layer 5 Session, Layer 6 Presentation (encryption, encoding), Layer 7 Application (HTTP, DNS, SMB — the services users actually touch). Mnemonic bottom-up: All People Seem To Need Data Processing.

Each layer wraps the one above it — encapsulation. Your HTTP request (L7) gets a TCP header (L4), then an IP header (L3), then an Ethernet header (L2), then it hits the wire (L1). The receiving side unwraps in reverse. When something breaks, exactly one envelope is usually at fault — the model's whole value is telling you which one.

Troubleshoot bottom-up: find the HIGHEST layer that still works, and the break is the layer just above it. Ping to 8.8.8.8 works but names fail? Layers 1–3 are healthy (ICMP is L3), so the break is Layer 7 DNS. Ping fails but ARP shows the gateway's MAC? Layer 2 works (ARP resolved), Layer 3 doesn't. Dark link light? Don't even think about Layer 7 — you're at Layer 1.

The protocol-to-layer-to-tool map is what makes the model operational, not academic: HTTP/DNS live at L7 — test with curl.exe or nslookup / Resolve-DnsName. TCP/UDP live at L4 — test with netstat or Test-NetConnection -Port. IP/ICMP live at L3 — test with ping and tracert. Ethernet/ARP live at L2 — check with arp -a. The cable lives at L1 — check the link light and Get-NetAdapter status. One layer, one protocol family, one command.

Two layers people blur: L4 vs L7. If ping works and DNS resolves but the website won't load, L3 and L7-name-resolution are fine — the break is L4 (the TCP port is closed/filtered) or the L7 application itself. Test-NetConnection -ComputerName example.com -Port 443 splits them cleanly: TcpTestSucceeded True means L4 is fine and the problem is the app; False means the port never opened.

The TCP/IP model is the older, four-layer sibling you'll meet in interviews: Link (OSI L1+L2), Internet (OSI L3), Transport (OSI L4), Application (OSI L5+L6+L7). Same network, coarser map. When someone says 'the TCP/IP model,' they mean these four — don't recite seven layers at them, map between the two.

example.code:
# One command that tests three layers at once — then you read it bottom-up.
Test-NetConnection -ComputerName example.com -Port 443

# Typical output, annotated by layer:
#   ComputerName          : example.com     <- L7: the NAME resolved (DNS worked)
#   RemoteAddress         : 93.184.216.34   <- L7 answer: name -> IP mapping
#   PingSucceeded         : True            <- L3: ICMP echo got a reply (IP path works)
#   TcpTestSucceeded      : True            <- L4: TCP handshake on port 443 completed
#
# Reading it: name resolved (L7-DNS ok) + ping ok (L3 ok) + TCP 443 ok (L4 ok)
# = the network path is healthy; if the site still won't load, the fault is
#   the L7 APPLICATION (the web server itself), not the network.

# The per-layer toolkit:
Resolve-DnsName example.com          # L7: DNS specifically (bypasses the browser)
ping 93.184.216.34                  # L3: raw IP reachability, no names involved
Test-NetConnection example.com -Port 443   # L4: is the TCP port open?
arp -a                              # L2: who is on my local wire?
Get-NetAdapter | Select-Object Name, Status, LinkSpeed  # L1: does the OS see a link?
curl.exe -I https://example.com     # L7: real HTTP (curl.exe — see note below)

# NOTE: in Windows PowerShell, bare 'curl' is an ALIAS for Invoke-WebRequest,
# not the real curl. 'curl.exe' forces the actual curl binary. When a tutorial
# says 'curl' and the flags behave oddly, check Get-Command curl first.
example.walkthrough: Test-NetConnection is the teaching command because one run exercises three layers and its output labels them: the resolved name proves L7 DNS, PingSucceeded proves L3 ICMP, TcpTestSucceeded proves L4 TCP — so if all three are True and the site still fails, you have eliminated the network and the fault is the application. The per-layer toolkit below it is the same idea decomposed: when the combined test shows a failure, you run the single-layer command to isolate exactly which envelope broke. Resolve-DnsName tests names without the browser's cache confusing you; ping with a raw IP tests L3 with L7 removed from the picture; arp -a shows L2 neighbors; Get-NetAdapter shows whether the OS even sees a physical link. The curl note is the classic gotcha — Windows PowerShell aliases curl to Invoke-WebRequest, so curl.exe with the .exe is how you get the real tool tutorials assume.

pitfalls: Starting at Layer 7 ('reinstall the application') when the link light is dark — always verify bottom-up. Thirty seconds checking L1 (cable, port, Get-NetAdapter status) saves hours of reinstalling software that was never broken.

Memorizing the seven layers without attaching a command to each — the model only earns its keep when 'Layer 3' automatically makes you type ping/tracert and 'Layer 7' makes you type nslookup. Layer names without tools are trivia; with tools, they're a diagnostic procedure.

Answering a TCP/IP-model question with the seven OSI layers — interviewers ask about both deliberately. Four layers (Link, Internet, Transport, Application) for TCP/IP; know the mapping cold: TCP/IP Application = OSI 5+6+7, Internet = OSI 3.
lessons.try_it: Run Test-NetConnection -ComputerName example.com -Port 443 and label each line of the output with its OSI layer. Then run Resolve-DnsName example.com and ping 93.184.216.34 — say out loud which layer each command tests and why.

lessons.title: Hashing, Encryption, and the Registry
concepts: Hashing is a one-way fingerprint: feed any data in, get a fixed-length string out (SHA-256 gives 64 hex characters). Same input always gives the same hash; change one byte and the hash changes completely (the avalanche effect). One-way means you cannot reverse it — there is no 'unhash.' Its job is integrity: hash a downloaded ISO with Get-FileHash and compare it to the vendor's published hash; match means the file wasn't corrupted or tampered with.

Encryption is reversible scrambling with a key: ciphertext plus the key gives back plaintext. That reversibility is the whole difference — encryption protects data in transit/storage while someone authorized can still read it. If you can decrypt it, anyone who steals the key can too, which is why key management is the actual hard part of encryption.

Hashing vs encryption, the interview answer: hashing is one-way (verify integrity, store passwords), encryption is two-way (protect data that must be read back). Passwords are HASHED, never encrypted — if the password database is stolen, hashes can't be reversed into passwords (attackers must guess-and-hash each candidate, which is why we add salt: a random value mixed in so identical passwords hash differently and precomputed tables fail).

The Windows Registry is the operating system's central configuration database — a hierarchy of keys (folders) and values (settings). Two hives matter most: HKLM (HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE) holds machine-wide settings that apply to every user — installed software, services, drivers; HKCU (HKEY_CURRENT_USER) holds the current user's settings — desktop, preferences. HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services is where every Windows service's startup configuration lives.

Group Policy and the registry are the same settings wearing different clothes: most policies are just registry values written by the GPO engine. Machine policies land in HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies, user policies in HKCU\SOFTWARE\Policies. This mapping is diagnostic gold — if a GPO 'isn't applying,' check whether the registry value actually arrived; if it did, the policy worked and the app is ignoring it.

Regedit safety is non-negotiable because the registry has no undo button: always export the key before editing (File > Export, or 'reg export'), change values don't delete keys unless you know the default will regenerate (most won't), and keep the .reg backup until you've rebooted and verified. Restore is 'reg import backup.reg' — one command that reverses the edit exactly.

example.code:
# 1. HASHING: verify a download's integrity (the real-world use)
Get-FileHash -Path C:\Install\server-2025.iso -Algorithm SHA256

# Output: Algorithm SHA256, Hash 9F2C41..., Path C:\Install\server-2025.iso
# Compare that 64-character string to the vendor's published hash character
# by character. Match = the file is exactly what the vendor shipped.
# (Try it: hash any file twice — identical output — then change one byte and
#  hash again. The avalanche: a totally different hash from a 1-byte change.)

# 2. REGISTRY BACKUP: export BEFORE you touch anything
reg export "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies" C:\Backup\policies-backup.reg
# This writes the entire Policies key — every value — to a .reg text file.
# It is your undo button. Keep it until after the reboot + verification.

# 3. READ a value (safe, changes nothing) — e.g. what is the logon shell?
reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon" /v Shell
# Expected: Shell    REG_SZ    explorer.exe

# 4. RESTORE: the surgical reversal of any edit under that key
reg import C:\Backup\policies-backup.reg
# Rewrites every value from the backup. Reboot, verify, THEN delete the backup.
example.walkthrough: Get-FileHash is hashing made concrete: -Algorithm SHA256 picks the current standard (MD5 and SHA-1 are broken for security use — fine for checksums, never for trust), and the output hash is compared against the vendor's published value. Identical strings mean identical files; that is the entire integrity story. The reg.exe commands are the registry survival kit: 'reg export' snapshots a key to a .reg file BEFORE editing — the step that turns a registry disaster into a one-command recovery. 'reg query /v' reads a single value without changing anything, which is how you confirm a GPO actually landed (check HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies for the value the policy should have written). 'reg import' writes the backup back over the live key — the exact inverse of your edit, which is why exporting first is the rule that matters more than any other registry advice.

pitfalls: Saying passwords are 'encrypted' in the database — the correct term is hashed (with salt). 'Encrypted' implies reversible, which implies a key that an attacker could steal. Interviewers ask this specifically to check you know the difference.

Editing the registry without exporting first — regedit has no undo, and 'I'll remember what I changed' fails at 2 AM. The export takes five seconds; the rebuild after a bad delete takes a weekend. Export, edit, reboot, verify, then delete the backup.

Deleting a registry key to 'reset' a setting — deletion is not the inverse of editing. Windows rarely regenerates deleted keys (the Winlogon key will NOT come back), so you trade a wrong value for a missing one, which is worse. Set the value back to its original instead.
lessons.try_it: Hash any file twice with Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 and confirm the outputs match. Then open the file, change one byte, hash again — watch the avalanche. Separately: run 'reg query' against HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon /v Shell and confirm it reads explorer.exe (look, don't touch).

lessons.title: TCP/IP In Depth
concepts: TCP vs UDP is the reliability tradeoff at Layer 4. TCP is the careful courier: it opens a connection (the three-way handshake — SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), numbers every segment, retransmits lost ones, and delivers data in order. Web pages, email, file transfers use TCP because a missing byte corrupts the file. UDP is fire-and-forget: no handshake, no retransmission, no ordering — just datagrams thrown at the destination. DNS, DHCP, live video and voice use UDP because a late retransmitted packet is worse than a dropped one — the conversation already moved on.

Ports are how one IP address serves many conversations: the IP is the apartment building, the port is the apartment number. A socket is the full address — IP plus port, like 192.168.10.5:443. Well-known ports are conventions every admin memorizes: 443 HTTPS, 80 HTTP, 3389 RDP, 22 SSH, 53 DNS, 445 SMB, 25/587 mail. 'Connection refused' on a port usually means nothing is listening there — check with netstat or Test-NetConnection before blaming the firewall.

ICMP is the network's signaling protocol at Layer 3 — ping and tracert are both ICMP. Ping sends an echo request and times the echo reply (reachability + latency). Tracert abuses the TTL field: it sends packets with TTL=1, the first router decrements it to 0, the packet 'dies,' and the router must send back a 'time exceeded' message — revealing its address. TTL=2 reveals the second hop, and so on. That is the entire trick behind the hop-by-hop map.

MTU is the largest packet the path allows — 1500 bytes on standard Ethernet — and fragmentation is what happens when a bigger packet meets a smaller pipe: the router chops it up (unless the DF, Don't Fragment, flag is set, in which case it drops it and complains). VPN tunnels add encapsulation overhead that shrinks the effective MTU, which is why 'small pages load but big downloads stall' after a VPN change is almost always MTU/fragmentation, not bandwidth.

The packet journey, end to end: your app hands data to TCP (L4), which cuts it into segments and adds port numbers; IP (L3) adds source/destination addresses making packets; Ethernet (L2) adds MAC addresses making frames; the NIC (L1) turns frames into signals. Each router strips L2, reads the L3 destination, re-wraps in new L2, and forwards. The destination unwraps in reverse. Every troubleshooting question is asking 'which envelope failed.'

Reading failures by layer: 'DNS_PROBE_FINISHED' with working ping = L7 DNS (not the network). Ping fails but ARP resolves the gateway = L3 past the local link. TCP port test fails but ping works = L4 (closed/filtered port). Dark link light = L1. Big transfers stall on VPN = L3 MTU. Name the layer first and the tool picks itself.

example.code:
# 1. Where does the path die? Tracert maps every hop using the TTL trick.
tracert 8.8.8.8
# Each line is one router that sent back 'time exceeded.' A row of * * * means
# that hop doesn't answer ICMP (common, not necessarily broken) — the path is
# only broken where EVERYTHING after a hop also times out.

# 2. Find your path's MTU ceiling: -f sets Don't Fragment, -l sets payload bytes.
#    1472 = 1500 (Ethernet MTU) - 20 (IP header) - 8 (ICMP header). No magic:
#    it is the largest payload that fits unfragmented in a 1500-byte frame.
ping -f -l 1472 8.8.8.8
# 'Reply from 8.8.8.8: bytes=1472' = 1500-byte path MTU confirmed.

ping -f -l 1473 8.8.8.8
# 'Packet needs to be fragmented but DF set.' = 1473 does NOT fit.
# The ceiling is between the largest -l that replies and the smallest that
# complains. Over a VPN, expect a lower ceiling (tunnel overhead eats bytes).

# 3. Is the PORT open, not just the host alive? (L4, not L3)
Test-NetConnection -ComputerName fileserver01 -Port 445
# TcpTestSucceeded : True  -> SMB is listening; the path AND the port work.
# TcpTestSucceeded : False -> host is up (ping may work) but nothing listens
#   on 445, or a firewall drops it. Check the service BEFORE the firewall.

# 4. What is listening locally? (the other end of the socket)
netstat -ano | Select-String 'LISTENING' | Select-String ':443'
# Shows the PID holding port 443. 'Connection refused' + no LISTENING line
# = the service isn't running. Start there, not at the firewall.
example.walkthrough: Tracert's output is only mysterious until you know the TTL trick: each hop is a router that killed a packet whose TTL expired and was forced to identify itself. Stars at one hop with responses after it mean that router just doesn't answer ICMP — cosmetic. Stars from some hop onward mean the path genuinely dies there. The ping -f -l pair is MTU discovery with no tools to install: -f (Don't Fragment) turns the router's 'too big' response into a clean yes/no per size, and 1472 is arithmetic, not magic — 1500 minus the 20-byte IP header minus the 8-byte ICMP header. The largest -l that replies is your ceiling; VPN overhead lowers it, which is the whole explanation for post-VPN 'big downloads stall.' Test-NetConnection -Port splits L3 from L4: ping proves the host, the port test proves the service — a False here with a working ping means nothing listens or a firewall filters, and netstat -ano confirms which by showing (or not showing) the LISTENING socket and its PID. Order of operations, always: is the service listening (netstat) before is the firewall blocking (policy).

pitfalls: Calling UDP 'worse than TCP' — it's a tradeoff, not a downgrade. DNS over TCP would be slower for no benefit; a file transfer over UDP would corrupt data. The interview answer names what each sacrifices and why the application chose it.

Blaming the firewall before checking whether anything listens — 'connection refused' with no LISTENING line in netstat means the service is down, and no firewall rule will fix a service that isn't running. netstat first, firewall second.

Forgetting MTU on VPN tunnels — the classic 'worked before the VPN, now large transfers stall' ticket. Tunnel encapsulation shrinks the effective MTU below 1500; ping -f -l finds the real ceiling in thirty seconds, and the fix is clamping MSS or lowering MTU on the tunnel, not adding bandwidth.
lessons.try_it: Run ping -f -l 1472 8.8.8.8, then -l 1473, and watch the 'Packet needs to be fragmented but DF set' message appear — that boundary is your path MTU talking. Then run Test-NetConnection -ComputerName example.com -Port 443 and state which layer each True/False belongs to.

lessons.title: Next-Gen Firewalls From Zero
concepts: A firewall is a bouncer for your network: every packet shows its ID (source, destination, what it's carrying) and the firewall decides who gets in, who gets out, and who crosses between network segments.

A NEXT-GEN firewall (NGFW) is a bouncer with a brain: beyond IPs and ports it inspects content — antivirus scans files, IPS blocks known attack patterns, web filter blocks bad site categories. Fortinet bundles these as UTM profiles attached to policies.

Policies are evaluated TOP-DOWN and the firewall stops at the FIRST match. Specific allows go at the top; a general deny-all goes at the bottom as the safety net. LOGIC CHECK: a perfect allow rule below a broad deny is decoration — order is logic.

NAT lets many private devices share one public IP. Source NAT rewrites outbound traffic (your 192.168.1.x becomes the firewall's public IP); destination NAT / VIP maps a public IP and port to a private server. It is stateful — replies are un-translated automatically, so no second rule is needed for return traffic.

Anything matching NO policy hits the IMPLICIT DENY and is dropped silently. Best practice: write your own explicit deny-all at the bottom so the drop is logged and visible in hit counts instead of vanishing.

example.code:
config firewall policy
    edit 10
        set name "LAN-to-WAN-web"
        set srcintf "port1"
        set dstintf "port2"
        set action accept
        set service "HTTP" "HTTPS"
        set nat enable
    next
end
example.walkthrough: Read it like a sentence: policy 10 says traffic FROM port1 (LAN) TO port2 (WAN) using HTTP/HTTPS is ACCEPTED, with source NAT so private IPs hide behind the public IP. 'edit 10' creates-or-opens policy number 10; each 'set' fills one field; 'next' saves. Three ideas in one policy: direction (srcintf/dstintf), match (service), verdict (action) — plus NAT so the return path works.

pitfalls: Putting the deny-all above the allow rules and then debugging the allow rule's syntax for an hour — the syntax was fine, the ORDER was wrong.
Forgetting NAT on the outbound allow: internal hosts' packets leave, but replies can't find their way back — enable source NAT on LAN-to-WAN allows.
lessons.try_it: Open the FortiGate simulator's Policy Board, send an HTTPS packet from 192.168.1.50, and read the evaluation log line by line until you can predict which policy fires before you click.

lessons.title: FortiGate Deep Dive
concepts: FortiOS config lives under 'config' paths: 'config system interface' for ports and IPs, 'config firewall policy' for the rule table, 'config firewall vip' for inbound NAT, 'config vpn ipsec phase1-interface' and 'phase2-interface' for tunnels.

The edit/set/next/end dance: 'edit <id>' opens (or creates) an entry, 'set <field> <value>' fills fields, 'next' saves and stays, 'end' saves and exits. 'set' outside an edit context fails — the CLI answers 'Command fail. Return code -1'.

A VIP (virtual IP) is destination NAT: 'set extip 203.0.113.10' plus 'set mappedip 10.0.10.50' plus port-forwarding publishes one public address that lands on a private DMZ server. Pair it with a policy allowing WAN-to-DMZ toward that server.

Site-to-site VPN is phase 1 (IKE: authenticate the peer and agree on crypto — remote-gw, psksecret, proposal) then phase 2 (IPsec: which subnets ride inside the tunnel — src-subnet, dst-subnet). Phase1-UP with Phase2-DOWN means the trust is fine but the crypto or the subnet pairs disagree.

'diagnose' is your witness stand: 'diagnose firewall policy list' shows live hit counts per policy (which rule is actually firing); 'diagnose vpn tunnel list' shows tunnel up/down state. LOGIC CHECK: 'show' tells you what EXISTS; 'diagnose' tells you what is HAPPENING.

example.code:
FortiGate # diagnose firewall policy list
id   name              src -> dst        action   hits
---  ----------------  ----------------  -------  ----
2    LAN-to-WAN-web    port1 -> port2     accept   14932
1    deny-all          port1 -> port2     deny     317
example.walkthrough: This is the money output in a firewall incident. Policy 2 (the web allow) has 14,932 hits — it is doing its job. Policy 1 (deny-all) has 317 hits — something is being blocked; investigate whether those 317 SHOULD have been allowed (a missing allow rule, or wrong order). When a user says 'the firewall is blocking me,' you don't guess — you watch these counters while they retry.

pitfalls: Referencing an address object in a policy before creating it — FortiOS requires the object to exist first ('entry not found in datasource'). Build addresses, then policies.
Leaving 'set allowaccess' wide open on the WAN interface — that exposes admin login (HTTPS/SSH) to the internet. Keep WAN allowaccess to ping only.
lessons.try_it: In the FortiGate simulator terminal, build a VIP publishing 203.0.113.10:443 to 10.10.10.50:443, then run 'show firewall vip' and read your config back like an auditor.

lessons.title: Palo Alto and App-ID
concepts: PAN-OS thinks in ZONES first: Trust (inside), DMZ (public servers), Untrust (internet). Interfaces join zones; security rules say which zones traffic may cross (Trust to Untrust). Evaluation is top-down, first match wins — the same universal principle as FortiGate.

App-ID identifies the APPLICATION itself — web-browsing, file-sharing, remote-access — by behavior and signatures, not by port number. A rule says 'allow web-browsing' and it works whether the app uses port 443, 8080, or anything else.

Port-based thinking fails in both directions: it BLOCKS legitimate apps on odd ports (a dashboard on 8080 missed by a tcp/443 rule) and ALLOWS rogue apps hiding on standard ports (malware tunneled over 443 sails through). LOGIC CHECK: if your rule says 'allow tcp/443', you have allowed EVERY application capable of using port 443.

Service 'application-default' means 'whatever ports this app normally uses — App-ID decides.' NAT lives on its own tab and is evaluated BEFORE security policy, so security rules must match the POST-NAT addresses and zones.
Action 'deny' sends back a rejection (polite but chatty); action 'drop' discards silently (stealthy — scanners learn nothing). Facing Untrust, drop is usually the safer default.

example.code:
set rulebase security rules allow-web from Trust
set rulebase security rules allow-web to Untrust
set rulebase security rules allow-web application web-browsing
set rulebase security rules allow-web service application-default
set rulebase security rules allow-web action allow
example.walkthrough: Five lines, one complete application-based policy: from Trust to Untrust, the APPLICATION web-browsing (not 'tcp/443'), on its default service ports, is ALLOWED. Because matching is by application identity, this rule still fires when the web app moves to port 8080 — and a companion rule can deny look-alike applications even when they ride port 443. That is the whole App-ID value proposition in a single rule.

pitfalls: Writing application 'any' plus service 'tcp/443' on a Palo Alto and calling it a web rule — that is port-based thinking on an App-ID box; you paid for application identity and then didn't use it.
Writing the security rule against the PRE-NAT destination IP — NAT is evaluated first, so the rule must match the translated (post-NAT) address and zone or it will never fire.
lessons.try_it: In the Palo Alto simulator, send 'web-browsing on TCP 8080' from Trust with only the baseline rules and watch it die on block-all — then build the App-ID allow rule and watch the SAME packet get allowed. That contrast is the lesson.

lessons.title: Proxmox VE From Zero
concepts: A hypervisor lets one physical server run many virtual servers; Proxmox VE is a Type-1 (bare-metal) hypervisor — it installs directly on hardware, no desktop OS underneath
Proxmox ships two engines: KVM for full virtual machines (own kernel — runs Windows, BSD, any Linux) and LXC for containers (shared host kernel — Linux guests only, ~50 MB idle)
Every VM/container gets a numeric VMID (100+); qm manages VMs, pct manages containers — same pattern: <tool> <action> <id> [options]
A Linux bridge (vmbr0) is a virtual switch: VMs plug virtual NICs into it; a bridge with no physical port is an isolated lab network
Storage pools: local holds ISOs/templates/backups, local-lvm holds thin-provisioned VM disks (space consumed only as the guest writes)
Live migration moves a running VM between nodes with near-zero downtime — it moves running state (RAM/CPU), so shared storage is the prerequisite

example.code:
qm list
qm create 120 --name lab-web --memory 2048 --cores 2 --net0 virtio,bridge=vmbr1
qm start 120
qm status 120
pct create 210 debian-12 --hostname dns01 --memory 512
pct start 210
example.walkthrough: WHAT: qm = VM manager, pct = container manager. HOW: list what's there, create by ID with resources, attach the NIC to a bridge, start it. WHY: the CLI is scriptable and works over SSH when the web UI is unreachable — assessments reward CLI speed. WHEN: creating lab VMs, bulk provisioning, verifying state (qm list) before and after every change. Open sims/proxmox-sim.html and run this exact sequence in the CLI Console tab, then find each machine in the Web UI tree.

pitfalls: VMID collisions: qm create fails if the ID exists — plan an ID scheme (100s web, 200s db) before creating
RAM is reserved, vCPU is shared: over-provisioning CPU is normal, over-provisioning RAM prevents VMs from starting
Putting lab VMs on vmbr0 (with uplink) when you meant isolated — check the bridge, not just the VM
Expecting containers to run Windows: shared kernel means Linux guests only
lessons.try_it: In sims/proxmox-sim.html: complete the guided lab 'Deploy a 3-VM lab with isolated networking' (create vmbr1 with no uplink, 3 VMs on it, verify with qm list + ip link show), then wipe it and rebuild from memory in free mode.

lessons.title: Linux Terminal From Zero
concepts: The orient-list-move loop is 80% of terminal work: pwd (where am I?), ls (what's here?), cd (go there)
One filesystem tree from /: /etc = configuration, /var = growing data (logs in /var/log), /home = people, /opt = add-on software, /tmp = scratch
Everything is a file: devices (/dev), kernel state (/proc) — read the system by reading files
Permissions are three audiences x three powers: owner/group/other x read(4)/write(2)/execute(1); add per audience to get octal (755 = rwxr-xr-x)
On files, x = may execute; on directories, x = may enter/traverse — that's why directories are 755 and data files 644
grep finds text, find finds files, tail -f watches logs live, pipes (|) chain tools: ps aux | grep nginx

example.code:
pwd
ls -lt /var/log
tail -20 /var/log/syslog
grep -i error /var/log/syslog | head
ls -l deploy.sh
chmod 755 deploy.sh
example.walkthrough: WHAT: a triage sequence — orient, find the newest log, read its tail, search for errors, check a script's permissions, fix the missing execute bit. HOW: -t sorts newest-first; -i ignores case; | feeds one command's output into the next. WHY: 'something broke' always starts with the newest log and the exact permission bits — guessing wastes the clock. WHEN: every troubleshooting session, in this order. Run it verbatim in sims/terminal-mastery.html.

pitfalls: rm has no trash can — rm -r on the wrong path is permanent; never rm -rf near /
chmod 777 'to make it work' — fixes the symptom by deleting all security; fix the exact missing bit instead
Forgetting -r on grep/find when searching directory trees (grep -r, find /path -name)
Editing configs without a backup: cp nginx.conf nginx.conf.bak takes two seconds
lessons.try_it: In sims/terminal-mastery.html: finish all three Challenges (find the newest log, fix deploy.sh to exactly 755, beat your best time on the navigation drill), then score 5/5 in the Permission Lab practice.

lessons.title: Git & GitHub From Zero
concepts: Git tracks three places: working directory (edited) -> staging area (git add) -> commits (git commit); git status tells you which files are where
A commit is a permanent snapshot with a message explaining why; the graph of commits is the project's history
Branches are safe sandboxes: never commit straight to main — branch, change, push, open a pull request
A pull request = 'review my branch, then merge': discussion plus automated checks before code lands
A merge conflict = both sides changed the same lines; resolve by editing, git add, git commit — the merge commit keeps both parents
GitHub hosts the repo for teams: push sends commits up, pull brings teammates' commits down; Issues track work, Actions run automation

example.code:
git clone https://github.com/interstitium-labs/infra-docs.git
git checkout -b fix/vpn-keepalive
edit vpn.md   # change keepalive = 30 -> 60
git add vpn.md
git commit -m "Raise VPN keepalive to 60"
git push origin fix/vpn-keepalive
example.walkthrough: WHAT: the full professional loop — clone, branch, change, stage, snapshot, publish. HOW: each command moves work one step along the three-place pipeline; the branch keeps main clean until review. WHY: this is the exact workflow infrastructure teams use for firewall rules, Terraform, and runbooks — reviewed, tested, reversible. WHEN: every change, every day. Run it in sims/git-simulator.html (Git Terminal tab) and watch the Repo Visual tab repaint after each command.

pitfalls: Committing straight to main — the #1 beginner habit; branches exist so review can happen
git commit without -m (or with 'fix stuff'): messages are for your future self at 3 AM — say what and why
Fearing merge conflicts: they're routine questions from Git, resolved by edit -> add -> commit
Pushing secrets (.env, private keys): once pushed, consider them compromised — use .gitignore before the first commit
lessons.try_it: In sims/git-simulator.html: complete the guided lab (clone -> branch -> change -> PR, all 6 steps), then run the merge-conflict walkthrough and inspect the two-parent merge commit in the graph.

lessons.title: Hypervisors Compared
concepts: Type-1 (bare metal: Proxmox VE, Hyper-V, ESXi) installs on hardware — production standard; Type-2 (VirtualBox, Workstation) runs inside a desktop OS — lab/testing only
Proxmox VE: free/open-source, KVM VMs + LXC containers side by side, HA/live migration/backups included, web UI + qm/pct CLI
Hyper-V: Microsoft's hypervisor, included with Windows Server — natural where Windows licensing already exists; managed via Hyper-V Manager / PowerShell
ESXi: Broadcom's enterprise hypervisor — dominant in large VMware estates; advanced features (vMotion, vCenter) are licensed tiers
Concepts transfer 1:1 — learn once, translate vocabulary: Linux bridge = virtual switch, storage pool = datastore, live migration = vMotion / Live Migration
Interview framing: describe fit ('dominates large VMware shops', 'natural with existing Microsoft licensing', 'enterprise features at open-source cost') — never disparage a vendor

example.code:
Proxmox:  bridge vmbr0  | storage pool local-lvm | qm migrate 100 pve02 (live)
Hyper-V:  virtual switch  | CSV / datastore        | Live Migration
ESXi:     vSwitch        | datastore              | vMotion
Same idea, three dialects.
example.walkthrough: WHAT: a concept-translation table. HOW: read each row left to right — one idea, three vendor names. WHY: interviewers test whether you understand virtualization or just memorized one console; translating proves understanding. WHEN: any 'compare hypervisors' or 'what's your virtualization experience' question. Study the full table in sims/proxmox-sim.html (Compare tab).

pitfalls: Naming a 'best' hypervisor absolutely — the right answer is always 'it depends on budget, existing licensing, and scale'
Trashing a vendor's product in an interview — frame by fit, not by rivalry
Confusing Type-1 and Type-2 — know which one you'd stake production on and why
Forgetting containers: Proxmox's built-in LXC is a genuine differentiator for Linux-heavy shops
lessons.try_it: Explain the table aloud in 60 seconds: cost, VM tech, containers, management, and migration for all three — then give the one-sentence fit summary for each without naming a loser.

lessons.title: Event Log Analysis: Get-WinEvent, Get-EventLog, and wevtutil
concepts: The logs that matter: System (drivers/services), Application (apps), Security (logons/auditing), Setup, Forwarded Events
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable is the fast path — it filters server-side before anything crosses to you
Get-EventLog is the legacy cmdlet: classic logs only, slow on big Security logs — prefer Get-WinEvent
wevtutil qe runs XPath queries from CMD; wevtutil epl exports a whole log to .evtx for evidence

Event IDs worth memorizing: 4624/4625 logon success/failure, 4740 account lockout, 1074 clean shutdown/restart, 6005/6006 event log service start/stop, 6008 dirty shutdown, 41 Kernel-Power unexpected shutdown, 7000/7009/7031 service failures, 10016 DCOM permission noise
NEVER clear a log on a live incident — exported .evtx is evidence, a cleared log is a destroyed crime scene

example.code:
# Who failed to log on in the last hour, and as which account?
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; ID=4625; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddHours(-1)} |
  Select-Object TimeCreated, @{N='User';E={$_.Properties[5].Value}}, @{N='From';E={$_.Properties[19].Value}}

# Unexpected shutdowns this week (41 = power loss, 6008 = dirty shutdown, 1074 = planned):
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='System'; ID=41,6008,1074; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddDays(-7)} |
  Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, Message | Format-List

# CMD equivalent — XPath query, text output, last 5 hits:
wevtutil qe Security "/q:*[System[(EventID=4625)]]" /f:text /c:5

# Export for the incident folder BEFORE you touch anything:
wevtutil epl Security \\FILESRV\IR\2026-10-10\security.evtx
wevtutil epl System   \\FILESRV\IR\2026-10-10\system.evtx
example.walkthrough: Start every log hunt with a time window and an ID, not with scrolling. -FilterHashtable with LogName + ID + StartTime runs the filter inside the event service, so a million-event Security log returns in seconds instead of minutes — piping Get-WinEvent into Where-Object drags every event through PowerShell first. For 4625 failed logons, Properties[5] is the target username and Properties[19] the source IP, which turns the query into an instant brute-force detector. wevtutil is your CMD-side twin: qe queries with XPath, epl exports the raw .evtx so the evidence survives even if the server does not. Logic Check: query the log for the symptom's time window FIRST and let the events pick the theory — reading logs to confirm a theory you already chose is how you miss the real cause sitting two lines above.

pitfalls: Piping Get-WinEvent into Where-Object on the Security log — minutes of runtime vs seconds with -FilterHashtable
Using Get-EventLog for the Security log — it is legacy, slow, and cannot do structured filtering
Forgetting the XPath quotes in wevtutil qe — the /q:"..." quoting must survive CMD parsing
Clearing logs to 'make the alert stop' during an incident — that is evidence destruction
lessons.try_it: Find every unexpected shutdown on your machine this month: Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='System'; ID=41,6008} | Select TimeCreated, Id. Then export the System log with wevtutil epl and confirm the .evtx opens in Event Viewer.

lessons.title: Service Management: Get-Service, sc.exe, and Dependencies
concepts: Get-Service reads state fast; sc.exe (Service Control) changes config from CMD — learn both, you will need both on Server Core
sc.exe config <name> start= auto — the space after 'start=' is REQUIRED, not a typo
Set-Service -StartupType Automatic is the PowerShell equivalent; 'Automatic (Delayed Start)' exists for non-critical services
Dependencies decide startup order: Get-Service -RequiredServices shows what it needs, -DependentServices shows what needs it
The 'Log On As' account needs the 'Log on as a service' right — change the password and forget the right, the service dies at next boot
Recovery tab: first/second/subsequent failure actions (restart service, run a program, restart computer); Event IDs 7000 (failed to start), 7009 (timeout), 7031 (terminated unexpectedly)

example.code:
# State of everything, worst first:
Get-Service | Where-Object Status -eq 'Stopped' | Sort-Object StartType -Descending |
  Select-Object Name, Status, StartType

# What does the print spooler depend on, and what depends on it?
Get-Service Spooler | Select-Object -ExpandProperty RequiredServices | Select-Object Name, Status

# CMD deep-dive: full config including the logon account and failure actions:
sc.exe queryex Spooler
sc.exe qfailure Spooler

# Change startup type (note the space after start=) and set recovery to restart twice:
sc.exe config Spooler start= auto
sc.exe failure Spooler reset= 86400 actions= restart/60000/restart/60000/""/60000

# PowerShell equivalent for the startup type:
Set-Service -Name Spooler -StartupType Automatic

# Why did it die? Ask the System log, filtered to service control manager IDs:
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='System'; ID=7000,7009,7031; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddDays(-1)} |
  Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, Message
example.walkthrough: Diagnose before you configure. A service that starts and then stops is a service that tried to tell you something — the System log's 7000/7009/7031 entries from the Service Control Manager name the failure, and the Application log often carries the service's own last words. Get-Service -RequiredServices maps the dependency chain so you fix the actual broken link instead of restarting symptoms. When you do change config, remember sc.exe's infamous syntax: 'start= auto' with the space, or the command silently misparses. And the Log On As account is a two-part change — the password in the service properties AND the 'Log on as a service' user right, or the next reboot is your outage. Logic Check: if the service ran fine for a year and died today, the service did not change — something around it did (password expired, dependency patched, disk full). Fix the delta, not the service.

pitfalls: sc.exe config <svc> start=auto (no space) — silently fails; the space after = is mandatory
Setting every service to Automatic — boot storms and circular waits; Delayed Start exists for a reason
Changing the service account password without updating the service — guaranteed 3 AM page
kill -9 style thinking: 'restart the service' without reading why it stopped, three times in a row
lessons.try_it: Pick a stopped manual service on your lab box: read its RequiredServices, check the System log for 7000/7009/7031 in the last day, then flip it to Automatic (Delayed Start) with Set-Service and confirm with sc.exe query.

lessons.title: Disk Management: diskpart, Get-Disk, and Volume Tasks
