concepts: Get-Disk shows every disk: Number, FriendlyName, OperationalStatus, PartitionStyle (RAW = uninitialized), Size
New disk bring-up sequence: Initialize-Disk -PartitionStyle GPT → New-Partition -UseMaximumSize -DriveLetter E → Format-Volume -FileSystem NTFS
diskpart is the CMD twin: list disk → select disk N → clean → convert gpt → create partition primary → format fs=ntfs quick label=Data → assign letter=E
MBR caps at 2 TB per disk — anything bigger needs GPT, no exceptions
Resize-Partition grows into contiguous free space; Get-PartitionSupportedSize tells you the ceiling first
chkdsk /f fixes logical errors (needs exclusive access), chkdsk /r also scans bad sectors (slow); Optimize-Volume -Defrag for HDD, -Retrim for SSD

example.code:
# Find the new uninitialized disk:
Get-Disk | Where-Object PartitionStyle -eq 'RAW' | Select-Object Number, FriendlyName, Size

# Bring it online: GPT, one big partition, NTFS, drive E:
Initialize-Disk -Number 2 -PartitionStyle GPT
New-Partition -DiskNumber 2 -UseMaximumSize -DriveLetter E
Format-Volume -DriveLetter E -FileSystem NTFS -NewFileSystemLabel Data -Confirm:$false
Get-Volume -DriveLetter E | Select-Object DriveLetter, FileSystem, SizeRemaining, Size

# CMD/diskpart equivalent as a script file (run: diskpart /s provision.txt):
#   list disk
#   select disk 2
#   clean
#   convert gpt
#   create partition primary
#   format fs=ntfs quick label=Data
#   assign letter=E

# How far can E: grow right now?
Get-PartitionSupportedSize -DriveLetter E | Select-Object SizeMin, SizeMax
example.walkthrough: The bring-up order is fixed: initialize, partition, format — skip a step and the next cmdlet fails with a confusing error. Get-Disk is your pre-flight: confirm the disk is RAW and the SIZE matches the disk you think you are touching, because 'select disk 2' in diskpart followed by 'clean' is one wrong number from a resume-generating event. Prefer GPT unless you have a specific legacy reason; MBR's 2 TB ceiling will bite exactly when the array grows. For growth, Resize-Partition only extends into adjacent free space — Get-PartitionSupportedSize tells you the real ceiling before you promise anyone a bigger drive. Logic Check: list disk, select disk, list disk AGAIN — the second listing is the one that saves your job, because disk numbers shift when hardware changes.

pitfalls: diskpart 'clean' on the wrong disk — no undo, no recycle bin; verify with list disk twice
MBR on a >2 TB disk — the space past 2 TB silently vanishes
Format-Volume on the wrong drive letter — Get-Volume first, format second
Running chkdsk /r on a multi-TB production volume at noon — it takes the volume offline for hours
lessons.try_it: On a lab VM with a spare VHDX: run Get-Disk, walk the Initialize → New-Partition → Format-Volume sequence, then write the equivalent diskpart script and compare the two paths step for step.

lessons.title: Windows Update Management: sconfig, usoclient, and PSWindowsUpdate
concepts: Server Core has no Settings app — sconfig option 6 (Download and Install Updates) and option 5 (update settings) are the native path
usoclient StartScan and usoclient StartInstall are the modern command-line triggers (wuauclt /detectnow is legacy)
Get-HotFix | Sort-Object InstalledOn -Descending is the fastest 'what is installed' audit
PSWindowsUpdate module: Get-WindowsUpdate -ListOnly to preview, Install-WindowsUpdate -AcceptAll -AutoReboot to deploy, Get-WUHistory for the record
WSUS client-side targeting: GPO sets the target group so the WSUS server sorts machines into rings
Rollback is a KB uninstall: wusa /uninstall /kb:5034441 /quiet /norestart — know it BEFORE you need it

example.code:
# Audit: what patches are actually on this box?
Get-HotFix | Sort-Object InstalledOn -Descending | Select-Object -First 10 HotFixID, InstalledOn, Description

# Am I missing a specific KB?
Get-HotFix -Id KB5034441 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

# Server Core native path (interactive menu):
sconfig   # then 6 = download & install, 5 = update settings

# Trigger a scan + install from the command line (silent — check Get-WindowsUpdate history after):
usoclient StartScan
usoclient StartInstall

# PSWindowsUpdate (install once: Install-Module PSWindowsUpdate -Force):
Get-WindowsUpdate -ListOnly | Select-Object KB, Title, Size
Install-WindowsUpdate -KBArticleID 'KB5034441' -AcceptAll -IgnoreReboot
Get-WUHistory | Select-Object -First 5 Date, Title, Result

# Rollback a bad KB:
wusa /uninstall /kb:5034441 /quiet /norestart
example.walkthrough: Patch state is an audit question before it is an install question: Get-HotFix sorted by InstalledOn tells you in seconds whether the box is current or six months behind, and Get-HotFix -Id answers 'is KBxxxx installed?' without scrolling. On Server Core, sconfig is the sanctioned UI — option 6 does the whole download-and-install cycle. usoclient is the scriptable trigger but it runs silent, so always follow it with a history check. PSWindowsUpdate is the fleet tool: -ListOnly previews so you never blind-install, and -AcceptAll is what makes it non-interactive (without it, the cmdlet stops and asks). The discipline that separates admins from outage-creators: a canary ring first, and a known rollback — wusa /uninstall with the KB number — rehearsed before the change window, not discovered during it. Logic Check: patching is a change like any other — if you cannot name the rollback path and the canary group, you are not ready to click Install.

pitfalls: Install-WindowsUpdate without -AcceptAll in a script — it prompts and your automation hangs forever
-AutoReboot on a production box without a maintenance window — that flag IS the outage
usoclient gives no progress output — silence is not failure, verify with Get-WUHistory
Patching the DCs, the hypervisor hosts, and the VMs all in the same window — stagger by role
lessons.try_it: Audit your lab box: list the 10 newest HotFixes, check for one specific KB by ID, then run Get-WindowsUpdate -ListOnly (install the module if missing) and read what it would install — without installing anything.

lessons.title: GPO Backup, Restore, and Migration: Backup-GPO and Import-GPO
concepts: Backup-GPO -All -Path <folder> snapshots every GPO into per-GPO folders (GUID + manifest.xml) — this is your change-window insurance
Restore-GPO brings a backup back into the SAME domain it came from — fast undo for a bad edit
Import-GPO migrates a backup into a DIFFERENT domain or a new GPO — use a migration table to remap SIDs/UNC paths
Back up BEFORE every GPO change, and name the folder with the date — 'GPOBackups\2026-10-10' beats 'GPOBackups\final2'
After any restore or import, verify: Get-GPO, gpresult /r, and re-check security filtering and WMI filter links

example.code:
# Insurance first — back up ALL GPOs into a dated folder:
$stamp = Get-Date -Format 'yyyy-MM-dd'
Backup-GPO -All -Path "\\FILESRV\GPOBackups\$stamp"

# Single-GPO backup before editing the risky one:
Backup-GPO -Name 'Sales-Wallpaper' -Path "\\FILESRV\GPOBackups\$stamp"

# The edit went sideways — restore it into the same domain:
Restore-GPO -Name 'Sales-Wallpaper' -Path "\\FILESRV\GPOBackups\$stamp"

# Migrate a GPO into the test domain (or clone it under a new name):
Import-GPO -BackupGpoName 'Sales-Wallpaper' -Path "\\FILESRV\GPOBackups\$stamp" `
  -TargetName 'Sales-Wallpaper-Test' -CreateIfNeeded

# Prove the restore landed:
Get-GPO -Name 'Sales-Wallpaper' | Select-Object DisplayName, ModificationTime
gpresult /r /scope:computer
example.walkthrough: GPO edits are the highest-blast-radius clicks in Windows administration — one bad setting replicates to every machine in the OU within 90 minutes. Backup-GPO -All is cheap insurance: each GPO lands in its own GUID-named folder with a manifest, and the dated parent folder turns your backup share into a timeline you can roll back to. Restore-GPO is the undo button but only within the same domain; the moment you cross domains (prod to lab, or company merger), you need Import-GPO plus a migration table to remap domain-specific SIDs and UNC paths, otherwise the imported GPO references security principals that do not exist. After any restore, verify like a skeptic: Get-GPO for the timestamp, gpresult for the winning set, and a glance at security filtering — a restored GPO with the wrong filter applies to everyone or no one. Logic Check: a GPO with no backup is a rumor — if you cannot restore it in under five minutes, your change window just became a research project.

pitfalls: Restore-GPO in a different domain — it only works where the backup was taken; cross-domain needs Import-GPO
Importing without a migration table — SIDs and UNC paths point at the old domain and the policy silently misfires
Backing up to C:\Temp on the DC — the backup dies with the server it was meant to save; use a share
Forgetting to re-verify security filtering after a restore — the settings are back but the audience changed
lessons.try_it: Back up all GPOs to a dated folder, create a throwaway test GPO, delete it, then Restore-GPO it back and confirm with Get-GPO — the full insurance cycle, rehearsed before you need it.

lessons.title: Windows Firewall Rules From the Command Line: netsh advfirewall and New-NetFirewallRule
concepts: Three profiles — Domain, Private, Public — each with its own on/off and defaults; the ACTIVE profile is what matters, check with Get-NetConnectionProfile
netsh advfirewall firewall add rule: the fastest path on Server Core — name, dir, action, protocol, localport, remoteip, profile
New-NetFirewallRule is the PowerShell twin with the same fields plus -DisplayName; Get-NetFirewallRule / Enable-NetFirewallRule / Disable-NetFirewallRule manage lifecycle
Rule precedence refresher: explicit BLOCK beats explicit ALLOW beats default — order within allows does not matter, block always wins
Logging: Set-NetFirewallProfile enables pfirewall.log; a DROP line with your app's port is the diagnosis, not a mystery
Always scope -RemoteAddress — an allow rule with remoteip=any on a management port is an exposure, not a fix

example.code:
# Which profile is actually active on this NIC?
Get-NetConnectionProfile | Select-Object Name, NetworkCategory

# CMD path — allow the app's HTTPS port from the app subnet, Domain profile only:
netsh advfirewall firewall add rule name="Allow App HTTPS" dir=in action=allow protocol=TCP localport=8443 remoteip=10.1.20.0/24 profile=domain

# PowerShell twin — same rule, object-oriented:
New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "Allow App HTTPS" -Direction Inbound -Protocol TCP `
  -LocalPort 8443 -RemoteAddress 10.1.20.0/24 -Action Allow -Profile Domain

# Prove it exists and is enabled:
Get-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "Allow App HTTPS" | Select-Object DisplayName, Enabled, Action, Direction
netsh advfirewall firewall show rule name="Allow App HTTPS"

# Turn on logging so the NEXT failure explains itself:
Set-NetFirewallProfile -Profile Domain -LogFileName "%systemroot%\system32\logfiles\firewall\pfirewall.log" `
  -LogBlocked True -LogMaxSizeKilobytes 16384
Get-Content "$env:SystemRoot\System32\LogFiles\Firewall\pfirewall.log" -Tail 5
example.walkthrough: Firewall work starts with the active profile, not the rule — a perfect allow rule on the Domain profile does nothing for a NIC that Windows classified as Public, and that mismatch is the single most common 'but I made a rule!' failure. Both CLIs build the same rule: direction, protocol, port, and — critically — a scoped RemoteAddress, because remoteip=any on RDP or WinRM is how test rules become incidents. netsh is terser and works everywhere including Core; the NetSecurity cmdlets give you objects you can filter and pipe. After creating the rule, prove it with Get-NetFirewallRule AND a connection test — the rule existing and the traffic flowing are two different facts. And enable the firewall log on every server you touch: when the next app fails, the pfirewall.log DROP line names the port, the IPs, and the verdict, which turns a two-hour mystery into a five-minute fix. Logic Check: when the app fails right after a firewall change, the firewall log is the witness — a DROP line with your app's port is a confession, not a mystery.

pitfalls: Writing the rule for the Domain profile while the NIC sits on Public — Get-NetConnectionProfile first, always
remoteip=any on management ports — scope every rule to the subnets that need it
Assuming rule order decides allow-vs-allow — only block-vs-allow has precedence; allows do not compete
netsh on a fresh build with the firewall service disabled — the rules exist but nothing enforces them
lessons.try_it: Create an inbound allow for TCP 8443 scoped to one /24 on the Domain profile with BOTH netsh and New-NetFirewallRule (different display names), list both with Get-NetFirewallRule, enable blocked-packet logging, then delete the test rules.

lessons.title: Reading Packet Captures: Wireshark and tshark for Admins
concepts: Capture filters (BPF, set BEFORE capture: 'host 10.1.1.50', 'tcp port 443') shrink the file; display filters (set AFTER: ip.addr==10.1.1.50) shrink the view
tshark is Wireshark for the terminal: tshark -i eth0 -f 'tcp port 443' -w cap.pcap captures; tshark -r cap.pcap -Y 'dns' reads back
The three-way handshake is the whole story: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK means the path and the port are alive
SYN with no SYN-ACK = server not listening or something filtering; RST right after SYN = port actively refused/closed
DNS in a capture: query goes out, response comes back — query with no response is a resolver/upstream problem, not a client problem
TLS stall after ClientHello with no ServerHello = cipher suite or protocol version mismatch
tcp.analysis.retransmission display filter finds the pain instantly on a 'slow network' complaint

example.code:
# Capture 60 seconds of HTTPS to the app server, then read it back:
tshark -i eth0 -f "tcp port 443 and host 10.1.5.20" -a duration:60 -w /tmp/app.pcap
tshark -r /tmp/app.pcap -Y "tcp.flags.syn==1 && tcp.flags.ack==0" -T fields -e ip.src -e tcp.dstport

# Wireshark display filters for the classics:
#   ip.addr==10.1.5.20 && tcp.port==443      one host, one service
#   dns.qry.name contains "corp.local"       who is asking for what
#   tcp.analysis.retransmission               where the slowness lives
#   icmp.type==3                              destination-unreachable answers

# Did the handshake complete? Look for the pattern in order:
#   10.1.1.50 -> 10.1.5.20  SYN
#   10.1.5.20 -> 10.1.1.50  SYN, ACK
#   10.1.1.50 -> 10.1.5.20  ACK
# Missing line 2 = filtered or down. RST instead of line 2 = port closed.
example.walkthrough: Read a capture like a transcript of an argument: who spoke last tells you who is waiting. The handshake is always the first thing to check — a complete SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK means the network path works and the service is listening, so your problem is above layer 4; a SYN with no answer means the packet died in transit or at a filter, and an immediate RST means the host is up but nothing listens on that port (the network equivalent of a slammed door). Use capture filters to keep files small — capturing all traffic on a busy server interface will fill a disk while you blink — and display filters to interrogate what you caught. tcp.analysis.retransmission is the cheat code for 'the network is slow' tickets: retransmissions cluster exactly where packets die. Logic Check: the capture never lies about what it saw, but it only saw one vantage point — capture on the client AND the server when you need to prove where packets vanish, and sync clocks first or the timelines will gaslight you.

pitfalls: Capturing on the wrong interface — check ip -br addr before you start, not after an hour of empty files
No capture filter on a busy link — multi-GB pcaps that take longer to open than the outage lasted
Forgetting promiscuous mode when you need someone else's traffic on a mirrored port
Comparing two captures with unsynced clocks — the 'delay' you found is just clock skew
lessons.try_it: Capture your own ping with tshark -f icmp, then apply display filters for echo request vs reply. Next, capture a curl to an HTTPS site and find the ClientHello → ServerHello → handshake completion in the packet list.

lessons.title: NAT and Port Forwarding
concepts: SNAT/masquerade: many private addresses share one public IP; the NAT table remembers each session so return traffic finds its way back
DNAT/port forwarding: inbound publicIP:port rewrites to internalIP:port — needs a matching WAN-side firewall allow, the NAT rule alone is not enough
PAT (overload) multiplexes thousands of sessions onto one public IP via source-port remapping
Hairpin NAT: an internal client reaching the server via its PUBLIC IP — fails unless the router supports hairpinning; use split-DNS instead
Double NAT (ISP router + your firewall both NATing) silently breaks all inbound forwarding — bridge the ISP CPE or forward on both
Windows Server NAT for labs: New-NetNat -Name LabNAT -InternalIPInterfaceAddressPrefix 192.168.10.0/24

example.code:
# Lab NAT on a Windows Server acting as the edge (Hyper-V internal switch scenario):
New-NetNat -Name LabNAT -InternalIPInterfaceAddressPrefix 192.168.10.0/24
Get-NetNat | Select-Object Name, InternalIPInterfaceAddressPrefix

# On a real edge firewall the inbound path is TWO rules, not one:
#   1. DNAT:  WAN 203.0.113.10:8443  -->  10.1.5.20:443
#   2. ALLOW: WAN interface, TCP 8443, source any, dest 10.1.5.20
# Forget rule 2 and the NAT translation succeeds while the firewall drops the packet.

# Troubleshooting 'works inside, fails from outside':
#   - From LAN, curl https://10.1.5.20:443     (tests the SERVER)
#   - From outside, curl https://203.0.113.10:8443  (tests NAT + firewall)
#   - Server OK + outside fails = NAT rule, WAN firewall rule, or double NAT at the ISP CPE.
example.walkthrough: Think of NAT as a translator with a memory: outbound, it rewrites the source and memorizes the session; inbound, a port-forward rule rewrites the destination before the firewall ever sees the packet — which is exactly why the forward and the WAN-side allow rule are a pair that must be configured together. The classic assessment trap is 'reachable by internal IP, unreachable by public IP': the server is fine (LAN test proves it), so the fault is in the translation path — a missing WAN allow rule, a forward pointing at the wrong internal IP, or double NAT where the ISP's router ate the inbound packet before your firewall ever saw it. Hairpin NAT is the other classic: internal users hitting the public IP of an internal server loop through the edge and fail on routers that do not support it — the enterprise answer is split-DNS (internal clients resolve the internal IP directly), not fighting the router. Logic Check: NAT is a translator with a memory — if the return packet cannot find its session entry, the conversation dies at the door; verify the session/translation table, not just the rule.

pitfalls: Creating the DNAT rule but not the WAN firewall allow — translation succeeds, packet gets dropped anyway
Two DNAT rules on the same external port — first match wins, the second is dead config
Testing inbound forwarding from inside the LAN — hairpin behavior makes the test lie; test from a real external path
Forgetting that the ISP modem is also a router — double NAT breaks inbound silently
lessons.try_it: Build the lab: New-NetNat on a server with an internal Hyper-V switch, put a VM behind it, and prove outbound works. Then diagram (on paper) the two-rule inbound path for publishing that VM's web port, and list what breaks if the ISP CPE is also NATing.

lessons.title: Linux Survival for Windows Admins: Files, Permissions, Processes
concepts: Everything is a file, and the truth is in plain text — logs, configs, and devices all read with the same tools
Permissions are rwx for user/group/other: chmod 750 = rwxr-x---; chmod 640 = rw-r-----; chown changes WHO owns, chmod changes WHAT they can do
sudo runs one command as root — the Linux equivalent of 'Run as Administrator', and it logs every use
Processes: ps aux | grep <name> finds it, kill <pid> asks nicely (SIGTERM), kill -9 <pid> is the fire axe — SIGTERM first, always
Disk: df -h shows filesystems, du -sh * shows which directory is eating the disk — run both before you delete anything
Text plumbing: cat, less, head/tail -f, grep -R, pipes — the whole admin toolkit is composable one-liners

example.code:
# Where am I, what's here, who owns it:
pwd; ls -lah /etc/ssh
# -rw------- 1 root root  sshd_config  -> only root can read/write. Good.

# Safe permission fix for a web directory (NOT 777, ever):
chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www/app
find /var/www/app -type d -exec chmod 750 {} \;
find /var/www/app -type f -exec chmod 640 {} \;

# Find the runaway process and end it politely first:
ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head -5
kill 1842        # SIGTERM: 'please shut down'
sleep 5; ps -p 1842 || echo "gone"
kill -9 1842     # only if it ignored SIGTERM

# Disk full drill — find the hog before you touch anything:
df -h /
du -sh /var/* 2>/dev/null | sort -rh | head -5

# Always back up a config before editing:
cp /etc/ssh/sshd_config /etc/ssh/sshd_config.bak-$(date +%F)
example.walkthrough: Your Windows instincts transfer directly: Task Manager becomes ps/top, Event Viewer becomes /var/log and journalctl, the Services console becomes systemctl, and Disk Management becomes df/du. The mindset shift is that Linux exposes everything as text you can read with the same five tools — when something breaks, you are never more than a grep away from the answer. Permissions deserve respect: the octal digits are user-group-other, and 777 ('everyone can do everything') is never the fix, it is the vulnerability you will explain in the postmortem. Same for kill -9: SIGTERM lets the process flush buffers and close cleanly, SIGKILL can corrupt whatever it was writing — escalate, do not start at the top. And the config-backup habit (cp file file.bak-date) costs one second and has saved more careers than any other single practice. Logic Check: Linux tells you the truth in plain text — if you cannot explain a failure from the log file, you have not read the log file yet.

pitfalls: chmod 777 to 'fix' a permission error — you just made the file world-writable; fix the owner/group instead
kill -9 as the first resort — corrupted databases and half-written files are the usual reward
Editing a config with no backup — one typo in sshd_config and your next logout is permanent
rm -rf with a trailing space or a variable that expanded to empty — the legends are all true
lessons.try_it: On any Linux box or WSL: run ls -lah on /etc/ssh, decode the permission strings into octal, use find to list files writable by 'other' under /tmp, and practice the df → du drill to find the three biggest directories under /var.

lessons.title: Reading Linux Logs: journalctl and /var/log
concepts: journalctl is the systemd journal: journalctl -u sshd --since '1 hour ago' shows one service's story with a time window
journalctl -xe jumps to the end with explanations; journalctl -p err -b shows only errors since this boot
/var/log is the classic layout: syslog (Debian) / messages (RHEL) for the system, auth.log (Debian) / secure (RHEL) for logins, kern.log for the kernel
tail -f /var/log/auth.log | grep -i fail is the live brute-force watch — learn it, you will use it weekly
dmesg | tail shows kernel/hardware events (disk errors live here); last shows logins, lastb shows FAILED logins
logrotate keeps logs from eating the disk — a 40 GB log usually means logrotate is missing or broken, not that you need a bigger disk

example.code:
# The SSH service's last hour — the single most useful log command:
journalctl -u sshd --since "1 hour ago" --no-pager | tail -30

# Everything the system flagged as an error since boot:
journalctl -p err -b --no-pager | head -20

# Classic files — know both distro names:
tail -100 /var/log/auth.log  | grep -i "failed"   # Debian/Ubuntu
tail -100 /var/log/secure    | grep -i "failed"   # RHEL/CentOS

# Brute-force census: who is hammering SSH, and how often?
grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log | awk '{print $(NF-3)}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10

# Kernel/hardware truth — disk errors announce themselves here:
dmesg -T | grep -iE "error|fail|I/O" | tail -10

# Who logged in, and who TRIED and failed:
last | head -10
lastb | head -10

# How big is the journal, and is log rotation healthy?
journalctl --disk-usage
ls -lh /var/log/auth.log* /var/log/syslog*
example.walkthrough: Log triage is a funnel: start narrow with the failing service's own journal (journalctl -u <service>), then widen to the system log only if the service log is silent. The --since flag is your time machine — 'since 1 hour ago' or 'since today' turns a million-line journal into the fifty lines that matter. On classic files, remember the distro split or you will stare at a nonexistent /var/log/secure on Ubuntu: auth.log vs secure, syslog vs messages. The failed-password pipeline (grep → awk → sort → uniq -c → sort -rn) is worth memorizing cold — it turns any auth log into a ranked attacker list in one line, and assessors love watching it typed from memory. And when a disk is full, check the logs before you buy storage: ls -lh on the rotated logs plus journalctl --disk-usage usually reveals one runaway log that logrotate should have tamed. Logic Check: start with the service's own journal, then widen to the system log — the answer to 'why did it fail' is almost always within fifty lines of the failure timestamp.

pitfalls: Reading /var/log/secure on Ubuntu (it is auth.log there) or auth.log on RHEL (it is secure) — know your distro
journalctl without --no-pager in a script — the pager swallows your pipeline
Deleting a 40 GB log that a process still holds open — the space does NOT free until the handle closes; truncate (: > file) or restart the service instead
Ignoring timestamps' timezone — correlate with the application's own logs or chase ghosts
lessons.try_it: Run the brute-force census pipeline against your auth log (or generate failures with bad ssh attempts to localhost first), then pull journalctl -p err -b and explain each error line in one sentence.

lessons.title: Linux Services and Networking: systemctl, ip, and nmcli
concepts: systemctl status/start/stop/restart/enable/is-enabled <service> — and ENABLED is not RUNNING: check both, the reboot tests the one you forgot
systemctl list-units --failed shows everything broken right now — the fastest health check on an unfamiliar box
ip addr show (addresses), ip route show (gateway/routes), ip link set <dev> up/down — the modern replacements for ifconfig/route
ss -tulpn replaces netstat: every listening TCP/UDP port with the owning process, in one screen
nmcli device status / nmcli con show — NetworkManager's view; /etc/resolv.conf may be auto-generated, check before hand-editing
firewalld: firewall-cmd --list-all — the host firewall is a suspect in every 'connection refused from remote, works locally' case

example.code:
# Service health in 10 seconds:
systemctl list-units --failed --no-pager
systemctl status sshd --no-pager | head -12
systemctl is-enabled sshd   # 'enabled' = survives reboot. 'disabled' + running = dies on reboot.

# Full network picture, modern tools:
ip -br addr                 # addresses per interface, one line each
ip route show               # default via <gateway> must exist
nmcli device status         # NetworkManager's view of each NIC

# What is listening, and who owns the port?
ss -tulpn | grep -E ':443|:80'

# Connectivity ladder — stop at the first failure:
ping -c4 10.1.5.20          # layer 3 to the host
ping -c4 db01.corp.local    # now with name resolution
traceroute 10.1.5.20        # where the path breaks (or tracepath, no root needed)

# Host firewall suspect?
sudo firewall-cmd --list-all | grep -A5 services
example.walkthrough: The 'enabled vs running' distinction is the highest-value two seconds in Linux service work: a service can be running-but-disabled (dies on reboot — your change did not stick) or enabled-but-failed (reboot will not save it — something is broken now). systemctl list-units --failed is the triage shortcut on any unfamiliar machine — it lists every broken unit before you even know what the box does. For networking, the ladder is sacred: ip addr (do I have an address?), ip route (do I have a gateway?), ping the gateway (layer 3?), ping by name (DNS?), ss -tulpn (is anything listening on the port?). Stop at the first rung that fails — every rung you skip is a wrong theory you will have to unlearn. And the host firewall (firewalld/iptables) is ALWAYS a suspect when local connections work and remote ones do not; --list-all shows the truth in one screen. Logic Check: enabled is not running and running is not enabled — check both, because the reboot will test the one you forgot.

pitfalls: Using ifconfig/netstat on a modern distro — they may not even be installed; ip and ss are the natives
Hand-editing /etc/resolv.conf when NetworkManager manages it — your edit vanishes on the next DHCP renew
'It works locally but not remotely' without checking firewalld — the default zone drops most inbound
Restarting a service to 'fix' it without systemctl status first — the status output usually names the cause
lessons.try_it: On a Linux box: run the failed-units check, pick one service and verify both is-enabled AND is-active, then walk the connectivity ladder (ip addr → ip route → ping gateway → ss -tulpn) and write down what each step proves.

lessons.title: Hyper-V Export, Import, and Dynamic Memory
concepts: A VM is files: the .vmcx config, the .vhdx disks, and any checkpoint .avhdx chain — name all three or you cannot move it
Export-VM -Path packages config + disks into a portable folder; Import-VM -Copy -GenerateNewId brings it onto the new host without ID collisions
Import modes: Copy (duplicate into place, safest), In-Place (register where the files sit), Restore (back to the original location)
Post-import fixups: virtual switch names must exist on the target host, and VM version must be ≤ what the host supports (Get-VMHostSupportedVersion)
Dynamic memory: Set-VMMemory -DynamicMemoryEnabled with Minimum/Startup/Maximum — the host reclaims idle guest RAM via ballooning
Never use dynamic memory for SQL/Exchange-style workloads — ballooning fights the database buffer pool; and do not overcommit vCPUs past physical cores without a reason

example.code:
# Export the VM (safe while running, but checkpoint-free is cleaner):
Get-VM WEB01 | Select-Object Name, State, Version
Export-VM -Name WEB01 -Path 'D:\Exports'
Get-ChildItem 'D:\Exports\WEB01' -Recurse | Select-Object Name, Length

# On the TARGET host — first make the world match:
Get-VMSwitch | Select-Object Name, SwitchType          # the vSwitch name from source must exist here
Get-VMHostSupportedVersion | Select-Object Version     # VM version must be <= host support

# Import as a copy with a fresh identity (no SID/VM-ID collision):
$vmcx = Get-ChildItem 'D:\Exports\WEB01\Virtual Machines\*.vmcx' | Select-Object -ExpandProperty FullName
Import-VM -Path $vmcx -Copy -GenerateNewId -VirtualMachinePath 'D:\VMs' -VhdDestinationPath 'D:\VMs\VHDX'

# Dynamic memory for the right workloads (web/app tiers, not databases):
Set-VMMemory -VMName WEB01 -DynamicMemoryEnabled $true `
  -MinimumBytes 512MB -StartupBytes 2GB -MaximumBytes 8GB -Buffer 20
Get-VMMemory -VMName WEB01 | Select-Object DynamicMemoryEnabled, Minimum, Startup, Maximum

# Who is actually using what?
Measure-VM -VMName * | Select-Object VMName, AvgCPU, AvgRAM
example.walkthrough: Moving a VM is a file operation with an identity problem. Export-VM gathers the three file types into one folder, but the import is where moves die: the .vmcx references a virtual switch BY NAME, so if the target host's switch is called anything different, the import fails or the VM boots with no network — create the matching switch first. -GenerateNewId is non-negotiable when the source VM still exists anywhere on the network; without it you get duplicate VM IDs and AD computer-account collisions that manifest as bizarre, intermittent failures. Check Get-VMHostSupportedVersion too: a VM created on a newer host carries a configuration version the old host cannot read. For memory, dynamic is a gift for bursty web/app tiers — the host reclaims idle RAM via the balloon driver — but databases manage their own memory and fight the balloon, so SQL gets static RAM, full stop. Logic Check: a VM is files — if you can name every file the VM needs (vmcx, vhdx, checkpoints), you can move it anywhere; if you cannot, you are hoping.

pitfalls: Import without -GenerateNewId while the original still exists — duplicate VM IDs and phantom AD conflicts
Forgetting the vSwitch name mismatch — VM imports fine, boots with no network, and the ticket says 'migration broke networking'
Dynamic memory on SQL Server — the balloon driver and the buffer pool fight, and performance loses
Exporting WITH a checkpoint chain and wondering why the export is huge — merge first
lessons.try_it: Export a lab VM, then import it onto the same host with -Copy -GenerateNewId under a new name. Verify the vSwitch mapping, boot it, and confirm the original and the clone coexist — then set dynamic memory bounds and watch Get-VMMemory.

lessons.title: ThreatLocker Allowlisting: Default-Deny Application Control
concepts: Default-deny vs default-allow: traditional antivirus allows everything except known-bad; allowlisting blocks everything except known-good
File identification: hash (SHA256), certificate, path, or file attributes - hash is most secure
Approval workflow: request → review → approve/deny - maintains security while enabling business
Built-in applications: ThreatLocker maintains a catalog of known-good applications for fast approval
Elevation of trust: applications can be permitted temporarily with automatic expiration
lessons.example: A user downloads a new version of Chrome. The hash doesn't match the approved version. ThreatLocker blocks execution and prompts for approval. The admin reviews the file (verifies it's legitimate Chrome from Google), approves the new hash, and the user can proceed. The old hash remains approved for rollback if needed.
pitfalls: Approving by path alone (C:\Tools\app.exe) - malware can replace the file at that path
Whitelisting entire folders - defeats the purpose of allowlisting
Disabling protection for "just a minute" - attackers only need a minute
Forgetting to remove temporary permits after they expire
lessons.try_it: Think through: A developer needs to run a custom-compiled tool. What information would you need to approve it securely? (Answer: file hash, publisher info, business justification, scope of permit - specific machines or all?)

lessons.title: ThreatLocker Ringfencing: Containing Application Behavior
concepts: Application containment: even allowed apps have boundaries on what they can do
Child process control: prevent apps from launching other processes (e.g., Word shouldn't launch PowerShell)
Network restrictions: limit which apps can access the network and to where
Registry/file system guards: prevent apps from writing to sensitive locations
Defense in depth: if an app is exploited, Ringfencing contains the blast radius
lessons.example: Adobe Reader is allowed to run (via Allowlisting). Ringfencing policy: Reader can open PDFs and print, but CANNOT launch child processes, CANNOT access the network, CANNOT write to registry. When a malicious PDF tries to exploit Reader to download malware, Ringfencing blocks the network access and child process creation - the attack fails even though Reader was exploited.
pitfalls: Overly restrictive policies that break legitimate functionality - test before deploying broadly
Forgetting that Ringfencing applies to the application, not the user - the user can still do things directly
Not considering update mechanisms - apps need to update, plan for that
Assuming Ringfencing replaces patching - it contains exploits, doesn't fix vulnerabilities
lessons.try_it: Design a Ringfencing policy for Microsoft Word: What should Word be able to do? What should it NEVER do? (Hint: Word needs to open/save documents and print. It should never launch PowerShell, access the network except for specific update servers, or write to system directories.)

lessons.title: Zero Trust Architecture: Never Trust, Always Verify
concepts: Core principle: no implicit trust based on network location - every access request is verified
Identity as perimeter: user and device identity replace the network boundary
Least privilege: grant minimum access needed, for minimum time needed
Micro-segmentation: break the network into small zones with strict controls between them
Continuous verification: trust is not permanent - re-verify regularly

ThreatLocker as Zero Trust: Allowlisting (verify apps), Ringfencing (limit app behavior), Network Control (verify connections), Elevation Control (verify privilege), Storage Control (verify data movement)
lessons.example: Traditional: User on corporate LAN is trusted, can access file server. Zero Trust: User on LAN must still authenticate, device must be compliant, application must be approved, and access is limited to specific files needed for the task. Location provides zero trust - every factor is verified independently.
pitfalls: Thinking Zero Trust is a product - it's an architecture, ThreatLocker implements it
Trying to do everything at once - start with identity, then devices, then apps, then data
Forgetting user experience - security that blocks work gets bypassed
Neglecting visibility - you can't verify what you can't see, logging is essential
lessons.try_it: Map each ThreatLocker control to a Zero Trust principle: Allowlisting → ?, Ringfencing → ?, Network Control → ?, Elevation Control → ?, Storage Control → ? (Answers: Verify applications; Limit blast radius/least privilege; Verify network access; Least privilege/just-in-time access; Verify data movement)

lessons.title: Entra ID: Cloud Identity Fundamentals
concepts: Entra ID (formerly Azure AD): Microsoft's cloud identity provider - not the same as on-prem AD
Hybrid identity: on-prem AD synced to Entra ID via Entra Connect - users have one identity for both
Cloud-only vs synced users: synced users originate on-prem; cloud-only exist only in Entra ID
Authentication methods: password hash sync, pass-through authentication, federation (AD FS)
Single sign-on: users authenticate once to access M365, Azure, and integrated SaaS apps
lessons.example: Contoso has on-prem AD with user jdoe@contoso.local. Entra Connect syncs this to jdoe@contoso.com in Entra ID. The user logs in to their workstation with on-prem credentials, then accesses outlook.office.com - SSO means they don't re-enter credentials. Password changes on-prem sync to cloud via password hash sync.
pitfalls: Confusing Entra ID with on-prem AD - they're different directories with different capabilities
Forgetting that synced users are managed on-prem - can't change passwords in cloud
Not monitoring sync health - sync failures cause login issues
Assuming all M365 features work without proper licensing
lessons.try_it: Check your understanding: A user is synced from on-prem. Where do you reset their password? (Answer: On-prem AD - the cloud is read-only for synced attributes. Password hash sync will propagate the change.)

lessons.title: Microsoft 365 Services: Exchange, SharePoint, Teams Administration
concepts: Exchange Online: cloud email - mailboxes, distribution groups, mail flow rules, anti-spam/anti-malware
SharePoint Online: document management - sites, libraries, permissions, sharing policies
Teams: collaboration - teams/channels, meetings, chat, app integration
OneDrive: personal cloud storage - sync, sharing, retention
Admin centers: each workload has its own admin center plus the unified M365 admin center
lessons.example: New project team needs: a Team for chat/meetings, a SharePoint site for documents, a shared mailbox for external communications. You create the Team (which auto-creates the SharePoint site), add members, create the shared mailbox in Exchange admin center, and configure permissions. The Team channels map to SharePoint folders.
pitfalls: Assigning licenses but not verifying service provisioning - users can't access what isn't provisioned
Over-sharing in SharePoint - "Anyone with the link" is convenient but risky
Forgetting Teams retention policies - chat data accumulates
Not configuring anti-phishing policies in Defender for Office 365
lessons.try_it: A user reports they can't access a SharePoint site. What do you check? (Answer: 1) Do they have a license with SharePoint? 2) Are they a member of the site? 3) Is the site shared with them? 4) Check sharing settings - is external sharing blocked?)

lessons.title: OSI Model: The 7 Layers of Networking
concepts: Layer 7 Application: HTTP, DNS, SMTP - what the user interacts with
Layer 6 Presentation: encryption, compression - TLS/SSL lives here
Layer 5 Session: connections between applications - NetBIOS, RPC
Layer 4 Transport: TCP (reliable) vs UDP (fast) - ports live here
Layer 3 Network: IP addressing and routing - routers operate here
Layer 2 Data Link: MAC addresses, switches, VLANs - Ethernet lives here
Layer 1 Physical: cables, hubs, signals - the actual wires
Troubleshooting: start at Layer 1 (is it plugged in?) and work up
lessons.example: User can't access a website. Layer 1: Is the network cable plugged in? Layer 2: Does the switch port show link? Layer 3: Can you ping the gateway? Can you ping 8.8.8.8? Layer 4: Can you telnet to port 80? Layer 7: Does DNS resolve the hostname? Each layer builds on the one below.
pitfalls: Jumping to Layer 7 without checking lower layers - "the website is down" might be "the cable is unplugged"
Confusing TCP and UDP - TCP is connection-oriented (HTTP, SMB), UDP is connectionless (DNS, DHCP)
Forgetting that firewalls operate at multiple layers - packet filter (L3), stateful (L4), application (L7)
lessons.try_it: A user can ping 8.8.8.8 but can't browse websites. Which layer is the problem? (Answer: Layer 7/Application - specifically DNS. Ping uses IP (Layer 3), browsing needs DNS resolution (Layer 7). Try nslookup.)

lessons.title: Windows Registry: Configuration Database Fundamentals
concepts: Hives: HKLM (machine-wide), HKCU (current user), HKU (all users), HKCR (file associations)
Keys vs values: keys are folders, values are the actual settings (name, type, data)
Value types: REG_SZ (string), REG_DWORD (32-bit number), REG_QWORD (64-bit), REG_BINARY, REG_MULTI_SZ
Group Policy maps to registry: most GPO settings write registry values
Backup before editing: export the key before making changes - registry edits are immediate
lessons.example: You need to disable USB storage via registry (when GPO isn't available). The key is HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\USBSTOR, value "Start", type REG_DWORD. Set to 4 to disable, 3 to enable. Export the key first, then modify. Changes take effect on reboot or service restart.
pitfalls: Editing without backup - one wrong delete can make the system unbootable
Confusing HKCU and HKLM - HKCU is per-user, HKLM is machine-wide
Forgetting that 32-bit apps on 64-bit Windows use Wow6432Node - registry redirection
Using REG_SZ when you need REG_DWORD - type matters
lessons.try_it: Where would you look for a setting that applies to all users on the machine vs just the current user? (Answer: HKLM for all users (machine-wide), HKCU for current user only.)

lessons.title: Hashing and Encryption: Integrity vs Confidentiality
concepts: Hashing: one-way function - input → fixed-size output, cannot reverse. Used for integrity verification.
Common hashes: MD5 (broken, don't use), SHA1 (weak), SHA256 (current standard)
Password hashing: store hashes, not passwords. Use bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2 - not SHA256 alone
Encryption: two-way function - plaintext ↔ ciphertext with a key. Used for confidentiality.
Symmetric (AES): same key encrypts/decrypts - fast, key distribution is hard
Asymmetric (RSA): public key encrypts, private key decrypts - slow, solves key distribution
TLS: uses asymmetric to exchange symmetric key, then symmetric for data - best of both
lessons.example: You download an ISO. The site provides a SHA256 hash. You run Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 on your download. If the hashes match, the file wasn't corrupted or tampered with. This is integrity (hashing), not confidentiality - anyone can read the ISO, but you know it's authentic.
pitfalls: Using MD5 or SHA1 for security - they're broken, use SHA256 or better
Confusing hashing and encryption - hashing is one-way (verification), encryption is two-way (secrecy)
Storing passwords with plain SHA256 - use proper password hashing (bcrypt/Argon2) with salt
Forgetting that encrypted data is only as secure as the key management
lessons.try_it: You need to verify a file wasn't modified in transit. Do you use hashing or encryption? (Answer: Hashing. You don't need secrecy, you need integrity verification. Compute the hash and compare.)

lessons.title: Project Build Guide: AD Homelab in a Weekend
concepts: What you need: Hyper-V (built into Windows 10/11 Pro) or VirtualBox (free), Windows Server eval ISO (free 180-day trial from Microsoft), 8GB RAM minimum
VM 1 - Domain Controller: 2 vCPU, 4GB RAM, 60GB disk. Install Windows Server, promote to DC (contoso.local), install DNS and DHCP
VM 2 - Client: 2 vCPU, 4GB RAM, 40GB disk. Install Windows 10/11, join to domain
OU Structure: Create OUs for Departments (IT, HR, Finance), Service Accounts, Workstations. This shows you understand AD design.
Bulk user creation: PowerShell script with New-ADUser in a loop - create 10 test users from a CSV. This is your automation demo.
GPO 1 - Security Baseline: Password policy (14 chars, complexity), lockout policy (5 attempts, 30 min), audit policy
GPO 2 - Mapped Drives: Drive Maps preference to map S: to \\fileserver\shared - shows you know Group Policy Preferences
GPO 3 - Software Restriction: Block execution from %AppData% - this is your "poor man's allowlisting" demo, maps to ThreatLocker concepts
Documentation: GitHub README with architecture diagram, step-by-step build notes, screenshots of each GPO, PowerShell scripts used
lessons.example:
Your GitHub README structure:
# AD Homelab - Enterprise Administration Demo
## Architecture (diagram: DC + Client, network 192.168.1.0/24)
## Build Steps (numbered, with commands)
## OU Design (screenshot of ADUC)
## GPOs Deployed (screenshots of each GPO setting)
## Automation Scripts (New-Hire.ps1 with examples)
## Lessons Learned (what broke, how you fixed it)

In the interview: "Let me show you my homelab. Here's the OU structure I designed, here are the GPOs I deployed, and here's the PowerShell script I wrote to onboard users. The software restriction GPO demonstrates the same default-deny principle as ThreatLocker Allowlisting."
pitfalls: Trying to build too much - scope to DC + 1 client, 3 GPOs, 10 users. Done is better than perfect.
No documentation - if it's not on GitHub with screenshots, it didn't happen (for interview purposes)
Forgetting to take screenshots DURING the build - do it as you go
Not testing - verify each GPO applies with gpresult /r on the client
lessons.try_it: Start now: Download Windows Server 2022 eval ISO from Microsoft. Create the DC VM. Install AD DS. Take a screenshot of Server Manager showing AD DS installed. That's step 1 done. Commit to GitHub.

lessons.title: Project Build Guide: PowerShell Toolkit That Gets You Hired
concepts: Repository structure: /Scripts (the .ps1 files), /Docs (usage examples), README.md (overview)

Script 1 - New-HireOnboarding.ps1: Parameters (FirstName, LastName, Department, Title). Creates AD user, generates username (first initial + last name), sets temp password, adds to department groups, creates home folder, outputs credentials for HR. This is the money script.

Script 2 - Test-InfrastructureHealth.ps1: Tests DC replication (repadmin /replsummary), DNS resolution (Resolve-DnsName), DHCP scope utilization, disk space, service status. Outputs color-coded results. Run this daily.
Script 3 - Get-SystemInventory.ps1: Queries Win32_ComputerSystem, Win32_OperatingSystem, installed software. Exports to CSV. Essential for audits.
Script 4 - Backup-Verification.ps1: Checks last backup timestamp, verifies backup files exist, tests restore of a single file. Because backups that aren't tested aren't backups.
Each script needs: comment-based help (.SYNOPSIS, .DESCRIPTION, .PARAMETER, .EXAMPLE), parameter validation, try/catch error handling, verbose output option
GitHub: Public repo, MIT license, professional README with badges, each script has its own documentation
lessons.example:
New-HireOnboarding.ps1 in action:
.
New-HireOnboarding.ps1 -FirstName "Jane" -LastName "Doe" -Department "IT" -Title "Help Desk Technician"

Output:
✓ Created AD user: jdoe
✓ Generated temp password: [secure]
✓ Added to groups: IT-Department, VPN-Users
✓ Created home folder: \\fileserver\users\jdoe
✓ Mailbox provisioning requested
✓ Credentials exported for HR (secure)

In the interview: "Here's my onboarding script. It reduces a 30-minute manual process to 2 minutes and eliminates errors. Let me walk you through the code."
pitfalls: No error handling - scripts that crash on bad input look amateur
Hardcoded values - use parameters, not "CN=Users,DC=contoso,DC=local" buried in code
No documentation - if I can't figure out how to run it from the README, it's useless
Copying without understanding - if you can't explain every line, don't include it
lessons.try_it: Write Script 2 (Health Check) today. Start with: Test-Connection to your DC, Resolve-DnsName for your domain, Get-Service for DNS/DHCP. Three checks, 20 lines. Commit it. You now have a portfolio.

lessons.title: How to Present Projects in the Interview
concepts: The 3-minute demo: "Let me show you what I built" - have GitHub open, walk through the README, show a script running, explain a design decision
STAR method for projects: Situation (what problem), Task (what you needed to do), Action (what you built), Result (what it accomplishes)
Connect to ThreatLocker: "My AppLocker demo implements the same default-deny principle as ThreatLocker Allowlisting. Here's the policy, here's what it blocks."

Connect to the JD: Map each project to a JD requirement. AD Homelab → "Deploying/managing Active Directory". PowerShell Toolkit → "Scripting". Troubleshooting Runbook → "Creating technical documentation".
Bring a laptop: Have the homelab VMs ready to demo, or screen recordings if VMs aren't portable. GitHub repos should be public.
Anticipate questions: "Why did you choose this OU structure?" "How would you scale this?" "What would you do differently?" Have answers ready.
lessons.example:
Interview flow:
Interviewer: "Tell me about your Active Directory experience."
You: "Let me show you. [Opens GitHub] I built a complete AD homelab - here's the OU design [shows diagram], here are the three GPOs I deployed [shows screenshots], and here's the PowerShell script I wrote to automate onboarding [shows code, runs it]. The software restriction GPO uses the same default-deny approach as ThreatLocker Allowlisting."

You just proved: AD design, GPO deployment, PowerShell automation, documentation, AND ThreatLocker conceptual understanding. In 3 minutes.
pitfalls: Apologizing for homelab - "It's just a homelab" sounds weak. Say "I built an enterprise AD environment to develop my skills." Own it.
Not having it ready - if you say "I have a project" but can't show it, you lose credibility. Have GitHub open before the interview.
Over-explaining - 3 minutes per project max. Let them ask follow-ups.
Forgetting the business value - always connect to "this saves time" or "this improves security" or "this reduces errors"
lessons.try_it: Practice your 3-minute AD homelab demo right now. Set a timer. Open your GitHub (or imagine it). Walk through: 1) What I built (30 sec), 2) Key design decisions (60 sec), 3) Demo a script or GPO (60 sec), 4) How it maps to this role (30 sec). Do it out loud.

lessons.title: CompTIA Security+ (SY0-701): Your Best Next Cert
concepts: Why Security+: Validates the security concepts you mastered in this CBT - Zero Trust, encryption, access control, threat mitigation
Domain 1 - General Security Concepts (12%): Zero Trust architecture (you learned this!), control types, change management - COVERED
Domain 2 - Threats, Vulnerabilities, Mitigations (22%): Malware, social engineering, vulnerabilities - PARTIALLY COVERED (focus on endpoint)
Domain 3 - Security Architecture (18%): Cloud security, virtualization, data classification - COVERED (Entra ID, Hyper-V)
Domain 4 - Security Operations (28%): SOC, SIEM, incident response, digital forensics - PARTIALLY COVERED (troubleshooting methodology)
Domain 5 - Security Program Management (20%): Risk management, compliance, governance - MENTIONED (documentation, SOPs)
Your CBT advantage: ThreatLocker products map directly to Security+ concepts - Allowlisting (application control), Ringfencing (containment), Network Control (firewall)
Study gap: Focus on cryptography details (PKI, certificates), threat actor types, and incident response procedures
lessons.example: Security+ exam question: "A security administrator needs to implement a solution that ensures only authorized applications can execute on workstations. Which solution BEST meets this requirement?" Your CBT knowledge: "Application allowlisting - default-deny execution control. ThreatLocker Allowlisting does this, and I implemented the same concept with AppLocker in my homelab." Answer: Application allowlisting/whitelisting.
pitfalls: Underestimating the exam - Security+ is broad, not deep. You need breadth across all 5 domains.
Ignoring the "management" domain - 20% is governance, risk, compliance. Don't skip it.
Not practicing performance-based questions - the exam has simulations, not just multiple choice
lessons.try_it: Take a Security+ practice test. For each question you miss, map it back to CBT content: "This was covered in the Zero Trust lesson" or "This is a gap I need to study." Focus your study on the gaps.

lessons.title: Cisco CCNA (200-301): Networking Deep Dive Validation
concepts: Why CCNA: Validates the networking skills you built - subnetting, VLANs, routing, switching. The CBT covered CCNA-level networking depth.
Network Fundamentals (20%): OSI model (you learned this!), TCP/IP, cabling - COVERED
Network Access (20%): VLANs, trunking, STP, EtherChannel - DEEP COVERAGE (you configured these!)
IP Connectivity (25%): Routing tables, OSPF, static routing - COVERED (longest-prefix-match, router-on-a-stick)
IP Services (10%): DHCP, DNS, NAT, NTP - COVERED (DHCP scopes, DNS troubleshooting)
Security Fundamentals (15%): VPNs, ACLs, Layer 2 security - COVERED (IPsec, ACL rule order, port security)
Automation (10%): REST APIs, JSON, SDN - GAP (the CBT doesn't cover network automation)
Your CBT advantage: The subnetting math, VLAN configuration, and troubleshooting scenarios directly prepare you for CCNA simlets
lessons.example: CCNA simlet: "Configure VLAN 10 on the switch, assign ports, configure trunk to router." Your CBT knowledge: You did this in the lab! "Switch# configure terminal, vlan 10, name SALES, interface range fa0/1-12, switchport mode access, switchport access vlan 10, interface gi0/1, switchport mode trunk." The CBT drills built this muscle memory.
pitfalls: The automation section (10%) - study REST APIs, JSON, and Cisco DNA Center basics separately
OSPF details - the CBT mentions OSPF but CCNA requires configuring it. Lab this specifically.
Wireless - the CBT covers WPA3 concepts but CCNA needs WLC configuration knowledge
lessons.try_it: Use the CBT's Cisco IOS terminal to practice: "show vlan brief", "show ip route", "show interfaces trunk". These are the exact commands CCNA tests. Time yourself - CCNA simlets are timed.

lessons.title: Microsoft Certifications: AZ-900, AZ-104, MS-102
concepts: AZ-900 (Azure Fundamentals): Entry-level. Validates cloud concepts, Entra ID basics, M365 overview. Your CBT covers: cloud identity (Entra ID lessons), Zero Trust (applies to Azure). Good first Microsoft cert.

AZ-104 (Azure Administrator): Associate-level. Manage Entra ID users/groups, hybrid identity (Entra Connect - you learned this!), virtual networks, storage. Your CBT covers: Entra Connect sync troubleshooting, Conditional Access policies, hybrid identity concepts.

MS-102 (M365 Administrator): Associate-level. Manage M365 tenants, Entra ID, Exchange Online, SharePoint, Teams, security/compliance. Your CBT covers: M365 licensing, Entra ID user management, Conditional Access, Exchange/SharePoint/Teams admin concepts.
Your CBT advantage: The O365/Entra ID domain directly maps to MS-102 objectives. The Entra Connect troubleshooting scenario is exactly what MS-102 tests.
Certification path: AZ-900 → AZ-104 OR MS-102 (choose based on role: Azure infra vs M365 admin). The ThreatLocker role aligns better with MS-102 (endpoint + identity + M365).
lessons.example: MS-102 exam question: "You need to ensure users can only access M365 from compliant devices or trusted locations. What should you configure?" Your CBT knowledge: "Conditional Access policy - require compliant device OR trusted location, block otherwise. I learned this in the Entra ID scenario." This is direct CBT-to-exam mapping.
pitfalls: Microsoft exams change frequently - always check the current skills outline on Microsoft Learn
Hands-on matters - use the free M365 developer tenant (90-day trial) to practice. The CBT taught concepts; you need clicks.
Powershell for M365 - learn the Microsoft Graph PowerShell SDK (replaces MSOnline module). The CBT taught PowerShell fundamentals; apply them to M365.
lessons.try_it: Sign up for a free M365 E5 developer tenant (developer.microsoft.com). Create a test user, assign a license, create a Conditional Access policy requiring MFA. You just did what MS-102 tests.

lessons.title: CompTIA Network+ and A+: Foundational Validations
concepts: CompTIA A+ (220-1101/1102): Two exams. Validates foundational IT: hardware, OS, troubleshooting, security basics. Your CBT covers: troubleshooting methodology (in depth!), Windows administration, security concepts. A+ is ideal if you're new to IT - it validates the foundations.

CompTIA Network+ (N10-009): Single exam. Validates networking: OSI model (you learned this!), TCP/IP, subnetting (you mastered this!), DNS/DHCP, network security. Your CBT's networking domain is Network+ level and beyond.
Why get them: A+ and Network+ are vendor-neutral, DoD-approved, and widely recognized. They validate what the CBT taught and make your resume ATS-friendly.

Your CBT advantage: The troubleshooting scenarios, OSI model lesson, subnetting drills, and DNS/DHCP content directly prepare you. The CBT is actually MORE advanced than Network+ in some areas (VLANs, IPsec).
Stacking: A+ → Network+ → Security+ is the classic CompTIA trifecta. With this CBT, you can likely skip A+ (you're beyond it) and go straight to Network+ or Security+.
lessons.example: Network+ question: "A technician needs to divide 192.168.1.0/24 into 4 subnets. What is the new subnet mask?" Your CBT knowledge: "/24 → 4 subnets = /26 (borrow 2 bits). Mask: 255.255.255.192. You did 30 of these in the subnet sprint drill." This is muscle memory now.
pitfalls: A+ has a lot of hardware/printer content the CBT doesn't cover - study those domains separately if pursuing A+
Network+ includes cloud and virtualization concepts - the CBT covers virtualization (Hyper-V) but review cloud networking models
Don't underestimate - even "easy" certs require studying the specific objectives
lessons.try_it: If you can complete the CBT's 30-task subnet sprint in under 15 minutes with 90%+ accuracy, you're ready for Network+ subnetting questions. That's the benchmark.

lessons.title: Your Certification Action Plan
concepts: Immediate (before Tuesday interview): No cert needed. The CBT + portfolio projects are your proof. Mention "studying for Security+" to show initiative.
30 days post-hire: CompTIA Security+ - validates the security knowledge, DoD-approved, directly relevant to ThreatLocker role
60-90 days: Microsoft MS-102 - validates M365/Entra ID administration, directly maps to JD requirements
6 months: Cisco CCNA - if role involves networking infrastructure. Or AZ-104 if more cloud-focused.
Study strategy: For each cert, take a practice test first. Map missed questions to CBT content ("covered") vs gaps ("need to study"). Focus only on gaps - don't re-study what the CBT already taught.
Cost: Security+ ($404), CCNA ($300), AZ-104 ($165), MS-102 ($165). Many employers pay for certs - ask ThreatLocker about their policy on Tuesday!
Maintenance: CompTIA certs require CEUs every 3 years. Microsoft role-based certs renew annually (free online). Factor this into your plan.
lessons.example: Tuesday interview talking point: "I've been preparing with a comprehensive CBT covering infrastructure and security. I'm planning to pursue Security+ next month to validate the Zero Trust and security concepts, then MS-102 for M365 administration. Does ThreatLocker support certification pursuits?" This shows initiative, planning, and asks about their investment in you.
pitfalls: Certification chasing without purpose - each cert should map to a career goal, not just resume padding
Ignoring hands-on - certs validate knowledge, but the portfolio projects prove you can DO the work. Both matter.
Waiting for "perfect" preparation - schedule the exam. A deadline focuses study.
lessons.try_it: Right now: Go to CompTIA.org, download the Security+ objectives (free PDF). Highlight every objective you can already answer from CBT knowledge. Count them. That's your starting point. The unhighlighted items are your study list.

lessons.title: From Static Diagrams to Living Systems
concepts: A textbook diagram shows you one part in isolation — a living systems view shows you how all parts move together in sequence
The four-step systems anatomy method: (1) See the whole in context, (2) Cut it open to reveal layers, (3) Walk through the process step-by-step, (4) Pull apart into labeled pieces
Apply this to any infrastructure: start with the user action, trace through every system it touches, watch the data flow
Interview power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'the packet starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

example.code:
USER clicks login
  → DNS resolves the name (see the query walk the hierarchy)
  → TCP handshake opens the connection (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK)
  → TLS negotiates encryption (watch the certificates exchange)
  → Kerberos authenticates (AS-REQ, TGS-REQ, AP-REQ — tickets flowing)
  → GPOs apply in order (LSDOU — watch each layer add settings)
  → User sees desktop

Each arrow is a living handoff, not a static box.
example.walkthrough: This is the 'jet engine cutaway' for IT: instead of memorizing that 'DNS resolves names', you see the query leave the client, hit the resolver, walk up to root, down to authoritative, and return — as a moving sequence. In the interview, narrate this journey.

pitfalls: Memorizing port numbers without understanding the conversation they enable
Drawing a network diagram as boxes without showing the data flow between them
Answering 'how does VPN work?' with 'it encrypts traffic' instead of walking through IKE, ESP, encapsulation
lessons.try_it: Open the terminal and run a real DNS trace. Watch the living system: each query is a step in the journey.

lessons.title: Anatomy of Authentication: Kerberos as a Living System
concepts: Kerberos is a three-act ticket exchange: AS-REQ (prove who you are) → TGS-REQ (get service permission) → AP-REQ (present ticket to service)
See it as a journey: client → KDC → client → service, with encrypted tickets as the physical tokens being handed off
Time synchronization matters because tickets have lifetimes — clock skew > 5 minutes breaks the entire chain
ThreatLocker relevance: Elevation Control and Ringfencing depend on knowing WHO is asking — Kerberos provides that identity foundation

example.code:
Act 1: AS-REQ
  Client → KDC: 'I am alice, here is my pre-auth timestamp (encrypted with my key)'
  KDC → Client: TGT (Ticket Granting Ticket) + session key

Act 2: TGS-REQ  
  Client → KDC: 'Here is my TGT, I want to access FILESERVER'
  KDC → Client: Service ticket for FILESERVER

Act 3: AP-REQ
  Client → FILESERVER: 'Here is my service ticket'
  FILESERVER: 'Ticket valid, access granted'

Watch each ticket as a sealed envelope being passed hand-to-hand.
example.walkthrough: Use the Kerberos Explorer in the Visuals section. Click through each step and watch the tickets move. This is the 'exploded view' — each message pulled apart and labeled.

pitfalls: Confusing the TGT (proves identity to KDC) with the service ticket (proves authorization to the resource)
Forgetting that Kerberos requires UDP/TCP 88 and time sync — two infrastructure dependencies
Not connecting authentication to ThreatLocker's identity-based policies
lessons.try_it: Open visuals/kerberos-explorer.html and step through the full exchange. Narrate each handoff out loud.

lessons.title: Anatomy of a Packet: From Click to Response
concepts: Every packet is a layered onion: Ethernet frame → IP packet → TCP segment → TLS record → HTTP request. Each layer is added as it descends, stripped as it ascends
Follow one packet: application creates data → transport adds port numbers → network adds IP addresses → data link adds MAC addresses → physical sends bits
Firewalls inspect at different layers: packet filters (L3/L4), stateful (connection tracking), application-aware (L7 deep inspection)
ThreatLocker Network Control operates here — understanding packet anatomy lets you explain exactly what gets blocked and why

example.code:
Outbound (encapsulation - layers added):
  [HTTP GET /index.html]
  [TCP: src 49152 → dst 443, SEQ 1000] + HTTP
  [IP: src 192.168.1.50 → dst 93.184.216.34] + TCP + HTTP
  [ETH: src AA:BB:CC → dst DD:EE:FF] + IP + TCP + HTTP
  → Bits on wire

Inbound (decapsulation - layers stripped):
  Bits → ETH (is it for my MAC?) → IP (is it for my IP?) 
  → TCP (which port/socket?) → TLS (decrypt) → HTTP (render)

Each layer asks: 'Is this for me? What do I add/remove?'
example.walkthrough: This is the 'cut the engine open' moment: peel each header to see what it contributes. In the interview, draw this as a stack and peel layers as you explain.

pitfalls: Saying 'the firewall blocks it' without specifying which layer and which rule matched
Confusing NAT (rewrites IP addresses) with PAT (rewrites ports for many-to-one)
Forgetting that VPN adds ANOTHER layer of encapsulation around the entire packet
lessons.try_it: Use the terminal to capture a real packet. Peel each layer and identify every header field.

lessons.title: VPN vs ZTNA: Where Remote Access Is Going
concepts: A traditional VPN is a moat-and-drawbridge: once a remote user authenticates, the drawbridge drops and their device lands INSIDE the network with broad reachability — the tunnel trusts the user, so the network trusts the device. ZTNA (Zero Trust Network Access) removes the drawbridge entirely. There is no 'inside.' A broker checks WHO you are and WHAT device you're on for every single application connection, then stitches together exactly one encrypted path to exactly one app — and nothing else on the network is even visible to you. Logic Check — here's the reasoning: a VPN answers the question 'is this user allowed on the network?' once, at login; ZTNA answers 'is this user, on this device, allowed to reach THIS application, right now?' on every connection — which is why a stolen password alone gets an attacker nothing in a ZTNA world: no approved device, no connection.

WHAT: ZTNA is a remote-access model built on Zero Trust principles (never trust, always verify; assume breach; grant least privilege per connection). ThreatLocker's ZTNA (launched March 2026 alongside Zero Trust Cloud Access) brokers traffic rather than tunneling it: no inbound ports are opened on the firewall, internal resources are never exposed to the internet, and access requires BOTH an authorized user AND an approved device — so compromised credentials are useless on their own. This is the same deny-by-default philosophy as ThreatLocker's endpoint controls, extended from 'what may run' to 'what may connect.'

HOW: In a brokered ZTNA flow, (1) the agent/connector on the internal side dials OUT to the cloud broker and holds that outbound connection open — nothing listens inbound; (2) the user authenticates (ideally with MFA) and the client presents device identity (certificate/posture); (3) policy evaluates user + device + application; (4) the broker stitches the user's session to the connector's session for that one app; (5) the session is continuously evaluated and dies the moment policy stops matching. Contrast with IPsec/SSL VPN: gateway listens on UDP 500/4500 or TCP 443, tunnel comes up after authentication, and routing decides reachability after that.

example.code:
Same user, same laptop, two worlds:

LEGACY VPN:
  1. User logs into VPN portal (password + MFA)
  2. Tunnel up -> laptop gets 10.8.0.14 on the corporate LAN
  3. Laptop can now reach file servers, printers, RDP hosts,
     the unpatched test box in the corner — everything routable
  4. Attacker with the user's phished password + a passed MFA
     push gets the same wide-open seat

BROKERED ZTNA:
  1. User authenticates; client presents device certificate
  2. Policy: user OK + device approved -> allow 'FileServer' app only
  3. Broker stitches one session to that one application
  4. File server's ports never exposed; nothing else is reachable
     or even discoverable
  5. Attacker with the password but no enrolled device: denied
     at the broker — there is no tunnel to hijack
example.walkthrough: Think of the VPN as a building keycard that opens the whole floor once you're through the lobby. ZTNA is an escort who walks you to exactly one office, watches the door, and re-checks your badge at every doorway. When an interviewer asks 'VPN vs ZTNA?' the winning answer names three things: per-application (not per-network) access, device identity bound to user identity, and no inbound exposure — then ties it to deny-by-default: the same philosophy ThreatLocker applies to applications, applied to connectivity.

pitfalls: Treating ZTNA as 'a better VPN client': the architecture differs (brokered, outbound-only connectors), not just the branding — interviewers probe for exactly this confusion

Forgetting the device half: user authenticates fine but the connection is denied because the device isn't enrolled/approved — the #1 ZTNA helpdesk ticket after a rollout, and it is the security working as designed
Opening inbound firewall ports 'to make ZTNA work': brokered ZTNA needs NO inbound listeners; if you're punching holes, you've rebuilt a VPN with extra steps
lessons.try_it: On paper, take your last VPN design and re-draw it as brokered ZTNA: list every inbound port you can now close, every network segment that becomes invisible to remote users, and the exact policy (user + device + app) for three roles. Then write the helpdesk script for the 'I can log in but can't reach the file server' call.

checks.hint: The Orlando OU was not found — did step 2 complete? Try Get-ADOrganizationalUnit -Filter 'Name -like "Orlando"' to look for it.
tuser1 is not in the Orlando Users OU — check the -Path value on your New-ADUser calls; the full chain OU=Users,OU=Orlando,DC=corp,DC=lab must match exactly.

labs.objective: Create a delegated OU structure (office, then Users and Workstations beneath it) and bulk-create users with New-ADUser, verifying placement with Get-ADUser.
steps: Open an elevated PowerShell session on your lab domain controller (or a workstation with RSAT and the ActiveDirectory module).
Create the office OU, protected from accidental deletion: New-ADOrganizationalUnit -Name 'Orlando' -Path 'DC=corp,DC=lab' -ProtectedFromAccidentalDeletion $true
Create the child OUs: New-ADOrganizationalUnit -Name 'Users' -Path 'OU=Orlando,DC=corp,DC=lab' and repeat with -Name 'Workstations'.

Create five users inside the Users OU: New-ADUser -Name 'Test User1' -SamAccountName tuser1 -Path 'OU=Users,OU=Orlando,DC=corp,DC=lab' -AccountPassword (Read-Host -AsSecureString 'Password') -Enabled $true (repeat for tuser2 through tuser5).
Verify placement: Get-ADUser -Filter * -SearchBase 'OU=Users,OU=Orlando,DC=corp,DC=lab' | Select-Object Name, SamAccountName, DistinguishedName

labs.title: Deploy a GPO and Prove Precedence

checks.hint: netdom query fsmo should list all five roles — run it from a domain-joined machine with connectivity to a DC.

checks.hint: Total addresses 4096 minus network and broadcast = 4094 usable.
/23 block size is 2 in the third octet: .0, .2, .4 ... .14.
A /23 broadcast always ends in .255 in the last octet.

labs.objective: Given 172.16.0.0/20, produce a complete subnet plan for 8 departments and verify every calculation two ways (block-size and binary AND).
steps: Compute the /20 mask, block size, total addresses, and usable host count. (Check: 172.16.0.0/20 = 4094 usable.)
Split 172.16.0.0/20 into eight equal /23 subnets. List each network ID, broadcast address, first usable, and last usable.
Assign: pick any /23 for the server VLAN and write its gateway as the first usable address; document why .0 and the broadcast are excluded.
Verify ONE of your /23s with the binary AND method on paper: AND the IP with 255.255.254.0 and confirm the network ID matches.
Run a cross-check in PowerShell: use [Net.IPAddress] parsing or ipcalc (Linux) to confirm your broadcast address for the server VLAN.
labs.success_message: Subnet plan complete and double-verified: you can carve address space on paper and prove it two ways — the core networking skill for the interview whiteboard.
labs.title: Subnet Planner: Carve a /20 for the New Office

checks.hint: Hard-set trunk mode; never leave DTP on auto for inter-switch links.
Both ends of the trunk must agree on the native VLAN.
Prune the trunk to only the VLANs that need to cross.
SVIs plus 'ip routing' move inter-VLAN forwarding into the switch.

labs.objective: Configure access ports, an 802.1Q trunk, and inter-VLAN routing on lab switches, then diagnose a deliberate native-VLAN mismatch.
steps: On Switch A: create VLANs 10 (servers) and 20 (workstations); assign two access ports to each with 'switchport mode access' + 'switchport access vlan'.
Connect Switch A to Switch B and configure both ends as trunks: 'switchport mode trunk', native VLAN 99, 'switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,99'.
On the Layer 3 device: create SVIs (interface Vlan10 / Vlan20) with gateway IPs, enable 'ip routing', and verify inter-VLAN ping works.
BREAK IT: change the native VLAN to 1 on Switch B's trunk only. Run 'show cdp neighbors detail' / 'show interfaces trunk' and capture the mismatch warning.
FIX IT: restore native VLAN 99 on both ends, confirm CDP warning clears, and re-verify inter-VLAN ping. Document the symptom->cause->fix chain.
labs.success_message: VLANs trunked, routed, broken, and repaired — you now have a war story about native VLAN mismatches for the interview.
labs.title: VLANs and Trunks: Build It, Break It, Fix It

checks.hint: 'No matching proposal' is always Phase 1: cipher, hash, DH group, lifetime, or PSK.
Phase 1 UP + no IPsec SA = Phase 2: proxy IDs or transform set.
ESP has no ports; NAT-T wraps it in UDP 4500.

labs.objective: Diagnose three broken site-to-site tunnels from logs alone and classify each as Phase 1, Phase 2, or NAT-T failure with the exact fix.
steps: Case A: log shows 'no matching proposal found from peer' repeating. Compare the two Phase 1 proposals (encryption/hash/DH/lifetime/auth) line by line and identify the mismatch; fix it.
Case B: 'show crypto isakmp sa' shows QM_IDLE but 'show crypto ipsec sa' is empty. Write both sides' crypto ACLs as source->destination pairs and find the proxy-ID disagreement; correct the ACL.

Case C: tunnel worked until the branch moved behind a NAT router; capture shows IKE on UDP 500 succeeding but ESP (IP proto 50) one-way. Enable NAT-T on both peers and confirm UDP 4500 traffic appears.
For each case, write a one-line diagnosis in the format: 'PHASE: <1|2|NAT-T> CAUSE: <...> FIX: <...>'.
labs.success_message: Three tunnels diagnosed from logs alone — you can now walk an interviewer through Phase 1 vs Phase 2 vs NAT-T failures with confidence.
labs.title: IPsec Troubleshooting: Read the Tunnel Like a Log

checks.hint: SSTP rides TCP 443 — indistinguishable from HTTPS to egress firewalls.
Use tracert / Test-NetConnection to prove which path each destination takes.
State the tunnel mode explicitly and the routing evidence for it.

labs.objective: Compare SSTP and L2TP/IPsec client VPNs from a restrictive network and measure the split-tunnel vs full-tunnel routing difference.
steps: From a phone hotspot or guest Wi-Fi, attempt a Windows native L2TP/IPsec connection; record whether UDP 500/4500/1701 + ESP survive (note failures).
Connect with SSTP (TCP 443) from the same network; record the result and note why TCP 443 traverses where the L2TP ports did not.
With the VPN connected in FULL tunnel mode, run 'tracert 8.8.8.8' and 'Test-NetConnection internal-app.corp -Port 443'; record the first hops.
Switch the VPN profile to SPLIT tunnel (only corporate subnets/DNS through VPN); re-run both tests and compare the paths.
Write a recommendation: which protocol for road warriors, and which tunnel mode for the security policy — with the trade-off stated.
labs.success_message: VPN shootout complete: you have firsthand evidence for the SSTP recommendation and a defensible split/full-tunnel policy position.

labs.title: Backup chain restore with NORECOVERY
labs.objective: Back up a test database and restore the full-plus-log chain, keeping the database in the restoring state until the final log.
steps: Confirm FULL recovery: SELECT recovery_model_desc FROM sys.databases WHERE name = 'LabDB';
Take the full backup: BACKUP DATABASE [LabDB] TO DISK = N'C:\Backup\LabDB_Full.bak' WITH INIT;

Create a canary file (C:\RestoreTest\canary.txt with today's date), let the backup run or trigger a one-time backup with 'wbadmin start backup'.

Delete the canary file, then restore it: 'wbadmin start recovery -version:<id> -itemType:File -items:C:\RestoreTest\canary.txt -recoveryTarget:C:\RestoreTest\Recovered\ -quiet' (get the version id from wbadmin get versions).
Verify the recovered file's contents match, note how long the restore took, and write a 5-line runbook entry: what was backed up, where, how to recover, and the measured RTO evidence.

Build a Process-Hunting One-Liner, Step by Step
labs.objective: Progressively build a single pipeline — list processes, filter by CPU, select properties, sort, export to CSV — learning why each stage sits where it does.
steps: Open PowerShell and run Get-Process. Study the columns: each row is a live object, not text. Pick out the CPU and Id properties — you will use them next.

Filter to CPU hogs: Get-Process | Where-Object CPU -gt 100. Logic: filter FIRST so fewer objects travel downstream — filtering a thousand objects then selecting is faster than selecting from a thousand then filtering.

Keep only useful properties: Get-Process | Where-Object CPU -gt 100 | Select-Object Name, CPU, Id. Logic: select AFTER filtering, because the filter needed the CPU property — an early Select-Object would have thrown it away and the filter would fail on missing data.
