Sort hungriest-first: append | Sort-Object CPU -Descending. -Descending flips the default ascending order — without it the biggest hog hides at the bottom of the list where nobody looks.

Export: append | Export-Csv C:\Assessment\hungry.csv -NoTypeInformation. Logic: -NoTypeInformation suppresses the '#TYPE System.Diagnostics.Process' header line Export-Csv writes by default — without it, row 1 is metadata garbage and Excel/Import-Csv misreads the file.

Verify the file: Import-Csv C:\Assessment\hungry.csv | Format-Table. Format-Table is safe HERE because it is LAST — nothing downstream needs the objects anymore. This is the one place formatting belongs.

checks.hint: Step 2's filter never ran. The pattern is Get-Process | Where-Object CPU -gt 100 — the pipe hands process OBJECTS (not text) to Where-Object, which keeps rows where the CPU property exceeds 100. Check your history: did the pipe and the comparison both make it in?

Step 3's Select-Object is missing. It must come AFTER Where-Object: Select-Object Name, CPU, Id keeps only those columns. If you selected before filtering, Where-Object would have no CPU property left to compare — order matters because each stage only sees what the previous stage passed on.

Step 4's sort is missing or not descending. Sort-Object CPU -Descending puts the hungriest process on top. Without -Descending you get ascending order and the worst offender hides at the bottom of the list.

Step 5 exported without -NoTypeInformation, so row 1 of your CSV is a '#TYPE ...' metadata line instead of data. Excel and Import-Csv choke on it. Re-run the export WITH -NoTypeInformation — the flag exists because the default header helps almost nobody and breaks imports.

labs.success_message: Pipeline built progressively and exported cleanly — you filtered objects (not text), ordered the stages correctly, and produced an import-safe CSV. That is the exact muscle memory the assessment rewards.

labs.title: Script the Full AD Account Lifecycle
labs.objective: Write a .ps1 script that creates a user, sets the password, disables, re-enables, and unlocks the account — narrating every step with Write-Host — then execute it under RemoteSigned.
steps: Check the policy first: Get-ExecutionPolicy -List. If CurrentUser shows Restricted, run Set-ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser. Logic: -Scope CurrentUser needs no admin rights and changes nothing machine-wide; -Scope Process would evaporate when this console closes, forcing you to redo it mid-assessment.

Create C:\Assessment\UserLifecycle.ps1 starting with a param block: param([string]$SamAccountName). Logic: a typed parameter rejects bad input immediately and makes the script reusable — no hardcoded usernames baked into automation.

Block 1 — create: Write-Host 'Creating account...' then New-ADUser -Name 'Lifecycle Test' -SamAccountName $SamAccountName -Path 'OU=Users,OU=Orlando,DC=corp,DC=lab' -AccountPassword (Read-Host -AsSecureString 'Temp password') -Enabled $true. Logic: -Enabled $true because new accounts default to DISABLED; -Path because the default Users container dodges every OU-linked GPO.

Block 2 — password: Write-Host 'Setting password...' then Set-ADAccountPassword -Identity $SamAccountName -NewPassword (Read-Host -AsSecureString 'New password') -Reset $true. Logic: -Reset $true selects the ADMIN code path — without it the cmdlet demands the old password like a user change and fails.

Block 3 — disable and VERIFY: Write-Host 'Disabling...' then Disable-ADAccount -Identity $SamAccountName; verify with Get-ADUser -Identity $SamAccountName -Properties Enabled | Select-Object SamAccountName, Enabled. Logic: verify AFTER the change — examiners score what you can prove, and a disable you never confirmed is a guess. Note -Properties: Enabled is not in the default property set.

Block 4 — re-enable and unlock: Write-Host 'Re-enabling...' then Enable-ADAccount -Identity $SamAccountName; Unlock-ADAccount -Identity $SamAccountName; verify Enabled is True again. Logic: these are DIFFERENT flags — a re-enabled account can still carry a lockout, so the lifecycle needs both cmdlets.

Run it: .\UserLifecycle.ps1 -SamAccountName 't.lifecycle' from C:\Assessment. Logic: the .\ prefix is mandatory — PowerShell will not run scripts from the current directory by bare name, by design (PATH is searched first, so bare names are a hijack vector).

checks.hint: The execution policy was never set — a .ps1 run under Restricted dies before line 1 executes. Run Set-ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser (user scope: no admin needed, nothing machine-wide), then re-run the script.

No New-ADUser in history. Minimum viable: New-ADUser -Name 'Lifecycle Test' -SamAccountName 't.lifecycle' -AccountPassword (Read-Host -AsSecureString 'pw') -Enabled $true. Remember -Enabled $true (new accounts are born disabled) and -Path to land in the right OU.

Set-ADAccountPassword ran without -Reset $true (or never ran). Without -Reset the cmdlet takes the USER code path and demands the old password — which you do not have. Admin resets REQUIRE -Reset $true to select the admin path.

Disable-ADAccount never ran. The lifecycle needs the disable step AND its verification: Get-ADUser -Identity <name> -Properties Enabled — note -Properties, because Enabled is not in the default property set and comes back blank without it.

Enable-ADAccount never ran — the account is still disabled and the lifecycle is incomplete. Re-enable with Enable-ADAccount -Identity <name>, then clear any lockout with Unlock-ADAccount -Identity <name>; they are separate flags.

No Write-Host narration found. The script must narrate each phase ('Creating account...', 'Disabling...') — in the assessment, narration is how you bank partial credit on a half-finished task. A silent script that breaks midway scores zero because the examiner cannot see your intent.

labs.success_message: Full lifecycle scripted and executed: create, password, disable, re-enable, unlock — every step narrated and verified. That is a complete, gradable automation artifact.

labs.title: Diagnose 'Can't Reach the Server' With CMD Tools
labs.objective: Work a 'can't reach the file server' ticket using CMD tools in strict OSI order — ipconfig, ping ladder, nslookup, tracert — and name the exact failing layer.
steps: Start with ipconfig /all. Write down the IPv4 address, subnet mask, default gateway, and DNS servers. Logic: everything downstream assumes local config is sane. If the address is 169.254.x.x (APIPA), STOP — DHCP failed and no higher-layer test is meaningful until the machine holds a real address.

Ping the loopback: ping 127.0.0.1. Logic: this tests your own TCP/IP stack with ZERO network involved. Failure here means the local stack or driver is broken — a repair/reinstall problem, not a network problem, and no cable-checking will fix it.
Ping the default gateway from step 1. Logic: this adds exactly one dependency — the local link. Success proves layer 1/2 to the gateway; failure isolates the fault to your cable, switch port, or NIC.

Ping 8.8.8.8 — an IP, deliberately not a name. Logic: this adds routing beyond your LAN while EXCLUDING DNS from the test. Gateway OK + 8.8.8.8 fails = routing fault past the gateway. Both OK + a name fails later = DNS fault. Without this step you cannot separate those two.

Resolve the name two ways: nslookup fileserver.corp.lab (your CONFIGURED resolver) and then nslookup fileserver.corp.lab <your-DNS-server-IP> (that SPECIFIC server). Logic: if the specific server answers but your default resolver does not, the RECORD is healthy and your client's resolver path is broken — fix the resolver or flush the cache, not the zone.

Trace the path: tracert -d fileserver.corp.lab. Logic: -d skips reverse-DNS so the trace finishes in seconds instead of minutes. Read hop by hop: '* * *' that RECOVERS on the next hop is a filtered ICMP hop, not a failure; a trace that DIES at the same hop every time names the fault location.

Write your verdict: which layer failed (local config / local link / routing / DNS / path) and the exact fix (e.g., ipconfig /release + /renew, ipconfig /flushdns, correcting the DNS server entry). Logic: a diagnosis without a named layer and a fix command is just a story — the assessment scores the verdict, not the wandering.

checks.hint: Step 1 never ran: ipconfig /all is the mandatory starting point. You need the IPv4 address (watch for 169.254.x.x APIPA, which means DHCP failed), the gateway, and the DNS servers written down BEFORE any ping — every later step depends on those numbers.

The loopback ping (ping 127.0.0.1) is missing. It is step 2 for a reason: it proves the local TCP/IP stack with zero network involved. Skip it and a broken local stack masquerades as a network outage, sending you chasing cables.

No ping of 8.8.8.8 found. Pinging an external IP — not a name — isolates ROUTING from DNS: gateway-OK plus 8.8.8.8-fails means a routing fault; both OK plus name-fails means a DNS fault. Without this step those two are indistinguishable.

No nslookup ran. Run it TWICE: once bare (tests your configured resolver) and once with the server IP appended (tests that specific server). Different results between the two is the single most informative DNS outcome — it separates 'record broken' from 'resolver broken'.

No tracert ran. Use tracert -d <target> — the -d skips reverse DNS and finishes in seconds. Read it hop by hop: stars that recover are filtered ICMP, not failures; a trace that DIES at one hop every time names the fault location.

labs.success_message: Diagnosis complete in OSI order with a named failing layer and a fix — that ladder (config, link, routing, DNS, path) is the exact method assessors watch for.

labs.title: Configure VLANs, Trunks, and an SVI From Scratch
labs.objective: From a blank switch in the simulated terminal: create VLANs 10 and 20, assign access ports, build a trunk, add an SVI, prove it with show commands, and save.
steps: Enter privileged mode and global config: enable, then configure terminal. Watch the prompt change: Switch> becomes Switch# becomes Switch(config)#. Logic: the prompt IS the mode documentation — config commands are rejected at the wrong prompt, so read it before every command instead of assuming the command is wrong.
Name the switch: hostname SW-LAB-01. Logic: the prompt becomes the hostname, so every later prompt tells you WHICH device you are configuring — the cheapest insurance on a multi-device assessment.

Create the VLANs: vlan 10, then name SERVERS, then exit; then vlan 20, name WORKSTATIONS, exit. Logic: creation and assignment are separate steps — each VLAN exists now but carries zero traffic until ports join it.

Assign access ports: interface range gi1/0/1 - 10, then switchport mode access, then switchport access vlan 10, then exit; repeat for gi1/0/11 - 20 with vlan 20. Logic: 'mode access' LOCKS the port — the default 'dynamic auto' negotiates trunking unpredictably. The range keyword configures ten ports in three commands instead of thirty.

Build the trunk: interface gi1/0/24, then switchport mode trunk, then switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20, then end. Logic: the allowed list is a FILTER — any VLAN you omit is silently dropped on this trunk, and 'VLAN 20 works locally but not across the trunk' is this exact omission. Explicit beats the 'allow all' default, which leaks every VLAN everywhere.

Add the SVI: configure terminal, then interface vlan 10, then ip address 10.1.10.2 255.255.255.0, then no shutdown, then end. Logic: IOS interfaces are DOWN by default so half-configured ports never forward traffic — a perfect config without 'no shutdown' shows down/down and passes nothing. The SVI is the switch's management address inside VLAN 10.

Prove it BEFORE saving: show vlan brief (VLAN 10 SERVERS should list Gi1/0/1-10), show interfaces trunk (Gi1/0/24 trunking with VLANs 10 and 20 allowed and forwarding), show ip interface brief (Vlan10 up/up). Logic: never save an unverified config — the show output is your proof, and proof is what gets graded.
Save: copy running-config startup-config. Logic: everything so far lived in RAM (running-config) — RAM evaporates on reboot, NVRAM (startup-config) survives. The grader reads what survives.

checks.hint: VLAN 10 was never created. Sequence: vlan 10, then name SERVERS, then exit. Watch the prompt — (config-vlan)# confirms you are in VLAN sub-mode. Without the VLAN in the database, 'switchport access vlan 10' assigns ports to a VLAN that does not exist.

No access-mode configuration found. Per port (or range): switchport mode access locks the port — never leave the 'dynamic auto' default — then switchport access vlan <id> assigns it. Use interface range to cover ten ports at once.

The trunk's allowed-VLAN list is missing or wrong. On interface gi1/0/24: switchport mode trunk, then switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20. Omit a VLAN here and it is silently dropped — 'works locally but not across the trunk' is this exact omission.

No 'no shutdown' found — your SVI is administratively down. IOS defaults every interface to down so half-configured ports never forward traffic. On interface vlan 10, after the ip address, run no shutdown, then confirm up/up with show ip interface brief.

show vlan brief never ran — this is the proof step. It should list VLAN 10 SERVERS with Gi1/0/1-10 and VLAN 20 WORKSTATIONS with Gi1/0/11-20. Verify BEFORE saving: an unverified config is a guess, and guesses do not survive grading.

The config was never saved. Everything lives in running-config (RAM) until copy running-config startup-config writes it to NVRAM. The assessment's next task may reboot the switch — unsaved work scores zero.

labs.success_message: Two VLANs, access ports, a filtered trunk, and a live SVI — verified with show commands and saved to NVRAM. That is a complete, gradable switch build.

labs.title: Write a PowerShell Function From a Spec
labs.objective: Write Get-DiskAlert from a written spec — typed parameters, pipeline support, BEGIN/PROCESS/END, comment-based help, and try/catch — then prove every requirement with Get-Command, Get-Help, and a pipeline test.
steps: Open PowerShell. You will define the function in this session — paste the whole function definition at the prompt (no file needed).
Spec, part 1 — name and help: the function is named Get-DiskAlert (approved verb Get). Start it with a comment-based help block (<# .SYNOPSIS ... #>) whose SYNOPSIS contains the word 'disk'.
Spec, part 2 — parameters: a param() block with [Parameter(ValueFromPipeline = $true)] [string[]]$ComputerName, defaulting to @($env:COMPUTERNAME) so it runs with no arguments too.

Spec, part 3 — blocks: a BEGIN block with a Write-Verbose line announcing the check; a PROCESS block that loops over each name in $ComputerName, uses try { Test-Connection -ComputerName $name -Count 1 -Quiet -ErrorAction Stop } catch { $reachable = $false }, and emits a [pscustomobject] with ComputerName, Reachable, and CheckedAt = Get-Date; an END block with Write-Verbose 'check complete'.
Prove it is a real function: run Get-Command Get-DiskAlert | Select-Object CommandType — you must see Function.
Prove the help exists: run (Get-Help Get-DiskAlert).Synopsis — you must see your synopsis containing the word 'disk'.
Prove the PROCESS block exists: run Get-Content Function:\Get-DiskAlert — the output must contain the word PROCESS.
Prove pipeline support: run "SRV1","SRV2" | Get-DiskAlert | Select-Object -ExpandProperty ComputerName — both SRV1 and SRV2 must appear, each processed by its own PROCESS invocation.

checks.hint: Get-Command did not report a Function — did you paste the whole Get-DiskAlert definition into this session?
The synopsis must contain the word 'disk' — check your <# .SYNOPSIS #> block.
No PROCESS block found — pipeline input needs its own PROCESS block; code outside named blocks runs once as END.
SRV2 did not come back — check ValueFromPipeline on $ComputerName and that the per-name work is inside PROCESS, not BEGIN.

labs.success_message: Get-DiskAlert is a real function: discoverable by Get-Command, documented by Get-Help, and pipeline-capable via PROCESS — the complete packaging for 'run repeatedly by humans.'

labs.title: Draw the Kerberos Exchange as a Sequence Diagram
labs.objective: Describe the 6-message Kerberos exchange as a numbered sequence diagram in a text file, in exact order — proving you can read and write the diagram type used for every authentication flow.
steps: Create a text file named kerberos-seq.txt (Notepad works, or run New-Item kerberos-seq.txt).
Write the exchange as 6 numbered lines, IN THIS ORDER. Each line: number, sender -> receiver, the message name, and what it carries in parentheses.
Line 1: Client -> AS : AS-REQ (requests a TGT — ticket-granting ticket).
Line 2: AS -> Client : AS-REP (returns the TGT).
Line 3: Client -> TGS : TGS-REQ (presents the TGT, requests a service ticket).
Line 4: TGS -> Client : TGS-REP (returns the service ticket).
Line 5: Client -> Server : AP-REQ (presents the service ticket to the server).
Line 6: Server -> Client : AP-REP (mutual authentication, optional).
Verify the order yourself: run (Get-Content .\kerberos-seq.txt | Select-String 'AS-REQ').LineNumber — it must print 1. Repeat for AS-REP (expect 2), TGS-REQ (3), TGS-REP (4), AP-REQ (5), AP-REP (6).

checks.hint: AS-REQ must be on line 1 — the client requests the TGT first, before anything else exists.
AS-REP must be on line 2 — the Authentication Service answers with the TGT.
TGS-REQ must be on line 3 — the client presents the TGT to the Ticket-Granting Service.
TGS-REP must be on line 4 — the TGS returns the service ticket.
AP-REQ must be on line 5 — the client presents the service ticket to the target server.
AP-REP must be on line 6 — the server's optional mutual-authentication reply closes the exchange.

labs.success_message: Six messages, correct order, each labeled with sender, receiver, and payload — that is a sequence diagram in text form, and you can now read any authentication flow drawn this way.

labs.title: Write a Mini-SOP: Reset a Locked AD Account
labs.objective: Write a complete, usable SOP for unlocking a locked AD account — every template section filled in — and verify each section is present.
steps: Create sop-unlock-account.md. Title it, and add a header line: version 1.0, today's date, and owner (you).
## Purpose: state when to use this SOP (user locked out after bad password attempts) and when NOT to (do not use for disabled or terminated accounts — that is a different procedure).

## Prerequisites: AD Users and Computers or RSAT, an account with unlock permission, and the user's identity verified — call back on the phone number on file. (Why the callback: unlocking for an impersonator is a breach, not a favor.)

## Steps: numbered, one action each, with the exact command and the expected result. Include: 1. Verify identity via callback. 2. Check lockout status: Get-ADUser <username> -Properties LockedOut. 3. Unlock: Unlock-ADAccount -Identity <username>. 4. Confirm: re-run the Get-ADUser check — LockedOut must now be False.
## Verification: the LockedOut=False check AND confirmation from the user (or a test logon). State why: 'looks done' is not done.
## Rollback: if you unlocked the wrong account — immediately re-lock or disable it with Disable-ADAccount, open an incident ticket, and notify security. Write the actual command.
Verify every section is present: run Get-Content .\sop-unlock-account.md | Select-String 'Purpose' (must match), then 'Prerequisites', 'Verification', 'Rollback', and 'Unlock-ADAccount'.

checks.hint: No Purpose section — state when to use the SOP and when NOT to (disabled/terminated accounts are a different procedure).
No Prerequisites section — list the tools, permissions, and the identity-verification callback.
No Verification section — how do you PROVE the unlock worked? (LockedOut=False plus a test logon.)
No Rollback section — what do you do if you unlocked the wrong account? (Disable-ADAccount, incident ticket, notify security.)
The Unlock-ADAccount command is missing from your steps — the SOP must contain the exact command, not just prose.

labs.success_message: Purpose, Prerequisites, Steps, Verification, Rollback — all present with real commands. That is a shippable SOP: a tech who has never done this can execute it at 2 AM.

checks.hint: VLAN 10 math is off — a /24 always yields 2^8 - 2 = 254 usable hosts (network .0 and broadcast .255 are reserved). Recompute from the mask.
The broadcast address of 10.10.20.0/24 is 10.10.20.255 — all host bits set to 1. Check your host-bit math.
The VPN pool is missing from your scheme — remote users need a subnet that does not overlap their home 192.168.1.0/24 networks. Add 10.10.100.0/24.

labs.objective: Write the Contoso Labs design document skeleton, compute the full subnetting math for the 10.10.0.0/16 plan (VLAN 10/20/30 + VPN), draw the text network diagram, and outline the build SOP. Applies the theory module 'Subnetting Mastery: CIDR Math That Never Lies' plus 'Network Diagrams and Change Records'.
steps: Step 1 — Open the design document (a text file or wiki page) and create four sections: Decisions Log, IP Address Scheme, Network Diagram, SOP Outline. Why first: every later phase (VLANs, DHCP, firewall rules, docs) reads this document — if the plan lives only in your head, phase 2 starts with a meeting, not a build. Nothing in phases 2-7 proceeds without a written plan to check against.

Step 2 — Reserve the supernet: 10.10.0.0/16 (RFC 1918 private space). Why this block: it never collides with employees' 192.168.1.0/24 home routers (VPN routing breaks on overlap), and a /16 gives 2^16 - 2 = 65,534 addresses — room for 256 /24s, so the company can grow for a decade without renumbering. Why not 192.168.x: the single most common home-router range on earth; your VPN users would route office traffic into their living rooms.

Step 3 — Carve VLAN 10 (users): 10.10.10.0/24. The math, shown fully: mask 255.255.255.0 = /24 = 24 network bits, 8 host bits. Usable hosts = 2^8 - 2 = 254 (subtract the network address 10.10.10.0 and the broadcast 10.10.10.255 — all-zeros and all-ones in the host portion are reserved). Usable range: 10.10.10.1 through 10.10.10.254. Verify: write 'network .0 / broadcast .255 / 254 usable' next to the entry — if any block shows a different count, your host-bit math slipped. Common mistake: counting .0 or .255 as usable — fix by remembering the rule: a host may never own the all-zeros or all-ones address.

Step 4 — Repeat for the remaining blocks and build the reservation table: VLAN 20 servers 10.10.20.0/24 (network .0, usable .1-.254, broadcast .255); VLAN 30 management 10.10.30.0/24; VPN pool 10.10.100.0/24. Inside each /24, reserve .1 for the gateway (the SVI you will create in phase 2 — convention, not law, but every admin expects the gateway at .1), .2-.49 for static infrastructure (servers, printers, switch management IPs), and hand .50-.250 to DHCP. Logic Check: 50 users today at ~20% of 254; doubling twice (50 -> 100 -> 200) still fits. And the third octet names the function — when a firewall log shows 10.10.20.11, you know instantly it is a server without a lookup table.

Step 5 — Draw the text network diagram: ISP -> firewall/router -> core switch -> three VLAN trunks/access ports; label CL-DC01 at 10.10.20.10, CL-FS01 at 10.10.20.11, gateway SVIs at .1 of each VLAN, VPN pool 10.10.100.0/24 terminating on the firewall. Why now: the diagram is the contract between the plan and the build — phase 2's switch config and phase 3's DHCP scopes are just this picture turned into commands.

Step 6 — Write the SOP outline: one numbered section per build phase (2-network, 3-servers, 4-virtualize, 5-data, 6-secure, 7-document), each with three sub-bullets: exact commands, verification ('run X — you should see Y'), rollback. What breaks out of order: writing SOPs after building means documenting what you did instead of deciding what to do — the build drifts and the doc describes the drift. Logic Check: if a phase cannot be expressed as commands + verification + rollback, you do not understand it well enough to build it yet.

Step 7 — Troubleshooting self-check: the classic failure is 'saving space' with /25s or /26s ('126 hosts is plenty'). The fix is arithmetic plus experience: address space is free, renumbering costs weekends, and the first surprise hire wave always exceeds the plan. If your scheme cannot absorb the 3-year growth projection, redo step 4 — this is the cheapest moment to be wrong.
labs.success_message: Design doc skeleton written, subnetting math verified for all four blocks, diagram drafted, SOP outlined — the blueprint every later phase builds from is now on paper, not in your head.
labs.title: Phase 1 Build: The Address Plan and Design Doc

checks.hint: 'show vlan brief' should list VLANs 10 (USERS), 20 (SERVERS), 30 (MGMT) as active with ports assigned. If a VLAN is missing, its 'vlan N' + 'name' block never ran — VLANs must exist before ports can join them.
The trunk to the router must explicitly allow VLANs 10, 20, and 30. If traffic for a VLAN dies at the trunk, the allowed-VLAN list is the first suspect.

Inter-VLAN ping from a user port to a server gateway failing? Walk the logic tree: (1) is your PC on the right access VLAN? (2) does 'show interfaces trunk' show the trunk up with all three VLANs allowed? (3) is the SVI up ('show ip interface brief')? Fix the first broken link.

labs.objective: Configure VLANs 10/20/30 on the switch (IOS-style), assign access ports, trunk to the router, create SVI gateways, and write the inter-VLAN firewall rules. Applies the theory modules 'VLANs, Trunks, and Inter-VLAN Routing' and 'Switching Resilience: STP, Port Security, EtherChannel'.
steps: Step 1 — Create the VLANs (global config mode). Why first: a port cannot join a VLAN that does not exist — every later step references these IDs. Commands: enable, configure terminal, then: vlan 10 / name USERS / exit, vlan 20 / name SERVERS / exit, vlan 30 / name MGMT / exit. Verify: show vlan brief — you should see VLANs 10, 20, 30 listed as active with no ports yet. Common mistake: naming without creating (typing 'name' at the wrong prompt) — the verify catches it.

Step 2 — Assign access ports to endpoints: interface range fa0/1-24, then switchport mode access and switchport access vlan 10. Why access, not trunk: an endpoint speaks one untagged VLAN; a trunked PC port invites VLAN-hopping and misconfigurations. Why ports 1-24 for users: physical grouping matches the logical plan — the next admin reads the patch panel, not a spreadsheet. Verify: show vlan brief — VLAN 10 should now show Fa0/1-24. Reserve a few ports on VLAN 30 for the jump box and switch management.

Step 3 — Build the trunk to the router/firewall: interface gi0/1, switchport mode trunk, switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,30, switchport trunk native vlan 999 (create vlan 999 / name UNUSED first). Why an unused native VLAN: the native VLAN carries untagged frames — leaving it as default VLAN 1 is the classic VLAN-hopping vector. Why explicit allowed list: a trunk that allows 'all' will happily carry a VLAN you create by typo someday. Verify: show interfaces trunk — you should see Gi0/1 trunking, native 999, VLANs 10/20/30 allowed and active.

Step 4 — Create the SVI gateways (the .1 addresses from your phase-1 plan): interface vlan 10 / ip address 10.10.10.1 255.255.255.0 / no shutdown, then repeat for vlan 20 (10.10.20.1) and vlan 30 (10.10.30.1). Why SVIs: they are the default gateways your DHCP scopes will hand out, and the point where inter-VLAN traffic can be policed. Order matters: SVIs come after the trunk, because a gateway for a VLAN that cannot reach the router is a black hole. Verify: show ip interface brief — all three Vlan interfaces should show 'up/up'.

Step 5 — Write the firewall rules at the inter-VLAN boundary (on the router/firewall SVI or firewall-on-a-stick). Why here: every inter-VLAN packet crosses this point — it is the one choke point you fully control. Rules: access-list USERS-TO-SERVERS extended permit tcp 10.10.10.0 255.255.255.0 10.10.20.0 255.255.255.0 eq 445 (SMB); permit tcp ... eq 443 (HTTPS); permit udp ... eq 53 (DNS); then access-list SERVERS-TO-USERS extended deny ip 10.10.20.0 255.255.255.0 10.10.10.0 255.255.255.0 (servers never initiate to users — this kills lateral movement). Logic Check: every 'permit' must map to a stated business requirement from phase 1's evidence; a permit you cannot justify is a hole, not a rule.

Step 6 — Verification pass, end to end: from a PC on an access port, ping 10.10.10.1 (own gateway — proves access VLAN + SVI), ping 10.10.20.1 (proves trunk + inter-VLAN routing), then ping 10.10.20.11 (a server — proves firewall rules pass required traffic). You should see replies at each hop; the first failing hop names the broken layer. Also test a denied path: from a server, ping a user PC — you should see failure (the deny rule working). A firewall you never test in both directions is a rumor.

Step 7 — Troubleshooting logic tree: NATIVE VLAN MISMATCH. Symptom: trunk shows up, but management VLAN is unreachable or the log fills with 'native VLAN mismatch' CDP messages. Diagnose: (1) show interfaces trunk on both ends — compare the native VLAN values; (2) if they differ (say 1 vs 999), untagged frames from one side land in the other's native VLAN — traffic arrives on the wrong network and looks like a ghost outage; (3) fix: set both ends to 999, then (4) verify with show interfaces trunk and a ping across the SVIs. The reasoning chain: untagged frames have no 802.1Q tag, so each side assigns them to its own native VLAN — mismatched natives mean mismatched destinations. Second common fault: a VLAN works locally but not across the trunk — check the allowed-VLAN list before anything else; the simplest explanation (a missing 'allowed vlan') beats exotic theories every time.
labs.success_message: VLANs 10/20/30 live, access ports assigned, trunk carrying all three to the router, SVI gateways up, firewall rules enforcing least privilege — and you can diagnose a native VLAN mismatch from symptoms, not guesses.
labs.title: Phase 2 Build: VLANs, Trunks, and Firewall Rules

checks.hint: The forest root should be corp.contoso.com. If Get-ADDomain fails, the Install-ADDSForest promotion did not complete — promotion must finish (and the server reboot) before any AD cmdlet works.
The Contoso OU tree is missing — OUs must exist BEFORE users, computers, and GPO links reference them. Re-run the New-ADOrganizationalUnit steps.
No DHCP scope found — the scope must be created and activated AFTER the DC/DNS is up, since clients need DNS pointing at the DC from their first lease.

labs.objective: Install Windows Server, promote the first DC (Install-ADDSForest), build the Contoso OU tree, configure DNS forwarders, create per-VLAN DHCP scopes with exclusions, and link baseline GPOs. Applies 'AD, DNS, and DHCP Administration One-Liners', 'Group Policy: Precedence, Enforcement, and Troubleshooting', and 'FSMO Roles and Replication Health Checks'.
steps: Step 1 — Install Windows Server 2025 (Server Core recommended for DCs — smaller attack surface, fewer patches) and set a STATIC IP before anything else: New-NetIPAddress -InterfaceAlias 'Ethernet' -IPAddress 10.10.20.10 -PrefixLength 24 -DefaultGateway 10.10.20.1, then Set-DnsClientServerAddress -InterfaceAlias 'Ethernet' -ServerAddresses 127.0.0.1. Why static first: a DC that gets its address from DHCP can lose its identity on a lease hiccup, and DNS must point at itself because it is about to BECOME the DNS server. What breaks out of order: promoting with DHCP addressing registers garbage in DNS and AD replication chases a moving target.

Step 2 — Install the AD DS role: Install-WindowsFeature AD-Domain-Services -IncludeManagementTools. Why a separate step: the role lays down the binaries; promotion (next step) creates the actual directory. -IncludeManagementTools pulls the AD PowerShell module and admin tools you will use for everything after. Verify: Get-WindowsFeature AD-Domain-Services | Select-Object Installed — you should see True.

Step 3 — Promote to the first DC of a new forest: Install-ADDSForest -DomainName 'corp.contoso.com' -DomainNetbiosName 'CONTOSO' -ForestMode WinThreshold -DomainMode WinThreshold -InstallDns -SafeModeAdministratorPassword (Read-Host -AsSecureString 'DSRM password'). Parameter logic: -DomainName is the DNS name everything joins; -InstallDns because AD cannot function without DNS (SRV records locate DCs); the DSRM password is the break-glass account for directory recovery — write it into the sealed credential inventory, never the doc. The server reboots automatically — that is expected, not a crash. Why forest root now: every later object (OUs, users, GPOs) hangs off this name; renaming a domain later is a migration project, so get it right while it is cheap. Verify after reboot: Get-ADDomain — you should see corp.contoso.com.

Step 4 — Configure DNS forwarders: Add-DnsServerForwarder -IPAddress 1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8. Why: your DC is authoritative for corp.contoso.com but knows nothing about the internet — forwarders resolve everything else. Why two: redundancy; if one provider has an outage, name resolution (and therefore logons, which need DNS) survives. Order logic: forwarders come after promotion because there was no DNS server to configure before. Verify: Get-DnsServerForwarder — you should see both addresses; then Resolve-DnsName www.example.com — you should get an answer, proving the full chain (client -> DC -> forwarder -> internet).

Step 5 — Build the OU tree BEFORE any users or GPOs: New-ADOrganizationalUnit -Name 'Contoso' -Path 'DC=corp,DC=contoso,DC=com' -ProtectedFromAccidentalDeletion $true, then New-ADOrganizationalUnit -Name 'Users' -Path 'OU=Contoso,DC=corp,DC=contoso,DC=com', and repeat for 'Workstations' and 'Servers'. Why this order: users, computers, and GPO links all reference OUs by distinguished name — creating them afterward means moving objects and relinking policies. -ProtectedFromAccidentalDeletion guards the tree against a careless delete (the number-one OU outage cause). Verify: Get-ADOrganizationalUnit -Filter * -SearchBase 'OU=Contoso,DC=corp,DC=contoso,DC=com' — you should see all four OUs.

Step 6 — Create DHCP scopes per VLAN with exclusions for static infrastructure: Add-DhcpServerv4Scope -Name 'VLAN10-Users' -StartRange 10.10.10.50 -EndRange 10.10.10.250 -SubnetMask 255.255.255.0 -State Active; then Add-DhcpServerv4ExclusionRange -ScopeId 10.10.10.0 -StartRange 10.10.10.1 -EndRange 10.10.10.49; then Set-DhcpServerv4OptionValue -ScopeId 10.10.10.0 -Router 10.10.10.1 -DnsServer 10.10.20.10. Why exclusions: .1-.49 holds gateways, servers, printers — handing those to a random laptop creates an IP conflict that presents as a 'haunted' outage. Why DNS = 10.10.20.10 (the DC) and ONLY the DC: AD clients must resolve SRV records only the DC hosts — a public DNS here breaks logons and group policy. Repeat the pattern for VLAN 30 (management). Logic Check: the scope range (.50-.250) must sit inside the /24 (.1-.254) but outside the exclusion — draw the three ranges on one number line; any overlap is a future outage.

Step 7 — Create and link baseline GPOs: New-GPO -Name 'Contoso Password Policy' | New-GPLink -Target 'OU=Contoso,DC=corp,DC=contoso,DC=com'; New-GPO -Name 'Contoso Baseline Security' | New-GPLink -Target 'OU=Workstations,OU=Contoso,DC=corp,DC=contoso,DC=com'. Why link at the OU, not the domain root: domain-linked policies hit domain controllers too — a workstation lockdown policy applied to DCs can break replication. Why separate GPOs per purpose: one policy per intent means you can disable 'Password Policy' for troubleshooting without touching security baselines. Verify: Get-GPO -Name 'Contoso Password Policy' and gpresult /r on a test client — you should see the GPO in the applied list. Common mistake: linking to the default Users/Computers containers — GPOs cannot link there; that is exactly why step 5's OU tree exists.

Step 8 — Promote the SECOND DC on host 2 (repeat steps 1-3 with Install-ADDSDomainController instead of Install-ADDSForest, IP 10.10.20.11). Why: one DC is a single point of failure for authentication, DNS, and DHCP — and you can only patch a DC safely when another one serves logons. Verify replication health: repadmin /replsummary — you should see zero failures; dcdiag /q — you should see no errors. Troubleshooting logic tree: repadmin shows failures -> (1) check DNS on the failing DC (must point at a working DC, never itself first during join... actually itself is fine post-promotion, but during promotion it must resolve the existing DC); (2) check time sync (w32tm /query /status — Kerberos dies beyond 5 minutes skew); (3) check the firewall (RPC/445 between DCs). Fix the first broken dependency — replication is always downstream of DNS, time, and connectivity, in that order.
labs.success_message: Forest corp.contoso.com live on two DCs, OU tree protected and populated, DNS forwarding verified, DHCP scopes serving each VLAN with DNS pointed at the DCs, baseline GPOs linked — identity is now the floor everything else stands on.
labs.title: Phase 3 Build: Domain Controllers, OUs, DNS, DHCP, GPOs

checks.hint: No External virtual switch found — production VMs need an External switch bound to the physical NIC to reach the LAN. Internal/Private switches cannot substitute.
Expected VMs not found — New-VM must complete for each guest. Remember: enable the Hyper-V feature (and reboot) BEFORE creating switches or VMs.
Checkpoint listing came back odd — if you see a long AVHDX chain on a production VM, merge it. Checkpoints are change-undo, not backup.

labs.objective: Enable Hyper-V, create External and Private virtual switches (New-VMSwitch with -SwitchType explained), build the CL-DC01 and CL-FS01 VMs, and set a sane checkpoint policy. Applies 'Virtual switches: External, Internal, Private' and 'Checkpoints done right: types, chains, and merging'.
steps: Step 1 — Enable Hyper-V and reboot: Enable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName Microsoft-Hyper-V -All, then Restart-Computer. Why first, before anything virtual: the hypervisor installs beneath the OS — switches and VMs cannot exist without it, and the reboot is mandatory, not optional. -All pulls the management tools too. What breaks out of order: every New-VMSwitch/New-VM before this fails with a feature-not-enabled error that looks scarier than it is. Verify after reboot: Get-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName Microsoft-Hyper-V | Select-Object State — you should see Enabled.

Step 2 — Create the External switch: New-VMSwitch -Name 'vSwitch-External' -SwitchType External -NetAdapterName 'Ethernet' -AllowManagementOS $true. Switch-type logic: External bridges VMs onto the physical LAN (VMs get real 10.10.20.x addresses clients can reach); Internal gives VMs a host-only network; Private gives VM-to-VM only. Production servers need External — nothing else puts them on the LAN. -AllowManagementOS $true keeps a virtual NIC on the host so YOU can still reach it; a host with no management path is a host you cannot patch. Verify: Get-VMSwitch — you should see vSwitch-External with SwitchType External. Common mistake: binding the wrong physical adapter on a multi-NIC host — Get-NetAdapter first and match the one with the LAN link.

Step 3 — Create the Private switch for the future isolated workload: New-VMSwitch -Name 'vSwitch-Private' -SwitchType Private. Why now: the malware-analysis VM arrives next quarter, and its isolation must be architectural (a switch type that physically cannot reach the LAN), not a firewall rule someone can fat-finger later. Verify: Get-VMSwitch — Private listed; note it has no NetAdapter binding — that absence IS the isolation.

Step 4 — Build the two VMs on host 1: New-VM -Name 'CL-DC01' -MemoryStartupBytes 4GB -NewVHDPath 'D:\VMs\CL-DC01\CL-DC01.vhdx' -NewVHDSizeBytes 80GB -Generation 2 -SwitchName 'vSwitch-External'; repeat for CL-FS01 (6GB RAM, 200GB VHDX for file shares). Parameter logic: Generation 2 = UEFI, faster boot, required for modern OS; separate VHDX per VM = separate failure and backup units; memory sized to role (DC is light, file server caches). Why separate VMs per role: patching or rebooting the file server must never take down authentication. Verify: Get-VM — both should show State Off; then Start-VM CL-DC01 and install the OS (this VM becomes the phase-3 DC — virtualization underpins identity, which is why this phase precedes... note: in the real build you would virtualize FIRST, then promote the guest to DC; the lab order here teaches each layer separately).

Step 5 — Set the checkpoint policy: on production VMs, allow only PRODUCTION checkpoints (VSS-aware, application-consistent): Set-VM -Name 'CL-FS01' -CheckpointType Production. Then state the rule in the SOP: checkpoints are for pre-change undo (patch Tuesday, config edits), kept < 24 hours, never more than 2 deep, and NEVER a backup. Why: a checkpoint is a differencing disk (AVHDX) chained to the parent — it lives on the SAME storage, grows silently, costs merge I/O, and a long chain can corrupt or fill the volume. Production (not Standard) checkpoints quiesce VSS writers so SQL/AD inside the guest stay consistent. Logic Check: ask 'does this survive the failure it protects against?' — a checkpoint does not survive host storage failure, ergo it is not a backup. Backups go to separate storage (phase 5's strategy).

Step 6 — Troubleshooting logic tree: VM HAS NO NETWORK. Symptom: guest OS shows 'unidentified network', no DHCP. Diagnose in order: (1) Get-VMNetworkAdapter -VMName CL-DC01 — is it connected to vSwitch-External? (2) Get-VMSwitch — is the switch External and bound to the live physical NIC? (3) Inside the guest: ipconfig — APIPA address (169.254.x.x) means DHCP never answered, so check the phase-3 scope and that the VM's virtual NIC is on VLAN 20's path. The chain is always: guest NIC -> virtual switch -> physical NIC -> physical switch port -> VLAN -> DHCP. Fix the FIRST broken link; everything downstream of it is a symptom. Second fault: host unreachable after switch creation — you set -AllowManagementOS $false; recreate the switch with $true.

Step 7 — Document the VM inventory in the design doc: name, role, vCPU/RAM/disk, switch, backup method, checkpoint policy. Why: phase 7's handover pack needs this table, and writing it now (while true) beats reconstructing it during an outage later.
labs.success_message: Hyper-V live, External switch carrying production VMs, Private switch reserved for isolation, CL-DC01/CL-FS01 built per-role, checkpoint policy set to production-only short-lived undo — virtualization is now the floor identity stands on.
labs.title: Phase 4 Build: Hyper-V Switches, VMs, and Checkpoint Policy

checks.hint: No FULL backup found — the backup chain must START with a FULL. Log and differential backups are meaningless without the base full to anchor them.
No transaction log backup found — with 15-minute log backups required for the 1-hour RPO, BACKUP LOG must run on a schedule after the full.
The restore chain is wrong — every restore except the FINAL one must use WITH NORECOVERY, or the chain ends early and later files cannot be applied.

labs.objective: Install SQL Server, create ContosoDB in the FULL recovery model, take FULL/DIFF/LOG backups on schedule, simulate data loss, and restore the full chain with NORECOVERY. Applies 'Backup, restore, and recovery models' and 'Backup Strategy: 3-2-1, Chains, RTO/RPO, and Testing'.
steps: Step 1 — Install SQL Server (Developer or Standard edition per licensing) on CL-FS01 or a dedicated VM, choosing: Database Engine Services (the core), and during setup set the data/log/backup directories to SEPARATE volumes (D:\SQLData, L:\SQLLogs, B:\SQLBackup). Why separate volumes: logs and backups on the data volume die with it — the whole phase-5 strategy assumes the backup survives the data disk's death. Set the SQL Server service to a dedicated domain service account (least privilege), not LocalSystem. Verify: in SSMS or sqlcmd, SELECT @@VERSION — you should see the installed build; services.msc should show SQL Server running under the service account.

Step 2 — Create the database in the FULL recovery model: CREATE DATABASE ContosoDB; then ALTER DATABASE ContosoDB SET RECOVERY FULL;. Why FULL, not SIMPLE: SIMPLE truncates the transaction log on checkpoint, which destroys point-in-time recovery — with SIMPLE your RPO is 'whenever the last full ran' (24 hours), violating the 1-hour requirement. FULL keeps every transaction in the log until you back it up, which is what makes 15-minute log backups meaningful. Order logic: set FULL immediately at creation — any transactions committed while in SIMPLE are unrecoverable to a point in time; the model must be FULL before real data lands. Verify: SELECT name, recovery_model_desc FROM sys.databases WHERE name = 'ContosoDB'; — you should see FULL.

Step 3 — Take the base FULL backup (the anchor of everything): BACKUP DATABASE ContosoDB TO DISK = 'B:\SQLBackup\ContosoDB_Full.bak' WITH INIT, COMPRESSION;. Why first: differential and log backups are deltas — they record changes SINCE the full. A log backup with no base full is a diff against nothing: un-restorable. WITH INIT overwrites any previous file (fresh chain); COMPRESSION shrinks the 40 GB database dramatically. Why to B:\ (separate storage): the backup must survive the data volume. Verify: RESTORE VERIFYONLY FROM DISK = 'B:\SQLBackup\ContosoDB_Full.bak'; — you should see 'The backup set on file 1 is valid.' A backup you never verify is a hope.

Step 4 — Schedule the chain: DIFFERENTIAL every 6 hours (BACKUP DATABASE ContosoDB TO DISK = 'B:\SQLBackup\ContosoDB_Diff.bak' WITH DIFFERENTIAL;), transaction LOG every 15 minutes (BACKUP LOG ContosoDB TO DISK = 'B:\SQLBackup\ContosoDB_Log_<time>.trn';). Why this cadence: the 15-minute logs cap worst-case loss at 15 minutes (inside the 1-hour RPO); the 6-hour diffs keep the restore chain short — at disaster time you restore ONE full + ONE diff + a handful of logs instead of hundreds of logs (this is what keeps the restore inside the 4-hour RTO). Implement via SQL Server Agent jobs. Logic Check: narrate the restore before the disaster — 'full, latest diff, then each log in sequence' — and count the files; if the count scares you, the diff interval is too wide.

Step 5 — SIMULATE data loss (the only way to prove the strategy): create and load a table (CREATE TABLE dbo.Orders (OrderID int IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, OrderDate datetime2 DEFAULT SYSDATETIME(), Amount decimal(10,2)); INSERT a few rows), take a log backup, note the time, then DELETE FROM dbo.Orders; (the 'oops'). Take another log backup — the delete is now IN the log chain, which is exactly what point-in-time recovery undoes. Do NOT panic: this is the drill the business is paying for.

Step 6 — Restore the chain, in order, with NORECOVERY until the final step: RESTORE DATABASE ContosoDB FROM DISK = 'B:\SQLBackup\ContosoDB_Full.bak' WITH NORECOVERY; then RESTORE DATABASE ContosoDB FROM DISK = 'B:\SQLBackup\ContosoDB_Diff.bak' WITH NORECOVERY; then each log in sequence RESTORE LOG ContosoDB FROM DISK = 'B:\SQLBackup\ContosoDB_Log_1.trn' WITH NORECOVERY; ... and the LAST log WITH RECOVERY (or STOPAT = '2026-10-10 10:16:00' for point-in-time, to land just before the delete). Why NORECOVERY: RECOVERY runs crash recovery and brings the database online — an online database cannot accept further restores, so recovering early ENDS the chain and strands the remaining logs. The final RECOVERY (optionally with STOPAT) is what replays the log up to the chosen instant and undoes the delete. Verify: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM dbo.Orders; — your rows should be back; check the OrderDate values against the noted time to confirm you landed before the delete.

Step 7 — Troubleshooting logic tree: RESTORE FAILS WITH 'the log chain is broken'. Symptom: a log restore errors that it cannot be applied. Diagnose: (1) was there a FULL backup AFTER the database was created but BEFORE this log? (2) did someone take an ad-hoc full with INIT in the middle (forking the chain)? (3) are you applying logs in exact chronological order — RESTORE HEADERONLY on each file shows FirstLSN/LastLSN; each file's FirstLSN must equal the previous file's LastLSN. The reasoning: SQL Server replays a single continuous log sequence number chain — any gap or fork breaks continuity, and the fix is always 'find the missing link or restart the chain from the newest valid full.' Prevention: never take manual backups outside the Agent jobs without documenting them. Final step: write the restore procedure (this exact sequence with YOUR file paths) into the phase-7 runbook — during a real outage you will not be calm enough to derive it.
labs.success_message: ContosoDB in FULL recovery, scheduled FULL/DIFF/LOG chain running, simulated delete recovered via NORECOVERY chain with point-in-time STOPAT — you have now caused a data loss and undone it, which is the entire point of backups.
labs.title: Phase 5 Build: SQL Backup Chain and Point-in-Time Restore

checks.hint: SMBv1 status unverified — run Get-SmbServerConfiguration and confirm EnableSMB1Protocol is False. The legacy copier must be isolated or replaced, not an excuse to keep a wormable protocol.
Host firewall state unchecked — Get-NetFirewallProfile should show all three profiles Enabled. Default-deny on the host is the last line before the attacker.
LAPS unverified — each machine needs a unique, rotated local admin password retrievable via Get-LapsADPassword. Identical local admin passwords fleet-wide turn one compromise into all.

labs.objective: Execute the one-day hardening sequence: verify backups, patch, kill SMBv1, restrict RDP/SMB, enable default-deny host firewalls, deploy LAPS, set up Windows Event Forwarding conceptually, and write the 1-page incident response runbook. Applies 'Windows Server Hardening Baseline' and 'Incident Response Fundamentals for Sysadmins'.
steps: Step 1 — Verify backups FIRST (before touching anything): confirm last night's ContosoDB full exists on B:\, run RESTORE VERIFYONLY, and restore ONE file-server file from the file backup to a temp folder. Why first: every hardening step carries breakage risk — a patch can blue-screen, a firewall rule can lock you out. With a verified restore, any mistake is recoverable; without it, you are one misclick from an unrecoverable outage. This is also the phase-5 proof paying off. Verify: the restored test file opens correctly. If the restore fails, STOP hardening and fix backups — you just discovered the real priority.

Step 2 — Patch critical vulnerabilities: on the DCs, run sconfig (option 6) or Install-WindowsUpdate via PSWindowsUpdate; on clients, confirm the GPO-driven update ring. Why second: patching kills known remote-code-execution — the highest-severity, lowest-effort attack path. Why DCs first: they are the keys to the kingdom; a compromised DC is a compromised forest. Order logic: patch AFTER backup verification (step 1) because patches occasionally break things and you need the rollback. Verify: systeminfo | findstr 'Hotfix' or Get-HotFix — the current month's cumulative update should be listed; uptime should show the reboot happened.

Step 3 — Disable SMBv1 everywhere and contain the legacy copier: Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol (clients); Set-SmbServerConfiguration -EnableSMB1Protocol $false -Force (servers). Then audit: Get-SmbServerConfiguration | Select-Object EnableSMB1Protocol — you should see False. Why: SMBv1 is the EternalBlue/WannaCry-class worm vector — unpatchable by design, disabled by default for a decade. The legacy copier: it does NOT get an exception to keep SMBv1 fleet-wide; it gets an isolated VLAN/ACL (phase-2 firewall rules) or a replacement plan. Common mistake: disabling on servers but forgetting clients — verify BOTH. Logic Check: for every 'but we need it' exception, ask 'is this exception worth a wormable protocol?' — the answer is isolation, not exception.

Step 4 — Restrict RDP/SMB at the network edge: firewall rules allowing TCP 3389 and 445 to servers ONLY from the admin jump box (10.10.30.x), deny from user VLAN and internet. On hosts: Set-NetFirewallProfile -Profile Domain,Public,Private -Enabled True, then set inbound defaults to block and allow only required services. Why: RDP and SMB are the two most brute-forced/exploited Windows services — exposed to the LAN they are a password-guessing away from compromise. Why jump-box-only: one hardened, monitored ingress point beats 60 scattered ones. Verify: from a user PC, Test-NetConnection 10.10.20.11 -Port 3389 — you should see TcpTestSucceeded: False; from the jump box, True. Test BOTH directions — a rule you test one way is a rumor.

Step 5 — Deploy LAPS (Windows LAPS, built into modern Windows): configure the GPO (Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > System > LAPS: enable password backup to AD, set complexity/length/expiry), then verify per machine: Get-LapsADPassword -Identity 'CL-FS01' -AsPlainText — you should see a unique password with an expiration timestamp. Why: identical local admin passwords fleet-wide mean one compromised hash (pass-the-hash) equals EVERY machine — LAPS makes each machine's local admin unique and rotated, so a breach stays local. Why AD-backed: the passwords are retrievable by authorized admins (no sticky notes) and audited. Common mistake: enabling the GPO but never verifying retrieval — an unretrievable password is a lockout, not a control.

Step 6 — Stand up Windows Event Forwarding (conceptually + skeleton): on the collector (jump box or CL-DC02), run wecutil qc (configures the collector service); create a subscription (wecutil cs subscription.xml) forwarding Security logs (4624/4625 logons, 4688 process creation, 4720 account creation) from all domain computers. Why WEF: 60 machines' logs on 60 disks are 60 places an attacker wipes — forwarded to one hardened collector, tampering the local log no longer blinds you. Why these event IDs: 4625 bursts = password guessing; 4720 = possible backdoor account; 4688 with command line = living-off-the-land detection. This is week-one skeleton — SIEM tuning is the deferred week-two work from the phase-6 scenario decision. Verify: wecutil gr <subscription-name> — you should see active sources reporting.

Step 7 — Write the 1-page incident response runbook and file it in the SOP: sections — (1) DETECT: what the WEF alerts and user reports look like; (2) CONTAIN: isolate the host (disable switch port / firewall block), DO NOT power off (memory forensics); (3) ERADICATE: identify persistence (autoruns, scheduled tasks, new accounts via 4720), remove; (4) RECOVER: restore from the phase-5 verified backups, force password resets; (5) LESSONS: timeline + what changes. Include the call tree (who declares an incident) and the 'first 15 minutes' checklist. Why one page: a 40-page IR plan is never read at 2 AM; one page gets used. Why 'do not power off': volatile memory holds the attacker's tools — pulling the plug destroys evidence. Logic Check: read the runbook as the 2 AM on-call person — every step must be an imperative command with a verification, not an essay.
labs.success_message: Backups verified, patches current, SMBv1 dead, RDP/SMB jump-box-only, host firewalls default-deny, LAPS rotating unique admin passwords, security events forwarding to one collector, and a 1-page IR runbook that fits the 2 AM test — the highest-risk gaps closed in one day, in risk order.
labs.title: Phase 6 Build: One-Day Hardening Sprint

checks.hint: The as-built section is missing the addressing truth — it must list the actual IPs, VLANs, and roles (e.g., CL-DC01 at 10.10.20.10). A diagram without IPs is a poster.
No credential inventory — the pack must say WHERE each credential lives (sealed envelope / vault), never the passwords themselves. 'Ask the old admin' is not an inventory.
Missing SOP index / change log — without procedures-with-verification and a history of what changed, the new hire inherits mysteries, not a system.

labs.objective: Assemble the complete handover pack (as-built diagram, SOP index, credential inventory template, change log, runbooks) and run the 'new hire Monday' review. Applies 'SOPs and Runbooks That Survive Contact With On-Call' and 'Network Diagrams and Change Records'.
steps: Step 1 — Assemble the as-built section: the phase-1 diagram updated with REALITY (actual IPs, actual VLAN assignments, actual server names CL-DC01/CL-FS01/CL-DC02, firmware/OS versions, the VPN pool, the jump box). Why first: the diagram is the map — every troubleshooting session starts with 'what is it supposed to look like?' Update rule: the as-built is redrawn whenever reality changes, or it becomes fiction; date-stamp it. Verify: pick any cable in the rack and trace it on the diagram — if you cannot, the diagram is incomplete. Common mistake: shipping the phase-1 PLAN as the as-built — plans show intent, as-builts show truth; label which is which.

Step 2 — Build the SOP index: one entry per procedure from phases 2-6, each with: purpose, exact commands in order, verification ('run X — you should see Y'), rollback, and last-tested date. Why the verification line: a procedure without a success signal is a guess — the on-call person needs to know whether it worked. Why last-tested: an untested procedure rots; the date forces the quarterly test habit. Include the SQL restore chain from phase 5 VERBATIM with your file paths — during a real outage nobody derives T-SQL from principles.

Step 3 — Create the credential inventory TEMPLATE: a table with columns System | Account | Where the credential lives (sealed envelope # / vault entry) | Last rotated | Owner. Fill the 'where' column; NEVER the password column. Why the template matters more than the values: it proves no credential is 'tribal knowledge' — if the where-column has a blank, that account is one resignation from being lost. Why sealed, not in the doc: a handover pack gets emailed, printed, left on desks — passwords in it are a breach waiting for a photocopier. Logic Check: for each row ask 'if the owner quit today, could I still get in?' — a 'no' is a finding, not a shrug.

Step 4 — Write the change log (start it now, even if short): date | change | reason | who | rollback. Seed it with the build itself: '2026-10-13: disabled SMBv1 fleet-wide — worm vector — rollback: Enable-WindowsOptionalFeature SMB1Protocol'. Why: the change log is the first place you look when something breaks — 'what changed since it worked?' answers 80% of outages. A log started at build time has no gaps; a log started 'later' never starts.

Step 5 — Attach the incident response runbook (phase 6), the backup/restore runbook (phase 5), vendor/support contacts (ISP, hardware warranty, Microsoft support contract numbers), and license inventory. Why contacts and licenses: at 2 AM with a dead array, 'who do I call and what is the contract number' is not trivia — it is the difference between a 4-hour and a 4-day outage. Why licenses: an audit or a reinstall without license proof is a second crisis.

Step 6 — Run the FINAL REVIEW: the 'new hire Monday' test. Hand the pack to a colleague (or role-play it yourself) and answer, using ONLY the pack: (1) the file server is down — which page restores service? (2) a new hire starts — which page gets their account created? (3) the DC will not boot — which page has the DSRM recovery path? (4) what changed last Friday? Every question must have a page number. Any question without one is a gap — go back and write that page. Why this test: it is the only honest review — 'looks complete' is an opinion, 'answers all four' is a result. Logic Check: documentation's single test is 'does this page change what the on-call person does at 2 AM?' — if a section fails that test, cut it; bulk is not thoroughness.

Step 7 — Publish and protect: store the pack in TWO places (file share + offline copy — the pack that lives only on the server it documents is unavailable exactly when needed), set the review calendar (quarterly test of one restore + one SOP), and hand the sealed credential envelope to the founder. Why two places: the file server being down must not take the recovery docs with it. Final verification: the quarterly calendar invite exists and the offline copy opens. You are done when a stranger could survive Monday — and you have proven it, not asserted it.
labs.success_message: Handover pack complete: as-built truth, SOPs with verification, credential inventory (locations, not passwords), change log, runbooks, contacts — and it passed the new-handle Monday test. Contoso Labs is built, secured, and survivable without you.
labs.title: Phase 7 Build: The Handover Pack and Final Review
Provision a User Through a Mock REST API
labs.objective: Stand up a local mock REST API, then drive a full integration from PowerShell: GET a user list with an auth header, POST a new user with a JSON body, parse the responses as objects, and handle a 401 with try/catch.
steps: Open an elevated PowerShell session. Save the mock API server below as C:\LabApi\mock-server.ps1, then start it in a background job: $job = Start-Job -FilePath C:\LabApi\mock-server.ps1 — the server listens on http://localhost:8080/ and enforces a bearer token (demo-token-123), returning 401 for anything else, 404 for unknown paths. Verify it is listening: Test-NetConnection -ComputerName localhost -Port 8080 (TcpTestSucceeded should be True).

GET the user list with your auth header: $headers = @{ Authorization = 'Bearer demo-token-123' }; $users = Invoke-RestMethod -Uri 'http://localhost:8080/api/users' -Method GET -Headers $headers -UseBasicParsing — then prove the response is a real object: $users.Count and $users[0].displayName (no parsing code needed; Invoke-RestMethod converted the JSON for you).

POST a new user — build a HASHTABLE (never hand-concatenated JSON), convert it, and declare the content type: $newUser = @{ displayName = 'Noah Patel'; userPrincipalName = 'noah.patel@corp.local'; department = 'IT' }; $result = Invoke-RestMethod -Uri 'http://localhost:8080/api/users' -Method POST -Headers $headers -Body ($newUser | ConvertTo-Json) -ContentType 'application/json' -UseBasicParsing — then read the server's confirmation: $result.status (should be 'created') and $result.id.

Trigger the error path on purpose: re-run the POST with a bad token inside try/catch — try { Invoke-RestMethod -Uri 'http://localhost:8080/api/users' -Method POST -Headers @{ Authorization = 'Bearer wrong-token' } -Body ($newUser | ConvertTo-Json) -ContentType 'application/json' -UseBasicParsing } catch { $_.Exception.Message } — confirm the message contains (401) Unauthorized, and say out loud which part of the request that blames (the header — not the URL, not the body).

Verify end to end: GET the list again and confirm Noah Patel is present (($users2 = Invoke-RestMethod -Uri 'http://localhost:8080/api/users' -Method GET -Headers $headers -UseBasicParsing).displayName -contains 'Noah Patel'), then stop the server: Stop-Job $job; Remove-Job $job.

checks.hint: The GET step did not return user objects — did you include -Headers with 'Bearer demo-token-123' and -UseBasicParsing? The response should contain displayName fields.
The POST body was not built from a hashtable via ConvertTo-Json — the JSON reaching the server should contain the userPrincipalName field. Never hand-concatenate JSON strings.
The error-handling step did not surface the 401 — wrap the bad-token POST in try/catch and output $_.Exception.Message, which contains '(401) Unauthorized.'

labs.success_message: Full REST lifecycle from PowerShell — GET with an auth header, POST with a JSON body, parsed objects, and a caught 401 that told you exactly which part of the request was wrong. That is what 'API integration' means in practice.

labs.title: Write Pester Tests for Infrastructure State
labs.objective: Write a Pester test file that asserts real infrastructure state — a service is running, a file exists, a TCP port is listening — get a green run, then deliberately break one fixture and watch the test go red.
steps: Open an elevated PowerShell session and verify Pester 5 is available: Get-Module -ListAvailable Pester | Select-Object Name, Version — if nothing shows 5.x, install it for your user: Install-Module Pester -MinimumVersion 5.0 -Scope CurrentUser -Force -SkipPublisherCheck, then Import-Module Pester -MinimumVersion 5.0.

Create the fixtures your tests will assert on: New-Item -Path C:\LabPester -ItemType Directory -Force; New-Item -Path C:\LabPester\flag.txt -ItemType File -Force — the service fixture is the built-in EventLog service (always running on Windows), and the port fixture is a listener you start now in a background job: $listenerJob = Start-Job -ScriptBlock { $l = New-Object System.Net.HttpListener; $l.Prefixes.Add('http://localhost:18090/'); $l.Start(); while ($l.IsListening) { $c = $l.GetContext(); $b = [Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetBytes('ok'); $c.Response.OutputStream.Write($b,0,$b.Length); $c.Response.OutputStream.Close() } } — confirm it: (Test-NetConnection -ComputerName localhost -Port 18090 -WarningAction SilentlyContinue).TcpTestSucceeded should be True.

Save the test file as C:\LabPester\Infra.Tests.ps1 (the .Tests.ps1 suffix is how Pester discovers it): Describe 'Lab Machine Baseline' { Context 'Services' { It 'EventLog service is running' { (Get-Service EventLog).Status | Should -Be 'Running' } } Context 'Files' { It 'Flag file exists' { Test-Path 'C:\LabPester\flag.txt' | Should -BeTrue } } Context 'Network' { It 'Port 18090 is listening' { (Test-NetConnection -ComputerName localhost -Port 18090 -WarningAction SilentlyContinue).TcpTestSucceeded | Should -BeTrue } } } — note every test only OBSERVES state; none of them change anything.
Run the suite: Invoke-Pester -Path C:\LabPester\Infra.Tests.ps1 -Output Detailed — confirm all 3 tests pass ('Tests Passed: 3'). Read the output format now so you recognize it under pressure later.

Prove the tests actually test something: break one fixture on purpose — Rename-Item C:\LabPester\flag.txt C:\LabPester\flag.txt.hidden — re-run Invoke-Pester and watch exactly one test go red with 'Expected $true, but got $false.' Then restore it (rename back) and confirm green again. A test you have never seen fail is a test you cannot trust.
Clean up: Stop-Job $listenerJob; Remove-Job $listenerJob; Remove-Item C:\LabPester -Recurse -Force.

checks.hint: Pester 5 was not confirmed — run Get-Module -ListAvailable Pester and check the Version column shows 5.x before writing tests.
The Pester run did not report Passed — did Invoke-Pester -Path point at your .Tests.ps1 file, and were all three fixtures (EventLog running, flag.txt present, port 18090 listening) in place?
No Should assertions were found in a .Tests.ps1 file — each It block needs a Should assertion (e.g. (Get-Service EventLog).Status | Should -Be 'Running') inside a file ending in .Tests.ps1.

labs.success_message: Green suite, and you watched it go red on demand — you now own a machine-readable definition of 'healthy' that you can run after every change window instead of hoping nothing broke.

labs.title: Layered Diagnosis Drill
labs.objective: For five symptoms, name the broken OSI layer and run the single command that proves it — building the bottom-up diagnostic reflex: highest working layer found, break is the layer above.
steps: Symptom 1 — 'No website opens by name, but ping 8.8.8.8 replies fine.' Call the layer (L7 — DNS name resolution; IP itself works, so L1–L3 are healthy), then prove it bypassing the browser: Resolve-DnsName example.com — a clean answer section confirms L7-DNS is actually the break, not the browser.

Symptom 2 — 'Ping to the file server fails, but arp -a shows the gateway's MAC address.' Call the layer (L3 — ARP resolving proves L2 works; ICMP ping failing puts the fault at/above IP), then prove it: ping 192.168.10.5, and if it fails, tracert 192.168.10.5 to see exactly which hop the path dies at (remember: one hop of * * * with replies after it is cosmetic; stars from some hop onward is the break).

Symptom 3 — 'No network at all; the link light on the NIC is dark.' Call the layer (L1 — physical; no command fixes a dead wire), then confirm the OS agrees: Get-NetAdapter | Select-Object Name, Status, LinkSpeed — 'Disconnected' means hands-on next: reseat the cable, try another switch port, then suspect the NIC.

Symptom 4 — 'Ping works and names resolve, but the HTTPS site won't load.' Call the layer (L4 — the TCP port; L3 and L7-DNS are proven working, so the handshake itself is failing), then prove it: Test-NetConnection -ComputerName example.com -Port 443 — TcpTestSucceeded False means the port is closed or filtered; True would point past the network at the L7 application.

Symptom 5 — 'Since the new VPN went in, small pages load but large downloads stall.' Call the layer (L3 — MTU/fragmentation; tunnel overhead shrank the path MTU below 1500), then prove it: ping -f -l 1472 8.8.8.8 versus ping -f -l 1473 8.8.8.8 — the size where 'Packet needs to be fragmented but DF set' appears is your ceiling talking. (1472 = 1500 - 20 IP header - 8 ICMP header: arithmetic, not magic.)

checks.hint: Symptom 1 is L7/DNS — ping to a raw IP works, so L1–L3 are fine and only names fail. Prove it with Resolve-DnsName example.com (or nslookup), not by reinstalling the browser.
Symptom 4 is L4 — ping (L3) works and names resolve (L7-DNS), so the TCP handshake on the port is the suspect. Run Test-NetConnection -ComputerName example.com -Port 443 and read TcpTestSucceeded.
Symptom 3 is L1 — a dark link light is physical. Get-NetAdapter shows the OS's view of the link (Status); 'Disconnected' means reseat the cable and try another port.
Symptom 5 is L3 MTU/fragmentation — the VPN shrank the path MTU. Use ping -f -l 1472 (Don't Fragment + payload size) and find the largest size that still gets a Reply.

labs.success_message: Five symptoms, five layers, five commands — you diagnosed bottom-up every time: find the highest working layer, and the break is the one just above it. That reflex is the whole OSI model paying rent.

labs.title: Write 3 FortiGate Policies in Order
labs.objective: Create three firewall policies in correct top-down order — a web allow, a DNS allow, and an explicit deny-all last — then prove the order with 'diagnose firewall policy list' and a packet test.
steps: Enter the policy table: 'config firewall policy'.
Create policy 10: 'edit 10' — set name 'LAN-web', srcintf port1, dstintf port2, service 'HTTP' 'HTTPS', action accept, nat enable. Then 'next'.
Create policy 20: 'edit 20' — set name 'LAN-dns', srcintf port1, dstintf port2, service 'DNS', action accept, nat enable. Then 'next'.
Create policy 30: 'edit 30' — set name 'deny-all', srcintf port1, dstintf port2, service 'ALL', action deny. It must be LAST. Then 'end'.
Verify: 'show firewall policy' shows 10, 20, 30 in order; 'diagnose firewall policy list' shows all three; send an HTTPS packet on the Policy Board and confirm policy 10's hits climb.

checks.hint: Step 1: enter the policy table with 'config firewall policy' before editing anything.
Policies 10 and 20 need 'set action accept' — the web and DNS allows.
Policy 10's service must include HTTP/HTTPS — check: set service "HTTP" "HTTPS".
Policy 30 needs 'set action deny' with service ALL — the explicit deny-all safety net, in last position.
Prove it: run 'diagnose firewall policy list' — every policy should show, with hits on the ones that fired.

labs.success_message: Three policies, correct order — specific allows on top, deny-all as the last word. That ordering instinct is half of firewall work.

labs.title: Build an App-Based Allow Rule
labs.objective: Create an application-based security rule allowing web-browsing from Trust to Untrust with service application-default, placed above the catch-all deny — then prove App-ID by passing web traffic on a non-standard port.
steps: Open the Policy Builder tab: name the rule 'allow-web-trust-to-untrust'.
Set From zone Trust, To zone Untrust, Source any, Destination any.
Set Application to 'web-browsing' (NOT 'any') and Service to 'application-default'.
Set Action allow with logging on, then Commit — confirm it lands ABOVE 'block-all'.
Proof: on the Zones tab send web-browsing on TCP 8080 from Trust — it must be ALLOWED by your rule (App-ID sees the app, not the port).

checks.command_pattern: set rulebase security rules \S+ from Trust
checks.hint: The rule's From zone must be Trust — check the 'from' line of your set commands.
Application must be 'web-browsing', not 'any' — this is the App-ID point of the whole lab.
Service must be 'application-default' so App-ID identifies the app on any port.
Action must be 'allow' — then verify placement above block-all and run the 8080 proof test.

labs.success_message: Application-based policy, proven on a non-standard port — you now think in applications, not port numbers. That's the Palo Alto mindset.

labs.title: Deploy a 3-VM Lab with Isolated Networking
labs.objective: Plan VM IDs, create an isolated Linux bridge (vmbr1, no physical uplink), deploy three VMs attached to it, power them on, and verify the topology from the CLI — the design -> build -> verify loop.
steps: Plan your scheme on paper first: VMIDs 120/121/122, names lab-web / lab-app / lab-db (120s = lab network). Write it down — collisions are the classic beginner error.
Create the isolated bridge: in the real Proxmox UI this is Node -> Network -> Create -> Linux Bridge with no bridge port. (In sims/proxmox-sim.html Lab tab, step 2 simulates this Web-UI action.)

Create the three VMs, each with its virtual NIC on the isolated bridge: qm create 120 --name lab-web --memory 1024 --cores 1 --net0 virtio,bridge=vmbr1 (repeat for 121/lab-app and 122/lab-db with 2048/4096 MB).
Power them on: qm start 120, qm start 121, qm start 122.
Verify: qm list shows all three; ip link show shows vmbr1 with no physical port while vmbr0 holds eth0 — that is your evidence the lab is isolated.
Document the topology (IDs, bridges, what you proved), then wipe and rebuild from memory using only the CLI — free mode.

checks.hint: lab-db (VM 122) is missing from qm list — did all three qm create commands complete?
vmbr1 isn't there — the isolated bridge must be created before VMs attach to it.

labs.success_message: 3-VM isolated lab deployed and verified: 120/lab-web, 121/lab-app, 122/lab-db all on vmbr1 with no uplink. You proved ID planning, bridge design, qm create/start, and topology verification — the exact loop an infrastructure assessment tests.

labs.title: Linux Permissions: Read, Compute, Fix
labs.objective: Decode permission strings, compute octal from rwx, and fix a real 'permission denied' with the minimal correct mode.
steps: Open sims/terminal-mastery.html and run ls -l /home/admin/deploy.sh. Decode the string -rw-r--r--: which audience is missing which power?
Compute the octal by hand: r=4, w=2, x=1 per audience. Confirm 644 = rw-r--r--.
In the Permission Lab tab, click the rwx boxes until the display reads 755 (rwxr-xr-x). Read the live math line to confirm 4+2+1 / 4+1 / 4+1.
Back in the terminal, fix the script with the minimal correct command: chmod 755 /home/admin/deploy.sh. Verify with ls -l.
Explain aloud why not 777: who else gains what power, and what could they do with it?
Run the Permission Lab practice dice to 5/5, then complete Challenge 2 (verify button) and Challenge 3 (navigation drill) in the Challenges tab.

checks.hint: deploy.sh is not rwxr-xr-x yet — apply chmod 755 /home/admin/deploy.sh first.
The fix is chmod 755 on the script — targeted at the exact missing execute bit.

labs.success_message: Permissions mastered: you decode ls -l fluently, compute octal from rwx, fixed deploy.sh to exactly 755, and can articulate why 777 is never the answer. 'Permission denied' is now a 30-second fix, not a blocker.

labs.title: Git Workflow: Clone to Pull Request
labs.objective: Execute the complete professional Git loop — clone, branch, change, stage, commit, push, pull request — with the repo visual proving every state change.
steps: Open sims/git-simulator.html. In the Git Terminal: git clone https://github.com/interstitium-labs/infra-docs.git — note the 2 seeded commits and the origin remote.
Create your sandbox: git checkout -b fix/vpn-keepalive. Confirm the Repo Visual HUD shows the new branch.
Make the change: edit vpn.md (change keepalive = 30 to keepalive = 60) and save. Watch the working directory panel flag it modified.
Stage and snapshot: git add vpn.md, then git commit -m "Raise VPN keepalive to 60" — watch the commit graph grow a node on your branch.
Publish: git push origin fix/vpn-keepalive. Your branch is now on the 'remote'.
Open the pull request via the lab's step-6 button (GitHub tab): review the automated checks, then merge. Confirm the graph shows your commits on main.
Bonus: run the Merge Conflicts guided walkthrough so your first real conflict isn't on a deadline.

checks.hint: The branch isn't on the remote yet — push it before opening the PR.
Your keepalive commit isn't in history — did git add + git commit complete on the branch?

labs.success_message: Full Git loop complete: cloned, branched, changed, staged, committed, pushed, and merged via pull request — with the graph as your receipt. You also know the conflict drill: edit, add, commit, two parents.

labs.title: Hunt the Smoking Gun in the Event Logs
labs.objective: Use Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable and wevtutil to find failed logons, unexpected shutdowns, and service failures — and export the evidence.
steps: List the available logs and their sizes: Get-WinEvent -ListLog Security, System | Select-Object LogName, FileSize, RecordCount

Find failed logons in the last 2 hours: Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; ID=4625; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddHours(-2)} | Select-Object TimeCreated, @{N='User';E={$_.Properties[5].Value}}
Find unexpected shutdowns this week: Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='System'; ID=41,6008,1074} | Select-Object TimeCreated, Id
Find service failures in the last day: Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='System'; ID=7000,7009,7031; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddDays(-1)} | Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, Message
CMD cross-check with XPath: wevtutil qe Security "/q:*[System[(EventID=4625)]]" /f:text /c:3
Export both logs as evidence: wevtutil epl Security C:\IR\security.evtx; wevtutil epl System C:\IR\system.evtx — then confirm the files exist

checks.hint: Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; ID=4625; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddHours(-2)}
wevtutil epl Security C:\IR\security.evtx — export BEFORE you touch anything

labs.success_message: Logs queried server-side with -FilterHashtable and exported as .evtx evidence — you now triage by ID and time window instead of scrolling.

labs.title: Add a Static Route and Read the ARP Table
labs.objective: Install a persistent static route to a new branch subnet, verify it in the routing table, and confirm layer-2 reachability via ARP.
steps: Survey the current table: Get-NetRoute -AddressFamily IPv4 | Where-Object {$_.NextHop -ne '0.0.0.0'} | Select-Object DestinationPrefix, NextHop, InterfaceIndex
Add the persistent route (PowerShell): New-NetRoute -DestinationPrefix '10.9.0.0/16' -NextHop '192.168.1.254' -InterfaceIndex <idx> -PolicyStore PersistentStore
CMD equivalent for the muscle memory: route add 10.9.0.0 mask 255.255.0.0 192.168.1.254 -p
