Verify it landed and is persistent: Get-NetRoute -DestinationPrefix '10.9.0.0/16' | Select-Object DestinationPrefix, NextHop, Store
Prove layer 2: ping the next hop once, then arp -a | findstr 192.168.1.254 — confirm the gateway IP resolves to the expected MAC
End-to-end: Test-NetConnection 10.9.0.5 -TraceRoute and confirm the first hop is 192.168.1.254

checks.hint: New-NetRoute -DestinationPrefix '10.9.0.0/16' -NextHop '192.168.1.254' -InterfaceIndex <idx> -PolicyStore PersistentStore
arp -a | findstr 192.168.1.254 — the gateway must have a MAC, or layer 2 is your problem

labs.success_message: Persistent static route installed and verified, ARP confirms the next hop is alive at layer 2 — routing is a table entry plus a reachable neighbor.

labs.title: Provision a New Data Disk Two Ways
labs.objective: Bring a RAW disk online with PowerShell (Initialize/New-Partition/Format-Volume) and reproduce the same result with a diskpart script.
steps: Identify the RAW disk and double-check its size: Get-Disk | Where-Object PartitionStyle -eq 'RAW' | Select-Object Number, FriendlyName, Size
Initialize as GPT: Initialize-Disk -Number <N> -PartitionStyle GPT
Create one partition with a drive letter: New-Partition -DiskNumber <N> -UseMaximumSize -DriveLetter E
Format it: Format-Volume -DriveLetter E -FileSystem NTFS -NewFileSystemLabel Data -Confirm:$false
Verify: Get-Volume -DriveLetter E | Select-Object DriveLetter, FileSystem, Size

Write the diskpart equivalent to C:\provision.txt (list disk / select disk <N> / clean / convert gpt / create partition primary / format fs=ntfs quick label=Data / assign letter=F) and step through what each line does — do NOT run it against a live disk

checks.hint: New-Partition -DiskNumber <N> -UseMaximumSize -DriveLetter E
Format-Volume -DriveLetter E -FileSystem NTFS -NewFileSystemLabel Data -Confirm:$false

labs.success_message: Disk initialized, partitioned, and formatted both ways — initialize → partition → format is the order, and list-disk-twice is the religion.

labs.title: Back Up Every GPO, Then Prove the Restore Works
labs.objective: Create a dated backup of all GPOs, delete a throwaway test GPO, and restore it — the full insurance cycle.
steps: Create the dated backup folder: $stamp = Get-Date -Format 'yyyy-MM-dd'; New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path "C:\GPOBackups\$stamp"
Back up everything: Backup-GPO -All -Path "C:\GPOBackups\$stamp" — then count the per-GPO folders and compare to (Get-GPO -All).Count
Create a throwaway GPO: New-GPO -Name 'Restore-Test-DeleteMe' | New-GPLink -Target 'OU=Test,DC=corp,DC=local'
Back it up individually, then delete it: Backup-GPO -Name 'Restore-Test-DeleteMe' -Path "C:\GPOBackups\$stamp"; Remove-GPO -Name 'Restore-Test-DeleteMe'
Restore it: Restore-GPO -Name 'Restore-Test-DeleteMe' -Path "C:\GPOBackups\$stamp"
Verify the resurrection: Get-GPO -Name 'Restore-Test-DeleteMe' | Select-Object DisplayName, ModificationTime

checks.hint: Backup-GPO -All -Path "C:\GPOBackups\$stamp" — dated folder, every GPO
Restore-GPO -Name 'Restore-Test-DeleteMe' -Path "C:\GPOBackups\$stamp"

labs.success_message: Full backup taken and a single-GPO restore proven — a GPO with a tested restore is a policy; without one it is a rumor.

labs.title: Audit Patch State and Preview Updates
labs.objective: Determine exactly how patched a server is, preview pending updates without installing, and know the rollback command.
steps: Audit installed patches: Get-HotFix | Sort-Object InstalledOn -Descending | Select-Object -First 10 HotFixID, InstalledOn
Check for one specific KB: Get-HotFix -Id KB5034441 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Open sconfig and note which menu option handles updates (option 6) — do not install from it in this drill
If PSWindowsUpdate is present: Get-WindowsUpdate -ListOnly | Select-Object KB, Title, Size — read what WOULD install
If missing: Install-Module PSWindowsUpdate -Force (lab only), then re-run the -ListOnly preview
Write down the rollback for one listed KB: wusa /uninstall /kb:<number> /quiet /norestart — say it out loud before you ever need it

checks.hint: Get-HotFix | Sort-Object InstalledOn -Descending | Select-Object -First 10 HotFixID, InstalledOn
Get-WindowsUpdate -ListOnly — preview first, install never (in this drill)

labs.success_message: Patch state audited and pending updates previewed — audit before install, canary before fleet, rollback rehearsed before the window.

labs.title: Deploy a Scoped Firewall Rule From the CLI
labs.objective: Create an inbound allow rule with both netsh and PowerShell, verify it, enable blocked-packet logging, then clean up.
steps: Check the active profile first: Get-NetConnectionProfile | Select-Object Name, NetworkCategory
netsh path: netsh advfirewall firewall add rule name="Lab App HTTPS" dir=in action=allow protocol=TCP localport=8443 remoteip=10.1.20.0/24 profile=domain
PowerShell path: New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'Lab App HTTPS PS' -Direction Inbound -Protocol TCP -LocalPort 8443 -RemoteAddress 10.1.20.0/24 -Action Allow -Profile Domain
Verify both: Get-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'Lab App HTTPS*' | Select-Object DisplayName, Enabled, Action, Direction
Enable blocked-packet logging: Set-NetFirewallProfile -Profile Domain -LogBlocked True; confirm the log path with Get-NetFirewallProfile -Profile Domain | Select-Object LogFileName
Clean up the lab rules: Remove-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'Lab App HTTPS*'; netsh advfirewall firewall delete rule name="Lab App HTTPS"

checks.hint: New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'Lab App HTTPS PS' -Direction Inbound -Protocol TCP -LocalPort 8443 -RemoteAddress 10.1.20.0/24 -Action Allow -Profile Domain
Get-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'Lab App HTTPS*' — prove the rule exists before you trust it

labs.success_message: Scoped rules built both ways, logging enabled, lab cleaned up — profile first, scope always, verify after.

labs.title: Find the SSH Attackers in the Linux Logs
labs.objective: Use journalctl and classic log files to identify brute-force SSH attempts, rank the attackers, and check for disk-eating logs.
steps: Pull the SSH service's recent history: journalctl -u sshd --since '2 hours ago' --no-pager | tail -30
Classic file check (Debian path shown; use /var/log/secure on RHEL): grep -i 'failed' /var/log/auth.log | tail -10
Rank the attackers: grep 'Failed password' /var/log/auth.log | awk '{print $(NF-3)}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10
Check failed logins via lastb: lastb | head -10
Kernel/hardware sanity: dmesg -T | grep -iE 'error|fail' | tail -5
Log hygiene: journalctl --disk-usage; ls -lh /var/log/auth.log* — is any single log eating the disk?

checks.hint: journalctl -u sshd --since '2 hours ago' --no-pager — the service's own journal first
grep 'Failed password' /var/log/auth.log | awk '{print $(NF-3)}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

labs.success_message: Attackers ranked, kernel checked, log sizes verified — service journal first, then the system, then the disk.

labs.title: "Automate This" in Bash: Fleet Disk Sweep
labs.objective: Write a Bash script that sweeps hosts for disk space and parses a log for errors — the Linux half of 'automate this'.
steps: Write sweep.sh: #!/bin/bash, then a for loop over three hostnames running ssh $h 'df -h / | tail -1' with an '== $h ==' header per host
Make it executable: chmod +x sweep.sh — then explain what the x bit does and why the script failed before it
Add error handling: if ssh fails, print "$h UNREACHABLE" and continue (|| with a message, not a silent skip)
Log parsing one-liner: grep -ci 'error' /var/log/syslog; then extract WHICH service errors most: grep -i 'error' /var/log/syslog | awk '{print $5}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5
Make it a report: redirect both sections into /tmp/disk-sweep-$(date +%F).txt with section headers

checks.hint: chmod +x sweep.sh — the execute bit is what turns text into a program
for h in web01 web02 db01; do echo "== $h"; ssh $h 'df -h / | tail -1'; done

labs.success_message: Bash loop written, made executable, errors handled, log parsed into a dated report — automate the boring, report the interesting.

simulations.title: Branch VPN tunnel down AND internal DNS failing
simulations.situation:
Two failures at once: the site-to-site VPN (an IPsec — Internet Protocol Security — encrypted tunnel between offices) is down AND internal DNS (Domain Name System) name resolution is failing. The reasoning for the triage order: these cascade — without DNS nothing can find anything, so the 'VPN is down' symptoms may be DNS in disguise — which means you fix name resolution first and re-test before touching the tunnel. Your job: determine which failure is primary, fix it first, and prove it with tests...

Monday 8:00 AM. The Orlando HQ to Tampa branch site-to-site VPN tunnel is down, and simultaneously Tampa users report they can't resolve internal hostnames (files.tampa.corp times out) though internet works. The Tampa firewall shows the tunnel in a down state, and nslookup against the Tampa DC returns SERVFAIL while external DNS resolves fine. You have 25 minutes before the branch manager escalates to the CIO.
simulations.prompt: Diagnose both failures, determine if they share a root cause, restore service, and document what you did.
evidence:
IKE Phase 1: DOWN (no response from peer 203.0.113.44)
IKE Phase 2: DOWN
Last successful: 2026-10-10 03:12

C:\> nslookup files.tampa.corp 192.168.20.5
Server:  dc-tampa-01.tampa.corp
*** dc-tampa-01.tampa.corp can't find files.tampa.corp: Server failed

2026-10-10 03:11:58 DENY udp 203.0.113.44:500 -> 198.51.100.10:500
policy: OUTBOUND-DEFAULT (no explicit allow for IKE)
choices: Tell Tampa users to use IP addresses instead of hostnames until the VPN comes back — DNS depends on the tunnel
Rebuild the entire VPN configuration from scratch on both firewalls — the tunnel config must be corrupted

Two independent failures from one overnight change: the HQ firewall policy push at 03:11 blocked UDP 500/4500 (killing IKE), and the Tampa DC's DNS service crashed — fix the firewall rule to allow IKE from the Tampa peer, restart the DNS Server service on dc-tampa-01 and verify zone loading, then confirm tunnel re-establishes and internal resolution works
Reboot the Tampa DC — that will fix both DNS and probably the VPN too
simulations.why: The evidence shows two failures with one trigger: the HQ firewall log shows IKE (UDP 500) denied starting 03:11, one minute before the tunnel's last success at 03:12 — an overnight policy push broke Phase 1. DNS SERVFAIL against the local DC with working external DNS points to the DNS Server service or zone on dc-tampa-01, independent of the tunnel (internal names resolve locally). Fix both at their actual layers: allow UDP 500/4500 for the peer, restart/verify DNS on the DC. Rebuilding the VPN or rebooting the DC treats symptoms; the 'use IPs' workaround concedes DNS unnecessarily.
simulations.hint: Line up the timestamps: when did the tunnel last succeed, and when did the deny start? And does internal DNS actually need the tunnel to work?
objectives: IKE troubleshooting and DNS service recovery

simulations.title: Hyper-V host out of disk: checkpoint sprawl
simulations.situation:
The Hyper-V host (the physical server running Microsoft's hypervisor) is out of disk space because of checkpoint sprawl — months of un-merged checkpoints (VM save points), each a differencing disk that only grows. VMs are pausing or crashing. The reasoning: every checkpoint freezes a differencing disk that records ALL subsequent writes, so an old checkpoint chain multiplies disk usage silently — and when the host disk hits zero, every guest on it halts. Your job: find the sprawl, merge it safely without losing data, and set the policy so it never happens again...

Your Hyper-V host HV-03 (2 TB volume, 40 GB free) is alerting critically. Get-VM shows 6 VMs; three have checkpoint chains 8-14 deep, some dating back months, including one on the production SQL VM. A junior admin suggests 'just delete the .avhdx files to free space.' The SQL VM cannot go down during business hours.
simulations.prompt: Reclaim the disk space safely without data loss or downtime on the SQL VM.
evidence:
PS C:\> Get-VMCheckpoint SQL-PROD | Sort CreationTime | ft VMName,Name,CreationTime

SQL-PROD  PrePatch-Jan     2026-01-14
SQL-PROD  PrePatch-Feb     2026-02-09
... (11 more, newest 2026-09-28)

PS C:\> Get-PSDrive C | ft Used,Free

Used: 1.96 TB | Free: 40 GB
choices: Export the SQL VM, delete everything, and reimport it — cleanest way to collapse the chain
Pause the SQL VM, delete all its checkpoints at once, and resume — fastest path to free space
Delete the oldest .avhdx files directly from disk — they're just old snapshots nobody needs

Never delete .avhdx files manually — remove checkpoints with Remove-VMCheckpoint (merges differencing disks into the parent), starting with the oldest on non-critical VMs; for SQL-PROD, remove checkpoints one at a time during a maintenance window or low-activity period since merges are I/O heavy, and verify each merge completes before removing the next
simulations.why: Checkpoints are differencing-disk chains (.avhdx) — deleting files manually orphans the chain and corrupts the VM. The safe path is Remove-VMCheckpoint, which merges each differencing disk back into its parent; removing oldest-first collapses the chain correctly. Merges are I/O-intensive on a production SQL VM, so they belong in a maintenance window or low-activity period, one at a time with verification — a failed mid-merge leaves you worse off. Export/reimport is downtime you don't need; pausing and bulk-deleting risks a long merge with the VM down.
simulations.hint: What does a checkpoint actually consist of on disk, and what has to happen to that chain for space to be reclaimed without losing the data in the differencing disks?

simulations.title: Restore SQL database to 2 hours ago after accidental deletion
simulations.situation:
Someone deleted critical rows two hours ago, and the business needs the SQL Server database rewound to just before the deletion — a point-in-time restore. The reasoning: the transaction log records every change in order, so replaying the log up to a chosen second reconstructs the past — but only if you have the full CHAIN (last full backup, the differential, every log backup) with no gaps. Your job: assemble the chain, restore against the clock, and verify the data...

At 11:30 AM a developer ran a DELETE without a WHERE clause on the orders table in the PROD-APP database — 40,000 rows gone. The last full backup was at 2:00 AM, transaction log backups run every 15 minutes, and the database is in FULL recovery model. The business needs the data back as of 9:30 AM (before the bad delete, after the morning batch at 8:00 AM). It's now 11:45 AM.
simulations.prompt: Restore PROD-APP to its 9:30 AM state with minimal data loss and document the steps.
evidence:
msdb backupset: FULL 2026-10-10 02:00 | LOG every 15 min, latest 11:45
recovery_model: FULL

Target: 2026-10-10 09:30:00 | Bad delete: 11:30
Tail-log backup required before restore begins
choices: Restore the 2:00 AM full backup WITH RECOVERY right now — fastest, and the 8 AM batch can just be re-run

Take a tail-log backup immediately (WITH NORECOVERY), restore the 2:00 AM full WITH NORECOVERY, apply log backups in sequence WITH NORECOVERY up to the 9:30 log, then STOPAT '2026-10-10 09:30:00' WITH RECOVERY on the final log restore — verify row counts against the morning batch, then bring the app back online
Detach the database, copy the MDF/LDF files as a backup, and reattach — the files contain everything up to now
Restore the full backup over the live database and then replay today's log backups after the 11:30 delete to 'undo' it
simulations.why: Point-in-time recovery in FULL recovery model is a strict sequence: tail-log backup first (captures everything since 11:45 including the delete, preserving your options), then full restore WITH NORECOVERY (keeps the database in restoring state so logs can apply), then each 15-min log in order WITH NORECOVERY, and the final log restore uses STOPAT 09:30 WITH RECOVERY to stop at the target and bring the database online. Restoring the full WITH RECOVERY immediately ends the sequence — no logs can apply after. Replaying logs past the delete re-applies the delete.
simulations.hint: The keywords are NORECOVERY vs RECOVERY and STOPAT. What state must the database stay in while you're applying the log chain, and which restore ends the chain?

simulations.title: DHCP scope exhaustion taking down a floor
simulations.situation:
An entire floor is offline: the DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) scope — the pool of addresses the server hands out — is exhausted, so new devices get no IP address and can't even start talking. The reasoning for the investigation order: first confirm it's exhaustion (not a dead server or a rogue DHCP imposter), then free or expand the pool for immediate relief, then find WHAT ate all the leases — because without the root cause (a too-short lease time, a device hoarding addresses, a new department that was never scoped), it refills and dies again. Your job: confirm, relieve, root-cause, and prevent the repeat...

The 4th floor (VLAN 40, 192.168.40.0/24) reports 'no internet' — 60 users affected. Their machines show 169.254.x.x APIPA addresses. The DHCP server is up and serving other VLANs fine. The VLAN 40 scope shows 0 available addresses, and you notice the lease duration is 8 days with 200 reservations for devices that left in a move six months ago. It's 9:15 AM and the floor is dead.
simulations.prompt: Restore connectivity now, then fix the root cause so it doesn't recur.
evidence:
Scope 192.168.40.0/24: 254 total | 0 available
In use: 254 (54 active leases, 200 stale reservations)
Lease duration: 8 days

C:\> ipconfig
IPv4 Address: 169.254.23.41 (APIPA)
DHCP Server: unreachable
choices: Immediate: reconcile and delete the 200 stale reservations to free addresses, shorten the lease to 8-24 hours for this scope; then verify clients renew. Root cause fix: audit reservations quarterly, set scavenging-appropriate lease times, add scope utilization alerting at 80%, and plan a scope split or superscope if growth continues
Expand the scope to a /23 immediately by changing the subnet mask on the DHCP scope only — more addresses instantly
Give the 60 users static IPs as a permanent fix — DHCP is unreliable
Reboot the DHCP server — the scope statistics are probably just not refreshing
simulations.why: APIPA + 0 available addresses + 200 stale reservations = exhaustion from dead reservations, not a server failure. Deleting stale reservations frees 200 addresses immediately; the 8-day lease is wrong for a dynamic floor (shorten to hours so addresses recycle). Changing the mask on DHCP alone without changing the VLAN subnet, gateway, and every static device creates a broken split network — a /23 expansion is a real project, not a 9:15 AM fix. Static IPs for 60 users trades one outage for permanent toil.
simulations.hint: Where are the 254 addresses actually going? Compare active leases to reservations — which number explains the outage, and which fix restores service in minutes?

simulations.title: AD replication failure between sites
simulations.situation:
Two Active Directory sites have stopped replicating — each domain controller (DC) now holds a diverging copy of the user database, so a password changed in Orlando doesn't work in Miami. The reasoning for the fix order: replication rides on DNS (DCs locate each other through DNS records) and the site-to-site network, so you check DNS first, then connectivity, then the AD service — and you check for a tombstoned DC (one offline so long the others stopped trusting it) before forcing anything, because forcing replication from a tombstoned DC corrupts the database. Your job: find the break and get the copies converging again...

Password changes made at HQ aren't reaching the Tampa DC — users who reset passwords Monday can't log in at the branch. repadmin /replsummary shows Tampa's inbound replication failing for 3 days with error 1722 (RPC server unavailable). The Tampa DC responds to ping, and its firewall shows no drops. A new hire started in Tampa this morning and their account doesn't exist on dc-tampa-01.
simulations.prompt: Diagnose the replication failure, restore it, and get the new hire working.
evidence:
Source DSA: dc-hq-01 | Destination: dc-tampa-01
Failures: 48 consecutive | Last error: 1722 (0x6ba)
Last success: 2026-10-07 06:00

PS C:\> Test-NetConnection dc-tampa-01 -Port 135
TcpTestSucceeded: False
choices: Seize the FSMO roles to the Tampa DC — replication is broken so Tampa should become authoritative
Demote and repromote the Tampa DC immediately — 3 days of failures means the DC is unrecoverable

Error 1722 + TCP 135 failing with correct DNS = RPC endpoint mapper blocked or the RPC service down on dc-tampa-01 — check the Windows Firewall RPC rules and the Remote Procedure Call service on the Tampa DC, fix, then force replication with repadmin /syncall and verify the new hire's account replicates before having them log in
Manually create the new hire's account on dc-tampa-01 so they can work today, and deal with replication later
simulations.why: Error 1722 (RPC server unavailable) with correct DNS resolution and failed TCP 135 points at the RPC endpoint mapper path — either the firewall's RPC dynamic-port rules or the RPC service itself on the destination DC. Ping working rules out basic connectivity; DNS resolving correctly rules out name resolution. The fix is at that layer, then repadmin /syncall to catch up 3 days of changes. Seizing FSMO roles is for dead DCs, not sick ones; demote/repromote is the last resort; creating a duplicate account on the Tampa DC guarantees a conflict when replication resumes.
simulations.hint: 1722 is RPC-specific. Ping works, DNS resolves — so which exact piece of the RPC conversation is failing, and what listens on TCP 135?

simulations.title: GPO not applying to the finance OU
simulations.situation:
A GPO (Group Policy Object) linked to the Finance OU (Organizational Unit) isn't applying — the settings never reach the workstations. The reasoning for the checklist order: the suspects form a hierarchy of likelihood — LSDOU precedence (a higher layer overriding it), security filtering (the GPO only applies to the groups it's scoped to), a GPO that's linked but disabled, or replication delay to the DC the client happened to talk to — so you eliminate them with gpresult and the event log instead of re-linking things at random. Your job: work the checklist and prove which suspect it was...

You linked a new hardening GPO to the Finance OU requiring screen lock at 5 minutes, but finance workstations still lock at 15. gpresult on FIN-WS-07 shows the GPO as 'Denied' with reason 'Inaccessible'. Other OUs get their GPOs fine. The GPO was created by a former admin, and you notice the Authenticated Users group was removed from the security filter and replaced with a group called 'Finance-Users' that contains user accounts only.
simulations.prompt: Fix the GPO so it applies to finance workstations correctly.
evidence:
GPO: FIN-Hardening-ScreenLock
Denied Reason: Inaccessible (security filtering)
Applied from: n/a

Security Filtering: Finance-Users (user accounts only)
Authenticated Users: REMOVED

Since MS16-072 (2016), computer must have READ access to the GPO
object even for user policies — Authenticated Users read required
choices: Set the GPO to Enforced — enforcement overrides security filtering denials

Add Authenticated Users (or Domain Computers) with Read permission on the Delegation tab while keeping Finance-Users in security filtering for Apply — since MS16-072 the computer account needs Read access to retrieve the GPO, and removing Authenticated Users broke retrieval for computer-targeted processing
Recreate the GPO from scratch — a GPO touched by a former admin can't be trusted
Move the finance computers into the Finance-Users group — then security filtering will match
simulations.why: Since MS16-072, GPOs are retrieved using the computer's security context, so the computer account needs Read permission on the GPO object — removing Authenticated Users removed that read path and the GPO shows 'Inaccessible'. The fix preserves the intent (Apply only to Finance-Users) while restoring retrieval: grant Authenticated Users or Domain Computers Read on the Delegation tab. Putting computer objects in a user group is wrong; Enforced affects precedence, not filtering; recreating the GPO repeats the same misconfiguration.
simulations.hint: The GPO is denied as 'Inaccessible', not 'filtered out'. Since 2016, whose credentials fetch the GPO from SYSVOL — the user's or the computer's?

simulations.title: Ransomware detonation on the file server: first 30 minutes
simulations.situation:
Ransomware is detonating on the file server — files are being encrypted NOW. The reasoning for the order of operations: every second of network connectivity is another second of spread (to mapped drives, to other servers), so CONTAIN first — isolate the host before anything else — and preserve evidence second (do NOT reboot: memory and logs are the crime scene, and rebooting destroys them). Investigation comes third, recovery fourth. This is the incident-response drill where doing the right things in the wrong order is the same as doing the wrong things...

10:00 AM: helpdesk reports files on \\FILE-02\shared opening as garbage with a .locked extension, and a ransom note in every folder. Your EDR shows the encryption process started at 09:40 from WS-SALES-114 (a workstation) via a mapped drive. FILE-02 also hosts the Veeam backup repository on a separate volume. 200 users are mapped to the share. The CEO is asking 'should we pay?'
simulations.prompt: Execute the first 30 minutes of incident response. What do you do, in order?
evidence:
09:40 encryption begins (WS-SALES-114 -> \\FILE-02\shared)
10:02 ransom notes appear | 10:05 helpdesk ticket opened

200 users mapped to \\FILE-02\shared
Veeam repo: D:\Backups on FILE-02 (same host, separate volume)
choices: Isolate WS-SALES-114 from the network immediately (keep powered on); disable the shared folder / block SMB to FILE-02 to stop encryption spread; preserve evidence (memory, logs, ransom note, EDR timeline) to a protected share; assess whether the Veeam repository volume is compromised before trusting any backup; escalate to security leadership/IR with the timeline — do NOT pay or wipe anything yet
Immediately start restoring FILE-02 from the Veeam repository on its D: drive — speed of recovery is everything
Pay the ransom — 200 users are down and the business needs the files today
Power off FILE-02 and WS-SALES-114 right now to stop the encryption, then investigate
simulations.why: The first 30 minutes are contain and preserve, not recover: isolate the source workstation (powered on for memory forensics), cut the attack path to the file server (disable the share/SMB, not the whole server — you need its logs), preserve volatile evidence with chain of custody, and critically verify the backup repository's integrity before trusting it — it's on the same host, so it may be encrypted too. Restoring from a possibly-compromised repo spreads the problem; powering off destroys memory evidence; paying funds crime, doesn't guarantee decryption, and the decision belongs to leadership with counsel, not the first responder.
simulations.hint: The backup repository lives on the same host as the encrypted share. What does that mean for your recovery plan, and what must happen before any restore begins?

simulations.title: Storage latency crippling the VM cluster
simulations.situation:
The VM cluster is crawling — and the culprit is storage latency: the disks can't serve read/write requests fast enough, so every VM on the shared storage queues up. The reasoning for proving it first: slow VMs can be CPU, RAM, network, OR storage, and each has a different fix — performance counters (disk queue length, latency in milliseconds) convict the storage before you touch anything. Then the cause hunt: a failed disk in the RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks) set forcing degraded reads, a backup job hammering the array, or a thin-provisioned volume out of space — your job is to prove it's storage, find the cause, and relieve it...

Users report the ERP is 'unusable' since 8 AM. The ERP VM lives on a 3-node Hyper-V cluster backed by an iSCSI SAN. Task Manager in the VM shows 100% disk active time with 80ms+ average response. The SAN management shows one controller's cache battery failed overnight, forcing write-through mode. A teammate suggests adding more vCPUs to the ERP VM.
simulations.prompt: Diagnose the real bottleneck and resolve it.
evidence:
Disk active time: 100% | Avg response: 84ms | Queue length: 32
vCPU: 45% utilized

Controller A cache battery FAILED 2026-10-10 02:14
Cache policy: forced WRITE-THROUGH on Controller A
CSV volumes healthy | No path failures | MPIO active
choices: Add 4 more vCPUs to the ERP VM — 100% disk active time means the VM needs more compute
Enable Storage QoS to throttle the ERP VM's disk — that will smooth out the latency
Live-migrate the ERP VM to another host — the host must be the problem

The failed cache battery forced write-through caching — every write now waits for spinning disk, explaining 84ms latency with low CPU. Fail storage I/O to Controller B (healthy cache) or replace the battery and restore write-back, verify latency drops, then monitor — do not add vCPUs to a storage-bound VM
simulations.why: The evidence chain is complete: cache battery failed at 02:14 → controller forced write-through → every write hits disk directly → 84ms average response with a queue depth of 32, while vCPU sits at 45%. This is a storage-cache problem, not compute or host placement — more vCPUs can't fix write latency, and live migration keeps the same SAN path. The fix is at the storage layer: fail over to the healthy controller or replace the battery to restore write-back caching, then confirm latency normalizes. Throttling the victim VM with QoS would make it worse.
simulations.hint: CPU is at 45% while disk response is 84ms. Which resource is actually saturated, and what changed on the SAN at 02:14 that explains it?

simulations.title: Expired certificate killing mail flow and VPN
simulations.situation:
The certificate — the cryptographic ID card proving 'this server really is mail.company.com' — has expired, and now mail flow AND the client VPN are both dead (both trusted that same cert). The reasoning: certificates are trust with an expiry date, and every TLS (Transport Layer Security) connection checks that date — one expired cert breaks every service bound to it simultaneously, which is why two 'unrelated' outages share one root cause. Your job: confirm the expiry, renew from the CA (Certificate Authority), bind the new cert to each service, and set up expiry monitoring so this never ambushes anyone again...

Monday 7:30 AM: Outlook clients show certificate warnings, ActiveSync stopped syncing overnight, and the SSL VPN portal throws ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID. All three services terminate on the same reverse proxy, which presents a wildcard cert for *.corp.example.com. The cert expired at midnight. The CA is an internal AD CS deployment, and the new cert was issued last week but never installed. 300 users affected.
simulations.prompt: Restore all three services with the least risk and prevent recurrence.
evidence:
Subject: CN=*.corp.example.com | Expired: 2026-10-10 00:00 UTC
Issuer: CORP-ADCS-CA | New cert issued: 2026-10-03 (in CA database)

Outlook: cert warning | ActiveSync: 0 syncs since 00:00
SSL VPN portal: ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID
choices: Generate a brand-new CSR and reissue from scratch — the week-old cert can't be trusted

Install the already-issued replacement cert on the reverse proxy (complete the pending request / import the PFX with private key), bind it to all three listeners, verify the full chain (intermediate CA cert present) from an external client, then create a 30-day-expiry monitoring alert and a calendar runbook for renewal
Tell users to click through the certificate warning — the cert is only expired, traffic is still encrypted
Renew via the public CA instead — internal CA certs are the problem
simulations.why: The replacement cert already exists in the CA database — the failure was operational (never installed), not cryptographic. Installing the issued cert with its private key and binding it to each listener restores all three services at once since they share the proxy; verifying the full chain (including the intermediate) from outside catches the classic 'installed the cert but not the chain' follow-up outage. Clicking through warnings trains users to ignore MITM attacks. The recurrence fix is monitoring (alert at 30 days) plus a renewal runbook — expiry is a solved problem with alerting.
simulations.hint: The new cert was issued a week ago. What's the actual broken step here — issuance or installation — and what do all three broken services have in common?

simulations.title: Emergency patch: print spooler RCE under active exploit
simulations.situation:
An emergency out-of-band patch: the Print Spooler has a remote-code-execution (RCE) flaw under ACTIVE exploit — it's in CISA's KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) catalog, meaning attackers are using it right now. The reasoning for skipping the normal patch rings: rings exist to contain PATCH risk, but a KEV-listed RCE on an exposed service means the ATTACK is certain and already happening — certain compromise beats possible patch side-effects. Your job: assess exposure (is the spooler even running on servers? it shouldn't be), contain (disable the service where it's not needed), patch, and verify...

Friday 4:00 PM: Microsoft releases an out-of-band patch for a print spooler RCE with confirmed in-the-wild exploitation; CISA KEV lists it with a short deadline. Your fleet: 400 workstations, 60 servers, 12 print servers running the spooler service (required). The last cumulative broke a line-of-business app and took a week to unwind. Leadership says 'patch everything tonight.'
simulations.prompt: Build the emergency patch plan that satisfies both speed and safety.
evidence:
CVE-2026-XXXX: Windows Print Spooler RCE | KEV added 2026-10-10
Exploitation: confirmed in-the-wild | Deadline: 21 days

400 workstations | 60 servers | 12 print servers (spooler required)
Last cumulative: broke LOB app, 1-week rollback
choices: Patch all 472 machines tonight with no testing — the KEV deadline and leadership's order override the testing concern
Uninstall the patch from the one server where the LOB app breaks and leave everything else patched — exceptions are fine
Wait for the normal patch Tuesday cycle — the spooler RCE probably won't hit us before then

Tonight: disable the spooler service on all non-print servers and workstations that don't print (immediate mitigation, zero patch risk); deploy the out-of-band patch to a pilot group including the LOB app within hours, then ring it out — print servers first with the app validated in the lab in parallel, full fleet inside the KEV deadline; document the spooler-disable as the compensating control
simulations.why: Active exploitation compresses the timeline but doesn't eliminate the need for validation — the last cumulative's week-long rollback is the cautionary tale. Disabling the spooler where it isn't needed is an instant, zero-risk mitigation that buys the testing window; then a compressed ring (pilot with the LOB app → print servers → fleet) beats the 21-day KEV deadline with evidence the app survives. Patching everything untested risks repeating last month's outage; waiting for Patch Tuesday ignores confirmed exploitation; ad-hoc unpatching creates unmonitored exceptions.
simulations.hint: You have two levers: reduce exposure immediately without patching, and patch quickly with validation. What can you turn off tonight that costs nothing, and what does that buy you?

pitfalls: Rambling through every command you typed — interviewers want judgment and communication, not a terminal transcript
Ending at 'I fixed it' with no follow-up — for an infrastructure role, the post-incident hardening is the real answer
points: Situation/Task: name the system, the blast radius (users/services affected), and what 'critical' meant in business terms — not just the tech
Action: show your triage order — how you scoped impact first, communicated status, then fixed; mention what you deliberately did NOT do (e.g., no untested changes at 2 AM)
Result: quantify recovery time, and close with the preventive action you took after (monitoring alert, runbook, automation) so it doesn't repeat
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you were on call and a critical system went down. Walk me through it.

pitfalls: Framing the teammate as wrong and yourself as the hero — it signals you'll be painful on a small in-office team
Choosing a trivial disagreement ('tabs vs spaces') — it wastes the question and suggests you avoid real conflict
points: Pick a real technical disagreement (e.g., change timing, tool choice, architecture tradeoff) — show you can argue the engineering merits, not personalities
Show how you evaluated both options against shared criteria: risk, rollback ability, business impact — and how you reached a decision together
End with what the outcome taught you about collaborating under pressure, especially with someone you'll share on-call with
behavioral.prompt: Describe a disagreement you had with a teammate about a technical approach. How did you resolve it?

pitfalls: Saying 'I document everything' with no example — it's unverifiable and every candidate says it
Describing documentation nobody ever read — pride should come from docs that got used, ideally by someone who isn't you
points: State your habit concretely: SOPs written during/after the fix (not 'later'), diagrams kept with the change, handover notes as a default
Give the example: what the doc covered, who used it, and a specific time it saved someone (an on-call engineer, a new hire, yourself at 2 AM)
Connect it to the team: documentation as how a small infrastructure team scales — it multiplies everyone, not just you
behavioral.prompt: How do you approach documentation? Give me an example of documentation you're proud of.

pitfalls: Claiming you 'mastered' something in a weekend — fast learning is credible; instant mastery isn't
Picking something trivial — the question tests how you handle genuine unfamiliarity under pressure
points: Name the technology, the deadline pressure, and why existing knowledge wasn't enough — set the stakes
Show your learning method: docs first, lab/test environment, small proof of concept before production — not 'I Googled it in prod'
Result: what you shipped with it, and what stuck — the durable skill or mental model you kept, not just the one-off fix
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you had to learn a new technology quickly to solve a problem.

pitfalls: Siding entirely with security ('users just need to deal with it') — ThreatLocker sells security to customers; empathy for the user side matters
Siding entirely with convenience and bypassing the control — that answer fails a security company's interview on the spot
points: Name the tension honestly (e.g., MFA rollout resistance, patching downtime, least-privilege pushback) — both sides had legitimate needs
Show how you found the workable middle: phased rollout, scoped exceptions with compensating controls, or better UX for the secure path
Result: security posture improved AND the business kept moving — and what you'd do differently about the communication next time
behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to balance security requirements against user convenience or business speed.

pitfalls: Picking a 'humblebrag' failure ('I worked too hard') — interviewers see through it and it wastes your best credibility-building question
Blaming others or the tools — ownership of failures is a core signal for an infrastructure role with production access
points: Own it plainly: what the change was, what broke, and the impact — no minimizing, no blaming the vendor or the previous admin
Show the recovery: how you detected it, executed the backout plan (or improvised one), communicated to stakeholders during the incident
Close with the systemic fix: what changed in your process afterward (better testing, staged rollout, checklist, peer review) — the failure bought something
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a change you made that went wrong. What happened and what did you do?

pitfalls: Claiming mentorship you didn't do — 'I help everyone' without a specific person and outcome reads as filler
Framing the mentee as incompetent — the story should show their growth, not your superiority
points: Describe the person and the gap honestly (a junior helpdesk tech, a teammate new to PowerShell) — mentoring starts from where they are
Show the method: pairing on real tickets, reviewing their runbooks, giving them the safe-but-real tasks — not lectures
Result: what they can do now that they couldn't before, and what mentoring taught you about your own knowledge gaps
behavioral.prompt: Have you mentored junior engineers or helped teammates grow? Give an example.

pitfalls: Generic praise ('great company, love cybersecurity') — it could apply to any security vendor and shows no research
Saying anything negative about remote work or your current situation — frame in-office as a pull toward the team, not a push away from something
points: Why ThreatLocker: connect your background to their mission — five years of remote support taught you what endpoint chaos looks like; you want to build the controls (allowlisting, hardening) that prevent the incidents you spent years firefighting
Why in-office: be concrete — after five years remote, you want the collaboration speed of a NOC-adjacent team, hands-on lab/hardware work, and mentorship proximity you can't get over chat
Why Orlando/now: tie it to your situation honestly — you're relocating, available immediately, and choosing in-office deliberately rather than settling for it
behavioral.prompt: Why ThreatLocker, and why are you specifically looking for an in-office role in Orlando?

pitfalls: Picking something trivial ('I forgot to enable virtualization in BIOS') — they asked for the HARDEST problem; bring the one that took real digging
Rambling through every command you typed — judgment and communication, not a terminal transcript
Ending at 'I fixed it' with no follow-up — no runbook, no automation, no lesson learned makes it a story about luck instead of skill
points: Situation/Task: name the actual project and stack — what you were building, on what hardware or hypervisor, and what 'broken' meant in concrete terms (not 'it didn't work' but the weirdest symptom you saw)

Action: show your debugging ORDER — how you isolated layers (hardware vs hypervisor vs guest vs network), what logs you checked, how you reproduced it, what you ruled out and why. Interviewers are scoring your process here, not just the fix — narrate your assumptions out loud the way you would in their onsite troubleshooting round

Result: the fix, plus what you did so it never happens again — the monitoring check, the documented runbook, the scripted rebuild, the config backup. For an infrastructure role, the post-fix hardening is the real answer
Close the loop to the role: 'that is the same isolate-verify-document loop I would run on your infrastructure tickets' — make the homelab a preview of you on the job, not just a hobby story
behavioral.prompt: After you described your homelab, the interviewer asks: 'What is the most technically difficult problem you have run into setting up those environments, and how did you solve it?'

pitfalls: Blaming the customer ('they didn't follow instructions') or trash-talking a previous tech — instant fail on a customer-facing role
Promising a timeline to calm them down and then missing it — a kept 2-hour promise beats a broken 30-minute one
Telling a story where you were the hero and the customer was the villain — they are testing whether you take the customer's side
points: Situation/Task: set the stakes fast — who the customer was, what broke, and what it cost them (downtime, a deadline, money). One angry-customer story from years of remote support and retention work — pick the one where the customer had a real reason to be upset

Action: the de-escalation sequence — let them finish without interrupting, acknowledge the impact in THEIR terms ('your team could not invoice for three hours'), take personal ownership ('I'm on this until it is resolved'), set a concrete next-update time and keep it, then fix the problem. Name what you deliberately did NOT do: no blaming the customer, no blaming the previous tech, no promises you could not keep

Result: the technical resolution AND the relationship outcome — did they stay, did they escalate further, what did they say after. Retention-role experience counts here: calming someone down IS the skill being tested

Close with the systemic fix: the KB article, the proactive alert, or the process change you made so the next customer never hits it — support maturity is preventing the repeat, not just surviving the call
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you had to deal with a frustrated or angry customer. How did you handle it?

pitfalls: Generic answers ('I love cybersecurity,' 'great culture') that could apply to any security company — if you could swap in another company's name, rewrite it
Leading with salary, location, or 'I need a job' — true for everyone, persuasive for no one
Reciting their marketing copy back at them — they wrote it; show them what it means to you instead
points: Make it personal and specific, not a mission statement: years of remote IT support meant watching what malware actually does to real users — the locked files, the panicked calls, the cleanup that never fully restores trust. Zero Trust and default-deny match how you already think about protecting systems: stop deciding whether things are bad, and only let the good run

Connect the craft to the company: this is an infrastructure-plus-security role at a security company — the rare seat where the internal IT work directly serves the mission. Your homelab, your hardening habits, and your support background all point at prevention rather than cleanup

Show you did homework without reciting the About page: reference something real — the free 6-week Zero Trust bootcamp they run in Orlando, ThreatLocker University being open to anyone, the allowlisting philosophy — and say what you want to LEARN there, not just what you bring

Keep it forward-looking: where this role sits in your trajectory — deepening infrastructure and security engineering at a company whose product you would be proud to demo — and mean it. Interviewers can tell the difference between flattery and alignment
behavioral.prompt: Why ThreatLocker? Why do you want to work here specifically?

cheatsheet.title: Subnetting Quick Chart
cheatsheet.body: /24 = 254 hosts | /25 = 126 | /26 = 62 | /27 = 30 | /28 = 14 | /29 = 6 | /30 = 2. Hosts = 2^(32-prefix) - 2. Block size = 256 - interesting octet mask value.

cheatsheet.title: Common Ports
cheatsheet.body: DNS 53/udp+tcp · DHCP 67/68/udp · HTTP 80 · HTTPS 443 · SMB 445 · RDP 3389 · WinRM 5985/5986 · LDAP 389 · LDAPS 636 · Kerberos 88 · SQL 1433 · SQL Browser 1434/udp · IKE 500/udp · NAT-T 4500/udp · ESP IP-50 · SSTP 443 · SSH 22 · SNMP 161/udp

cheatsheet.title: GPO Precedence (LSDOU)
cheatsheet.body: Local → Site → Domain → OU. Later wins. Enforced GPOs beat Block Inheritance. gpresult /r /scope:computer · gpupdate /force

cheatsheet.title: RAID Cheat Sheet
cheatsheet.body: RAID 0: stripe, n×d, lose 0 · RAID 1: mirror, 1×d, lose 1 · RAID 5: parity, (n-1)×d, lose 1 · RAID 6: dual parity, (n-2)×d, lose 2 · RAID 10: stripe of mirrors, (n/2)×d, lose 1 per pair

cheatsheet.title: SQL Backup Chain
cheatsheet.body: FULL → DIFFERENTIAL → LOG → LOG. Restore: FULL WITH NORECOVERY, then DIFF/LOGs WITH NORECOVERY, last WITH RECOVERY. Point-in-time: RESTORE ... WITH STOPAT. Recovery models: Simple (no log backups) / Full / Bulk-Logged.

cheatsheet.title: PowerShell One-Liners
cheatsheet.body:
Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties LastLogonDate | Sort-Object LastLogonDate | Select-Object -Last 10 — -Filter * means 'every user' (the cmdlet refuses to run with neither -Filter nor -Identity); -Properties LastLogonDate because the DEFAULT ~10 properties EXCLUDE it (blank output = unrequested property, not missing data); Sort-Object orders oldest-first; Select-Object -Last 10 keeps the final 10 = the 10 stalest logons. Result: your dormant-account hit list.
Test-NetConnection fileserver -Port 445 — tests TCP port 445 (SMB), not just ICMP. Ping OK + this fails = host is up but the port is firewalled. Logic: ping proves layer 3 (host alive); -Port proves layer 4 (service reachable). When 'ping works but the app fails,' this is the next command, not more pings.
Get-VM | Where-Object State -eq 'Running' — Where-Object keeps only VMs whose State property equals 'Running'. Swap in 'Off' for the powered-down set. Faster than opening Hyper-V Manager, and the pattern (Get → Where) works on every noun.
Resolve-DnsName web01.corp.lab -Server 10.1.10.10 — resolves via THAT server (-Server), not your configured resolver. No -Server = tests YOUR resolver; with -Server = tests THE ZONE. Different answers between the two = resolver problem, not a record problem.
Get-DhcpServerv4Lease -ScopeId 10.1.10.0 — lists current leases in the scope. -ScopeId takes the NETWORK ID (10.1.10.0), not a range address — the classic mix-up. Pipe to Where-Object HostName -like 'PC-*' to hunt one machine.
Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 5 Name, CPU — top-5 CPU hogs in one line: sort hungriest-first (-Descending, else the worst hides at the bottom), keep 5, show two columns. The assessment's favorite triage shape: Get → Sort → Select.
Get-ADUser -Filter 'Enabled -eq $false' -Properties PasswordLastSet | Where-Object { $_.PasswordLastSet -lt (Get-Date).AddDays(-180) } — disabled accounts with passwords older than 180 days. Logic Check on the syntax: single-quoted -Filter so PowerShell does NOT expand $false first (the AD provider parses the string); the curly-brace Where-Object form is required here because the comparison uses a COMPUTED date, not a simple value — the simplified 'Where-Object Prop -op value' form cannot call .AddDays().

cheatsheet.title: VPN Troubleshooting Flow
cheatsheet.body: 1) Ping peer? 2) IKE Phase 1 up? (PSK/proposal match) 3) Phase 2 up? (subnets/transform-set match) 4) NAT-T needed? (UDP 4500) 5) Firewall allowing ESP/500/4500? 6) Interesting traffic defined?

cheatsheet.title: RTO vs RPO
cheatsheet.body: RTO = how long until systems are BACK (downtime tolerance). RPO = how much data you can LOSE (backup frequency). Lower RPO = more frequent backups. 3-2-1: 3 copies, 2 media, 1 offsite.

cheatsheet.title: PowerShell Verb-Noun Quick Reference
cheatsheet.body:
I need to READ something → Get-*: Get-Process | Get-Service | Get-ADUser -Filter * | Get-VM | Get-DhcpServerv4Lease -ScopeId 10.1.10.0 (Get never changes anything — always safe to run)
I need to CREATE something → New-*: New-ADUser -Name 'Jane Doe' -SamAccountName jdoe -AccountPassword (Read-Host -AsSecureString 'pw') -Enabled $true · New-ADOrganizationalUnit -Name 'Orlando' -Path 'DC=corp,DC=lab' -ProtectedFromAccidentalDeletion $true · New-VM -Name 'WEB01' -MemoryStartupBytes 4GB -Generation 2
I need to CHANGE something → Set-*: Set-ADAccountPassword -Identity jdoe -NewPassword (Read-Host -AsSecureString 'pw') -Reset $true (-Reset $true = the ADMIN path, skips the old-password check; without it the cmdlet fails demanding the old password)
I need to DELETE something → Remove-*: Remove-ADUser -Identity jdoe (run with -WhatIf first to preview)
I need to FILTER rows → Where-Object <property> -<operator> <value>: Where-Object CPU -gt 100 · Where-Object Status -eq 'Running' (operators: -eq -ne -gt -lt -ge -le -like -match; never = or ==)
I need to PICK columns → Select-Object Name, CPU, Id (goes AFTER Where-Object — the filter needs the properties Select would drop)
I need to SORT → Sort-Object CPU -Descending (default is ascending; -Descending puts the biggest first)
I need to INSPECT an object → Get-Process | Get-Member (lists every property and method — run before guessing property names)
I need to EXPORT → Export-Csv out.csv -NoTypeInformation (-NoTypeInformation kills the '#TYPE ...' garbage header row that breaks imports)
SAFETY: append -WhatIf to any New-/Set-/Remove- to preview without executing · Format-Table/Format-List go LAST — they destroy objects and anything after them sees formatting records, not data

cheatsheet.title: CMD Network Commands
cheatsheet.body:
I need the full IP picture → ipconfig /all (IP, mask, gateway, DNS servers, DHCP server, lease times, MAC)
I need a fresh DHCP lease → ipconfig /release THEN ipconfig /renew (always pair them — /release alone leaves you addressless; 169.254.x.x = DHCP failed)
I need to clear bad DNS → ipconfig /flushdns (stale cached record) — inspect the cache first with ipconfig /displaydns
I need to test the local stack → ping 127.0.0.1 (zero network involved — failure = local TCP/IP broken, not a network problem)
I need to test the local link → ping <default gateway> (from ipconfig /all)
I need to test routing, NOT DNS → ping 8.8.8.8 (an IP, not a name — separates routing faults from DNS faults)
I need to test a PORT, not just ping → PowerShell: Test-NetConnection <host> -Port 3389 (ping = ICMP/layer 3; apps = TCP/layer 4 — ping OK + app dead = port blocked)
I need the path → tracert -d <target> (-d skips reverse DNS = fast; '* * *' that recovers = filtered ICMP, NOT failure; trace DYING at one hop = fault there)
I need to test DNS → nslookup <name> (YOUR resolver) vs nslookup <name> <server-IP> (THAT server — separates 'record broken' from 'resolver broken')
I need listening ports → netstat -ano (-a = all + listening, -n = numeric/fast, -o = PID → match with tasklist; LISTENING = waiting, ESTABLISHED = live)
I need to set a static IP → netsh interface ipv4 set address name="Ethernet" static 10.1.10.50 255.255.255.0 10.1.10.1 (order: name, static, IP, mask, gateway)
I need to set DNS → netsh interface ipv4 set dnsservers name="Ethernet" static 10.1.10.10 primary (quote names with spaces: "Ethernet 2")
I need DHCP back → netsh interface ipv4 set address name="Ethernet" source=dhcp

cheatsheet.title: T-SQL Backup/Restore Syntax
cheatsheet.body:
I need a FULL backup → BACKUP DATABASE Orders TO DISK = 'E:\Backups\Orders_Full.bak' WITH INIT, COMPRESSION, STATS = 10 (INIT = overwrite the file's old sets; NOINIT = append; COMPRESSION = smaller at CPU cost; STATS = 10 = progress every 10%; the SERVICE account needs write rights on the folder)
I need a DIFFERENTIAL → BACKUP DATABASE Orders TO DISK = 'E:\Backups\Orders_Diff.bak' WITH DIFFERENTIAL (changes since the last full only — useless without its verified base full)
I need to VERIFY a backup file → RESTORE VERIFYONLY FROM DISK = '...' (checksums the file, restores nothing — an unverified backup is a hope, not a backup) · RESTORE HEADERONLY FROM DISK = '...' (what sets live in the file: D/I/L, dates) · RESTORE FILELISTONLY FROM DISK = '...' (logical-to-physical file map for restores to different drive letters)
I need to RESTORE a chain → RESTORE DATABASE Orders FROM DISK = '...Full.bak' WITH NORECOVERY, REPLACE; then RESTORE DATABASE Orders FROM DISK = '...Diff.bak' WITH RECOVERY (NORECOVERY = 'not done yet, keep stacking' on EVERY file except the last; RECOVERY only on the LAST file = 'commit, go online'; RECOVERY too early orphans the rest of the chain; REPLACE = allow overwrite of the existing DB)
I need backup HISTORY → SELECT database_name, backup_start_date, type FROM msdb.dbo.backupset WHERE database_name = 'Orders' ORDER BY backup_start_date DESC (type: D = full, I = differential, L = log — lives in msdb, survives even when the user DB is gone)
SAFETY: UPDATE/DELETE always carry a WHERE — write the SELECT version of the WHERE first, count the rows, then convert

cheatsheet.title: IOS Switch Config Commands
cheatsheet.body:
I need privileged mode → enable (Switch> becomes Switch#)
I need config mode → configure terminal (Switch# becomes Switch(config)#) · exit = back ONE level · end or Ctrl+Z = jump back to #
I need to name the switch → hostname SW-01 (the prompt BECOMES the hostname — read it before every command; wrong-prompt commands get rejected)
I need a VLAN → vlan 10 → name SERVERS → exit (creation and assignment are separate — empty VLANs carry no traffic)
I need access ports → interface range gi1/0/1 - 10 → switchport mode access → switchport access vlan 10 (ONE vlan, UNTAGGED, for end devices; 'mode access' locks the port — never leave 'dynamic auto')
I need a trunk → interface gi1/0/24 → switchport mode trunk → switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20 (MANY vlans, TAGGED 802.1Q, for switch-to-switch; omitted VLANs are SILENTLY dropped on the trunk)
I need a switch IP (SVI) → interface vlan 10 → ip address 10.1.10.2 255.255.255.0 → no shutdown (interfaces are DOWN by default — no shutdown is mandatory, then confirm up/up)
I need to VERIFY → show vlan brief (VLANs + member ports) · show interfaces trunk (trunk status + allowed/forwarding VLANs) · show ip interface brief (up/up health scan) · show ip route (routing table on L3) · show running-config (the LIVE config)
I need to SAVE → copy running-config startup-config (RAM → NVRAM; everything unsaved evaporates on reboot — configure, verify with show, THEN save)

cheatsheet.title: Windows Service Management
cheatsheet.body:
I need service states fast → Get-Service | Where-Object Status -eq 'Stopped' | Sort-Object StartType -Descending
I need the full config from CMD → sc.exe queryex <name> (state, PID, exit codes) · sc.exe qfailure <name> (recovery actions)
I need to change startup type → sc.exe config <name> start= auto (SPACE after start= is mandatory) · PowerShell: Set-Service -Name <name> -StartupType Automatic
I need dependencies → Get-Service <name> | Select-Object -ExpandProperty RequiredServices (what it needs) · -DependentServices (what needs it)
I need recovery actions → sc.exe failure <name> reset= 86400 actions= restart/60000/restart/60000/""/60000 (restart twice, then nothing)
I need why it died → Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='System'; ID=7000,7009,7031} (7000 failed to start · 7009 timeout · 7031 crashed)
I need the logon account → sc.exe qc <name> (check the SERVICE_START_NAME) — after a password change, update the service AND the 'Log on as a service' right
LOGIC CHECK: a service that ran for a year and died today did not change — something around it did (password, dependency, disk). Fix the delta, not the service.

cheatsheet.title: Disk & Volume Commands (diskpart + PowerShell)
cheatsheet.body:
I need to see all disks → Get-Disk | Select-Object Number, FriendlyName, OperationalStatus, PartitionStyle, Size (RAW = uninitialized)
I need to bring up a new disk → Initialize-Disk -Number <N> -PartitionStyle GPT → New-Partition -DiskNumber <N> -UseMaximumSize -DriveLetter E → Format-Volume -DriveLetter E -FileSystem NTFS -NewFileSystemLabel Data -Confirm:$false
I need the diskpart version → list disk → select disk <N> → clean → convert gpt → create partition primary → format fs=ntfs quick label=Data → assign letter=E (list disk TWICE before clean)
I need to grow a volume → Get-PartitionSupportedSize -DriveLetter E (check the ceiling) → Resize-Partition -DriveLetter E -Size (Get-PartitionSupportedSize -DriveLetter E).SizeMax
I need volume info → Get-Volume | Select-Object DriveLetter, FileSystem, SizeRemaining, Size
I need to check/repair → chkdsk E: /f (logical errors, needs exclusive access) · chkdsk E: /r (adds bad-sector scan — slow, off-hours only)
I need to optimize → Optimize-Volume -DriveLetter E -Defrag (HDD) · Optimize-Volume -DriveLetter E -Retrim (SSD)
LOGIC CHECK: MBR caps at 2 TB — anything bigger is GPT, no exceptions. And 'clean' has no undo: verify the disk NUMBER, not just the size.

cheatsheet.title: Windows Update Commands
cheatsheet.body:
I need patch state fast → Get-HotFix | Sort-Object InstalledOn -Descending | Select-Object -First 10 HotFixID, InstalledOn
I need one specific KB → Get-HotFix -Id KB5034441 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue (silent = not installed)
I need the Server Core UI → sconfig → option 6 (download & install) · option 5 (update settings)
I need to trigger from CLI → usoclient StartScan → usoclient StartInstall (silent — verify with Get-WUHistory after)
I need fleet-grade control → Install-Module PSWindowsUpdate -Force → Get-WindowsUpdate -ListOnly (preview) → Install-WindowsUpdate -AcceptAll -IgnoreReboot (without -AcceptAll it prompts and hangs automation)
I need history → Get-WUHistory | Select-Object -First 10 Date, Title, Result
I need to roll back → wusa /uninstall /kb:5034441 /quiet /norestart (know this BEFORE the change window)
I need WSUS targeting → GPO: Computer Config → Policies → Admin Templates → Windows Components → Windows Update → 'Enable client-side targeting' (target group name)
LOGIC CHECK: patching is a change — canary ring first, rollback rehearsed, never -AutoReboot on production without a window.

cheatsheet.title: Linux Admin One-Liners
cheatsheet.body:
I need the service story → journalctl -u <svc> --since '1 hour ago' --no-pager · journalctl -p err -b --no-pager (errors since boot) · journalctl --disk-usage
I need service control → systemctl status/is-enabled/start/stop/restart <svc> · systemctl list-units --failed --no-pager (triage any box in 10s)
I need the network picture → ip -br addr (addresses) · ip route show (gateway) · nmcli device status · ss -tulpn (listening ports + owning process)
I need connectivity ladder → ping -c4 <gateway> → ping -c4 <name> (DNS?) → ss -tulpn (listening?) — stop at the first failure
I need disk triage → df -h (filesystems) → du -sh /var/* 2>/dev/null | sort -rh | head (the hog)
I need processes → ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head · kill <pid> (SIGTERM first) · kill -9 <pid> (last resort)
I need logins → last | head (successful) · lastb | head (failed)
I need permissions → ls -lah (decode rwx) · chmod 640 file · chmod 750 dir · chown user:group file (NEVER 777)
I need text plumbing → grep -R 'error' /var/log/ · tail -f /var/log/auth.log | grep -i fail · awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
I need the host firewall → sudo firewall-cmd --list-all
LOGIC CHECK: enabled is not running and running is not enabled — the reboot tests the one you forgot.

cheatsheet.title: Packet Capture & ARP Reading
cheatsheet.body:
I need to capture → tshark -i eth0 -f 'tcp port 443 and host 10.1.5.20' -a duration:60 -w /tmp/cap.pcap (capture filter = BPF, BEFORE capture, keeps files small)
I need to read it back → tshark -r /tmp/cap.pcap -Y 'dns' -T fields -e dns.qry.name
I need display filters → ip.addr==10.1.5.20 · tcp.port==443 · dns.qry.name contains 'corp.local' · tcp.analysis.retransmission (find the slowness) · tcp.flags.syn==1 && tcp.flags.ack==0 (unanswered SYNs)
I need the handshake verdict → SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK = alive · SYN with no SYN-ACK = filtered/down · RST after SYN = port closed
I need the ARP table → arp -a (IP → MAC mappings) · arp -a | findstr 192.168.1.254 (is the gateway resolved?)
I need to clear ARP → arp -d * (admin; temporary — a rogue re-announces in seconds)
I need duplicate-IP proof → same IP, two MACs across minutes = two devices claiming one identity; trace via switch mac address-table
LOGIC CHECK: read a capture like an argument transcript — who spoke last tells you who is waiting. A SYN with no SYN-ACK is being left on read.

cheatsheet.title: Windows Firewall CLI (netsh + NetSecurity)
cheatsheet.body:
I need the active profile FIRST → Get-NetConnectionProfile | Select-Object Name, NetworkCategory (a Domain-scoped rule does nothing on a Public NIC)
I need a rule from CMD → netsh advfirewall firewall add rule name='Allow App' dir=in action=allow protocol=TCP localport=8443 remoteip=10.1.20.0/24 profile=domain
I need a rule from PowerShell → New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'Allow App' -Direction Inbound -Protocol TCP -LocalPort 8443 -RemoteAddress 10.1.20.0/24 -Action Allow -Profile Domain
I need to verify → Get-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'Allow App' | Select-Object Enabled, Action, Direction · netsh advfirewall firewall show rule name='Allow App'
I need toggle → Enable-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'Allow App' · Disable-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'Allow App' · Remove-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'Lab*'
I need logging on → Set-NetFirewallProfile -Profile Domain -LogFileName '%systemroot%\system32\logfiles\firewall\pfirewall.log' -LogBlocked True → Get-Content <log> -Tail 5 (DROP + your port = confession)
I need precedence → explicit BLOCK beats explicit ALLOW beats default (allows do not compete with each other)
LOGIC CHECK: scope every rule with -RemoteAddress — remoteip=any on a management port is an exposure, not a fix.

cheatsheet.title: Robocopy & File Shares
cheatsheet.body:
I need to mirror a share → robocopy \\SRV1\Share \\SRV2\Share /MIR /ZB /R:3 /W:5 /LOG:C:\logs\robo.log /TEE (/MIR = mirror incl. deletions · /ZB = restartable+backup mode · /R:3 /W:5 = 3 retries, 5s wait)
I need copy-not-mirror → robocopy <src> <dst> /E /ZB /R:2 /W:2 (/E = subdirs incl. empty; no /MIR = never deletes at destination)
I need what WILL happen first → add /L (list-only dry run — always /L before /MIR on production)
I need share inventory → net share (local shares) · Get-SmbShare | Select-Object Name, Path
I need to map a drive → net use Z: \\SRV\Share /persistent:yes · PowerShell: New-PSDrive -Name Z -PSProvider FileSystem -Root \\SRV\Share -Persist
I need share vs NTFS perms → share permissions are the OUTER gate, NTFS the INNER — effective access = most restrictive of the two; set with icacls D:\Data /grant 'Domain Users:(OI)(CI)M'
LOGIC CHECK: /MIR deletes at the destination — one flipped source/destination and you mirror NOTHING onto EVERYTHING. /L first, always.

cheatsheet.title: GPO Backup & Recovery
cheatsheet.body:
I need insurance → $s = Get-Date -Format 'yyyy-MM-dd'; Backup-GPO -All -Path "\\FILESRV\GPOBackups\$s" (per-GPO folders: GUID + manifest.xml)
I need one GPO backed up → Backup-GPO -Name 'Sales-Wallpaper' -Path "\\FILESRV\GPOBackups\$s"
I need undo in the same domain → Restore-GPO -Name 'Sales-Wallpaper' -Path "\\FILESRV\GPOBackups\$s"
I need cross-domain migration → Import-GPO -BackupGpoName 'Sales-Wallpaper' -Path "\\FILESRV\GPOBackups\$s" -TargetName 'Sales-Wallpaper-Test' -CreateIfNeeded (+ migration table for SIDs/UNC paths)
I need proof it landed → Get-GPO -Name 'Sales-Wallpaper' | Select-Object DisplayName, ModificationTime · gpresult /r /scope:computer
I need link management → New-GPLink -Name 'X' -Target 'OU=Sales,DC=corp,DC=local' -LinkEnabled Yes · Remove-GPLink -Name 'X' -Target <OU>
LOGIC CHECK: a GPO with no backup is a rumor — if you cannot restore it in under 5 minutes, your change window is a research project.

glossary.def: Microsoft's directory service — a centralized database on Windows servers storing every user account, computer account, group, and security policy in a company network. When you log into a work computer, AD verifies your identity.
A Windows server running Active Directory Domain Services. It holds the AD database and authenticates logins. Always have at least two — if the only DC dies, nobody can log in.
A container inside Active Directory for organizing users, computers, and groups (e.g., OU=Sales, OU=Servers). Group Policies are linked to OUs to control settings for everything inside them.

Rules pushed from Active Directory to computers and users — password requirements, desktop settings, security policies, software installs. Applied in LSDOU order: Local, Site, Domain, OU (later wins on conflict).
The internet's phone book — translates human-readable names (fileserver01) into IP addresses (192.168.1.10). AD cannot function without working DNS.
Automatically assigns IP addresses, subnet masks, gateways, and DNS settings to devices when they join the network. Eliminates manual configuration and prevents duplicate addresses.
A 32-bit number (IPv4) identifying a device on a network, written as four decimal octets (e.g., 192.168.1.10). Every device needs a unique one to communicate.
A 32-bit number that divides an IP address into network and host portions. 255.255.255.0 (/24) means the first 24 bits are the network, the last 8 are hosts (254 usable addresses).
Shorthand for a subnet mask counting the network bits: /24 = 255.255.255.0, /16 = 255.255.0.0. Higher number = smaller network.
The router address devices send traffic to when the destination is on a different network. Without a correct gateway, a device can only talk to its local subnet.
Logically segments a physical switch into multiple isolated broadcast domains. VLAN 10 (Sales) can't see VLAN 20 (Engineering) without a router, even on the same switch.
A switch port carrying traffic for multiple VLANs simultaneously, using 802.1Q tagging to identify which VLAN each frame belongs to. Used between switches and to routers.
The IEEE standard for VLAN tagging — inserts a 4-byte tag into Ethernet frames identifying the VLAN ID (1-4094).
A network device that forwards packets between different networks/subnets using routing tables. Operates at Layer 3 (Network) of the OSI model.
A network device connecting devices within the same network, forwarding frames based on MAC addresses. Operates at Layer 2 (Data Link).
Filters network traffic based on rules (allow/deny by source, destination, port, application). Sits between network zones enforcing security policy.
Encrypted tunnel over an untrusted network (like the internet) connecting remote sites or users to a private network. Types: site-to-site (IPsec), client/remote-access.
Protocol suite for encrypted IP communication. Used for site-to-site VPNs. Two phases: IKE Phase 1 (establish secure channel) and Phase 2 (negotiate encryption for data).
Rewrites source or destination IP addresses as packets pass through a router/firewall. Lets many private addresses share one public IP (PAT/overload).
Microsoft's Type-1 hypervisor for running virtual machines on Windows Server. VMs share physical hardware but run isolated operating systems.
A software-emulated computer running on a hypervisor. Has virtual CPU, RAM, disk, and network — behaves like physical hardware to its OS.
Software that creates and runs virtual machines. Type-1 (bare-metal: Hyper-V, ESXi, Proxmox) runs directly on hardware; Type-2 (VirtualBox, VMware Workstation) runs on top of an OS.
Hyper-V point-in-time snapshot of a VM's state. Useful before changes, but NOT a backup — checkpoints depend on the original VM files.
Microsoft's relational database management system. Stores structured data in tables; queried with T-SQL. Critical for business applications.
Transact-SQL — Microsoft's extension of SQL for querying and managing SQL Server databases (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, BACKUP DATABASE, etc.).

Redundant Array of Independent Disks — combines multiple physical disks for performance, redundancy, or both. Common levels: 0 (striping, no redundancy), 1 (mirroring), 5 (striping+parity, 1 disk fault tolerance), 6 (2 disk fault tolerance), 10 (mirrored stripes).
Maximum acceptable downtime after a disaster. RTO of 4 hours means systems must be restored within 4 hours.
Maximum acceptable data loss measured in time. RPO of 1 hour means backups must be frequent enough that you never lose more than 1 hour of data.
Keep 3 copies of data, on 2 different media types, with 1 copy offsite. The baseline for any serious backup strategy.
Microsoft's task automation framework — a command-line shell and scripting language built on .NET. Uses Verb-Noun cmdlets (Get-ADUser, New-VM). The primary admin tool for Windows Server.
A PowerShell command following the Verb-Noun pattern (Get-, Set-, New-, Remove-). Discoverable via Get-Command and self-documenting via Get-Help.
The authentication protocol used by Active Directory. Uses encrypted tickets instead of sending passwords over the network. Three parties: client, KDC (on DC), and service.
Lightweight Directory Access Protocol — the standard protocol for querying and modifying directory services like AD. Think of it as the query language for the AD database.
7-layer conceptual model for network communication: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application. Troubleshooting goes layer by layer.
The practical protocol suite powering the internet. TCP (reliable, ordered delivery) and UDP (fast, no guarantees) run on top of IP (addressing and routing).
Dividing a large network into smaller sub-networks by borrowing host bits for network bits. Controls broadcast domains, improves security segmentation, and organizes addressing.
The set of devices that receive each other's broadcast traffic. Routers and VLANs divide broadcast domains; switches do not.
Prevents network loops on switches with redundant links by blocking redundant ports. Without it, broadcast storms crash the network.
Open Shortest Path First — a dynamic routing protocol where routers share link-state information to calculate best paths automatically.
Input/Output Operations Per Second — measures storage performance. Higher IOPS = faster disk. Critical for database and VM workloads.
Maximum Transmission Unit — largest packet size a network path supports (typically 1500 bytes on Ethernet). VPN encryption overhead can cause MTU issues.
ThreatLocker's core Zero Trust approach — only explicitly approved applications are permitted to run; everything else is blocked by default. Opposite of traditional antivirus (blocklist).
ThreatLocker feature controlling what approved applications can do — limit which files, registry keys, network destinations, and child processes an app can access.
Security model assuming no implicit trust: verify every user, device, and application explicitly before granting access. 'Never trust, always verify.'
Step-by-step documented procedure for performing a task consistently. Includes purpose, prerequisites, steps, verification, and rollback.
The default command-line shell on most Linux systems. Used for navigation, file management, scripting, and system administration.
Distributed version control system tracking changes to files over time. Enables branching, merging, and collaboration. GitHub hosts Git repositories online.
Open-source Type-1 hypervisor platform (Debian-based) for VMs (KVM) and containers (LXC), with web UI, clustering, and built-in backup.
Fortinet's next-generation firewall appliance. Provides firewalling, VPN, intrusion prevention, and UTM features in one device.
Palo Alto Networks' firewall operating system. Known for App-ID (application-based policies instead of port-based) and zone-based security.
Network protocol analyzer capturing and displaying packet-level traffic. Essential for diagnosing network issues — see exactly what's on the wire.
Windows tool for reading system, application, and security logs. First stop when troubleshooting Windows Server issues.
